title: Paper Trail
pitch: Say it once - one sentence about your life event, and every agency, insurer, and employer form gets filled, cross-checked, approved by you, and receipted.
about_excerpt: Say it once - one sentence about your life event, and every agency, insurer, and employer form gets filled, cross-checked, approved by you, and receipted. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every big life event arrives with a hidden invoice: not money, but paperwork . A birth triggers 15–40 separate actions scattered across the Social Security Administration, the health insurer, and the employer's HR portal — each with its own login, its own forms, its own deadlines (add a dependent within 30 days or wait for open enrollment), and its own ways of spelling the same name. Humans have always been the integration glue between these portals: re-typing identical data, making format mistakes, missing windows. When we read the WebMCP spec, one sentence rewired how we think: websites can hand agents structured capabilities instead of forcing them to screenshot pixels. The paperwork layer is the biggest unclaimed prize for that idea — so we built the app we wished existed: say it once, and the whole bundle gets done, with the human still sovereign. What it does Type one sentence — "We had a baby girl on June 3rd at General Hospital." One interview , no forms: the hub derives the facts and materializes an action bundle across three independent portals, with deadline math computed live (DOB June 3 + 30 days → insurer window closes July 3). Each portal owns a tool surface : walking into a page dynamically registers its tools and walking away unregisters them ( AbortController ). The agent only ever sees the tools for the page it's on. Drafts fill from one canonical profile — and a reconciliation engine catches cross-portal conflicts (the hospital's "Okafor-Reyes, Amara" vs. the profile's "Amara Okafor-Reyes"; "Jun 03, 2026" vs. "2026-06-03"), explains them in plain language, and standardizes only on the human's say-so. Nothing files without a human click. Every write tool is a two-call gate: the first call opens an on-page dialog showing every field about to be filed; the second call executes only if the human actually approved — enforced in code, not in a prompt. Replay a confirmation id → unknown_confirmation_id . Let the agent approve itself → human_approval_missing . File twice → already_submitted . Everything ends in a receipt ledger : payload digest → confirmation number → timestamp → human-approval flag. The showpiece : pt_cascade_update . The family moves mid-flow; one call re-derives the whole situation — deadlines recomputed, every pending draft re-filled across all three portals — while filed actions stay untouched, because receipts preserve what was actually submitted. How we built it A zero-dependency, zero-build static SPA — classic scripts, no framework, no backend, deployable anywhere (it even runs from file:// ). mcp.js — the WebMCP layer: registerTool with readOnlyHint annotations, per-portal AbortSignal lifecycles, and a guarded executor (activity-rail logging, ~1.5K output budgets, throws → typed errors agents can self-correct from). portals.js — three fictional portals (SSA, Meridian Health, employer HR) with schemas, strict in-code validation whose errors are written for the agent, the two-call ConfirmGate , and the reconciliation engine. hub.js — the one-sentence interview resolver and the hub tool surface ( pt_start_life_event_interview , pt_get_action_bundle , pt_reconcile_field_conflicts , pt_get_receipt_ledger , pt_cascade_update ). store.js / bundle.js — canonical profile, dependency-aware bundle, deadline math, event-sourced receipts — plus a store subscription so the page the human is watching re-renders live when the agent mutates state through the protocol. 26 tools across 4 surfaces; 13 annotated read-only; 3 gated writes. A /diag.html page probes the runtime (API presence, live registration, getTools() visibility, abort lifecycle) — 11/11 checks pass in Chrome 150 with #enable-webmcp-testing . Challenges we ran into The runtime diverges from the spec text. In the real Chrome build, modelContext.registerTool() returns undefined , not a Promise — our .then() chain silently died at boot. We caught it only by testing against the actual enabled runtime, and now handle both styles. That bug alone justified building a diagnostics page. Tool identity is page-scoped. Re-entering a portal risks a synchronous Duplicate tool name throw; abort-then-re-register had to be proven clean (it is — verified via getTools() ). The "shared live app" requirement is real work. When the agent conducts the interview through the protocol, the human's screen must react — we wired store-driven re-rendering so the bundle materializes on screen as the tool call lands. Timezones and dates. "Jun 03, 2026" vs. "2026-06-03" needed part-wise date comparison, not toISOString() gymnastics that silently shift days across UTC offsets. Making the gate genuinely binding. The tempting shortcut is a confirm dialog the agent can talk its way past. We made approval a server-side-of-the-page fact: the finalize call checks the human's actual click in code, and we proved the negative paths on camera. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full judge experience runs through the runtime's own executeTool : interview → surface swap → gated filing (pending → human approval → submitted) → reconciliation → cascade → ledger. Not a scripted path — the protocol path. Receipts as evidence : every filing carries a payload digest and confirmation number; the ledger reads like an audit trail, because that's what it is. Honest degradation : without a WebMCP runtime the chip says so, the human buttons drive the same code paths, and the app still demonstrates every flow. A dark, full-height activity rail that narrates every tool call — the human and the agent visibly share one live artifact. What we learned Protocol depth is a design material, not a checkbox. Dynamic surfaces, annotations, and elicitation-shaped gates changed the architecture, not just the API calls. Human-in-the-loop belongs in code. A prompt saying "ask first" is a suggestion; a gate that physically cannot finalize without the human's click is a guarantee. Test in the real judging environment early. The single most dangerous bug we fixed was invisible in every browser except the one with the flag enabled. Agents need agent-legible errors : strict in-code validation with messages written for self-correction turns failures into progress. What's next for Paper Trail Move and bereavement event packs — the bundle engine takes new event types without architecture changes. Native requestUserInteraction elicitation as a progressive enhancement of the two-call gate. An accessibility operator mode — the same tool surfaces are a better substrate than the visual DOM; narration and pacing ride the protocol for free. Handoff export — the remaining human-only actions (notary visits, in-person verifications) as a calendar file, because a good agent knows what it can't do. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Headroom - Transfer Window
pitch: An AI agent runs your premier league football transfer window and the page refuses every deal that breaks the rules.
about_excerpt: An AI agent runs your premier league football transfer window and the page refuses every deal that breaks the rules. Like Comment Story Updates Transfer Window Sandbox Demo screen Sign Osihmen - processing Sign Osihmen - refused Sell Kamara instead of Rogers The transfer window/plan ready for submission Inspiration I'm a huge Premier League fan and follow the transfer market closely, so I wanted to explore how AI could make complicated transfer decisions clearer. I built this to help understand how transfer fees, wages, amortization, and PSR rules actually affect a club's decisions and possibly automate the transfer market old legacy brute force system with modern Agentic AI application software. With WebMCP, the AI can make recommendations and decisions while the website remains the source of truth for the calculations and rules. Premier League clubs aren't allowed to lose more than £105m (about $133m) over three seasons . Break it and you don't get a fine — you lose league points. Everton were docked 10 points for going £16.6m over, then 2 more for a second breach. Nottingham Forest lost 4 points for going £34.5m over. Points decide relegation, and relegation costs a club around £100m . And the maths behind it is genuinely counterintuitive. A transfer fee isn't a cost when you pay it — it's spread across the contract, capped at five years since 2023 . A £110m signing is a £22m charge this season, not £110m. A sale books its profit immediately, and an academy graduate has a book value of zero, so their whole fee is pure profit. That's why clubs sell their own young players every June, racing a June 30 accounting deadline that Sky Sports calls football's unofficial transfer deadline day . So I tried asking ChatGPT to do it, with no tools. It got close it knew about amortisation. But I had to hand it every single number, and it still told me flatly: "headline accounts alone cannot establish a breach." It couldn't answer, and it knew it couldn't. That's the whole idea. Not "AI is bad at maths" but that an agent with no access to the real numbers can only ever guess, and in this domain guessing costs you league points. What it does You manage a Premier League club through a transfer window, with an AI agent working alongside you. The page exposes 14 WebMCP tools it can call directly: search the market, price deals, rank sale candidates, edit the plan. What it cannot do is state a number it didn't get from the page. Ask it to sign a £110m striker with £20.3m of headroom and it doesn't apologise and comply. The plan turns red, submission is blocked, and it comes back with the exact figure: £12.1m over , £22m annual amortisation, £10.4m of wages. Then ask who to sell, and it gets genuinely interesting. It recommended Leon Bailey at £30m worth £34.2m to the PSR position, more than the fee, because you also shed his wages and remaining amortisation. And it noted that Morgan Rogers would be worth more (+£62.7m) but Bailey was the cleaner fix from a crowded midfield. It weighed a trade-off but every number in that trade-off came from the page. How I built it React + TypeScript + Vite. No backend, no auth, no API keys it deploys as static files. The rules engine ( src/engine/rules.ts ) is pure functions with a test suite: PSR aggregation, fee amortisation capped at five years, profit on sale against book value, and squad registration (25 seniors, max 17 non-homegrown, U21s exempt). The 14 tools are thin wrappers over it, so the model never does the arithmetic itself. The tools sit in three tiers with standard MCP annotations derived from the tier, so the hint an agent reads can't drift from what the UI shows: Read-only (9) — readOnlyHint , idempotentHint Reversible (4) — every change undoable Consequential (1) — submit_window , destructiveHint Crucially, agent and human mutate through the same store . A tool call and a button click run the identical code path, so the agent has no privileged back door and you watch the board change under its hands. Why WebMCP and not a normal MCP server submit_window doesn't return when called. It raises a confirmation in the page and suspends the promise resolves only when a human confirms or declines, and it honours the AbortSignal if the call is cancelled. An agent working against a REST API could always call POST /submit . Here there is no server, so there is nothing to call. The gate isn't a prompt asking the agent to behave; it's the only path through, and it needs a hand on it. Challenges The API is still moving. The W3C proposal exposes navigator.modelContext ; the Chrome docs show document.modelContext . Registration is either per-tool registerTool or a bulk provideContext . Rather than betting on one, I wrote a small adapter that detects whatever the browser provides one file to change when the spec settles. Making the gate genuinely block. My first version returned "awaiting confirmation" immediately, which let the agent wrap up while the decision was still open. Rewriting it to suspend inside the tool call is what turned "the agent chose to stop" into "the agent structurally cannot finish." Calibrating the data so the demo is honest. The rules are real, but I had to invent every financial figure and tune them so each club sits in a distinct, legible position Villa tight at £20.3m, Forest at £8.1m, Everton nearly gone at £2.6m. Villa also had to genuinely need a striker, so the story starts from a real problem. What I learned Good tool descriptions do more work than I expected. The agent correctly explained the five-year amortisation cap and derived its own spending formula 5 × (£20.3m − first-year wages) entirely from reading the tool descriptions. It extended the rule rather than just following it. I also learned the interesting failure mode isn't hallucination. It's a model being nearly right confidently, with working shown while missing the pieces it has no access to. Being off by £700k sounds trivial until you remember Everton lost 10 points for £16.6m. Honesty about the data Club and player names are real, because the constraints only mean something if you recognise them. Every financial figure is invented. They are not club accounts and shouldn't be cited as such. The rules are real and public that's what the page enforces, and it's the part worth learning. What's next Roles as tool tiers. The gate currently means any human. In a real club it would mean a specific one a scout gets read-only tools, an analyst can build a plan, and only a sporting director's click resolves submit_window . And beyond football. The failure mode here isn't specific to sport. It's what every agent does when handed a calculator-shaped problem and no calculator: assert arithmetic it can't actually do, somewhere being wrong carries a real penalty. Tax. Benefits eligibility. Medical billing. Export control. Give the page the rulebook, and make the agent ask. title: EZI ChemLab
pitch: A 3D chemistry and physics lab where an AI agent runs the experiment. Through WebMCP it mixes reagents, switches modes and writes the lab report, for schools without a safe lab.
about_excerpt: A 3D chemistry and physics lab where an AI agent runs the experiment. Through WebMCP it mixes reagents, switches modes and writes the lab report, for schools without a safe lab. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Many schools in Indonesia teach chemistry without a laboratory that is safe or complete enough for students to run experiments themselves. Teachers describe reactions on a whiteboard, and students memorise colour changes they have never actually seen. The missing piece is not information. It is the instructor standing beside you who pours the reagent, points at the bubbles as they form, and stops you before you make an unsafe combination. We wanted to find out whether an AI agent could take that role, and WebMCP is the first thing that makes it possible. A chatbot can describe a reaction. With WebMCP, it can run one. What it does EZI ChemLab is a 3D chemistry and physics lab that an AI agent drives from inside the browser. The student talks to the agent, and the agent operates the bench. There are three practical modes, mapped to Phases D, E and F of the Indonesian national science curriculum: Acids and bases , with indicator colour change and gas evolution Electrolyte and non-electrolyte solutions , tested with a conductivity lamp Density and buoyancy , the classic egg in fresh water against salt water The agent can switch topics, mix substances, read the current state of the bench, explain each stage, raise an educational safety warning, reset the experiment, and write up the observation report at the end. Reagents are not teleported into the beaker. Each one is measured out into its own graduated cylinder first, or lifted on a spatula if it is a powder, and only then poured in one at a time. The amount_ml the agent asked for is something you can read off the glass rather than take on trust. How we built it Seven tools are registered client side through the browser model context API: switch_experiment_mode , mix_substances , get_lab_state , explain_reaction_step , trigger_safety_alert , reset_experiment and render_lab_report . The frontend is Next.js with React Three Fiber. Every object on the page is built from geometric primitives in code, with no third party assets: the glassware is turned on a lathe from a profile the way real glassware is, and the floor tiles and the room the glass reflects are drawn to a canvas at runtime. Bubbles are capped at 110 instances so the simulation runs on the standard school laptops we are aiming at. The backend is Rust with axum, acting as a proxy so that no API key ever reaches the client. One decision shaped everything else: reaction outcomes come from a static lookup table, never from a language model. The visual result of a reaction is a scientific fact, and a hallucinated colour change would teach a student something false. The model writes prose. The table decides the chemistry. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP specification moved the API from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext in July 2026, and browsers in the field are still split across both locations. Every registration goes through a resolver that checks both, because a page that registers nothing looks exactly like a page that was never built. Refracting glass nearly cost us the experiment. The renderer builds the buffer that transmissive glass reads from opaque objects only, so anything marked transparent inside a beaker is not merely faint, it is absent: the liquid, the bubbles and the electrodes all disappeared behind the very glass that was meant to show them. Worse, our whole browser test suite stayed green while the beaker was empty on screen, because every check ran at 900 pixels and refraction only switches on from 1024 up. We now have a check that runs wide, hides the interface panels so that a text update cannot stand in for a reaction, and insists the contents are actually visible. We also had to design for a judging period that runs for weeks. An API quota running out in mid September would leave the lab looking broken, so step explanations are generated once, reviewed for scientific accuracy, and served as static content. Only the lab report, which depends on what the student actually did, calls a model at run time, and the backend accepts several numbered providers and moves to the next one when a call fails. That is not a claim on paper: in production the first provider currently fails on every request and the second answers, and the report still arrives. Every remaining failure path returns vetted static text with a 200 response rather than an error. Accomplishments that we're proud of Every execute handler returns a structured result containing the visual state, the temperature change and a plain language observation, so the agent narrates what actually happened instead of guessing. Unknown reagent pairs return a structured error listing the valid pairs, which lets the agent correct itself without the student ever noticing. We also built the lab so that it stays usable when WebMCP is not available. A status badge reports what the browser supports, a manual panel calls the exact same handlers rather than mock versions, and the topic buttons in the header run switch_experiment_mode the same way an agent does. The tool layer is genuinely separate from the interface. What we learned Reading matters as much as writing. get_lab_state returns the same view of the bench that the interface shows, so the agent can check what is actually there before it acts rather than assuming its last call succeeded. Together with the structured errors, it is what keeps a long conversation from drifting away from the simulation. We also learned that visible tool call indicators are not decoration. Every call is written to an activity console with the tool name, the outcome, and whether it came from an agent or was run by hand. Watching that line appear at the exact moment the liquid changes colour is what makes the whole thing legible, both to a student and to anyone evaluating it. What's next for EZI ChemLab Reaction rate is the next topic, and it is the one that rewards an agent most. It has four variables to manipulate and two beakers to compare, so the agent stops triggering effects and starts designing an experiment. Thermochemistry follows closely behind, since temperature data already flows through mix_substances . Beyond that: teacher accounts with printable worksheets, offline packaging for schools with limited connectivity, and coverage extending into Phase F electrochemistry. Built With axum docker docker-compose dokploy drei lets-encrypt next.js openai react react-three-fiber reqwest rest-api rust serde tailwind-css three.js tokio tower-http traefik typescript webgl webmcp zustand Try it out chemlab.eziedutech.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo entrant. I designed the product and made the calls on how the lab should behave: measuring each reagent before mixing so the amounts are visible, building the room and glassware as 3D geometry rather than using imported assets, and keeping reaction outcomes in a static table so the science cannot be hallucinated. I set up the infrastructure, VPS, domains, Dokploy, and the provider chain behind the lab report, and I tested the whole session in the ChatGPT desktop app. The implementation was written with AI coding agents working to those decisions, and I reviewed and tested what it produced. title: uk.gov Radar
pitch: Your agent reads everything the UK government published this month. You make the calls.
about_excerpt: Your agent reads everything the UK government published this month. You make the calls. Like Comment Story Updates The agent filled the profile. It stays blue until you keep it. A suggestion, its reason, the next step, and your note, on one card. Dropped, with a reason the agent reads before it suggests again. The weekly brief. Every claim links to its source page. One page, two hands. The founder and the agent point at the same row. I run Hyperdrift, a small AI studio in the UK. Every month the government publishes the grant, the consultation or the tender that could change a founder's quarter. Every month I miss it, because it's buried under sixty documents I don't have time to read. So I built a radar. It reads gov.uk, UKRI and Parliament for me. Useful, but not enough: a list of what changed still needs someone who knows my company to say which lines matter. WebMCP was the missing link. Open the radar in a browser that has an agent, and the page hands the agent its controls. It fills my profile from what it already knows about me. It works the list on my screen: filters move, cards light up, every suggestion comes with a reason and a date. Then I tell it something the website will never hear: my NHS partner has gone and I've got six weeks. The list re-ranks in front of me. I drop one, I say why, and it reads my reason before it speaks again. The site keeps the data. My agent keeps my context. I keep the last word. A plug-in on a server can't do that. Try it: radar.hyperdrift.io/explore, in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP on. Three prompts wait at the top of the page. Under the hood: seven tools on document.modelContext, one of them registered only once a shortlist exists; every tool calls the same functions the buttons call. Built this week on a pipeline from May; dated commits in WEBMCP.md. Independent project, not affiliated with HM Government. title: MusterMind - The wearability agent — buy, restyle, or skip
pitch: The first shopping agent that can tell you not to buy. Buy, restyle, wait or skip — every verdict cited to you, to product data, or to the rules, live over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The first shopping agent that can tell you not to buy. Buy, restyle, wait or skip — every verdict cited to you, to product data, or to the rules, live over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We started somewhere else. The first idea was a size recommender — obvious fashion-commerce problem. Then we opened DevTools on a live AJIO product page and found something that reframed the whole project. Sitting in window.__PRELOADED_STATE__ , invisible to any agent driving the DOM, was a size chart already converted to centimetres , an explicit measurementType: "Garment Measurement" provenance flag, live per-size stock counts, and — the thing we didn't expect — a crowd fit distribution: Perfect 64% · Tight 15% · Too Tight 5% · Loose 11% · Too Loose 3% over 2,100 raters The page already knew this garment runs small. It had no way to tell an agent. But the moment that actually defined the product came later. Our first working version ranked a ₹320 polo as the top buy for a client dinner. It was cheap, in stock, not a duplicate, and technically satisfied every constraint. It was also completely wrong — a polo does not become client-dinner appropriate because it is cheap. That is the failure mode of every shopping agent we've used. They can only say buy , so they optimise for the one signal they can read: price and availability. We rebuilt the engine around a different question — what if the agent could say no? What it does Mustermind is a wearability decision layer. You give it an occasion, a budget, a PIN code, a deadline, fits you avoid, and a rough list of what you already own. It scores live AJIO products on four axes: product facts, your constraints, purchase risk, and rewear value. Every garment gets one of four verdicts: Verdict Meaning buy Worth buying for this occasion restyle You can already assemble this look from what you own wait Right piece, wrong price or arrives too late skip Violates a stated constraint, duplicates something owned, or can't be delivered Every verdict carries the factors behind it, and every factor is tagged with its source — you, product data, or the rules. A real card from the running app: RESTYLE — You can get this look from what you own U.S. Polo Assn. · Men Button Down-Collar Tailored Fit Shirt · ₹1,175 + Within budget [user] ₹1,175 against a ₹3,000 ceiling − Close to what you own [rules] You already have White Shirts; this adds a colour, not a category · Rewear value [rules] Pairs with 1 item you already own + Right register [rules] Shirts suits client dinner + Fit confidence [product] 90% — garment measurements published, 77 fit ratings + Suggested size M [product] 16% of 77 raters found this loose vs 5% tight, so one size down · Deliverable, no date [product] Serviceable at 560029; the delivery API did not return a date That last line matters as much as the verdict. The delivery API returned no date, so the app doesn't invent one. Load the default brief and Mustermind recommends nothing. Two restyles, five skips, four different skip reasons. Then tell the agent "I could stretch to ₹5,500" and a blazer becomes the single buy — on screen, with the reason visible, and the change written to a Decision Ledger showing that you made it. How we built it Zero npm dependencies. Node 20 and vanilla HTML/CSS/JS. Nothing to install, no lockfile, no bundler — a judge can read the entire thing. It ships as a ~55 MB Alpine container running non-root. Five WebMCP tools , registered on document.modelContext with navigator.modelContext as a fallback probe, behind feature detection: Tool readOnlyHint untrustedContentHint get_current_style_brief ✅ — get_product_truth ✅ ✅ evaluate_wearability ✅ ✅ record_user_tradeoff — — prepare_purchase_handoff — — Five, deliberately. Tool selection degrades as the set grows, and each description is written as product surface — when to call it, what changes state, and when to ask instead of assert . The verdict engine is a rule engine, not a model. This was a deliberate constraint: the agent has to narrate why a verdict is what it is, and a scorer you cannot read gives it nothing to say. Gradient boosting would have scored marginally better and been useless on camera. Crowd fit becomes a directional prior. Too Tight and Too Loose count double — they signal a full size off, not a preference: $$\text{skew} = \frac{\left(t + 2t^{+}\right) - \left(l + 2l^{+}\right)}{100}$$ where $t, l$ are the tight and loose percentages and $t^{+}, l^{+}$ the too tight / too loose ones. We call RUNS_SMALL above a weighted gap of 6. At the rater counts these products carry, the standard error on a $p \approx 0.20$ proportion over $n = 2100$ is $$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \approx 0.0087 \approx 0.9\ \text{pp}$$ so a 6-point weighted gap is several standard errors — signal, not noise. Below 50 raters we return INSUFFICIENT_DATA and refuse to call it at all. Two public AJIO sources , called server-side only: the PDP aggregator and the delivery-promise API, with a 60-second cache and hard timeouts. The style-code invariant is strict — only codes this server obtained from AJIO's own search, or ships fixtures for. Never a code supplied by the browser. No anti-bot sensor header is sent, stored or committed anywhere. If a call would need one, the app falls back to clearly-labelled fixtures instead. There's a grep in the verification step that fails the build if such a string ever appears in the tree. 55 assertions, no test framework. node scripts/selfcheck.js . Challenges we ran into The WebMCP API is not the MCP API. Our tools returned {content:[{type:'text',text:...}]} — the envelope a remote MCP server uses. Chrome's execute returns a plain string . Every result would have arrived as a stringified wrapper the agent had to unwrap. We also assumed an unregisterTool method; there isn't one — unregistration is an AbortSignal passed at registration. Both were caught only by reading Chrome's docs against our own code. The silent one: origin isolation. WebMCP is only exposed in origin-isolated documents. Without Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 , document.modelContext is simply undefined — no error, no warning, nothing to debug. You'd naturally blame your Chrome version and go chasing an upgrade that was never the problem. Real data is hostile in small ways. numUserRatings is "2.1K" , a display string — parse it naively and you fabricate a rater count. Percentages arrive as "15 %" , with a space. The size chart is a superset of what's purchasable (8 charted, 5 buyable on one real product), so recommendations must come from the intersection. One live product returned a fittingType of " " — whitespace, which is truthy, and rendered a factor row with blank evidence. A truthful API answer that was useless. Our demo fixtures had invented SKUs. The live delivery API dutifully returned "not serviceable" for them — which is true, and means the SKU doesn't exist , not that the garment can't be delivered. We were putting fabricated products on real-looking hard fails. Fixture products no longer consult live delivery. A regression we caused ourselves. When live search landed, it loaded eight real style codes — and the PDP allowlist, which only knew about fixtures, rejected every one. The app rendered empty under a confident "Live AJIO data" badge. Fixing it meant sharpening the invariant rather than loosening it: codes AJIO's own search returned are server-obtained, so they earn a session allowlist; browser-supplied codes never do. Then the fix had its own bug — the search cache outlived the session allowlist, so the first Reset handed back codes the adapter then refused. Both are now regression-tested. Knowing when to stop being clever. The hardest call was making wrong register a hard stop instead of a weighted negative. Softening it makes price pull junk back to the top of the list, and the whole argument collapses. Accomplishments that we're proud of It opens with zero buys. A recommender that cannot say "you already own something that works" will eventually sell you a fourth white shirt. Getting the rules honest enough to recommend nothing — and then having that be the most compelling thing on screen — is the accomplishment. Four skips, four different reasons. Wrong register, already owned, avoided fit, undeliverable. Not one score threshold wearing four hats. The agent cannot spend your money. prepare_purchase_handoff is two-phase: it returns AWAITING_CONFIRMATION , a card appears, and only a real DOM click mints a single-use token — bound to style code and size, expiring in 60 seconds. Guessing an ID, replaying a used one, or swapping the size after confirmation all fail, and all four are asserted. There is no cart, checkout, login, orders or payment access anywhere in the codebase. It degrades honestly. Fixture mode is labelled in a banner, a header badge, and a per-card pill, and tool results carry dataSource so the agent discloses it. Serviceable-with-no-date says exactly that. title: StockPilot
pitch: StockPilot is an agent-native inventory management app where AI agent doesn't just read your data, it proposes actions, files them for approval, and you decide with a single click.
about_excerpt: StockPilot is an agent-native inventory management app where AI agent doesn't just read your data, it proposes actions, files them for approval, and you decide with a single click. Like Comment Story Updates StockPilot with WebMCP StockPilot Why WebMCP Is a Strong Fit Inventory management is fundamentally a shared-state problem . The dashboard shows data, but analyzing it requires cross-referencing products, suppliers, sales velocity, and profit margins — work that takes 30-60 minutes manually. WebMCP solves this by letting an AI agent operate on the same data, through the same logic, as the UI — not a copy, not a mirror, the identical code path. The agent doesn't just read data. It proposes actions (replenishment plans, purchase orders), but the human retains control over consequential decisions. This is only possible because WebMCP tools are registered on document.modelContext — they execute in the browser, against the same database, with the same server-side validation as the dashboard. How It Creates a Better User Experience Before WebMCP: User opens dashboard → sees health score, at-risk products, open POs User manually clicks each product → checks velocity → mental math on profit User opens spreadsheet → calculates which products are worth restocking User creates POs one by one, copying supplier data manually Time: 30-60 minutes for a weekly inventory review With WebMCP Agent: User types: "Protect my inventory with a $3,000 budget" Agent analyzes all products in one call → risk levels, velocity, profitability Agent proposes a budget-aware replenishment plan → grouped by supplier with cost subtotals User clicks Approve → POs are created → stock is received Time: 2 minutes for the same review The agent auto-navigates to relevant pages after each action. The Agent Activity Panel shows every tool call in real-time. The human always knows what the agent is doing. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult or Impossible Before Cross-Product Profitability Analysis : "Which products will make me $1,000 profit this month?" — impossible to answer manually without cross-referencing sales velocity, profit margins, and inventory levels across all products. The agent calls get_profitability_analysis once and returns sorted projections. Budget-Aware Replenishment : "Replenish my inventory with a $3,000 budget" — the agent prioritizes by urgency (critical → warning → watch), fits items within budget, and returns what fits vs. what's rejected. Manual equivalent: 2+ hours of spreadsheet work. Emergency Impact Simulation : "What if my electronics supplier delays 10 days?" — instant analysis of which products stock out, days until stockout, alternate suppliers available, total revenue at risk. Manual equivalent: calling each supplier, checking lead times, calculating impact. Agent Proposes → Human Approves : The agent can't unilaterally place orders. It files pending actions with reasoning and cost estimates. The human approves or rejects via the Agent Actions queue. Server enforces the approval gate — the agent can't bypass it. Real-Time Visibility : The Agent Activity Panel shows every tool call as it happens. The human watches the agent work, sees the reasoning, and can intervene at any point. How WebMCP Was Implemented Architecture : Shared domain logic in inventory.server.ts (~2,200 lines) is called by two entry points: UI : TanStack Start server functions via inventory.functions.ts WebMCP : 52 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() in tools.ts Tool Design : Each tool has: 4 annotations ( readOnlyHint , destructiveHint , idempotentHint , openWorldHint ) Zod → JSON Schema input validation (auto-generated, no manual drift) Structured error codes ( NOT_FOUND , CONFLICT , PRECONDITION_FAILED , INVALID_INPUT ) Audit trail logging to agent_tool_calls table Collaboration Model : 24 consequential tools are marked with agent hints ("only call after human approval") Server-side enforcement: PO state machine ( draft → approved → received ), decidedBy derived from session Agent Activity Panel: real-time visibility into every tool call Auto-navigation: 9 tools navigate to relevant pages after execution Deployment : Cloudflare Workers with D1 (SQLite) database. Live at https://stockpilot.aakas.workers.dev Tech Stack : TanStack Start, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Drizzle ORM, Cloudflare D1, TypeScript 5.7 Built With cloudflare react tailwind tanstack Try it out stockpilot.aakas.workers.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Aakash Shakya Like Share this project: Updates Aakash Shakya started this project — Sep 02, 2026 06:57 AM EDT

title: RecallOps WebMCP
pitch: The website gives agents tools to investigate and prepare - then withdraws them where human authority begins.
about_excerpt: The website gives agents tools to investigate and prepare - then withdraws them where human authority begins. Like Comment Story Updates Capability Sculpting: WebMCP tools appear only when workflow state permits; human-only authority stays outside the visiting agent. Architecture: WebMCP browser tools meet FastAPI policy, CockroachDB governed memory, AWS hosting, and an authority receipt chain. Governed evidence: mem_47 scores 0.94 but is rejected for version mismatch and failed outcome; reviewed mem_12 remains eligible. Immutable postcheck: after human approval, the app records recovery measurements and an independent policy verdict before reuse. Independent review: a separate reviewer certifies pending memory before it becomes eligible for future governed recall. Gallery overview: five proof screens show capability sculpting, architecture, governed evidence, postcheck policy, and reviewed recall. Problem Operational agents often mistake semantic similarity for permission. The closest historical fix may target the wrong service version, have a known failed outcome, belong to another tenant, or contain unreviewed experience. Asking an agent to “be careful” does not create an authority boundary, and an agent that can approve its own proposal or promote its own memories can turn one unverified outcome into future operational authority. Solution RecallOps demonstrates Capability Sculpting: a WebMCP incident room whose server-authoritative workflow state continuously changes what the visiting agent can do as control moves between agent, operator, application, and reviewer. The agent can inspect an incident and at most three policy-evaluated candidate decisions, stage an exact mitigation proposal, assess a server-created postcheck, and recall compatible evidence only after certification. It cannot approve the proposal, apply the simulator action, activate memory, switch role, or override policy. Those protected transitions remain server-enforced UI actions for distinct operator and reviewer identities. When the agent stages a proposal, propose_mitigation is withdrawn. Only after exact human approval, an allowlisted simulation, and an immutable observation does record_postcheck_assessment appear. The agent submits an attributable assessment, while the backend independently computes the policy verdict. The new memory remains PENDING_REVIEW and retrieval-ineligible until an independent reviewer decides its disposition. Why WebMCP is essential This is not a chatbot with a static tool list. WebMCP lets the website and visiting agent collaborate over the same incident state while the website retains control of the capability surface. Native document.modelContext.registerTool registrations are lifecycle-bound with separate AbortController s, reconciled against server epochs, and withdrawn on state changes. Stale callbacks and guessed protected operations fail server-side even if a client retained old JavaScript state. The page makes protocol behavior judge-visible through a Capability Inspector and chronological Activity Rail. Judges can watch authority move without opening DevTools. What humans and agents can now do together The agent rapidly investigates bounded evidence and prepares a precise, digest-bound proposal. The operator owns authorization and attests only the isolated simulator action. The application owns measurement and policy evaluation. The agent interprets—but cannot invent—the observation. A different reviewer governs whether the experience may influence a future incident. The resulting Authority Receipt links evidence, proposal, approval, observation, assessment, policy verdict, and review in one independently verifiable chain. Four WebMCP tools inspect_incident — bounded, read-only incident, workflow, and at most three candidate decisions; similarity is separate from eligibility and rejection codes are machine-readable. In POSTCHECK_READY , it also returns the server-issued immutable observation and independent policy verdict required for assessment. propose_mitigation — proposal-only mutation bound to incident, evidence, idempotency key, and action hash; it cannot approve or execute. record_postcheck_assessment — appears only after server-created evidence; accepts an observation ID plus attributable opinion and can create only a pending-review memory. recall_reviewed_memory — read-only compatible recurrence; absent until certified evidence is admissible and withdrawn when governance no longer permits reuse. Human-only operations Approve/reject proposal, attest the simulator action, certify/quarantine/reject/revoke memory, role handoff, and policy override are never WebMCP tools. Separation of duties is enforced by authenticated subjects and database/API invariants, not by hiding buttons. The claim is deliberately scoped to WebMCP-mediated authority; RecallOps does not claim to prevent general browser automation or prove physical-person independence. Demonstrated impact The headline synthetic case uses one identical candidate set. Similarity-only retrieval selects mem_47 at 0.94 , even though it is version-incompatible and has a known failed outcome. RecallOps rejects it before ranking and selects reviewed compatible mem_12 at 0.81 . Across the committed 12-case governed benchmark, similarity-only retrieval makes 11 unsafe selections and leaks two pending memories; RecallOps makes zero unsafe selections, leaks zero pending memories, and produces all three expected abstentions. These are deterministic synthetic policy-regression results, not production incident-rate or universal-safety claims. Execution and proof The no-signup judge flow is isolated per run and deterministic. It covers successful recurrence, observation unavailability, stale tools, replay/idempotency, separate reviewer authority, refresh, reset, and constrained layout. Candidate-bound local assurance reports: 498 Python tests collected, with the base suite plus real CockroachDB integration exercised in the combined coverage run; 100.00% Python statement and branch coverage: 5,454/5,454 statements and 1,224/1,224 branches; 74.06% mutation score: 1,519/2,051 killed, with zero untested mutations or timeouts; 10/10 browser, 2/2 judge-journey, and 4/4 native Chromium WebMCP tests; 2/2 public browser tests and a distinct native Chromium 151 live lifecycle proof; 15/15 exact independent-verifier outcomes across one valid and 14 materially tampered bundles; zero known vulnerabilities in the production and development lock audits. The receipt signature proves integrity and policy consistency of the supplied authority chain. It does not prove external truth, physical presence, trusted time, or completeness against a compromised signer. The product states those limitations next to the proof. How Codex was used OpenAI Codex helped convert the frozen product requirements into transactional and protocol boundaries, implement the WebMCP lifecycle, red-team authority paths, expand tests, identify real TOCTOU and production-lock defects, verify coverage and mutations, and generate deterministic evidence. Claims were accepted only when backed by executable checks or explicit external proof; remaining final-release gates stay red rather than being inferred from older evidence. Links Live URL: https://6n4hjbd6xh.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Public repository: https://github.com/milos-plavsic/recallops Demo video: https://youtu.be/C3lcckoKUbs Judge guide: https://github.com/milos-plavsic/recallops/blob/main/docs/JUDGE_GUIDE.md Evidence index: https://github.com/milos-plavsic/recallops/blob/main/docs/EVIDENCE_INDEX.md Existing-project comparison: https://github.com/milos-plavsic/recallops/compare/cee362c5ce3cb3bb44c63a4c1ba80b558881d21c...main Exact testing instructions for judges Open the live URL; no signup or credentials are required. Start the deterministic judge scenario for checkout-latency-42 . In ChatGPT's in-app browser or WebMCP-enabled Chrome, ask the agent to find a safe response and stage it without authorizing or executing anything. Confirm mem_47 is visible but rejected for SERVICE_VERSION_MISMATCH and KNOWN_FAILED_OUTCOME , while mem_12 remains eligible. After staging, confirm propose_mitigation disappears and authority changes to operator. Use the operator controls to approve the exact proposal and attest the labeled simulation. Confirm record_postcheck_assessment appears only after the server-created observation; let the agent record its assessment and confirm the memory is PENDING_REVIEW . Open the purpose-bound reviewer handoff. Confirm the reviewer page exposes zero WebMCP tools and activate the memory as the distinct reviewer. Confirm recall_reviewed_memory appears only after review; invoke it and verify the compatible checkout-latency-43 selected evidence authority changes, while the UI separately reports whether the bounded action changed. Download the Authority Receipt and run the documented network-free verifier if desired. Similarity can disco
video_title: RecallOps — WebMCP Incident Co-Control Room Demo
video_transcript_excerpt: RecallOps is an incident co-control room for WebMCP. The problem is simple. Operational agents can retrieve similar history, but similarity is not authority. The closest-looking fix can target the wrong service version, have a known failed outcome, or still be waiting for review. Here, the visiting agent works through ChatGPT's in-app browser using native WebMCP tools exposed by the page. At the start, RecallOps gives the agent only the safe investigation capability. The agent calls inspect_incident and receives bounded incident data for checkout-latency-42. The important part is visible here. One memory has 0.94 similarity, but RecallOps rejects it before ranking because it is for the wrong service version and has a known failed outcome. A lower similarity reviewed memory remains eligible. That is the core policy boundary. Similarity discovers experience. Policy decides whether it can be used. Next, the agent stages one bounded mitigation proposal. It can prepare, but it cannot authorize or execute. As soon as the proposal is staged, the WebMCP tool surface changes. propose_mitigation is withdrawn and authority moves to the human operator. The operator approves the exact proposal hash and attests the labeled sandbox action. This is not production infrastructure execution. It is an isolated deterministic checkout simulator. After that, the application creates the immutable post-check observation. Only now does the agent receive the post-check assessment tool. The agent can interpret the measurements, but it can't invent them, rewrite them, or decide policy. RecallOps keeps the measurement, the agent assessment, and the independent back-end verdict separate. The new memory is still not reusable. It remains pending review and excluded from governed retrieval. Now, a distinct reviewer opens the purpose-bound review page. Notice that this page exposes zero WebMCP tools. Certification is never delegated to the agent. After review, RecallOps opens the compatible recurrence, check out {dash} latency {dash} 43. Only now can the reviewed evidence be recalled and used safely. The system reports whether the selected evidence authority changed, whether the bounded action changed, and what recommendation is selected. Finally, the evidence packet and authority receipt bind the incident, proposal, approval, observation, assessment, verdict, and review into one verifiable chain. RecallOps demonstrates capability sculpting. The website changes what the agent can do as authority moves between agent, operator, application, and reviewer. Similarity can discover experience. Only reviewed evidence earns authority.

title: LabSpace Atlas
pitch: Tell LabSpace Atlas what you need. It shapes the room, knows where everything lives, and guides you from question to ready workspace—while every important decision remains yours.
about_excerpt: Tell LabSpace Atlas what you need. It shapes the room, knows where everything lives, and guides you from question to ready workspace—while every important decision remains yours. Like Comment Story Updates LabSpace Atlas connects synchronized 2D and 3D planning with inventory and exact-location evidence. Improved UI for Layout Editor and Inspector WebMCP UI Pop-up / Judges Mission and Use Cases Suggestions WebMCP UI Pop-up / Evidence Tracker with export WebMCP UI Pop-up / Tools UI Facility Viewer (For Research Institutions and University usage) Spatial Index Update With Agent Progress Tracker Confirmation Window for Human Approval / Reviewed Mode Process Tracker in Action / Go With The Experiment Step-by-Step Process Tracker Records Holder The New Universal Inventory Studio Storage Workspace - Assigning Items Location Couldn't Be Easier New Assets Detailed Viewer Spatial Index Update With Agent Placement Tracking Inspiration I am a biologist and researcher, not a programmer. LabSpace began with a familiar laboratory question: “Where is it?” The answer might be in a spreadsheet, on a label, or in the memory of the person who last used it. A floor plan tells me where a cabinet stands; an inventory list tells me a reagent exists. Neither necessarily helps me find the right drawer and get ready to work. I started LabSpace to bring those pieces together. For this challenge, I wanted to go further: could I describe what I need to a browser agent, watch it work with my actual laboratory, and still make the decisions myself? That became LabSpace Atlas. What it does Atlas is where I can plan a room, keep track of its contents, and find what I need for work. The three tasks in the video are just the tip of the iceberg. I chose them to tell one short story, not to limit what you can try. Once you have connected the browser agent, please make it your own. Open the Inspector's Tools tab and explore all 24 tools: plan an annex, inspect nested storage, check a room for placement problems, or validate a move before approving it. Change the requests, combine the tools, and bring a question from your own lab. The same checks and approval controls still apply. Here is the short journey I chose for the video: Build a place to work. I ask for a 38-square-metre researcher office, R-003, with three desks and matching chairs, doors and windows in specific positions, a locker, and basic safety equipment. After I enable Fast Draft, one request takes it through building, furnishing, and checking the layout. I can then inspect and edit the room in 2D and 3D. Record new stock. I ask it to add alpha-glucosidase and lipase, with quantities and expiry dates. Atlas prepares both entries together and waits for me to approve them inside the app. I have not specified a shelf, so it leaves storage unassigned. Later, I can add a photograph from my computer or an image URL, and place the record on a named shelf or drawer in the Storage workspace. Find the materials, then the workspace. I give the agent my DPPH checklist: reagent, pipette holder, 100 and 200 microlitre tips, and a microplate reader. It looks for those records, points out anything missing or uncertain, and recommends a work surface. I also ask about chloroform separately to show what happens when an item has no recorded match. That check does not add chloroform, methanol, or any other solvent to my checklist. Before the collection starts, I see the items and final workbench in Atlas's Review collection dialog. After I approve, I can move through the locations with Next and Previous, see supported drawers or doors open, and finish at the chosen bench. The guide stays below the scene, leaving the location details in view. I confirm each step myself. Following the guide does not deduct stock or approve the experiment. Why WebMCP fits this problem “Put this on the bench” sounds simple until there are several benches, different heights, and equipment already in the way. The agent needs to know which object I mean and whether the placement makes sense. The same is true when I ask for something inside a particular drawer. The 24 WebMCP tools give the browser agent those details: record IDs, dimensions, storage paths, stock information, and the results of the app's checks. It works with the same room and records that I see on screen. I can describe a task without knowing every menu or field. The browser agent interprets my request, and Atlas carries out the supported actions and checks. If the host supports voice, I can speak the request there too. There is no second chatbot inside Atlas. I also wanted to decide how much freedom to give it. Every session starts in Reviewed mode. I can switch on Fast Draft for a validated new blank room and its complete first blueprint, but that choice lasts only for the session. Inventory changes, moves, resizes, and changes to existing rooms still need review; a failed check cannot silently pass. The agent cannot enable Fast Draft or approve its own proposals. What existed before, and what I added for this challenge I brought an existing project to this challenge: LabSpace AI . It already had the synchronized 2D/3D editor, inventory and storage, a Spatial Index, placement checks, and local saving. I am not claiming that foundation as new challenge work. For the challenge, I added the WebMCP tools and the workflows around them: room and annex planning, inventory and layout proposals, Reviewed and Fast Draft modes, checklist assessment, and a collection guide with approval and exportable evidence. Getting that to work also meant revisiting the cameras, storage views, assets, and tests. A tool call succeeding was not enough if I still could not understand its result on screen. The repository's annotated pre-webmcp-2026-08-27 tag and dated implementation notes preserve that boundary. How we built it I came up with LabSpace from problems I encountered as a researcher and shaped its development into LabSpace Atlas. I defined the laboratory workflows, supplied reference photographs and equipment requirements, and directed the product design and AI-assisted development. I tested the application myself, set priorities for fixes, and kept revising layouts, cameras, and equipment models when they did not make sense in a real lab. I also planned, recorded, and edited the demonstration video. GPT-5.6 helped me turn those observations into requirements, and Codex helped implement, debug, test, and document the application. I repeatedly tested the results myself and pushed back when an arrangement, camera view, or equipment model did not make sense as a researcher. Hilal helped with end-to-end regression testing and debugging, including checking how natural-language requests worked through WebMCP. Eman helped review the designs and created reference diagrams to guide our work with GPT-5.6 Sol. She also checked for inconsistencies as the designs developed. The application uses React and TypeScript, React Konva for 2D planning, and Three.js/React Three Fiber for 3D. Detailed assets use optimized Blender-authored GLBs. Node and Express serve the Render-hosted app; SQLite supports local development, while each public visitor's workspace persists in that browser's IndexedDB. Under the hood, document.modelContext.registerTool registers each tool with an input schema and an execution handler. The handlers call the same search, planning, validation, and staging functions used by the app. I can inspect the calls and my decisions in the Inspector, or export them to review later. Atlas has no embedded language model and requires no application API key. Tool results are shared with the browser agent the user connects; that host's privacy policies and usage limits still apply. Challenges I ran into Getting the right record was only half the problem. Early camera views could leave it hidden behind a wall or another object. I refined the viewpoints around actual storage faces, with closer, slightly elevated framing and temporary wall cutaways. Trust also needed more than a confirmation sentence in chat. Inventory and collection approvals became visible product dialogs, with cancellation and recorded decisions. The collection guide was reorganized so it no longer competed with the evidence panel. Even connection setup mattered. Tools being registered on the page did not mean a new conversation had discovered them. Atlas now separates “connect once” from the shorter task prompts and makes that first step explicit. Accomplishments I am proud of The moment that matters to me is when the answer leaves the chat and appears in the room: the office is there, the inventory entry is saved after my approval, or the drawer I was looking for opens in front of me. There are 115 searchable assets that can be viewed from all sides, along with storage maps, item photographs, and reversible editing. I kept Low, Balanced, and High rendering options because extra visual detail should be a choice, especially on a slower devic

title: client-weave
pitch: ClientWeave: An agent-native workspace where buyers and AI scope services, calculate seller-governed pricing, and book consultations—with humans retaining final control.
about_excerpt: ClientWeave: An agent-native workspace where buyers and AI scope services, calculate seller-governed pricing, and book consultations—with humans retaining final control. Like Comment Story Updates buyer goal service discovery service details shared scope guided scope validation deterministic pricing consultation availability agent-capabilities human confirmation confirmed booking Inspiration Buying professional services is rarely a simple checkout flow. Buyers often begin with an incomplete goal, refine requirements through conversation, wait for a quote, and then schedule a consultation. AI agents can accelerate this process, but consequential actions—such as submitting a lead or booking time—should remain under direct human control. That tension inspired ClientWeave : an agent-native professional-services CPQ workspace where buyers and browser agents collaborate on the same scope, while the seller controls pricing and the buyer retains the final say. What it does ClientWeave creates a shared, attributed workspace for service discovery, scoping, pricing, and consultation booking. A browser agent can: Discover services relevant to the buyer’s goal Create and update a structured scope Calculate deterministic, seller-governed pricing Find available consultation times Finalize a confirmed lead or booking Every scope change records whether it came from the buyer or the agent, making the process transparent and auditable. The key safety boundary is intentionally simple: an agent cannot confirm an action on the buyer’s behalf. Before a lead is submitted or a consultation is booked, the buyer must directly confirm the exact current summary in the interface. If the scope or quote changes afterward, that confirmation becomes stale and finalization is rejected. How we built it ClientWeave is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Supabase, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, Zod, and TanStack Query . The application exposes six browser-native WebMCP tools: discover_services create_scope update_scope price_scope find_consultation_slots finalize_confirmed_scope These tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() with a compatibility fallback for older browsers. They use the same authenticated and audited HTTP boundaries as the regular user interface, so agent interactions do not bypass the application’s validation or security model. The codebase separates deterministic domain rules from framework and infrastructure concerns. Pricing uses canonical inputs, versioned rules, integer minor units, and per-line rounding to ensure that the same scope always produces a reproducible quote. Public scope links use restricted, expiring capabilities rather than owner-level access. We also added structured validation, origin checks, secure cookies, content security policies, rate limiting, redacted observability, audit events, and retention workflows. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was designing collaboration without silently transferring authority from the person to the agent. Hiding a confirmation button from an agent was not enough; the server also needed to verify that a human directly confirmed the exact scope, quote, and intended action currently being finalized. Another challenge was keeping state consistent across the visual interface, WebMCP tools, pricing engine, and database. An agent could update a scope while the buyer was reviewing it, so we needed freshness checks and clear invalidation rules to prevent stale quotes or confirmations from being used. Designing safe public access was also demanding. Buyers should be able to participate without creating an account, but a private scope link must grant access to only one scope and must never provide workspace-owner privileges. Finally, we wanted the agent experience to be reliable without depending on brittle DOM scraping. Creating narrow, well-described WebMCP tools—and ensuring they behaved exactly like the human-facing workflows—required careful contract and integration testing. What we learned We learned that agent-native software works best when agents receive structured capabilities rather than instructions to imitate clicks. WebMCP made the available actions explicit, typed, and easier to audit. We also learned that human oversight should be enforced as a system invariant, not presented as a warning message. Direct confirmation, confirmation freshness, limited capabilities, and server-side authorization all work together to preserve meaningful human control. Most importantly, attribution changes the quality of collaboration. When every change clearly shows whether it came from a person or an agent, users can review the process instead of merely trusting the final result. What’s next Next, we want to expand ClientWeave with richer seller-defined pricing rules, reusable scope templates, additional scheduling integrations, and collaborative comments. We also plan to explore approval policies for larger deals while preserving the same core principle: agents can help move work forward, but people remain responsible for consequential decisions. title: Verdiqt
pitch: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict.
about_excerpt: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI made building software cheap. It did not make building the right software cheap. People now ship a SaaS product in a weekend, and find out at launch that nobody wanted it. Verdiqt moves that painful discovery to before you write the first line of code. You put your idea on trial, and a court decides whether it deserves to live. What it does You file a case: your SaaS idea in a sentence, or a link to a public GitHub repo you already built. Then the courtroom goes to work, and you watch every step happen live: The case file. The court reads your idea and writes it up: who it's for, what problem it solves, what to search for. The investigation. Real research across five real communities : Hacker News, Reddit, GitHub, Stack Overflow, and Product Hunt. Every finding appears on screen with a link to its source, and every source reports honestly: gathered, failed, or empty. If the first search comes back thin, the court automatically widens its search. The deliberation. Six AI judges each take one question: "Is the pain real? Is anyone actively looking for this? Who already exists? Who would pay? Can you reach these people? Can you build it fast enough?" Each judge delivers their score the moment they finish, you literally watch the bench board fill in, one verdict at a time. The ruling. A presiding judge reads the entire case file and rules: BUILD, PIVOT, or KILL —> with a score out of 100, the reasoning behind every number, and exactly one recommended next step (a real, cheap test you can run this week). A full trial takes about a minute. And if you refine your idea and try again, the court remembers: the evidence you marked as important and the previous ruling follow your case, so every iteration builds on the last. How we built it Zero cash out of pocket. The whole product runs on free tiers and hackathon credits: one small server runs the website and the research pipeline, the AI judges run on free model APIs, and when one provider's daily quota runs dry, the court automatically switches to a backup provider mid-trial and keeps ruling. Constraints became design: the court paces itself under rate limits, shows its deliberation while it works, and never wastes a token. The model argues; the code rules. Anti-hallucination isn't a prompt, it's enforced in code. Judges may only cite evidence the court actually gathered: invented citations are stripped automatically, and a high score that loses its citations gets capped. When public evidence is thin, the judge is allowed to use domain judgment but the ruling must say so, out loud, in the rationale. Uncertainty is never dressed up as certainty. Privacy without accounts. No sign-up. Your browser gets an unguessable key; only its fingerprint is stored. Your cases are yours, anyone else asking for them gets an identical "not found.", don't worry. Challenges we ran into Running a multi-stage AI pipeline on free tiers meant treating every token and every request as scarce... the wait-and-retry pacing, the provider failover, and the one-at-a-time trial queue all exist because of it. And WebMCP is new enough that the tool contract itself was a design problem: we learned that the workflow belongs inside the tool descriptions, so agents teach themselves the journey. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, evidence-cited validation trial in about a minute. A deliberation you can actually watch. A surface that serves two audiences at once... humans get a courtroom, agents get a toolbox, and each can see the other working. What we learned Never think you have enough time to build something. What's next for Verdiqt GitHub sign-in to put your whole repo graveyard on trial at once, re-trials over time to watch a verdict change as markets move, and Reddit's expanded API access for even deeper community evidence.
