title: Take Five
pitch: A governed room for humans and agents on WebMCP: the phase you are in is the set of tools the page offers, and every act on the ledger says how we know who did it.
about_excerpt: A governed room for humans and agents on WebMCP: the phase you are in is the set of tools the page offers, and every act on the ledger says how we know who did it. Like Comment Story Updates Take Five — a governed room for humans and agents Live: https://take-five-lw7.pages.dev/ Code: https://github.com/arthapraha/take-five (MIT) Five phases — Open · Commit · Reveal · Ruling · Closed — where the phase the room is in is the set of tools the page offers an agent. Every act lands on an append-only, SHA-256 hash-chained ledger, and every entry records not just what happened, but how well we know who did it . Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP's defining move is that the page declares what an agent may do. That makes the page the right place to put a rule — and the natural unit of a rule is not a permission, it is a phase . A governed proceeding is a state machine with sharp edges: you may seal a position now and not open it; you may open it now and not seal a new one; a ruling may be ratified only once and only from Ruling. Every other agent integration expresses that as validation — a tool that exists always and refuses most of the time. WebMCP lets us express it as existence . In Commit, commit_to_round is registered and reveal_in_round is not. Advance, and commit_to_round is gone — unregistered by aborting its AbortSignal , not hidden, not stubbed, not returning an error. Where the browser fires toolchange the badge moves with it; where it does not — ChatGPT's in-app browser has no addEventListener on modelContext — the tool list still changes, because the surface genuinely changed and the render does not depend on the event. The page says which case it is in rather than implying the stronger one. That is a rule an agent cannot argue with, cannot be prompted past, and does not have to be told about. It reads the tools it has. The second fit is subtler and is why this project exists. When an agent rides your browser session, its acts and yours arrive inside the same authenticated session . Existing audit tooling records one agent's actions for its own operator. Nothing records acts between parties in a shared venue — and at the WebMCP door, for the first time, a page can see which path an act arrived by. That is not full attribution. It is more than anyone had, and it is exactly enough to record honestly. How it creates a better user experience By refusing to overstate what it knows. Every ledger entry carries three fields: seat identity , ingress path , and an evidence grade — client-asserted , server-observed , or inherited . The grade is derived from the door the act came through, never passed in by the caller, and the interface never renders an attribution stronger than its grade . An act arriving with no grade is refused outright. You can watch this work rather than take it on faith: The commit-reveal check runs off-page in a Cloudflare Pages Function, so the entry is graded server-observed . When that function is unreachable, the check falls back into the page, grades itself down to client-asserted , and states the reason in its own output. A silent fallback would let a strong label survive a check that never left the browser. Every status chip on the page says what it cannot do. Cross-origin exposure unavailable in this browser? The chip says so, and no cross-org claim is made. Verification runs in your browser, over the whole chain, and can fail: the test suite includes altered content, a severed link, and the rehash-one-entry repair attempt that still breaks every entry after it. A verifier that cannot fail proves nothing. The result is an interface a sceptical person can use as an instrument instead of as a claim. That is the better experience: not more confidence, but confidence you can check. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Share a venue and leave a record neither party controls. Before WebMCP, an agent acting on a web app was indistinguishable from its human at the door — the session was the identity, and the page had no view of the route. Take Five demonstrates three things that become possible when the page declares the surface: An agent cannot read the room without leaving a mark. The read tools are themselves acts. Ask the agent to read the ledger and the read appears on the ledger , graded and attributed, between the two calls it made. The ask and the answer stay separate. ratify_ruling is registered only in Ruling and cannot ratify . It raises a request and blocks on a human. Two entries land, never one — the ask is the agent's, through the WebMCP door; the answer is the host's, through the UI door. Collapsing them would credit an agent with a decision it only asked for. A declined ratification stays on the chain permanently. The division of labour is legible on the record, not just in the prose: the human sets the question, advances the phases and rules; the agent acts through the tools; the chain records both, each through its own door. Neither party can perform the other's acts without the ledger saying which door it came through. A claim can cross an organisational boundary and stay labelled as borrowed. A separate origin calls into the room via exposedTo , and the room records the claim verbatim , names the origin that made it, and carries a SHA-256 over the claim bytes that anyone can recompute — graded inherited : we did not witness this, we carried it; trust it exactly as far as you trust that origin. The digest is on the ledger row, so a reader watching the demo can check the room's arithmetic without being given anything but the picture. Cross-organisation tool access here is not ambient. The room delegates the tools Permissions Policy to a named frame, and exposedTo allowlists a named origin. Two independent gates, both auditable, neither of them ours. Produced live on 31 August in Chrome 151 behind the WebMCP testing flags, and again on 2 September in Chrome 152 on the deployed build — with a local agent attached to the same page at the same time, which was never offered the partner's tool. The inherited row is a thing that happens, not a row we describe. Bring your own agent. The page publishes its tools through WebMCP; a small local bridge in this repository lets any MCP client outside the browser call exactly the tools the page would show a riding agent — and nothing else. We built our own side panel, Take Five Agent , to show it: type a prompt, and an agent on your machine, calling a model you choose — in our run, glm-5.3 through a local Ollama client to Ollama's cloud — calls the page's own read_ledger , and the call lands on the chain as a tool: row through the WebMCP door, chained to a bridge_opened row that names the door it came through. The agent is not in the browser and not ours to vouch for; the row says so. Chrome asks, once, whether the site may "access other apps and services on this device" — you say yes, and that permission is the point: an agent touches your things only by a permission you deliberately grant. What a visitor to the live URL sees is the page publishing its tools; the agent is a local install. "Bring your own agent" is the true claim, not "open the link and watch it work." The two browsers in our film are two different consumers of one tool surface — a cloud assistant's in-app browser and a bring-your-own local agent — working against the same page. That is the protocol working as a protocol. And the recording was made under the same rules the product enforces: a clean chain, one page per relay, a permission asked once, a door recorded before any call. And what we found that we would rather not have There is currently no way to build a human-only gate on the web. We built the confirmation dialog, then tested it instead of trusting it. We advanced the room to Ruling, asked an agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser to ratify, and the owner touched nothing. The chain recorded ruling_ratified and closed the room. Asked plainly afterwards, he confirmed: "No I didn't touch anything." This falsified a sentence in our own shipped README. We had written that UI handlers and registered execute callbacks are disjoint code paths, so the distinction is real. The paths are disjoint; the inference was wrong. An agent driving the page can take the UI path , so a code path tells you how an act arrived and not who caused it. That sentence is now corrected in the README rather than softened, and the grade legend with it. What survived is the grade. client-asserted had already declined to vouch for the actor — so the ledger did not lie even in the case that falsified our prose about it. What was false was the gloss, written by the same author who wrote the grade and trusted his own summary more than his own code. The primitive intended for this, requestUserInteraction() , is absent from every environment we tested — the polyfill, Chrome behind the WebMCP flag, and ChatGPT's in-app browser. Where the browser can't do something, the page says so rather than pretending. Watch for it. Everything here sits behind document.modelcontext. The agent sees five read-only tools. Watch what happens when it uses one. The read itself lands on the chain. The agent cannot look at this room without leaving a mark. We are in commit. The agent can seal a position without disclosing it. The room stores only the hash of the position and a nonce. And commit around exists only in this phase. Advance, and it is gone. Not hidden, unregistered. Reveal in round has taken its place. That list is the agent's actual surface, not a menu we are drawing next to it. Or bring your own agent. The reveal recomputes the digest off page in a Cloudflare function, so this entry is graded server observed. If that function is unreachable, the check falls back into the page, grades itself down to client asserted, and says why in its own output. A silent fallback would let a strong label survive a check that never left the browser. Ratify.underscore.ruling cannot ratify. It raises a request and blocks on a human. The human sets the question and rules. The agent acts through the tools. The chain records both, each through its own door. Two entries land, never one. The ask is the agent's, the answer the host's. A refusal stays on the chain permanently. Now the part we would rather not have found. Web MCP's primitive for a human gate, request user interaction, does not exist. Not in in polyfill, not in flagged Chrome, not in chat GPT's browser. So, the room uses its own ratified dialogue and records what pressed it. This click was a person's and the row says the page cannot tell that from an agent driving the browser. A page cannot require a human today. Anything claiming to describe the convention, not a control. And when a claim arrives from another organization, the room records it verbatim, names the origin that made it, and hashes what it was given, then grades it inherited. We did not see this happen. We carried it. Trust it exactly as far as you trust that origin. Every hash recomputed, every link checked in your browser. Nothing here asks you to take the chain on trust. That is the product, not certainty about who acted, but an honest record of how well we know.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. With a passion for thoughtful, over-engineered UX flows. Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Luca Gugliemi started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:26 AM EDT

title: Meabs
pitch: When architects meet agents and WebMCP, who will break first
about_excerpt: When architects meet agents and WebMCP, who will break first Like Comment Story Updates Multi-Region Simulation Event Driven Reference Architectures Inspiration As an architect, I spend a lot of my time working with pictures. We use architecture diagrams to explain how systems work, how they connect and how we think they will behave. I wanted to bring those pictures to life and avoid my designs breaking things and getting people paged in the middle of the night :-) I wanted to be able to model a change and get an idea of what it might do to the design. What happens if the load increases? What if I lose a component or a zone? If I change something to recover, what impact does that have somewhere else? Having an agent working alongside me makes that much quicker to explore. The agent can stress the architecture, break things, inspect what happened and try to recover it. I can change the constraints or try a different idea and see how it responds. What it does Resilience Forge turns an architecture diagram into something I can experiment with. I can configure a scenario, change the workload and run deterministic simulations to see how the architecture responds. I can introduce failures such as losing a component or a zone, watch the impact on the architecture and metrics, and test different ways of recovering. An AI agent can work on the same scenario through WebMCP. It can inspect the architecture and metrics, run stress tests, introduce failures and make changes to try to recover the system. The agent and I work against the same state. If I change a constraint or make a decision in the UI while the agent is working, it sees that change and has to respect it. This means I can work with the agent rather than handing the whole simulation over to it. Resilience Forge also includes a flight recorder that shows the WebMCP calls as they happen, so I can see what the agent is doing and how those actions affect the simulation. For this project I've used deterministic simulations, so I can run the same scenario repeatedly and get consistent results. The idea could go much further by bringing in real telemetry, service limits, costs and other infrastructure data to create more realistic simulations. How we built it I used Codex to help with the coding and my knowledge of creating pictures as an architect :-) For hosting I am using the ChatGPT Sites capability The simulation and WebMCP tools work against the same application state. Every WebMCP mutation works against a version of that shared state. If I change the architecture while the agent is working, its old write is rejected as STALE_STATE rather than silently overwriting my change. The agent then has to read the current state and decide what to do next. Constraints such as pinned decisions are enforced in the application itself, not left to the prompt, and the Flight Data Recorder shows human and WebMCP actions against the same timelines. The WebMCP tools are domain operations rather than UI controls. The agent can inspect the architecture, run stress tests, inject failures, change scaling or traffic behaviour and apply remediations without having to work out how to click around the page. The same domain logic is used whether the change comes from me or from WebMCP. This was important because I didn't want the agent operating against a separate version of the architecture from the one I could see and change in the UI. Challenges we ran into The main one for me was keeping the state between the agent and the user aware of each other, as both parties can make changes and we need to make sure that the application is aware of those. Both can make changes while a simulation is running, so the application needs to keep them in sync. If I make a decision or add a constraint in the UI, the agent needs to know about it and respect it when deciding what to do next. Accomplishments that we're proud of Created my first ever YouTube video, and it has spurred me on to do more, I may be terrible at it for now but I will improve :-) What we learned WebMCP will change how agents and users interact with websites. When I'm designing user journeys, I now need to think about the agent journey as well as the human journey. WebMCP makes that much easier because the agent can interact with capabilities exposed by the application rather than having to pull information from the DOM and work out how to operate a UI designed for a human or have information locked away so that agents can't access it. What's next for Meabs I'm working on an agent that can read infrastructure source code such as Terraform and CDK and then model that infrastructure in Resilience Forge. I'd also like to integrate with vendors' MCP servers to bring in real-time information such as service limits. From there, I want to explore bringing in real telemetry and cost data so the simulations can move closer to the architectures I'm actually working with. This also builds on some of my other work around PEAR (Public Engagement AI-Readiness) and the Agent Observatory, where I've been exploring how we design applications for agents and how we observe what those agents are doing. Resilience Forge gave me a chance to put some of those ideas into a working application rather than leaving them as architecture diagrams or slide decks :-) Built With next.js/vinext react-19 tailwind-css three.js typescript vite Try it out github.com resilience-forge.gman72.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Garry Meaburn Like Share this project: Updates Garry Meaburn started this project — Sep 02, 2026 05:13 PM EDT

title: HumanAgentMultiplayer
pitch: A real-time WebMCP workspace where multiple humans and their agents safely co-edit contracts and visual canvases, with browser-held revision receipts and human commit controls.
about_excerpt: A real-time WebMCP workspace where multiple humans and their agents safely co-edit contracts and visual canvases, with browser-held revision receipts and human commit controls. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI copilots are useful one-on-one, but shared work becomes fragile when several people and agents edit at the same time. We wanted agents to collaborate directly inside a web app—not through screenshots or brittle UI automation—while protecting teammates from stale edits. What it does HumanAgentMultiplayer is a pair of live WebMCP workspaces for people and their agents: A shared contract editor with local human drafts, inline approval, immutable revision history, and reviewed restores. A shared Excalidraw canvas where people commit visual drafts, agents create, update, and delete structured elements, and every change appears in a revisions tab. For each agent, the browser keeps an opaque read receipt. Before changing either workspace, the agent reads the current state. If another person or agent has edited since then, the server returns only those intervening changes and rejects the stale mutation until the agent reviews and retries. Agents never send a revision number themselves. How we built it We built the UI with TypeScript, React, CodeMirror, and Excalidraw. Shared state uses Yjs with y-partyserver. A Cloudflare Worker and separate hibernating Durable Objects coordinate the daily document and canvas rooms, persist snapshots and revision metadata, and expose the WebMCP-safe API. Human restores use a browser confirmation flow protected by Cloudflare Turnstile. Challenges we ran into The hard part was making collaboration feel immediate without letting an incoming live update silently overwrite a person’s local work. We separated local human drafts from shared state, added visible commit controls, and treated Excalidraw hydration metadata as non-user changes so a refresh does not create a fake draft. We also designed the freshness protocol so the browser holds the agent identity and the server records what that agent actually read, rather than trusting a revision supplied by a tool call. Accomplishments that we're proud of Two distinct real-time demos under one human-agent collaboration model. Browser-registered WebMCP tools that operate on structured document and canvas state. Human review controls, immutable document history, and a visible canvas revision feed. A public, open-source Cloudflare deployment with daily isolated rooms. What we learned Real-time collaboration needs both low-latency sync and explicit intent. The useful safety boundary is not a caller-supplied version number: it is a browser-held record of what each agent actually saw. What's next for HumanAgentMultiplayer We’re turning this into a full multi-agent version of Google Docs: a shared workspace where multiple professionals can collaborate on the same document alongside their own agents. Each agent will work from what it has actually read, surface live changes and conflicts, and help its person contribute without overwriting anyone else. title: Infinite Canvas — Agent Design Lab
pitch: One WebMCP brief becomes three safe, editable design experiments a person can compare, cancel, promote, and undo.
about_excerpt: One WebMCP brief becomes three safe, editable design experiments a person can compare, cancel, promote, and undo. Like Comment Story Updates Infinite Canvas is a browser-based visual design canvas where people and AI agents inspect, create, and edit the same live document through native WebMCP tools. Problem Visual design applications are built for pointer-and-keyboard interaction. An AI agent approaching the same application usually has to infer state from pixels, guess which controls to click, and repeat brittle UI actions. That makes substantial design work slow, unreliable, and difficult for a person to supervise. Solution For this WebMCP Challenge proof of concept, one agent brief starts three named hypotheses in isolated editable branches. A person can keep working on the original while the lanes run, inspect status and layout checks, cancel a lane, promote one branch only if the source revision is still current, and undo that promotion in one history step. Why WebMCP Visual design is state-heavy and precision-dependent: selections, trees, styles, tokens, pages, and history. The app registers structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, so an agent operates on the live document model instead of guessing from rendered pixels. The same MobX stores and handlers power both the visible editor and agent calls. What people and agents can do together The person keeps working visually while delegating a bounded exploration task. The agent reads the real selection and tree, starts three hypotheses, and reports progress. The person can compare structured editable branches, cancel work, promote a result, or undo it. A fingerprint-based stale-revision check rejects a completed branch when the person changed the original instead of silently overwriting that work. Implementation The hosted build exposes 54 tools: 34 core canvas tools, 14 design-lab tools, and six experiment tools: start_design_experiment, get_experiment_status, compare_experiment, cancel_experiment_lane, promote_variant, and undo_experiment_commit. Experiment jobs are orchestrated together, while writes to the single editor document are serialized. Operation IDs make retries idempotent; cancellation is cooperative; promotion is atomic and undo-compatible. Live demo Open the public URL and use the judge prompt in the repository README. No login is required. title: Morphus - the 3D world editor your agent can operate
pitch: A WebGPU 3D world editor that hands its real authoring tools to your browser agent. Sculpt terrain, grow forests and build scenes by asking...the scene graph is the API, not the pixels.
about_excerpt: A WebGPU 3D world editor that hands its real authoring tools to your browser agent. Sculpt terrain, grow forests and build scenes by asking...the scene graph is the API, not the pixels. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most attempts to let an AI agent drive a creative tool try to make the model see the screen: screenshots, pixel coordinates, guessing where a button is and hoping the click lands. For a 3D editor that's close to hopeless, because the interesting state isn't on screen at all. It's a scene graph, a modifier stack, a spline running through a forest field. Meanwhile our editor already had a complete, precise description of everything it could do. Tool declarations written for its own built-in Copilot, each with a JSON Schema. That surface existed, and it was locked inside one chat panel. WebMCP is the piece that was missing. It lets a page hand its real command surface to whatever agent the user is already talking to. So the question stopped being "how does a model learn to use our UI" and became "why is our UI the interface at all?" What it does Morphus is a WebGPU 3D world editor that runs entirely in the browser. It sculpts terrain, grows forests, blocks out levels, casts combat VFX, and lays out procedural cities. With WebMCP it registers all 154 of its tools with the browser, so an agent can build a world in the page the person is looking at . No server, no API key, no separate MCP process. Ask it for a landscape and it calls create_mesh_terrain , then terrain_sculpt_stroke along a path of world-space points, then create_forest_field and grow_forest_field to plant a stand of trees along a spline. Ask it for a city and it runs a whole pipeline. generate_street_grid lays avenues and cross streets with real junctions, kerb returns and lane markings. generate_city_massing divides the blocks between them into lots that front the street and extrudes them into volumes. generate_city_buildings replaces the tallest of those with actual architecture: limestone banks, setback towers, corner headquarters with colonnades and cornices. Throughout, it reads back with get_terrain_state , get_street_network and list_nodes , so it acts on what's really in the scene rather than on what it assumed. The scene graph is the API. A heavy GPU application becomes operable by a model that never has to render a frame. How we built it The core decision was to build a bridge, not a second implementation : await document.modelContext.registerTool( { name: "terrain_sculpt_stroke", description: "Sculpts the terrain along a path of world-space points...", inputSchema: { /* JSON Schema, shared with the in-app Copilot */ }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: false, untrustedContentHint: true }, execute: async (input, { signal }) => { /* ... */ } }, { signal: controller.signal } ); WebMCP asks for exactly the shape the Copilot declarations already had, so src/lib/webmcp/tools.ts reuses both the declarations and the same executor. A browser agent and the in-app Copilot run identical code paths and cannot drift apart. The payoff showed up when we built the city. Nine new tools became agent-drivable the moment they existed, with no bridge changes, no registration code, and no separate schema to maintain. The surface went from 145 to 154 by writing the features. Everything else followed the platform's guidance rather than working around it: Annotations derived, not hand-listed. readOnlyHint comes from the tool's name prefix, because a hand-kept list of read tools beside 154 declarations goes stale the first time someone adds a get_ . One tool lies about itself: capture_mesh_modeling_base captures topology as the base of a live modelling stack , so it writes. It's named as an explicit exception. A tool wrongly marked read-only is worse than one left unmarked, because it invites an agent to call a mutation speculatively. Lifetimes via AbortSignal . There is no unregisterTool . Aborting the registration controller is how tools go away, so they disappear cleanly with the editor. A second signal on execute cancels a call mid-flight, which matters when a sculpt covers a 4 km terrain. A visible record. Tools run in the page, so the only trace of a call is the one the page chooses to show. The menu bar carries an AGENT readout: tools registered, and the name of the last call. Challenges we ran into We shipped a curated 20, then reversed it. The original argument was sound. A tool list is a prompt, and every entry spends the agent's attention. But it cuts the other way at this scale. The editor's real capability is the whole surface, and an agent that cannot inset a face or lay a street is operating a demo of the editor rather than the editor. Curation became the agent's job, and ours became making that job possible: order the list so read and world-building tools lead, and annotate every entry honestly. Character budgets are a design problem, not a formatting one. Chrome recommends 500 characters per description. Truncating the overruns turned out to be exactly wrong, because the tail of a good description is the part that says when not to reach for the tool. We rewrote those by hand, aliased four over-long names, and wrote a budget check that fails the build. The same logic applied to results. A silently truncated result reads as a complete answer, which is how an agent ends up confidently acting on half a scene graph. A forest was planted thirty metres underground, and reported success. The viewport draws two different terrains depending on renderer backend, and they are not the same surface. The forest sampled one; the viewport drew the other. Measured, they differ by 26 to 30 metres, so every stand was buried and every tool call returned "success": true . There is now exactly one function that answers "how high is the ground here", and everything placed on the ground goes through it, so forests, streets and buildings can only ever be wrong together. Roads that bridge their own kerbs. Sampling terrain once at a street's centreline and reusing that height across its full width buries the uphill kerb and floats the downhill one by half the width times the gradient. On a 16m avenue that was 2.3 metres of float. Sampling per edge took the worst deviation across 228 vertices from 2.303m to 0.000m. We later replaced the hand-rolled ribbon entirely with three-roads , an OpenDRIVE-style model that owns lanes, kerb returns and paint properly. A building grammar that can't build a city. We vendored procedural-bank , a shape grammar producing early-twentieth-century commercial architecture, and measured before trusting it: 142,552 triangles from 478 kit modules per building, in about 300ms. Turning every knob down, with no ornament, no colonnade and no crown, reached 117,660. A saving of 17%, because the cost is in the modules and not the decoration. Building all 456 volumes of a modest grid would be roughly 62 million triangles and two minutes of blocking work. So it generates a few dozen landmarks standing among massing boxes, which is what a downtown looks like anyway. Resizing a canvas is not resizing a renderer. On WebGPU the render targets and depth texture are allocated when the renderer is built, so a canvas that grows afterwards leaves them behind and every frame fails validation against a black viewport. The sting is in the fix. The poll that waits for a real size cannot use requestAnimationFrame , because a page that isn't being composited doesn't run animation frames at all. The one mechanism that looks right is guaranteed to be asleep exactly when it's needed. Testing an API most browsers don't have. WebMCP needs Chrome's origin trial or chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . So we built a stub. ?webmcp=stub installs a minimal modelContext plus a console harness, exercising the same registration path and the same tool code with no model in it. window.__webmcp.list().length; // 154 window.__webmcp.describe("generate_street_grid"); // the schema an agent sees await window.__webmcp.call("generate_street_grid", { columns: 4, rows: 3 }); It settles the deterministic half of the question, "did this tool run and return what it promised", that Chrome's own guidance says to answer before writing evals. Accomplishments that we're proud of No parallel implementation. The agent's tools and the app's tools are the same tools. Nine city tools shipped with zero bridge changes. Budgets enforced by a check that fails the build , rather than by good intentions. The human stays the one who understands the document. Geometry appearing in a 3D scene is ambiguous. Did the person do that, or the model? The activity readout answers it on every call. It degrades cleanly. In a browser without WebMCP the editor behaves exactly as before: no crash, no chip, no console noise. Bugs closed by measurement, not by eye. Planted heights matching terrain to 0.000m, road vertices conforming to 0.000m, triangle budgets sampled across seven configurations. On a project where the camera can sta

title: ShipCheap
pitch: Project-aware backend hosting decisions without billing jumpscares—powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Project-aware backend hosting decisions without billing jumpscares—powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Choosing a backend host looks simple until a developer has to reconcile runtime support, database needs, region availability, credit-card requirements, sleeping services, free-tier limits, and surprise usage bills. Most comparison pages make people translate one real project into dozens of filters and pricing tables. ShipCheap began as a human-first backend hosting decision board. For the WebMCP Challenge, I turned it into a shared workspace where a person can describe or link a real project, let an agent do the repetitive analysis, and still review every important result in the same visible interface. What it does ShipCheap helps developers: rank backend hosts from runtime, budget, database, uptime, card access, region, and risk tolerance; compare providers in a visible decision table; simulate 1,000 deterministic monthly billing scenarios; inspect percentiles, budget-overrun probability, and likely cost spikes; review provider-specific launch checks; sign in and link a public GitHub repository by URL; approve a read-only GitHub App for private repositories; detect a repository's stack and save project-specific hosting recommendations. Why WebMCP Hosting selection is structured but multi-step. Without WebMCP, an agent must guess which controls to click, scrape result cards, and reconstruct application state. ShipCheap exposes eight purpose-built tools instead: open_project_workspace list_linked_projects list_available_github_repositories start_github_app_installation analyze_github_repository recommend_backend_hosts open_backend_host_comparison preview_billing_risk The agent can turn plain-language constraints into ranked recommendations, open the exact comparison or simulator, and—after the user chooses a repository—build a project-aware analysis. The person and agent share the same visible state throughout. Human control and data protection The agent advises and configures; it cannot silently create an account, approve GitHub access, attach billing, spend money, or deploy infrastructure. Private repository access uses a read-only GitHub App. Project reads and writes are authorized server-side against the signed-in Clerk user ID, and the database enforces repository and installation constraints. How I built it ShipCheap is a Next.js 16 App Router application written in TypeScript and React, styled with Tailwind CSS, and deployed on Vercel. Prisma stores data in PostgreSQL on Neon. Clerk provides authentication, and a GitHub App provides read-only repository access. The WebMCP layer lives in src/components/WebMCPTools.tsx and registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool uses a strict JSON Schema, validates inputs during execution, cleans up registrations with an AbortController , and returns concise structured results. The integration is progressive enhancement: the site and public decision workflow still work when WebMCP or authentication is unavailable. What I changed during the challenge ShipCheap existed before the challenge. During the submission period I added the eight-tool WebMCP layer, expanded the provider catalog and comparison surfaces, connected the tools to the existing recommendation and billing-risk logic, added Clerk authentication, created the project workspace, integrated the read-only GitHub App, added repository stack detection and project-specific recommendations, migrated persistence to Neon PostgreSQL, documented the public testing flow, and verified all eight tools on the deployed app in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Challenges The hardest design problem was deciding where agent authority should stop. A hosting assistant that can silently install integrations, deploy, or spend money would be risky, so ShipCheap keeps approval and consequential actions with the person. The second challenge was maintaining one source of truth. WebMCP tools reuse the same provider data, recommendation functions, repository analyzer, and billing simulator as the visible UI instead of maintaining a separate agent-only model. Accomplishments A working deployed product rather than a WebMCP-only proof of concept. Eight non-trivial tools spanning public decisions and authenticated project analysis. Visible shared state between human navigation and agent actions. Repository-aware recommendations for public and approved private GitHub projects. Strict validation, server-side ownership checks, and explicit safety boundaries. A public MIT-licensed repository with reproducible setup instructions. What I learned Useful agent-native design is less about exposing many actions and more about exposing the right decision boundaries. Structured tools compress repetitive analysis, while visible state and explicit approval keep consequential choices understandable and human-controlled. What's next Next steps include live pricing-source verification, richer project reports, additional providers, and deeper authenticated end-to-end testing. These are future directions, not claims about the current submission. title: FlightSweeper
pitch: A browser agent buys a sandbox flight within exact, revocable limits set by the traveler.
about_excerpt: A browser agent buys a sandbox flight within exact, revocable limits set by the traveler. Like Comment Story Updates Untrusted supplier content cannot override the stored refundability and price rules. The issued sandbox ticket records policy evidence and resolves a duplicate request safely. Mission authority and the WebMCP-connected agent workflow. FlightSweeper lets a traveler delegate a complete sandbox flight purchase in one browser conversation—without letting the agent choose its own authority. The traveler sets the route, date, arrival deadline, cabin, connection limit, refundability rule, purchase cap, and execution mode. The agent searches, compares, and executes. FlightSweeper independently approves or denies the transaction and records why. The result is practical delegation with visible control: the traveler does not need to click through the booking flow, and the agent cannot silently expand the traveler’s limits. The proof in one transaction One supplier result contains an instruction telling the agent to ignore the traveler’s refundability rule. FlightSweeper marks the supplier output as untrusted and evaluates the exact quote against the stored mandate. The cheaper offer is denied. The agent then selects an eligible offer, refreshes the quote, requests policy evaluation, and issues one idempotent sandbox ticket. Repeating the purchase returns the original ticket instead of creating another transaction. The traveler can revoke future authority without erasing the evidence. This single flow demonstrates the core product idea: an agent can complete consequential work, but it cannot authorize itself. Why WebMCP Traditional browser agents infer controls from a visual interface. They can also carry stale or adversarial page content into a consequential action. WebMCP gives FlightSweeper a structured, page-scoped transaction surface with bounded inputs and explicit trust annotations. The human and agent share the same visible transaction state. All 10 tools remain discoverable so the agent can plan the complete workflow. Application-side checks expose the valid next actions and reject premature or prohibited calls. The responsibility split is explicit: The traveler owns purchasing authority. The agent owns search and execution. Suppliers own inventory. FlightSweeper owns policy enforcement and transaction evidence. A human can replace or expand the mandate. An agent can only narrow it. The traveler can revoke future authority at any time. What the traveler and agent do together The agent reads the mandate, searches sandbox inventory, compares visible offers, selects an exact quote, refreshes it, requests independent evaluation, purchases an eligible offer, and retrieves the receipt. The traveler watches the same mission, offer, authorization, and evidence states change on the page. This makes a multi-step booking executable through one agent conversation while preserving the limits that matter to the traveler. How we implemented WebMCP The page registers 10 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(), bounded input and result schemas, and accurate readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations. Every success returns data, mission status, and valid next actions. Every failure returns a typed error with the same state guidance. Human controls and WebMCP tools call the same application functions and persist state in versioned browser storage. Tool callers provide mission, offer, and idempotency identifiers—not price, passenger, payment, or authorization claims. Before every consequential decision, FlightSweeper reloads the stored mission and exact quote. Authorization, denial, and booking receipts record the policy and quote versions, stored limits, offered values, rule results, actor, timestamp, and resolution. We verified the complete lifecycle in ChatGPT desktop’s in-app browser and Chromium 151: adversarial denial, monotonic tightening, quote refresh, authorization, ticketing, replay, revocation, and receipt retrieval. What we built during the challenge Production FlightSweeper existed before the challenge. After the August 25, 2026 kickoff, we built this public, self-contained WebMCP Challenge Edition: sandbox inventory, the stable tool catalog, state-validated execution, the authority and policy engine, the adversarial fixture, durable evidence, repeat-safe ticketing, the browser interface, tests, documentation, and deployment. Production FlightSweeper remains private and unchanged. The challenge edition never charges a card or creates an airline order. It demonstrates authority, policy enforcement, quote binding, revocation, and idempotency controls. A live provider connection would require additional provider, payment, identity, operational, and regulatory controls. FinSync LLC operates FlightSweeper and is registered as a California Seller of Travel, CST 2172984-70. Registration as a seller of travel does not constitute approval by the State of California. I also own FinSync LLC, the registered California Seller of Travel that operates FlightSweeper (CST 2172984-70). For the challenge, I built a public MIT-licensed sandbox with ten browser WebMCP tools, a read-only MCP inspection API, and machine-readable contracts. I designed the human-controlled purchase mandate, agent authority limits, independent policy checks, revocation controls, repeat-safe execution, and durable decision records. I also built the interface, automated tests, security controls, documentation, and legal disclosures. I verified the complete flow in ChatGPT desktop and Chromium, deployed the custom domain, and produced the public demo. title: Rove
pitch: Rove turns open-web shopping into a shared workspace where people and browser agents research, refine, and save real retailer finds together.
about_excerpt: Rove turns open-web shopping into a shared workspace where people and browser agents research, refine, and save real retailer finds together. Like Comment Story Updates Threads of Clothes you saved Clothes and Styles for you by Agent Update Profile Welcome and Profile setup More Clothes List of Saved Prompts and their finds Inspiration Shopping across the open web is fragmented. Products live across dozens of retailer tabs, useful recommendations disappear inside chat transcripts, and the human often cannot refine an agent’s work without starting over. That inspired Rove: a shared fashion research workspace where a person and a browser agent work on the same shopping mission. The agent handles open-web research while the human stays in control of preferences, budgets, product review, selective replacement, and the final cart. What it does Rove turns a natural shopping request—such as “Find three shirts, three pants, sneakers, and a fragrance for four days in Cancún under C$450”—into a structured research mission. The browser agent can: Read the user-approved style profile. Translate the request into quantities, categories, occasions, and budgets. Claim prioritized retailer research targets. Browse live retailer pages. Progressively publish grounded products with direct images and canonical links. Enrich products with availability, pricing, materials, and variants. Report research progress and unresolved needs. Add exact products to the shared cart. At the same time, the human can: Watch products arrive progressively. Filter and compare recommendations. Inspect retailer provenance. Accept the complete edit or replace only selected items. Request completely fresh research without duplicate links. Save completed prompts and accepted products locally. Manage a cross-retailer cart called “Your Thread.” Rove keeps completed missions separate from the current mission, so previous research remains useful without confusing the active task. How we built it Rove is a client-only application built with Nuxt 4, Vue 3, strict TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and the imperative WebMCP API. It registers 17 tools through document.modelContext , covering profile setup, mission planning, retailer scheduling, candidate publication, product enrichment, recommendation review, research history, and cart management. The most important architectural decision was giving the interface and WebMCP tools the same typed domain action layer. Agent actions do not update a separate hidden system: they produce the same visible state changes as human actions. A deterministic research scheduler ranks retailer targets based on: Requested categories and quantities. Remaining unmet needs. Style and occasion relevance. Department compatibility. Per-item and overall budgets. Retailer capabilities. Scarce categories such as fragrance. Published candidates pass through validation for retailer domains, canonical product URLs, mission identity, budgets, duplicate history, and required imagery. Recommendation order combines relevance, budget fit, profile alignment, availability, freshness, and retailer diversity. The application uses browser-local persistence and requires no backend, database, account, API key, embedded chatbot, or OpenAI API call. It is deployed as a static Netlify application and remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making agent research behave like a reliable product workflow instead of an open-ended chat. Retailer information is inconsistent. Some products have sizes and colours, while fragrances and accessories may have neither. We had to introduce category-aware variant handling so a perfume could not accidentally inherit an invalid clothing colour or size. Selective replacement was another difficult problem. When the user rejected one product, the system initially risked replacing or hiding accepted products. We redesigned the review workflow so accepted products remain visible and only explicitly rejected items become new research targets. We also had to solve duplicate prevention across repeated missions. Rove now retains previously surfaced and accepted product links so “research again” can use past preferences as context without relisting the same products. Product imagery created additional complexity because retailer image URLs vary and can fail after publication. We added direct-image validation, visible fallbacks, and consistent image framing so missing or differently sized assets do not break the interface. Finally, we had to balance a sophisticated agent workflow with a simple human experience. Mission state, research queues, replacement context, saved history, and the cart all needed to remain understandable without exposing internal orchestration details. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that Rove feels like a complete fashion product rather than a WebMCP demonstration screen. Key accomplishments include: Seventeen working WebMCP tools with closed schemas and clear annotations. One shared action boundary for human and agent operations. Progressive multi-retailer research with visible state changes. Quantity-aware and budget-aware mission fulfilment. Selective product replacement without disturbing accepted items. Fresh research that avoids previously listed links. Category-aware cart variants for clothing, fragrance, and accessories. Saved missions with locally preserved prompts and accepted edits. A polished, responsive, accessible Rove interface. A deterministic test suite with 68 passing tests, strict type checking, and verified production builds. What we learned We learned that useful agent experiences depend more on state design and tool contracts than on one large prompt. Small, purpose-built tools with explicit schemas gave the browser agent clearer responsibilities and made failures easier to understand. A persisted state machine also made the collaboration resilient: the agent could report what it had completed, what remained unresolved, and what it should do next. We also learned that human control must be visible. Users need to see what the agent changed, preserve decisions they already approved, and request corrections without restarting the entire workflow. Most importantly, WebMCP works best when it is integrated into the product’s real domain model. The tools should not sit beside the application—they should operate the application. What's next for Rove Next, we want to expand Rove with: More retailer adapters and stronger regional availability support. Better price and inventory freshness indicators. Optional, privacy-conscious cross-device synchronization. Visual style references and wardrobe-aware recommendations. Stronger accessibility and mobile interaction testing. User-controlled retailer preferences and sustainability signals. Cleaner retailer checkout handoffs while keeping purchasing on official retailer sites. Evaluations that measure duplicate rate, budget adherence, research completion, and recommendation acceptance. Our long-term vision is for Rove to become the open-web workspace where people and agents build confident shopping decisions together. title: Tracelayer
pitch: Give AI agents useful access, without giving away Human authority.
about_excerpt: Give AI agents useful access, without giving away Human authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration As AI agents become capable of using websites and taking actions on behalf of users, I kept coming back to one question: How do we give an AI agent useful access without also giving it full trust or Human authority? This becomes especially important in high-stakes applications. In cybersecurity, finance, administration, or access management, an Agent may be useful for gathering information and making recommendations, but a wrong action can have real consequences. I did not want to build another cybersecurity copilot that simply reads logs and produces a verdict. Instead, I used a synthetic security incident as a proving ground for a broader idea: a web application should decide what an Agent is allowed to do at every stage, preserve Human context and judgment, and keep consequential authority separate from Agent reasoning. That became TraceLayer . What TraceLayer does TraceLayer is a WebMCP-native reference architecture for Human-Agent collaboration in high-stakes web applications. The demo follows one synthetic cybersecurity case involving suspicious account and connected-application activity. ChatGPT investigates the case using structured tools exposed directly by the TraceLayer webpage through WebMCP. During the investigation, the Agent can read evidence, inspect entities, connect related events, link evidence, and maintain an assessment. But its capabilities are not static. As the case progresses, TraceLayer changes the Agent's WebMCP surface. During investigation, it can gather and record evidence. During response review, investigation writes disappear and the Agent can only read the case and propose a response. Once a consequential proposal is pending approval, the Agent becomes read-only. There is deliberately no WebMCP tool for authorization or execution . The Human also contributes something the Agent cannot determine from the exposed investigation data. In the demo, a login appears to originate from Singapore. The Agent initially treats that location as supporting evidence of compromise. The Human checks an internal company network reference and adds organizational context showing that the address is actually a sanctioned corporate VPN exit. The original event is never rewritten. Instead, the Agent reads the updated shared case and creates a new assessment that supersedes its earlier interpretation. This creates a collaboration loop where: Agent reasoning → Human context → Agent reassessment rather than treating the Agent's first answer as final. Why authentication matters The most important boundary appears when the Agent proposes a consequential action. Simply placing an Approve button on a webpage is not enough. A browser Agent may also be capable of interacting with ordinary webpage controls, so a click by itself is not strong evidence that a Human approved the decision. TraceLayer separates three responsibilities: Agent: investigates and proposes. Human: provides organizational context and authorizes consequential decisions. SYSTEM: performs an approved operation. Signing in with ChatGPT establishes the account identity, but identity alone is still not approval. For consequential actions, TraceLayer uses a fresh WebAuthn user-verification ceremony tied to the exact proposal and current case state. Only after that verification does TraceLayer record the Human authorization. A separate SYSTEM record then performs the simulated security action. In short: The Agent proposes. The Human authorizes. SYSTEM executes. The authorization flow is real. The cybersecurity telemetry and response effects in the demo are synthetic and simulated. How I built it TraceLayer is a browser-first application built around a single shared case state. The Human interface and the WebMCP interface both operate on the same underlying domain functions, so the Agent is not interacting with a separate demo backend or a scripted copy of the case. TraceLayer exposes seven generic WebMCP tools: get_case_state query_events inspect_entity correlate_entities link_evidence record_assessment propose_response_action The page dynamically registers only the tools appropriate for the current stage of the investigation. Application policy remains authoritative even if an Agent has stale knowledge of a previously available capability. The incident contains 40 immutable synthetic events. Some evidence is externally controlled and even contains instruction-like text aimed at automated review. TraceLayer still exposes that content as evidence, but that content does not gain authority over application policy, tool availability, authorization, or execution. The final workflow is: INVESTIGATING → RESPONSE_REVIEW → PENDING_AUTHORIZATION → POST_ACTION_REVIEW → CASE_COMPLETE At completion, TraceLayer produces an inspectable Decision Trail showing what the Agent assessed and proposed, what context and decisions came from the Human, and what actions were performed by SYSTEM. Challenges The hardest part was not getting the Agent to investigate the incident. ChatGPT could solve the synthetic case surprisingly quickly. The harder problem was designing an interaction where the Human genuinely mattered. Early versions risked becoming the familiar pattern of: AI recommends → Human clicks approve That was not enough. The Human needed to contribute knowledge that changed the investigation itself, not just appear at the end as a ceremonial approval button. That led to the organizational-context handoff and assessment-supersession model. Another major challenge was authority. At first, Human and SYSTEM actions were represented only as application-level actor labels. Testing showed that an Agent with normal browser interaction could potentially initiate ordinary UI controls. That forced a much stronger design: authenticated identity, real WebAuthn user verification, exact proposal binding, fresh challenges, replay protection, and separate SYSTEM execution. I also spent significant time trying to break the implementation rather than only proving the happy path. The final project includes tests for stale capabilities, replay attempts, wrong revisions, wrong users, rejected proposals, raw-evidence immutability, deterministic reset, hostile-content behavior, and multi-user authority isolation. The final suite contains 128 automated tests , alongside TypeScript, lint, build, accessibility, responsive, and published-host validation. What I learned The biggest lesson was that Agent capability and Human authority are different things . Giving an Agent access to useful tools does not mean it should inherit the authority of the Human using the application. I also learned that Human-Agent collaboration becomes much more meaningful when both sides contribute something distinct. The Agent is good at searching, correlating, and maintaining structured reasoning across machine-scale information. The Human contributes organization-specific knowledge, judgment, and verified authority over consequences. And the application itself has an important role: it controls which capabilities exist, preserves state, enforces valid transitions, and records how decisions were reached. WebMCP made this especially interesting because the capability boundary lives directly in the application. The webpage is not just displaying information to an Agent. It can expose a structured capability surface that changes as the application state changes. Why this is practical TraceLayer is not intended to replace existing SIEM, EDR, identity, or enterprise systems. Those systems can remain the telemetry and execution layers. TraceLayer demonstrates the Human-Agent control layer that can sit above them: where an Agent investigates, the Human contributes local knowledge and controls important decisions, and the application constrains what the Agent is allowed to do at each step. Cybersecurity is the proving ground, but the same trust pattern could apply anywhere an Agent can recommend an important action without automatically inheriting the user's authority. The goal is simple: give AI agents useful capabilities without automatically giving them trust or Human authority. title: Real Me • DeepMatch
pitch: Transformando desabafos em conexões humanas. O Real Me usa IA e WebMCP para ajudar pessoas a encontrar, com privacidade e consentimento, quem viveu experiências semelhantes.
about_excerpt:
Transformando desabafos em conexões humanas. O Real Me usa IA e WebMCP para ajudar pessoas a encontrar, com privacidade e consentimento, quem viveu experiências semelhantes.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Many people go through loneliness, life changes, relationship problems, professional uncertainty, grief, anxiety, or other difficult experiences without having someone they feel comfortable talking to. Real Me • DeepMatch was created around a simple idea: sometimes the person who can understand you best is someone who has already lived through something similar. 

 Instead of building another social network based on followers, likes, popularity, or public exposure, Real Me focuses on experiences. Users can share what they are going through and the platform can help identify people with similar experiences, always putting privacy, safety, and consent at the center of the interaction. 

 What it does 

 Real Me • DeepMatch is a web platform designed to transform personal experiences into meaningful human connections. 

 A user can share an experience or situation. Artificial intelligence helps interpret its context and the DeepMatch system can identify compatible experiences from other users. 

 The goal is not to replace human relationships with AI. AI acts as a bridge between people. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, we are extending Real Me so AI agents can discover structured tools provided by the platform and help users interact with Real Me through natural conversations. 

 How we built it 

 The existing Real Me application was created as a web application using technologies including React, Vite, Supabase, Netlify and AI-assisted development. 

 I am a non-technical founder building the project with the assistance of AI tools, particularly ChatGPT. AI has helped me transform product ideas into working software, understand technical concepts, debug problems and progressively build the platform. 

 Real Me existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the challenge, the project is being extended with WebMCP capabilities. This distinction is intentional and transparent: the existing platform provides the foundation, while the WebMCP integration is new work being developed specifically during the challenge period. 

 Our goal for the WebMCP implementation is to expose useful Real Me capabilities as structured tools that AI agents can discover and use with appropriate user consent. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges has been building a technology product without a traditional software engineering background. 

 Instead of treating that limitation as a reason not to build, I have been using AI as a development partner: learning each component, testing implementations, identifying errors and improving the product step by step. 

 The WebMCP Challenge introduces another challenge: moving from a traditional website interaction model toward an agent-native experience where AI can understand and use capabilities exposed directly by the application. 

 Privacy and consent are also fundamental challenges because Real Me deals with personal experiences. Agent actions must therefore be designed carefully so users remain in control of what is shared and what actions are performed. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Real Me evolved from an idea into a working web product. 

 The project already has the foundation for users to share experiences and for DeepMatch to explore compatibility between them. 

 Another accomplishment is demonstrating that AI-assisted development can allow a non-technical founder to move beyond prototypes and participate directly in building a real technology product. 

 For this challenge, our next milestone is making Real Me agent-accessible through WebMCP while maintaining the human-centered philosophy of the platform. 

 What we learned 

 Building Real Me has shown us that AI can do more than answer questions. It can help people create technology that previously required technical knowledge they did not have. 

 The WebMCP Challenge is also teaching us to think differently about websites. Instead of designing only for humans clicking interfaces, applications can expose structured capabilities that agents can understand and use. 

 For Real Me, this creates an interesting possibility: an AI conversation does not need to end with an AI response. With the user's permission, it can become the beginning of a meaningful human connection. 

 What's next for Real Me • DeepMatch 

 During the WebMCP Challenge, our immediate goal is to implement and test Real Me's WebMCP tools and demonstrate an end-to-end agent interaction. 

 After the challenge, we want to continue developing DeepMatch, improve privacy and safety mechanisms, expand the matching experience and explore how agent-native interfaces can make meaningful human connections easier to discover. 

 Our long-term vision is simple: 

 AI should not replace human connection. It should help people find it.

title: gpuiXwebmcp
pitch: A native developer debugger for WebMCP—inspect tools, execute calls, and trace browser-agent interactions.
about_excerpt:
A native developer debugger for WebMCP—inspect tools, execute calls, and trace browser-agent interactions.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 I wanted to explore how WebMCP could be used to make websites easier for AI agents to interact with. While working with WebMCP, I felt there was a missing developer tool for seeing what tools a webpage exposes and what happens when those tools are called. 

 So I built gpuiXwebmcp, a native debugger for WebMCP using Rust and GPUI. It connects to a WebMCP-enabled Chrome tab and lets you see the available tools, inspect their schemas, execute them, and view the execution results. 

 The main idea is simple: instead of guessing what an agent is doing inside a browser, developers should be able to see the tools and their execution clearly. 

 I built the project to learn more about WebMCP, GPUI, browser communication, and building native developer tools with Rust. One of the main challenges was connecting the browser environment with a native GPUI application and keeping the tool and execution state synchronized. 

 This project is still an early experiment. The next things I want to explore are agent execution, tool-call replay, better debugging information, and connecting local AI models to the WebMCP tools.
