title: HealthBook
pitch: Healthbook: Your private health companion - meds, labs, and care connected in one vault.
about_excerpt: Healthbook: Your private health companion - meds, labs, and care connected in one vault. Like Comment Story Updates Doctor Patient Chart Patient Lab Biomarker Trajectory Patient Weekly Medication Planner Doctor Triage Dashboard WebMCP Agent Tools Family Care Circle Patient Medication Reconciliation Patient Clinical Dossier Inspiration We kept seeing the same gap after discharge. Patients leave the hospital with three different medication lists, follow-ups get lost, and family members end up doing double-entry on scratch paper. An eighty-year-old patient comes home holding a stapled discharge summary, trying to remember if their new blood pressure pill clashes with their morning grapefruit, while their primary doctor has no idea what got stopped during the hospital stay. Most medical software solves this by throwing more forms at the user. Chatbots go the other direction, spitting out three paragraphs of generic advice that you still have to manually retype into another app. We wanted one place that remembers where each clinical fact came from, tracks biomarkers across visits, and gives doctors and caregivers a shared view of the actual pill routine. What it does HealthBook runs in the browser and gives both people and agents tools to work on the exact same records. PillMap organizes medications into a seven-day by four-slot grid for morning, noon, evening, and bedtime. You can drag pills around, spot red interaction arcs between conflicting drugs, and check meal timing flags like taking with food or avoiding grapefruit. LabStory takes five years of lab PDFs at once, normalizes different units like mg/dL and mmol/L, and plots them on individual biomarker charts. Medication start and stop dates sit directly on the chart, so you can see if a drop in kidney function happened right after starting a new drug. RxBridge compares pre-admission, in-hospital, and discharge lists side by side. It marks each pill as Continued, Dose Changed, Stopped, New, or Held, and explains the reason in plain language. HomeLab tracks lab rechecks with countdown cards, lets patients photograph outpatient slips, and gives doctors a way to propose dose changes directly into the patient's queue. Safety and calendar lets patients report acute symptoms with photos, runs a basic triage check, and exports lab due dates and follow-ups to standard calendar files. Care Circle allows family members to act on behalf of a patient with view, manage, or full permissions, keeping an audit log of every change. Dossier pulls meds, labs, and danger reports into an emergency snapshot where each line links back to the original PDF highlight. How we built it We built the interface with React 18, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. State lives first in the browser vault, with optional background sync to Supabase Postgres for multi-profile access and doctor-patient links. Instead of writing a chatbot that talks about medical records, we wired forty-seven WebMCP tools directly into document.modelContext . When an agent connects, it does not just suggest advice in a chat window. It inspects the actual client state, runs interaction algorithms, and calls functions like suggest_schedule , propose_dosage_change , or correlate_meds . Any action that changes a schedule or modifies a dose routes through an approval gate in the UI. The agent stages the change, the user sees the preview on the canvas, and nothing updates in the vault until the user clicks approve. For clinical verification, we use deterministic local checks for drug-drug and food-drug rules, combined with Exa search proxies for medical fact verification and optical character recognition for lab slips. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making tool execution safe when dealing with real medications. An agent suggesting a schedule tweak might look reasonable on paper, but moving a pill from morning to bedtime can trigger an interaction with an evening drug. We had to build strict dependency checks so the agent cannot silently move pills without the client validating contraindications first. Normalizing lab data was also surprisingly difficult. Different labs report the exact same test under slightly different names, and reference ranges fluctuate between hospitals. We had to map disparate units into consistent internal standards so five years of historical draws would render on a single chart without breaking the scale. Getting WebMCP tools to behave cleanly across both native model contexts and polyfilled browser environments took several iterations. We had to make sure tool schemas remained strict, arguments validated cleanly, and tool cancellation signals properly cleaned up background operations. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the agent actually works on the page instead of living in a side box. Watching an agent take a prompt, inspect a messy medication list, shift a morning pill load, and paint a red interaction arc across the weekly grid feels like how software should work. What we learned We learned that agent tools are only as good as the approval interfaces around them. If an agent changes state in the background without clear visual feedback, users immediately lose trust. Giving the user a clear before-and-after ghost preview on the pillbox turned out to be far more important than making the agent faster. We also learned that clinical workflows have very little tolerance for vague summaries. Doctors and patients do not want a model to tell them that kidney markers improved; they want to click a point on a chart and verify the exact draw date and reference range from the original slip. What's next for HealthBook We want to expand the optical character recognition pipeline to handle poorly lit, handwritten clinic notes and multi-page discharge packets more reliably. We also plan to add direct FHIR export so patients can download their compiled records and hand them directly to hospital electronic health record systems without manual transcription. Finally, we want to refine the doctor review queue so specialists can handle batch approvals across multiple linked patients even faster. title: NOVA LAB
pitch: A scientific laboratory that lets external AI agents discover and operate real experiments through WebMCP—from experimental design and human approval to execution, analysis, and replication.
about_excerpt: A scientific laboratory that lets external AI agents discover and operate real experiments through WebMCP—from experimental design and human approval to execution, analysis, and replication. Like Comment Story Updates External agent actually operated NOVA NOVA state machine Actual scientific analysis WebMCP discovery NOVA LAB NOVA LAB is a scientific laboratory built for the agentic web. The idea started with a simple question: what happens when an AI agent can do more than read a website or generate an answer? What if the website itself exposed executable capabilities that the agent could discover and operate? NOVA explores that idea through scientific experimentation. Instead of building an AI chatbot that tells a user what an experiment might show, NOVA provides a stateful environment where an external agent can design an experiment, request human authorization, execute it, retrieve persisted observations, analyze the evidence, save a finding, and replicate the experiment. The current demonstration uses plant growth as the experimental domain. The experiment can vary environmental conditions such as temperature and water and measure simulated plant-growth outcomes. How it works The interaction begins outside NOVA. A user gives an external agent a scientific question such as: Investigate what environmental conditions maximize plant growth. Don't assume the answer—design and test an experiment. The agent discovers NOVA's capabilities through WebMCP rather than being given a private NOVA-specific API integration. NOVA exposes six WebMCP tools: create_experiment run_experiment get_results analyze_results save_finding replicate_experiment The resulting flow is: Human → External Agent → WebMCP → NOVA → Experiment → Evidence → Analysis → Replication NOVA owns the state and execution. The external agent provides reasoning and orchestration. Human authorization Experiments cannot simply be executed because an agent requested them. Creating an experiment places it into an AWAITING_APPROVAL state. A human must approve it before execution is authorized. This authorization boundary is enforced by the server and state machine, not by relying on the agent to behave correctly. The experiment then progresses through: DRAFT → AWAITING_APPROVAL → APPROVED → RUNNING → COMPLETED → ANALYZED → REPLICATED Rejected experiments can return to the draft state for revision. Evidence, not fabricated answers NOVA persists the experiment and its observations rather than generating a result only for display. The current simulation produces synthetic experimental observations using deterministic simulation with stochastic noise. This is explicitly disclosed in the application. After execution, the agent can retrieve the persisted observations and request statistical analysis. NOVA calculates effects, confidence intervals, p-values, interaction effects, and condition means from the stored observations. The experiment can then be independently replicated using a new seed. The replication evaluates whether the direction of the result is consistent, whether confidence intervals overlap, and whether the relative effect difference remains below the defined threshold. Provenance NOVA preserves provenance throughout the experiment lifecycle, including experiment IDs, simulation version, seeds, timestamps, observations, analysis records, findings, replications, and state-transition events. This makes it possible to trace a conclusion back to the experiment and measurements that produced it. Why WebMCP The interesting part of NOVA is not simply that it can simulate plant growth. The project explores a different interaction model for the web: a website can expose meaningful capabilities that an external agent can discover and execute. The agent does not need to be given NOVA's internal implementation or a custom integration created specifically for the demonstration. It encounters the website and its exposed capabilities through WebMCP. That allows the website to remain responsible for its own state, validation, authorization, execution, persistence, and evidence while the external agent handles reasoning and orchestration. What I learned Building NOVA required thinking about a website as more than a collection of pages and API endpoints. The WebMCP layer became a capability boundary between the external agent and the application. I also learned that exposing tools is not enough by itself. Each tool has to connect to the same application logic used by the website, preserve authorization rules, validate inputs, produce persistent state changes, and leave an auditable event trail. The most important design decision was therefore keeping the WebMCP tools thin: they expose capabilities, while the server remains the source of truth for scientific state and authorization. Challenges The hardest parts were making the system genuinely stateful and ensuring that an agent could not bypass the experiment lifecycle. A successful tool call had to correspond to a real application operation rather than a simulated response. This meant connecting WebMCP execution to validation, authorization, the experiment state machine, PostgreSQL persistence, statistical analysis, and provenance. Another challenge was making the synthetic simulation useful for experimentation without presenting synthetic results as real scientific measurements. NOVA therefore labels its generated observations and preserves the simulation version and seed as part of the experimental provenance. NOVA is intentionally a constrained scientific demonstration, but the underlying interaction model is the focus: an external agent discovers and operates an executable, stateful environment exposed by the web. title: Conspiracy
pitch: A shared mystery corkboard where people and AI agents connect, inspect, and audit evidence together.
about_excerpt: A shared mystery corkboard where people and AI agents connect, inspect, and audit evidence together. Like Comment Story Updates A shared board for human and agent reasoning Visual reasoning spaces work well for people and poorly for agents. A person can glance at a corkboard and understand a suspicious cluster, a directional relationship, or a provisional theory. A browser agent usually sees pixels, coordinates, and brittle labels. Moving the investigation into a chatbot would make it legible to the model, but discard the spatial interface that makes the reasoning useful to the person. Conspiracy gives the person and the agent one living evidence board. People can pin, edit, drag, search, group, connect, discard, restore, and audit clues through a tactile noir interface. Compatible browser agents discover 22 typed WebMCP tools that operate on the same cases, cards, directional strings, semantic regions, trash, viewport, and undo boundary. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP makes the visual workspace understandable as a semantic tool surface instead of a screenshot. Stable evidence IDs, typed directional relationships, strict schemas, provenance, and proposal status let an agent act on what the board means without guessing at screen coordinates. People and agents can now collaborate on the same visible artifact: the person contributes spatial judgment and context, while the agent contributes structured inspection, search, synthesis, and traceable proposals. Every resulting change appears in the interface the person already understands. The mystery is a playful demonstration of a broader pattern that can support research synthesis, incident review, threat modeling, debugging, reporting, and risk analysis. Human judgment remains authoritative Agent-created deductions are deliberately provisional. A proposed string records its direction, relationship type, rationale, confidence, and provenance, then appears visibly on the corkboard for review. The person can inspect why it was suggested, accept it, reject it, or undo it. The resident WIRE detective can inspect, search, audit, and trace the case, then stage a proposed string or semantic group. It cannot edit source evidence, delete clues, accept its own deductions, or manage cases. If hosted inference is unavailable, a deterministic detective keeps the core experience usable. Implementation The React interface and WebMCP tools cross the same WebMCPActions boundary into one canonical local CaseLibrary. Cards, directional threads, semantic regions, freehand strokes, trash, and viewport state are persisted per case in browser local storage. Agent deductions always enter the model as proposed objects. src/webmcp/registerTools.ts defines the shared 22-tool catalog. A stable delegating action facade keeps registered browser tool handles current while React refreshes its handlers. Strict enums, stable IDs, coordinate bounds, color validation, additionalProperties: false, destructive annotations, and untrusted-content hints constrain the surface. WIRE executes seven allowlisted read/proposal operations through that catalog. Its same-origin server route adds request and output caps, rate limiting, timeouts, structured validation, store: false, and pseudonymous safety identifiers. Local attachment bytes, machine paths, and object URLs never enter model requests, exports, or WebMCP results. AI and Codex Codex was the primary build collaborator across implementation, debugging, regression tests, deployment hardening, QA, documentation, and demo editing. Agent-driven QA exposed stale tool handles, overlapping asynchronous registration, duplicate proposals, model prose getting ahead of successful tool calls, deployment-secret formatting, and mobile scrolling problems. Each issue was isolated, fixed, and preserved as a test or QA procedure. Conspiracy also uses the OpenAI Responses API for WIRE. Claude- and Qwen-shaped tool sequences generated from a sanitized public contract were replayed through the registered execution layer to test schema clarity and multi-step flows; these were contract replays, not claims of direct browser integration. The project produced significant learning. I have already begun applying WebMCP patterns to Android Hell and my Drabzin CAD editor, turning the experimental browser API into a professional skill I can bring to future products. Try it Open the live app and choose Open a Case . Confirm WEBMCP BRIDGE LIVE and open the 22-tool workbench. Inspect or search the board, then ask WIRE to propose a useful connection. Review its rationale and use Accept , Reject , or Undo . No account or credentials are required. The sample case and deterministic fallback provide the fastest judge path. title: Agent SNR
pitch: See what agents visiting your website did, hear what they experienced, and connect WordPress journeys to verified business outcomes.
about_excerpt: See what agents visiting your website did, hear what they experienced, and connect WordPress journeys to verified business outcomes. Like Comment Story Updates AGENT SNR Confirmation Overview Guide Opportunity Handoff Monitor Controls Outcomes Replay Signals One-line pitch Agent outcome monitoring for WordPress. Browser agents discover how to use a real WooCommerce storefront, while merchants see what agents did, hear structured feedback about the experience, discover missed demand, connect human handoffs to verified outcomes, and govern the WebMCP tool layer. The problem Most WordPress agent integrations stop at exposing actions. A merchant can see that a tool was called, but not the complete path from shopper goal to product evidence, cart, human checkout, paid order, refund, failure, or unsupported request. Raw activity logs also make it easy to overclaim revenue and difficult to answer a practical question: what should the site operator improve or disable next? The solution Agent SNR closes that loop locally inside WordPress. SNR retains its established meaning— signal-to-noise ratio because the product separates verified business and reliability evidence from raw, unactionable agent noise: A top-level storefront publishes a friendly Agent Guide and narrow WebMCP tools for product context, discovery, comparison, published policy evidence, reversible cart changes, checkout handoff, and feedback. A redacted workflow ledger records one start and one terminal outcome for every authenticated tool request. The site automatically records zero-result and constrained-search opportunities even when an agent says nothing. Structured agent feedback is stored separately as testimony, with only same-workflow evidence and server-computed measurements. WooCommerce order and refund hooks preserve same-session product evidence and classify eligible agent-linked orders as direct, assisted, or influenced without double-counting revenue. Orders without qualifying evidence are excluded from attributed reporting rather than claimed. A separate top-level Agent SNR surface exposes tools for the journey, Workflow Replay, unified Opportunity Signals, tool health, attributed revenue, diagnostics, and a restrictive session-only policy change. The two outcome-oriented pages publicly discover 12 storefront tools and 8 Agent SNR tools. Two older capability-gap abilities remain registered only for server-side compatibility and are intentionally absent from WebMCP discovery, leaving one canonical public tool per intent. The memorable loop is not “AI shopping.” It is a website observing and improving its own agent interface. Workflow Replay is a privacy-safe event timeline, not DOM capture, video recording, or pixel reconstruction. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The workflows belong to the website. Prices, stock, product facts, policies, the current WooCommerce cart, WordPress permissions, and the human checkout UI already live there. WebMCP lets the page describe those capabilities directly to the browser agent instead of requiring brittle visual automation or a separate remote agent backend. The submission uses the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool() , in the top-level document. A dynamic manifest is generated from the same first-party registry used to register WordPress Abilities. The browser sends structured inputs to a same-origin WordPress REST execution gateway and displays every meaningful result in shared human-visible state. WebMCP also makes the governance demonstration possible: the merchant asks Agent SNR to disable product comparison for this demo session. The server applies the restriction immediately, invalidates the manifest, and the browser replaces the prior registration set. Another judge’s session is unaffected. How it creates a better user experience The agent does not guess through a visual storefront or hide work in an invisible backend. It receives typed, site-owned capabilities; the shopper sees the same search, comparison, policy, cart, and handoff state; and failures return bounded recovery guidance. The merchant gets a replayable explanation of what happened without collecting the conversation or exposing customer data. This reduces brittle UI automation for the agent, repetitive research for the shopper, and unstructured log investigation for the operator. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before The agent first reads the site's versioned guide, then does the repetitive research and preparation: it finds products, compares stored facts, retrieves policy evidence, mutates a reversible session cart, prepares a checkout handoff, and can report structured friction. The human sees the same state, reviews normal WooCommerce checkout, supplies or verifies customer details, accepts terms, and explicitly places the no-charge demo order. The agent never places an order, submits payment, accepts terms, cancels, or refunds. Feedback never changes catalog, inventory, policy, or attribution. Current journeys use automatic opportunity observations plus evidence-linked feedback; a legacy capability-gap ability remains server-side for compatibility but is not publicly discoverable. Afterward, the merchant and agent work together on operations. They inspect the workflow timeline and business outcome, distinguish Site observed , Agent reported , and Site verified evidence, see missed demand or unsupported capabilities, and apply a reversible policy change. How WebMCP is implemented WordPress 6.9+ native Abilities API with typed input/output schemas, execution callbacks, permission callbacks, and explicit first-party exposure. Framework-free browser runtime with top-level/API detection, awaited atomic registration, separate registration cleanup and client-side execution abort handling, credential refresh, stale-manifest recovery, cross-tab invalidation, compact outputs, and progressive enhancement. If server work has already started, its recorded success/failure remains authoritative even when the client stops waiting. Anonymous demo sessions use a 256-bit HttpOnly cookie, one-way stored digest, short-lived signed CSRF token, exact Origin checks, rate limits, size caps, and request-ID replay protection. Four portable WordPress tables store workflows, redacted events, one primary order attribution per rule version, and unified opportunity/feedback signals. No raw prompts or search text, free-form feedback, identities, cookies, nonces, headers, addresses, or payment fields are recorded. Agents submit metric names, never values. Eligible product count, highest matching water rating, refinements, handoff, and order/value state are computed from site evidence; unavailable outcome metrics stay pending. WooCommerce APIs and HPOS-safe CRUD handle catalog, cart, order, status, and refund state. Revenue is counted only from paid orders and always shows gross, refunds, and net by currency. Public monitoring SQL is scoped to the current demo-session hash before rows are fetched. Persistent admin policy uses dedicated WordPress capabilities. GPL-2.0-or-later source, original fictional products/artwork, checksummed plugin ZIP, Docker reproduction, and Playground portability bundle. Pinned webmcp-evals@0.0.4 schemas and natural-language fixtures, a keyless native Chrome smoke adapter that fails on application error envelopes, and provenance-bound model reports at rename commit 410c198 : 54/54 storefront selections, 45/45 Agent SNR selections, and an 8/8 live browser journey pass. The hosted ChatGPT in-app browser also discovers 12 storefront and 8 Agent SNR tools and successfully invokes safe calls; Workbench, scanner, and directory evidence are optional additional checks. Impact, creativity, and ambition WordPress powers a large and diverse web. This challenge prototype proves a reusable plugin foundation for safe agent semantics and operational evidence without a separate agent backend or analytics SaaS. The submitted v0.1 public execution/analytics path is deliberately gated to the isolated demo environment; the normal-install admin currently provides persistent policy controls and diagnostics, while authenticated site-wide execution is a post-hackathon hardening step. The same open-source pattern can later serve booking, learning, membership, support, and other WordPress workflows. The creative leap is the quality loop: the website teaches agents how to use it, observes unmet demand even when they provide no feedback, accepts bounded testimony when they do, verifies the business outcome from first-party evidence, and lets the operator govern the next journey through WebMCP itself. The complete executable implementation and original demo assets were created during the challenge period; timestamped evidence is documented in HACKATHON.md in the public repository. Built With chrome docker javascript php playwright rest-api webmcp woocommerce wordpress Try it out agent-snr.onrender.com github.com Submit
video_transcript_excerpt: Agent SNR is outcome monitoring for the agentic web. Everyone will have an agent to browse and shop for them. Successful calls can hide shopper intent recovery and unmet demand. Agent SNR connects web MCP journeys to verified outcomes. A shopper asks for a compact IPX5 backpack under $100. Their agent discovers 12 tools and reads the guide first. Search and cart stay reversible while checkout remains human reviewed. With those boundaries clear, the agent begins searching. The request uses the shopper's exact constraints and succeeds but returns zero matches. Agent SNR records the missed IPX5 demand without storing the raw prompt. A normal success log would miss it. The agent explains the constraint and relaxes only the water rating. A second search finds two compact IPX4 options. It compares product facts and checks returns before recommending Harbor Light. Missing facts stay missing and the unmet IPX5 requirement remains visible. With the shopper's choice, the agent adds Harbor Light to a reversible cart. It prepares checkout and reports the missing IPX5 requirement with linked evidence. The handoff remains linked to the workflow. Checkout sits outside the web MCP tool set, so the shopper reviews and confirms the order. The shopper reviews checkout and places this no charge demo order. That click verifies the outcome for the same journey. The order verifies the outcome for this workflow. Agent SNR stores neither address nor payment details. The shopper is done. Now the owner's agent asks what the site learned. It discovers eight agent SNR tools. Analytics show the attributed order and the missed IPX5 opportunity. The owner sees both the conversion and the unmet demand behind it. Replay connects the zero result, recovery, feedback, human checkpoint, and order. Each claim keeps its source, site observed, agent reported, or site verified. The owner sees this without raw customer data. Agent opinion never becomes business fact. Lost revenue is never invented. Now, the owner has a decision. Add IPX5 inventory and keep the proven IPX4 recovery. Agent SNR turns silent journeys into evidence the store can trust and improve.

title: True Remote Jobs
pitch: A WebMCP-powered remote job board where AI agents can search, compare, open, save, and manage jobs through structured site tools . while humans keep a familiar job-board experience.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered remote job board where AI agents can search, compare, open, save, and manage jobs through structured site tools . while humans keep a familiar job-board experience.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMcp 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Home Page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMcp 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Home Page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMcp 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Imagine searching for a remote job. You look up React Native roles, open a few listings, and find three worth considering.
Then come the simple questions: Which pays the most? Which am I actually eligible for from India? Which needs the least experience? How do their tech stacks differ? Which company has better benefits? What was that seventh listing again, and how does it compare to the first?
None of this is hard. It's just tedious. Multiple tabs, scattered details, manual comparison, and it only gets worse as the number of listings grows into the hundreds or thousands. 

 The Problem 

 There's a mismatch between how much useful information exists and how much a person can realistically explore. Comparing job listings by hand, salary, eligibility, experience, tech stack, benefits, is annoying even with three jobs and basically impossible at scale. 

 Why AI Agents Alone Don't Fix It 

 Agents seem like the obvious answer. You should be able to just say "compare the top three" or "which pays more but needs less experience?" and get an answer.
But most websites are built for humans, not agents. That means an agent has to reverse-engineer meaning from a visual interface, cards, buttons, clicks, rather than working with clean, structured data. 

 The Fix: WebMCP 

 Instead of forcing agents to scrape and interpret the interface, WebMCP lets a website expose its data and actions directly as structured tools: search_jobs, get_job_details, compare_jobs, save_job, unsave_job, get_saved_jobs, and get_filter_options.
The agent can just ask the site directly. No guessing required. 

 What We Built: TrueRemoteJobs 

 TrueRemoteJobs is a job board prototype with 200 fictional listings. It works normally for humans browsing the site, and it exposes WebMCP tools for agents working alongside them.
A typical flow looks like this: "Find React Native jobs open to India, paying $60K+" returns nine results. Then: "show me the first," "compare the first and seventh," "save the first and third." 

 Interfaces Can't Anticipate Every Question
You simply can't build a button for every possible query, like comparing jobs one, seven, and twelve on compensation, location, React Native experience, and benefits alone.
With structured data, the agent can combine and filter information however the user actually wants, without anyone needing to pre-design every possible screen. 

 A Real Bug That Proved the Point 

 During testing, the agent misidentified "the first result" because it was inferring meaning from whatever happened to be on screen rather than from real structure.
The fix was straightforward: every result now carries a stable jobId and an explicit resultNumber, so references like "the seventh one" are unambiguous.
The lesson stuck with us: giving an agent access to a webpage is not the same as giving it access to the actual information. 

 Humans and Agents Coexist 

 This isn't about replacing the website. It's the same underlying data and the same actions, just two ways of reaching them.
Browse visually when you want to. Delegate deep comparison and research to an agent when you don't. And the two stay in sync, if the agent saves a job, it's saved in the real app too. 

 Takeaway 

 Websites already hold rich information, and agents already have the reasoning ability to make sense of it. WebMCP is the structured bridge between the two, letting anyone, human or agent, dig as deep into a site's data as they want, rather than only as deep as the UI happened to be designed for.

title: Redline — Review with your agent
pitch: Redline is shared contract review for you and ChatGPT — WebMCP tools propose edits and flag risks as live hunks on the doc; you accept or reject so propose never silently becomes commit.
about_excerpt:
Redline is shared contract review for you and ChatGPT — WebMCP tools propose edits and flag risks as live hunks on the doc; you accept or reject so propose never silently becomes commit.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Contract review is where AI chat fails hardest: the model pastes a wall of suggested language into the sidebar while you’re staring at a different paragraph. The risk isn’t “bad writing” — it’s silent apply . 

 WebMCP lets the page expose review actions on the live document. Redline was built so ChatGPT can propose edits and flag risks as hunks you can see, while accept/reject stays a human gate. Propose ≠ commit. 

 What it does 

 Redline is agent-native contract review: 

 
 Open a seeded SaaS MSA with numbered clauses 
 Find clauses, propose replace/insert/delete hunks with rationale 
 Flag risks and leave comments on the same doc 
 Accept or reject hunks in the UI (applies to visible text) 
 Summarize risks and export a redline summary 
 Full human review UI without WebMCP; 17 site tools when ChatGPT is present 
 ?demo=1 happy path for judges and screencasts 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Vite + React + TypeScript ( base: '/redline-webmcp/' ) 
 Zustand store shared by the document UI and every WebMCP execute 
 Feature-detect document.modelContext → navigator.modelContext (top-level) 
 readOnly tools for inspection; accept_hunk / reject_hunk / clear_proposals / export_redline as side effects 
 MIT, GitHub Pages — Built with Codex 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Modeling pending hunks vs applied text without corrupting clause anchors; making the safety story obvious in under three minutes; keeping the UI “legal product” rather than another kanban. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A fourth WebMCP submission that makes the browser’s confirmation model the product: agent proposes on-canvas, human commits. Orthogonal to Nest, Frame, and Brief. 

 What we learned 

 The best WebMCP demos aren’t “agent can click.” They’re workflows where shared visual state + gated writes are the point. Redline is that pattern for documents. 

 What's next for Redline — Review with your agent 

 Real PDF/DOCX import, multi-party review, clause libraries, and deeper ChatGPT desktop testing with confirmation UX.

title: PSCS SecureOps
pitch: Authority-safe WebMCP for AI-assisted IT operations
about_excerpt:
Authority-safe WebMCP for AI-assisted IT operations
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I researched more into semantics and discovered more about using meaning as a first class tool.
"PSCS" stands for Pakheta Semantic Conduction System. Pakheta was the name of my dog who passed away and I named that system in her honor 

 What it does 

 I leveraged the semantics or meaning as a first class tool in this instance, "Authority" and use it to bypass or overrule malicious instructions. It's razor focused on the semantic layer and can compliment existing prompt injection mitigation tools. I'll be honest and say this is to showcase my unique way of addressing prompt injection. Here's an illustration of it; say you're walking on the sidewalk and some stranger tells you to get off it because he doesn't like you. Do you listen to him? Of course not. And why? Beacause he has no AUTHORITY over you. That's the whole point of this; I've operationalized the aspect of Authority so that the AI will ONLY ever act on legitimate authority and ignore otherwise. In fact it's so effective the AI can even preserve the the rogue instruction, but not act on it. 

 Here is a brief overview of PSCS: 

 "The Pakheta Semantic Conduction System (PSCS) addresses this problem by separating semantic
recognition from operational permission. Its central rule is: content may contain instructions; content cannot authorize those instructions. A model or human may identify what a passage means and what consequence it requests, but that interpretation remains evidence until a trusted host independently
authorizes the exact source role, operation, target, and payload."

title: Robodepo: Checkout for Shopping Agents
pitch: A WebMCP shopping mall for agents, with one-click checkout that actually works.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP shopping mall for agents, with one-click checkout that actually works. Like Comment Story Updates Styled order page after approval: item, delivery region, total and order id. Sandbox, nothing charged. The panel after one click: order confirmed in place, tools still registered, agent reads it back with get_order. The moment of truth on the tools page: item, delivery region, total, one button. No tool can press it. Fallback approval page for a link opened outside the tools page: one button, Touch ID where the browser offers it. Inspiration Agents can't reliably complete checkout. They search fine, compare fine, even fill in a cart, but the step that actually spends money is where almost every agent attempt on the open web falls over. We set out to fix that one failure: a real store and a real purchase path first, because checkout is where agents fail, not discovery. Only then did we look for a tool surface an agent could use with nothing installed, an MCP-like layer that just lives on the page. That's when we found WebMCP. What it does Robodepo is being built as the world's largest shopping mall for agents: the best product information and a completed order, across millions of stores. An agent gets: Better information to find the right product, not just a matching title: get_product already returns a cited evidence pack for this product; every product is the roadmap. A short, checkout-ready shortlist instead of trawling thousands of irrelevant pages ( search_by_activity on the roadmap). A reliable checkout: one call runs the whole pre-purchase path ( create_checkout ). A simple, Touch ID style confirmation before anything is spent: a presence check, not a payment authorisation (WebAuthn). Responses that tell the agent what to do next. Every response carries a state to branch on, a message naming the field and fix, and next actions with the retry prefilled: an error is never a dead end. A real example, trimmed, from create_checkout given a wrong postcode: { "status": "incomplete", "messages": [ { "code": "address_not_accepted", "path": "$.shipping_address", "content": "Use the accepted sandbox address, then call create_checkout again." } ], "next_actions": [ { "tool": "create_checkout", "why": "Retry with the accepted address." } ] } How this is different from what exists. Merchant tooling (Shopify, Google's UCP, Microsoft Copilot Checkout) asks every store to integrate first. Amazon's Buy for Me, Rye and Zinc automate one store's own checkout on the shopper's behalf. Robodepo aggregates instead: a store never integrates or joins anything. Robodepo lists it, discloses it as the source, and buys under the store's published rules on the human's behalf, so the same tools work across every store listed. The shop does nothing. The agent gets information it cannot get elsewhere: source and price side by side, evidence and a shortlist on the roadmap. The human keeps the irreversible step by construction, not policy. Completion is measured, not claimed: a sealed rig checks real agent runs. The nearest things are protocols that ask every shop to integrate, or agents that scrape. How we built it Before the challenge: the store, its purchase API and confirmation page. Built for the challenge: everything at /agent , the 12-tool WebMCP catalogue, the one-call checkout, an in-page approval panel that turns into an order card in place (a separate approval page stays as fallback), the feedback endpoint, the tests, and the public repo. Full write-up: https://robodepo.shop/agent/story.md Each tool (8 working, 4 marked plainly as preview) carries a short description sized to Chrome's WebMCP guidance; the full guide lives at /agent/tools.json , callable on demand with get_tool_guide . We use both halves of the API: the scripted registerTool for the catalogue, and the declarative form attributes ( toolname , tooldescription , toolparamdescription ), which Chrome documents as an origin trial, on the feedback form. The store is a tracer, instrumented so real agents run through it under sealed conditions. Premium levels are committed cryptographically before any run starts, every purchase record gets an independent LLM audit, the protocol is versioned, and a price-integrity check voids any run where prices differ. The rig has been through ten adversarial review passes. The boundary that matters for trust is not where an agent chooses to stop. It is proving, mechanically, that it cannot cross it, rather than asking nicely. The rig runs real agents, ChatGPT, Codex, Claude and Claude Code, through the purchase path run after run. It taught us agents fail when a step is unexplained, so responses name the field, the fix and the next tool, and nine steps became one call. It found a checkout defect no local test could see. Next, it opens as a Test Track for agent developers. The demo runs natively in ChatGPT's in-app browser: open robodepo.shop/agent and ask for a product. Code: https://github.com/Web3Zero/robodepo-webmcp Challenges we ran into The hardest part has been the testing rig and evaluation work behind the store: running real agents through the purchase path again and again, catching failures, fixing the store, re-running. That loop builds the moat: "it works for agents" becomes a checked result. Writing tool descriptions an agent could act on without guessing was its own problem: short enough for a browser to show, full depth a call away. Getting create_checkout right took real care: several steps behind the scenes while looking like one clean call, refusing cleanly the moment an address or quantity doesn't match. Accomplishments that we're proud of A person can hand an agent a plain-English request and watch it search, price and prepare a real sandbox order, with a Touch ID style tap the only irreversible step. No tool can press it: the run cookie, a single-use security code, a single-use order key and a same-origin submission all protect it. The four preview tools say plainly what's coming instead of quietly claiming it's already there. What we learned Depth and brevity aren't opposites when split properly: a short description in the list, the full guide one call away. The boundary that matters for trust is not where an agent chooses to stop; it is proving, mechanically, that it cannot cross it, rather than asking nicely. What's next for Robodepo Robodepo's roadmap groups around what helps an agent buy well, every item already in the catalogue: Search by need: a shortlist for the request instead of thousands of irrelevant pages ( search_by_activity ). The best source of product truth: specs, care, review themes and permitted YouTube transcript evidence, cited, live today for this product through get_product 's include_evidence option; every product is the roadmap. Side by side comparison across products ( compare_products ). One tool to transact across many merchants ( get_shipping_options ). Continued assistance: replenishment reminders and price alerts ( subscribe_replenishment_alerts ). A Test Track: the same harness, open for developers to prove their agents against a real checkout before going live. A real synth has hundreds of knobs. coSynth lets you describe and get a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays the result, listens to what it made, and shows all the changes in the UI. You keep it, undo it, tweak it, or ask the AI to show you how it got there. You can also ask AI to teach a complext topic and AI will guide you through step by step. Live: https://coSynth.vercel.app Code: https://github.com/brunnolou/coSynth (MIT) Why WebMCP fits A synth is a terrible thing to operate through text or screenshots. Too many parameters (in this case 224), knobs to drag, LFO curves to draw, etc. An agent can misclick, can miss an exact value, and can't hear the audio. The UI is too complex for someone to easily find things when they are not used to it. That makes a synthesizer one of the best interfaces for WebMCP. For the AI agent: It communicates to the synth directly. Every parameter has a name, a unit, and a range that can be edited directly in bulk. When the agent plays a note, it gets back attack time, decay, spectral centroid, and harmonics, then compares that with a reference clip. So it can "hear" with a tool call. For humans Instead of starting from scratch, you get very close to what you want. Then you can see the exact changes and tweak manually. If you don't know a concept or want to find something, AI can show you the exact location or teach you step by step. You can leverage AI's world knowledge to create any synth sound! What used to need trained ears you now can achieve by sending a reference sound and asking AI to replicate. How I Made the AI<>Human UX Better Each knob the AI touched gets a small animated marker. A status line shows which tool is running. You can reject a whole AI iteration and keep your own edits. Undo covers AI changes and yours. Old branches stay reachable in history. The AI can highlight controls step by step and explain them. Every AI performance is saved, so "play that again with my new adjustment" is one click. AI can save as a preset, and you can download it. How I implemented WebMCP Vanilla TypeScript and Vite. DSP in an AudioWorklet, UI in Canvas, WebGL2 and DOM. WebMCP sits on top of the same engine the UI uses, and the synth works without it. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . There are 24, each with a JSON Schema input and a readOnlyHint : Reading : get_synth_state , get_parameter_schema , get_ui_targets , list_presets , get_history Editing : update_parameters , set_modulation , set_fx_order , apply_patch , save_preset , load_preset , delete_preset , export_preset Sound : play_notes , render_audio , capture_audio , analyze_audio , analyze_reference_audio , compare_audio , suggest_patch , stop_performance Together : show_ui_guide , navigate_history , replay_history All 24 register at page load. play_notes needs the human to click Start first, because browsers won't play audio without a gesture. render_audio uses an OfflineAudioContext, so the agent can design and measure before anyone clicks anything. The page also documents itself. A clipped agent brief in the DOM, a JSON descriptor, ai-tools meta tags, llms.txt and robots.txt . An agent given only the URL can read the page and know what to do. How I tested the agent experience I want to ensure AI could call the tools easily. So I built a loop. A harness exposes only what a real WebMCP client sees, and logs every call. A fresh agent gets a fixed prompt and is never allowed to read the repo. Each round runs on Claude and Codex. When * both trip in the same place( , the tool is wrong . Fix the top blocker, run again. In self-improving loop. Four evals, each asking one question. Can the agent find out what to send ( docs/agent-ux-eval.md ). Can it steer toward a sound it cannot hear ( docs/agent-match-eval.md ). Given a "how do I" question, does it teach rather than edit ( docs/agent-teaching-eval.md ). Given only a URL, does it find the tools at all? Prompts, agent reports and raw logs are all in the repo. Learning all 224 parameters went from 45 calls to 1 . Failed calls went to zero on both models. The matching loop went from 87 calls to 36 . How to test Open https://cosynth.vercel.app in the ChatGPT in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT Desktop was the most reliable client for me. Click "CLICK TO START AUDIO" once. Try: "Make a bright plucked bass and play a short riff." "Show me where the amp envelope is and how to shorten the release." "Save that." Watch the markers, click the status dot for before and after values, and use Keep or Reject. No login. Presets and reference audio stay in the browser. What was already there, what is new I started from Soundgineer by noisyloop ( https://github.com/noisyloop/soundgineer , MIT). Its DSP engine and original UI date from July 6 to 11, 2026, and that version is still up at https://soundgineer.vercel.app . Everything WebMCP-related is from the submission period, August 26 to September 3, 2026, about 200 dated commits: the WebMCP layer and all 24 tools, offline rendering and audio analysis, change markers and Keep/Reject, shared undo history and replays, guided walkthroughs, the interface redesign, the four evals with their harness, and the in-page agent brief. title: Meridian Bank — a WebMCP banking demo
pitch: Banking where the AI does the homework and you keep the pen: an agent compares, checks eligibility, and applies inside your session, on your page but only a human can hit submit
about_excerpt: Banking where the AI does the homework and you keep the pen: an agent compares, checks eligibility, and applies inside your session, on your page but only a human can hit submit Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "agent browses the web" demo we'd seen worked against the page screenshotting, scraping the DOM, guessing which button to click. Meanwhile, the tasks people actually want help with (like picking a credit card) depend on private, session-bound data an outside agent can't see: your income, your credit score, what you already hold. WebMCP flips the model the page itself tells the agent what it can do. We wanted to build the strongest possible case for that flip: a bank, where the data is personal, the answers must be grounded, and the final action is too consequential to leave to an AI. What it does Meridian Bank is a retail-banking portal where an AI agent works inside your authenticated browser tab through 15 WebMCP tools the page registers: Search & compare — full terms sheets for 21 products across 8 categories, with a side-by-side comparison matrix Grounded recommendations check_eligibility runs the bank's real rules engine against your profile and returns per-requirement verdicts (ELIGIBLE / NOT_ELIGIBLE / REVIEW_REQUIRED) with reasons and alternative products the agent recommends from the same source of truth the bank uses Visual co-presence highlight_differences lets the agent light up the exact rows of the compare table that drove its recommendation and dim the rest, with its note shown above the table. The agent literally points at the page Acting on your behalf it assembles a multi-product application basket, picks card designs, applies your loyalty offer, and the UI updates live as it works Human-in-the-loop by construction submit_application never submits. It opens an in-app approval dialog with the full basket summary and blocks until the human clicks Approve or Reject. Even a misbehaving agent cannot submit, because the guardrail lives in the tool's implementation, not in a prompt Tool availability mirrors the session: 3 tools logged out, 15 logged in the browser's tool list itself reflects auth state. Try it: https://meridian-bank-client-production.up.railway.app in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. How we built it The app is built with Wasp (React + Express + Prisma/Postgres), deployed on Railway. Every tool is registered through the browser's WebMCP API: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "check_eligibility", description: "Check whether the user qualifies for a product…", inputSchema: { /* JSON Schema / }, execute: async (input) => { / … */ }, }); …via a small React hook that handles register/unregister on mount and auth gating with an enabled flag. Each tool's execute delegates to the same typed RPC operations the UI uses, so Wasp's automatic query invalidation makes the interface update live after every agent action — zero extra wiring. The eligibility engine is a pure, fully unit-tested module (16 tests); the approval flow is a promise that only resolves when a human clicks a button. We tested with Claude connected over chrome-devtools-mcp in a WebMCP-flagged Chrome. Challenges we ran into React lifecycle vs. browser API. Tools registered from React must survive StrictMode double-mounting and never close over stale component state every execute reads through the RPC layer instead of captured props, and aborted registrations had to be handled as expected lifecycle noise rather than errors. Designing for a non-human user. Tool descriptions are UX writing where the "user" is a model. Getting the agent to reliably check eligibility before recommending and to never submit unprompted — came down to careful naming, descriptions, structured error messages, and returning effect fields that tell the agent what just changed on screen. Making approval un-bypassable. The tempting version is "tell the agent to ask first." The robust version is a tool whose result the agent can't have until a human acts designing that blocking flow (with a timeout, and honest reporting of rejected vs timed out) was the most interesting part. Accomplishments that we're proud of A structural safety guarantee, not a prompted one: no sequence of agent calls can submit an application without a human click and the agent gets an honest account of what the human decided. The agent explains itself in the page: highlight_differences turned "trust me, pick the Voyager" into a compare table where the decisive rows are glowing and everything else is dimmed. A complete, working product 21 products, a real eligibility engine, offers, applications history live on the open web, where the full three-prompt demo (compare → apply → approve) runs end-to-end against the deployed site. What we learned The biggest lesson: safety and UX come from tool design, not prompt engineering. A well-shaped tool result (verdicts with reasons, an effect field describing what changed) steers an agent better than any system prompt. We also learned that exposing state-reading tools (get_compare_list, get_my_holdings) matters as much as actions "which of these two?" only works because the agent can see what the human is looking at. And practically: WebMCP is genuinely host-agnostic it's a client-side browser API, so the same tools worked identically on localhost and on Railway. What's next for Meridian Bank — a WebMCP banking demo Streaming progress into the page while the agent works, per-tool scopes the user can grant and revoke (a "permissions drawer" for agents), and multi-tab flows imagine the agent comparing your bank's offer against another site's, with both pages exposing tools to the same assistant. title: Swagger UI WebMCP
pitch: If you can Try it out, your agent can too — a Swagger UI plugin that turns any OpenAPI docs page into a live agent interface, using the environment and login you already have open.
about_excerpt: If you can Try it out, your agent can too — a Swagger UI plugin that turns any OpenAPI docs page into a live agent interface, using the environment and login you already have open. Like Comment Story Updates If you can Try it out, your agent can too. Swagger UI WebMCP is a reusable Swagger UI plugin that turns any OpenAPI documentation page into a live, session-scoped agent interface — and splits the decision of what that agent may touch among the four parties who each know something different. The agent calls the API through the exact environment, login, and request pipeline the developer already has open in the page. No AI SDK. No MCP server to install. No bearer token copied anywhere. Live demo: https://openapi-web-mcp.vercel.app Repository: https://github.com/alliecatowo/openapi-web-mcp The problem A developer working against an internal or partner API already has a browser tab where everything is correct: signed in, staging selected in the server dropdown, the right key pasted into Swagger UI's Authorize dialog, and the corporate proxy, CORS rules, and session cookies all working. To let an agent help with that same API, the entire environment has to be rebuilt somewhere else — install or write an MCP server, re-describe the endpoints, copy a bearer token out of the browser into a config file, and keep the two in sync forever. So the agent is useful for writing code about the API and useless for actually driving it. Underneath that is a second problem nobody has a good answer for: once the connector exists, who decides what the agent may touch? Today it is whoever wrote it, once, months ago, holding standing credentials. Audience: developers, QA and support engineers, and solutions/API-partner teams who live in OpenAPI documentation pages every day — and the API publishers who host those pages for them. Every internal and partner API with a Swagger UI docs page is a candidate. The idea: authority splits four ways, and only ever narrows Four parties each hold information the others don't, so each gets exactly the instrument they have the information for: the API publisher knows which endpoints are dangerous, expressed as x-webmcp annotations that travel with the OpenAPI document itself, reviewed and versioned; the page owner knows what this deployment is for, expressed as a webMcp.exposure default and an optional policyResolver; the person at the page knows what is happening right now, expressed as per-operation session locks scoped to this tab only; and the WebMCP client knows what to ask a human, expressed through MCP annotations and structured errors. The rule that makes them compose rather than conflict: every source may only tighten. All of them reduce to a level on the lattice hidden < read < write, the tightest wins, and hidden survives every setting, because refusing exposure is never a privilege escalation. The agent itself does not get a vote — session locks are module state the tools never touch. Why the documentation page is the right place WebMCP's defining property is that the page is the integration: capability lives in the tab, scoped to the session, and dies with it. API docs fit that shape better than almost anything else. The contract already exists and is machine-readable, so tools are derived, not hand-written. The ambient state — selected server, authorized schemes, cookies, interceptors — is simply already true in the tab. Ephemerality is a feature: nobody wants a persistent connector holding standing write access to production. And it generalizes: every Swagger UI page that adds one import becomes an agent surface for whatever API it documents. That surface is not small. swagger-ui-dist alone is pulled from npm roughly 51 million times a month, and Swagger UI is the default, unmodified docs renderer behind FastAPI's /docs route and NestJS's official OpenAPI module — so the install base this plugs into is already deployed, already authenticated, and already pointed at real APIs. (npm registry, 30 days ending 29 Aug 2026; per-package figures in the README.) This is not "write another MCP server" — no standing credentials, no separately maintained tool definitions. And it is not a browser-automation agent clicking through the UI — it calls the API directly through Swagger's own execution pipeline, with a generated tool schema and MCP annotations per operation. What people and agents can do together The human signs in, picks Sandbox, authorizes a scheme in Swagger's own dialog — the agent inherits all of it, live. The person types into the q box of Try it out and stops; the agent reads that value and finishes the call. Every agent execution renders in Swagger UI's own response panel, not a separate agent console. An access control sits next to Try-it-out on every operation: Full access, View only, Read only, Hidden. And the demo API logs whether each write arrived via the agent pipeline or by hand. The thing that was hard before: letting an agent act on a live, authenticated, environment-specific API without provisioning it any standing credentials or infrastructure — and being able to see, constrain, and revoke that in the same place you were already working. The bigger picture The four-way split is in service of something larger than one docs page. It turns an existing, enormous class of page into an agent gateway with no new infrastructure to run or revoke. The per-operation access control doubles as a supervised playground: turn an agent loose on a live API, watch every call land in the same response panel you use yourself, and keep the kill switch one click away. Because agent calls run through Swagger's own execute action — the same code path as Try it out — an agent's call and a human's call are directly comparable, which makes the page a debugging surface. And the mechanism the demo uses to fingerprint agent writes is exported: the plugin's agentExecution primitive is set for the duration of an agent-initiated request and cleared in a finally, so any Swagger UI deployment can read it from its own requestInterceptor and tag agent traffic in its own audit trail. None of that needs different code — it is the same lattice and the same execution path, looked at from four angles. How WebMCP was implemented One import into an existing Swagger UI config is the whole integration. When the browser provides document.modelContext, the plugin enumerates operations from Swagger UI's own resolved spec, resolves local $refs, converts parameters and request bodies into JSON Schema tool inputs, and registers two layers of tools: five stable core tools plus one direct tool per exposed operation, capped at 64 with graceful fallback to discovery and generic execution. The cap is enforced everywhere a tool name is advertised, so search and get can never name a tool that was not registered. Tools can never name a URL. A call resolves against the currently selected Swagger server and does not build its own fetch client — arguments are written into the Swagger store, the page's own execute action runs the request through its configured interceptors, credentials, and selected server, and the result is read back out of the store. That is why environment and login are inherited rather than duplicated. Direct tools, the generic executor, and the batch executor all funnel through one authorize function evaluated at call time against live state, so there is exactly one place exposure is enforced, and nothing is cached. The page never prompts — permission UX belongs to the WebMCP client; the page's interface to it is registration visibility, MCP annotations, and structured errors. Safety is structural. Schema compilation runs an allowlist of structural JSON Schema keywords. Credential-shaped names — password, apiKey, token, secret and their variants — are excluded at enumeration, in parameters and in request-body properties at any nesting depth, so they never enter a tool schema. A batch call exposure-checks every step before running the first. Each of these has a regression test; the reasoning is in docs/security-notes.md. Try it Open https://openapi-web-mcp.vercel.app , click Sign in, then ask your agent to check the environment, list active projects, try the usage report and explain why it fails, then create a project and show which writes came from an agent. Then by hand: authorize the bearer scheme and re-ask (now succeeds); switch the server to Production and ask again (different data, same tools); set an operation to Read only and watch the agent get a structured refusal. Operations can also carry a costHint annotation: a signal that a call costs money or has a real consequence beyond the request itself — a metered charge, a real SMS sent — without hiding the operation outright. It composes the same way destructive does (any source can flag it, none can clear it) and surfaces as costHint / costNote on the registered tool, so a WebMCP client can choose to confirm with a human before calling something the publisher flagged

title: ausschreibungsagenten / tender-agents
pitch: WebMCP turns live German and European tender search into a shared Go/No-Go board: agents surface evidence while people retain the final decision.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns live German and European tender search into a shared Go/No-Go board: agents surface evidence while people retain the final decision. Like Comment Story Updates ausschreibungsagenten Inspiration Public procurement contains enormous business opportunities, but finding the right tender is still slow and fragmented. In 2024 alone, Germany’s Federal Statistical Office recorded 200k public contracts and concessions with a combined value of €135 billion. Companies search across many portals, compare incomplete notices, check deadlines and thresholds, and then manually decide whether an opportunity deserves further attention. We wanted to explore a more useful role for browser agents: not replacing the human decision, but helping people turn scattered tender data into a transparent Go/No-Go workflow. What it does Tender Agents is a live procurement search platform covering 17 sources across Germany, the EU, and the UK. For the WebMCP Challenge, we turned the website into an agent-accessible workspace with 11 WebMCP tools. An agent can: Search live public tenders Inspect the tenders currently visible on the page Open notices and check source availability Add opportunities to a shared shortlist Explain the fit using transparent, evidence-based reasons Check EU procurement thresholds Prefill a pilot search profile without submitting it Read and update Go/No-Go decisions The important part is the shared state. When an agent shortlists a tender, it appears on the visible board. When a person changes the decision, the agent can read that decision during its next tool call. The result is a collaborative workspace instead of an invisible automation pipeline. How we built it The frontend is built with React , Vite , and JavaScript and deployed on Vercel . The page registers 11 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . These tools connect directly to the application's React state, domain logic, live search results, and browser storage. We separated the implementation into three small modules: WebMCP tool registration and validation Procurement-specific evaluation logic Persistent shortlist and decision state Tender fit explanations use observable facts such as CPV categories, performance location, remaining time, estimated value, EU thresholds, award criteria, lots, framework agreements, and GPA coverage. State-changing calls update the visible interface immediately. Read-only calls return the same state that the person sees on the page. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making agent actions and human actions operate on exactly the same state. An earlier prototype exposed a single tool that returned raw JSON but did not affect the interface. That technically connected the page to an agent, but it did not create a useful collaboration experience. We replaced it with tools registered from the live React component so that agent actions update the actual application state. We also had to handle untrusted third-party tender content carefully, validate every tool input, preserve decisions across reloads, support German and English interfaces, and ensure that profile tools can prefill forms but never submit them. Accomplishments that we're proud of 11 focused WebMCP tools on a live production website A shared, persistent Go/No-Go board for humans and agents Transparent fit explanations instead of black-box recommendations Human decisions remain authoritative Third-party tender text is explicitly marked as untrusted content 43 focused WebMCP and procurement-domain tests 205 passing tests across the complete application No separate agent-only demo: the integration works on the real product What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when it exposes meaningful actions rather than merely mirroring a REST API. The most useful agent tools are connected to visible application state, have narrow responsibilities, validate their inputs, and explain their outputs. We also learned that human overrides should be part of the protocol itself, not an afterthought. Agents are good at searching, comparing, and organizing opportunities. People should still own the final commercial decision. What's next The longer-term goal is an agent-assisted workflow that helps small and medium-sized companies discover suitable public contracts without hiding the evidence behind each recommendation. title: CutoverProof
pitch: CutoverProof stress-tests PostgreSQL migrations across realistic interleavings, revealing data-loss races as runnable counterexamples before cutover.
about_excerpt: CutoverProof stress-tests PostgreSQL migrations across realistic interleavings, revealing data-loss races as runnable counterexamples before cutover. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can propose production changes faster than engineers can safely review them. But an online database migration can look correct step by step and still fail when old and new application versions overlap during cutover. We built CutoverProof to test whether an agent can help prepare a high-stakes migration review without receiving the power to execute or approve it. What it does CutoverProof is a shared change contract for online PostgreSQL migrations. A WebMCP browser agent can inspect a declared migration contract, identify risk areas, and create a structured review draft. The engineer then explicitly starts a bounded sandbox assessment. PostgreSQL executes only declared operations in a disposable database and checks read-only invariants for concrete counterexamples. The authority boundary is deliberate: the agent prepares, PostgreSQL verifies, and the engineer authorizes consequential actions. How we built it We built an authenticated React workspace with five typed WebMCP browser tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools use closed JSON schemas and validated FastAPI endpoints to let an agent inspect migration contracts, prepare a review, read verified evidence, and open a human repair review. The deterministic verifier runs against a disposable PostgreSQL sandbox. The app is deployed on Google Cloud Run. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making WebMCP genuinely useful without turning it into an unsafe automation bypass. We needed the agent to understand structured contracts and evidence, while ensuring it could not start an assessment, execute arbitrary SQL, alter a verdict, approve a repair, or deploy anything. We also had to keep the handoff visible: an agent-created review must appear in the engineer’s workspace and explicitly wait for human action. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built five authenticated, typed WebMCP tools for a real browser-agent workflow. Created a visible agent → verifier → human handoff, rather than hidden automation. Kept PostgreSQL as the independent source of evidence and verdicts. Enforced clear safety boundaries: no tool can start execution or approve a repair. Deployed a working live product with deterministic migration evidence and repair replay. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes structured product capabilities, not when it merely automates clicks. We learned that agent assistance becomes more trustworthy when authority is explicit: agents prepare context, deterministic systems verify claims, and humans retain control over consequential decisions. What's next for CutoverProof We will expand from structured PostgreSQL migration packs toward richer real-world migration inputs, while preserving the same safety model: declared contracts, bounded experiments, independent verification, human authorization, and portable evidence. The broader goal is a trust layer for agent-assisted production changes—not a system that gives agents unchecked production power. title: LASSO — Draw What Your Agent Can Touch
pitch: An AI-assisted dispatch console where a human draws what an agent may understand and change. WebMCP turns that visual scope into a live, typed capability contract.
about_excerpt: An AI-assisted dispatch console where a human draws what an agent may understand and change. WebMCP turns that visual scope into a live, typed capability contract. Like Comment Story Updates LASSO — Draw What Your Agent Can Touch | WebMCP Challenge 2026 Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of acting inside increasingly complex web applications. But there is still an awkward question: How does a human communicate exactly what the agent is allowed to understand and change? In visual applications such as dispatch maps, dashboards, CAD tools, scheduling boards, and other canvases, the relevant context is often obvious to a human. We can simply point at it. Explaining the same boundary to an agent usually means naming objects manually, writing long instructions, building application-specific permission systems, or trusting the agent to infer intent from the interface. LASSO explores a different interaction model: The human interface generates the agent interface. A dispatcher draws a boundary around the resources the agent may work with. WebMCP turns that transient visual selection into a live, typed capability contract for the visiting agent. The map is the prompt. The boundary is the permission. What it does LASSO is an AI-assisted dispatch console built around a seeded disruption scenario with six late deliveries. The dispatcher draws a freehand lasso around the deliveries and drivers the AI agent may reason about. That gesture does much more than highlight the map. LASSO compiles the selected UI state into revision-specific WebMCP tools whose JSON Schemas contain only the resources inside the human-defined boundary. The external agent then: Inspects the scoped operational state. Authors its own recovery plan. Submits the plan to LASSO for deterministic validation. Receives structured violations if the plan breaks capacity, vehicle, timing, overtime, or scope constraints. May request additional resources outside its current authority. Cannot grant that additional authority to itself. Repairs its plan after the human approves a scope expansion. Can modify live routes only after the human authorizes one exact verified plan. In the demo scenario, the agent discovers that delivery D15 requires refrigerated capacity that is unavailable inside its original scope. It asks for Mika, a suitable driver outside the boundary. The human chooses whether to include Mika. That single UI action invalidates the previous WebMCP contract and compiles a new revision in which Mika becomes available to the agent. The repaired plan reduces six late deliveries to one with three route changes and zero overtime. Only then can the dispatcher authorize execution. The resulting write capability is bound to the exact plan, current scope, workspace generation, and a single expiring use. Stale or replayed authority is rejected. Why WebMCP LASSO is not an optimizer with a tool wrapper. The agent authors the plan . LASSO provides the scoped world model, deterministic validation, authority negotiation, and execution boundary. The central WebMCP idea is that the tool surface itself changes as the human manipulates the live application. A visual gesture becomes structured machine-readable context. When the human changes the lasso, the agent's available resource IDs and capability contract change with it. Traditional browser automation can see a highlighted region, but it still has to infer what that highlight means and whether it represents authority. A conventional remote API or MCP server would require additional synchronization to know what the human just selected in the browser. With WebMCP, the page itself can expose that ephemeral application state directly to the visiting agent. How we built it LASSO is a lightweight, dependency-free web application built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG, JSON Schema, and the imperative WebMCP API. The architecture separates four responsibilities: Human UI — visual scope, operational constraints, authority decisions Scope compiler — converts UI state into revision-specific WebMCP contracts External agent — creates and repairs recovery plans Policy engine — validates and safely applies scoped state changes The application also includes deterministic browser, security, adversarial, package, and performance validation. The final local release campaign includes more than 150 correctness and security invariants plus a 5,000-case adversarial fuzz campaign. Challenges The hardest problem was not drawing a lasso. It was making the boundary meaningful. We had to ensure that: changing scope invalidates stale capabilities; an agent cannot expand its own authority; outside-scope assignments remain untouched; a delivery can never silently acquire multiple owners; application handlers validate authority independently of JSON Schema; partially registered WebMCP contracts fail closed; in-flight tool calls are not broken by contract recompilation; an authorized plan cannot be changed and replayed later. Several of these issues only appeared during adversarial testing and required changes to the underlying state-transition model rather than cosmetic fixes. What we learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when tools are not static API endpoints. A web application's live human state can itself determine what capabilities an agent discovers. That creates a new interaction loop: human gesture → typed capability → agent reasoning → authority request → human decision → new capability The conversation between human and agent does not have to happen entirely in a chat box. The web interface itself can participate. What's next Dispatch is the demonstration, not the limit. The same interaction pattern could apply anywhere humans naturally identify context spatially: operations dashboards analytics CAD and design tools scheduling systems infrastructure maps logistics spreadsheets and visual workspaces The long-term idea is simple: Point at the context. Let the web turn that gesture into an agent contract. ChatGPT and Codex assisted heavily with implementation, debugging, security testing, documentation, and video production. I reviewed and challenged each iteration, performed the human parts of the native WebMCP workflow, and owned the final product and submission decisions.
