title: Bandmate-WebMCP
pitch: Bandmate is a WebMCP musical sequencer, where you jam away on your instrument, and the agent arranges it all in one tab while the loop keeps playing, with creative collaboration happening in realtime.
about_excerpt: Bandmate is a WebMCP musical sequencer, where you jam away on your instrument, and the agent arranges it all in one tab while the loop keeps playing, with creative collaboration happening in realtime. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Four bars of melody and no idea what goes under it. Asking ChatGPT yields MIDI text to convert, import and audition five minutes later, and the model never heard your take. WebMCP suggested a third thing: the agent sits in the tab with the sequencer, reads your notes as structure, and writes into the bar you are still hearing. What it does Bandmate is a four-track loop sequencer (drums, bass, chords, lead; 4 bars, 64 steps) exposing 16 WebMCP tools. Play a riff on the piano or your computer keys; ask "what goes under this?"; the agent calls suggest_chords then add_chords, and teal notes cascade into the grid while the loop keeps playing. It adds bass and drums in three styles, and can play you two arrangements before committing one. Record live and its writers are unregistered until you stop. Export a Standard MIDI File into any DAW. Why WebMCP fits this use case Shared state beats generated text. The agent needs what you just played, what you just muted, and which bar you are looking at. All three live in the page's store; get_session serialises them in under 700 characters. The human must stay in the loop. Harmony is taste. audition is a tool whose execute() awaits a click; the agent's turn pauses until a human has listened. Capabilities should track the mode. While you record, writers are dangerous; during an audition they would corrupt the preview. Tool groups are disposed via AbortController and the browser fires toolchange, so the agent's tool list is truthful at every moment. No backend. One static site works in ChatGPT desktop, Chrome with the flag, or with a bring-your-own-key agent. How it improves the experience for people Five minutes per iteration becomes eight seconds. You never leave the grid or convert a file; every agent write is teal beside your amber notes and undoable in one click. The agent reacts to what you did by hand ("muted bass 5s ago"), and when it cannot decide it plays A and B instead of guessing. Students see why a chord works: numerals, names, borrowed and altered chords, a why per suggestion. What humans and agents can accomplish together that was previously impossible The agent hears your playing as structure, not audio, so it can answer "what goes under what I just played?" and drop the answer into the bar you are still hearing. A DAW has no ear for theory; a music generator has no room for you. And because the agent cannot hear, it asks your ears: it plays two options in your tab and waits for you to pick. How I built it Vite + vanilla TypeScript, Tone.js 15, no server. Registration. Each tool is a typed defineTool({name, description, inputSchema, annotations, execute}) registered via document.modelContext.registerTool(descriptor, {signal}). That is the only surface ChatGPT's browser and Chrome 152 expose; navigator.modelContext is probed only as a fallback for other builds. Tool groups and toolchange. Five ToolGroups (readers, writers, dialog, transport, recording), each with one AbortController. Recording or auditioning disposes the writers; leaving re-registers them. Abort unregisters natively, the browser emits toolchange, and the header pill shows idle 15 / recording 8 / auditioning 7. Annotations. Readers carry readOnlyHint. Exactly one tool, clear_track, carries consequentialHint: it is the only whole-track wipe, and it also asks the human first. untrustedContentHint appears nowhere, because no Bandmate content originates from a third party. Schema hygiene. Every schema is type:'object', additionalProperties:false, explicit required, enums for closed sets, numeric bounds, a description on every property. An Ajv strict test compiles all of them and enforces name ≤ 30, description ≤ 350, parameter ≤ 120. Bounded results. get_session ≤ 700 chars, get_track ≤ 1,500, everything else clipped with truncated:true. Notes use a compact b1: 1@1 3@5 5@9 degree format; drum lanes are 16-char velocity-class strings. Every result ends with hint or next. Audition as an awaiting tool. Each option is a full variant Session swapped into the store's transient layer at the next step; the engine tick reads store.current(), so previews are audible without rebuilds. Keep commits one undoable agent mutation; the promise resolves with chosen, listened, undo_id. On timeout it returns awaiting_human and the card stays open. Honours AbortSignal. Attribution and undo. Note.by / DrumHit.by are set by store.apply() from the caller's meta. Undo is a linear stack of deep-cloned snapshots (cap 50) tagged with author and label; the undo tool refuses when the top entry is human. Writers that would remove human notes call store.dryRun() then askHuman(). One clock. A single 64-step Tone.Sequence reads store.current() every 16th; no Parts, no rebuilds. Recording quantises keydown times to the nearest 16th and writes by:'human' live. Export. Pure SMF type-1 writer (PPQ 480, swing baked, drums on channel 10). The tool sets the Download button's href and spotlights it; the click is the human's. Challenges document.modelContext hands back inputSchema as a JSON string and executeTool takes one, which shaped the built-in agent and the Playwright harness. Keeping a promise pending inside execute() for up to 60 s and defining what happens after a host timeout (card stays; late click applies). Making agent writes audible on the next 16th without glitches. Autoplay: an agent transport play before any gesture must return muted_until_user_taps and spotlight Play. Accomplishments Sixteen tools that plain sentences route to across 12 eval cases; an audition whose promise waits for a human ear; a mode-driven tool list the browser reports truthfully; zero backend. What I learned Tool descriptions are UX: verb-first, one "use when", one constraint, and "returns undo_id" changed which tool the model picked more than schema tweaks did. Hinted results turn three calls into a conversation. Once every cell knows who wrote it, undo, confirmation and "what did I just do?" fall out for free. What's next WebMIDI input, more styles and time signatures, a per-bar "why this chord" explainer, auditions of fills and voicings, all as more tools on the same store. Built with webmcp typescript vite tone.js web-audio midi vitest playwright github-pages chatgpt-desktop Testing instructions for judges Open the live URL in ChatGPT desktop (macOS, in-app browser) or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Other browsers: open the agent drawer, paste your own OpenAI or Anthropic key, use the built-in agent. Press ▶ Play once (audio unlock). The demo riff loops. Ask Add lo-fi drums → teal drum cells. What goes under what I just played? → chord strip fills. Let me hear two bass options → press ▶ A, ▶ B, Keep one. Press ● Record: the pill drops 15 → 8 tools. Play keys (a w s e d f …), press Stop; back to 15. Ask Export this as MIDI, click the highlighted Download button, open the file in any DAW. Chrome: DevTools → Application → WebMCP lists the registered tools with annotations (15 idle, 8 recording); ?debug=1 opens the inspector. Repo: pnpm test. Tools reference: docs/tools.md, generated from the schemas. title: Can an Agent Fly a Plane?
pitch: I built a flight simulator, then used WebMCP to see if an AI agent could fly the thing, handle an emergency it didn’t know was coming, and somehow land.
about_excerpt: I built a flight simulator, then used WebMCP to see if an AI agent could fly the thing, handle an emergency it didn’t know was coming, and somehow land. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I've been watching a lot of pilot content lately, and I've always been interested in planes. An agent-driven flight evaluation sounded cool, and using STL, where I'm from, felt obvious. What it does This project is a real-time WebMCP evaluation for model developers and evaluation researchers. Your agent has to take off from STL on a flight to MDW in Chicago, handle a sealed emergency, coordinate a diversion with simulated ATC (air traffic control), and land safely back in St. Louis. ATC defines the route and checkpoints, but the agent decides how to fly them. It chooses the flight targets, aircraft configuration, and activation conditions. The simulator applies those targets continuously using 60 Hz physics at a fixed 2x time scale. It never pauses or changes that rate while the agent thinks, and the emergency decision window and mission deadline still use real elapsed time. Completing the flight requires hitting the route checkpoints and configuring the aircraft correctly. The score deducts points for slow emergency decisions, exceeding the mission window, high G-force, abrupt motion, hard or off-center landings, and crashes. The page registers six WebMCP tools for reading the manual, starting the flight, programming commands, coordinating with ATC, and waiting for events. WebMCP gives the agent structured state and validated actions instead of making it guess at visual controls. A person can fly the same aircraft manually, or start an agent evaluation and watch it go. The exported trajectory records every WebMCP call, action, result, latency, before-and-after state, score change, and simulator event. How I built it I used Codex to build and test each version. My first Cesium.js scene used a real route from STL to Chicago, but it hurt performance and was very buggy. I switched to Three.js and built a simplified but representative wide-body twinjet flight envelope. The simulation runs outside React render state at 60 Hz. The WebMCP layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool to expose the six tools, but the simulator still works manually without WebMCP if you want to fly it yourself. I went through probably 15 to 20 iterations of the world itself, adding audio and the minimap along the way. The hard part was deciding what the agent should actually control. We revised the tools until the agent was calling the shots instead of taking credit for decisions buried in the simulator. Challenges I ran into The V1 version was kind of cool, but it was too easy. The agent was basically on autopilot. The deterministic simulator controlled pitch, bank, and power while the agent only decided whether to return or continue. I set a /goal challenging Codex to make a fresh subagent complete the flight using the actual flight model. The results were pretty interesting. After 13 hours and 73 attempts, it finally got three runs to land with scores around 90, but of course it cheated. Somewhere along the way it decided the easiest way to fly a plane was to stop time whenever it needed to think. That obviously defeated the entire point. That exposed the most interesting part. As soon as the agent has to think, time becomes part of the problem. Even Terra at low reasoning could take long enough that the aircraft crashed or flew too far away. The solution was to meet in the middle. Simulated ATC supplies the route, but the agent writes the flight program before takeoff and replaces it after the emergency. The simulator tracks its targets at 60 Hz without pausing or deciding what comes next. I tested that version with ten agents in cold threads, and all ten failed. I decided they needed a “manual” explaining the aircraft and command interface. I really didn't want to do this, but they needed enough context to land without moving the decisions back into the simulator. The manual publishes rotation speed, climb and landing configuration, approach speed, flare limits, and the go-around sequence. It does not reveal the emergency, choose the diversion, or provide a program. The agent still has to fly. The resulting architecture completed three fresh blind runs in a row without pausing, changing the fixed simulation rate, or revealing the emergency early. Every WebMCP interaction was captured in the browser-side trajectory export. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that I didn't stop at “this works because the agent said it does” (which happens every single time lmao). I grilled Codex on how the simulation worked and kept pushing until the agent, rather than a hidden policy, owned the decisions. Thinking still hurts performance here, but I believe that is useful signal rather than something to hide. Models should be able to judge when deeper reasoning is worth the time. What I learned I learned a lot about building with WebMCP and understanding the agent experience. It isn't as simple as “give the agent all the information and let it do the thing.” I had to run fresh agents repeatedly and fix ambiguous tools without taking decisions away from them. The manual is part of the interface, not an answer key. The same applies to human UX. If people and agents get stuck at the same point, the interface probably is not communicating clearly enough. What's next? This could become an evaluation environment for model developers and researchers testing decisions under time pressure. Most evaluations I've seen analyze time after the run. Here, time changes the environment. A longer response means the aircraft has traveled farther, burned more fuel, and moved closer to failure. The sealed scenario and exported trajectory make that measurable. The idea also does not have to stop at flying a plane. The same setup could test an agent acting as ATC, coordinating a ground crew, or handling another system where the world keeps moving while the model thinks. The bigger question is whether models can learn when to reason deeply and when they need to act now. title: Panoptik
pitch: Panoptik is a browser-native video studio powered by WebMCP. In-browser AI agents inspect footage and propose smart cuts and zooms as reviewable staged diffs—100% locally.
about_excerpt: Panoptik is a browser-native video studio powered by WebMCP. In-browser AI agents inspect footage and propose smart cuts and zooms as reviewable staged diffs—100% locally. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP Toolcalls - 2 Zoom controls Voiceover and music Zoom points Stage WebMCP Toolcalls - 1 Text overlays Landing page Facecam controls Autogenerated captions using whisper agentic ediditing session Export menu Workspace Editor Panoptik × WebMCP — Project Story A browser-native video studio where humans and AI agents co-edit on the same canvas. > Decode, render, audio mixing, and export happen 100% inside your browser using WebCodecs and Canvas2D. No uploads, no render farm, zero data leakage. Inspiration Making demo videos for software products takes too much time. A punchy 90-second product demo requires 15+ camera zoom keyframes, dozens of subtitle snippets, manual silence excision, and canvas framing. In tools like ScreenStudio, Loom, or Premiere, this forces creators to spend 45 to 60 minutes scrubbing frame-by-frame, calculating focal centers, placing timeline diamonds, and proofreading speech. Because editing is so exhausting, many developers simply give up and ship raw, unpolished recordings. When we set out to build an AI agent to handle this tedious workflow, we ran into a core architectural barrier: video editing lives inside client-side canvas pixels. Backend MCP servers are blind to the browser session: The video file lives in the browser's Origin Private File System (OPFS), the playback state lives in an in-memory Zustand store, and the rendered UI exists only as Canvas2D pixel buffers. There is no remote server copy for an external API to inspect. Multimodal DOM-scraping is fragile and costly: Directing an agent via automated screenshots and synthetic cursor events consumes ~150 KB to 200 KB of token bandwidth per action, introduces seconds of latency, and frequently misclicks or desynchronizes with the timeline. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge provided the missing architectural link: an in-page, standardized communication bridge between browser-resident agents and client-side web applications. We built Panoptik so an in-browser agent can inspect the canvas, analyze project telemetry, and propose structured edits directly through 30 imperative WebMCP tools—while keeping the human firmly in control. What it does Panoptik is a screen recording and video production studio that runs entirely inside the browser: Zero-Upload Local Media Engine: Drop in raw recordings or capture screen, camera, and microphone directly. Decoding, real-time compositing, audio mixing, and MP4/WebM encoding run entirely client-side via WebCodecs, Canvas2D, and mediabunny. Proprietary dashboards, sensitive credentials, and internal code never leave your machine. 30 Granular WebMCP Tools: Panoptik exposes its editing engine via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Running inside ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, the agent inspects scene cadence, reads click coordinates, checks rendered frames, and orchestrates multi-track edits. The "Agent Proposes, Human Disposes" Diff Engine: The agent never silently mutates the timeline. Proposed cuts, zooms, captions, and transitions appear as non-destructive ghost edits (dashed amber keyframe diamonds, pending caption chips, and preview diffs). The creator can adjust any parameter manually and commit or discard the diff with a single click. Studio-Grade Polish: Dynamic Camera Zooms: Smooth continuous cubic camera translations with automatic viewport margin clamping. Visual Grounding: Three-tier focal resolution mapping agent requests (e.g., "zoom in on the login button" ) to exact coordinates via click telemetry, grid bounding boxes, or balanced fallbacks. Acoustic Snapping & Silence Removal: Automatic dead-air truncation that preserves natural speech cadence without clipping vocal phonemes. Word-Level Subtitles: Synchronized transcription with animated keyword highlighting. Pitch-Preserving Speed Adjustment: High-fidelity audio time-stretching via the WSOLA algorithm. Live Tool Trace Panel: A persistent inspector panel that surfaces every WebMCP call, runtime latency, input payload, and return value for total human oversight. How we built it Panoptik is structured as a monorepo containing the Next.js application ( apps/web ), the low-level media engine ( packages/engine ), and the shared type contract ( packages/project-schema ). ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser Tab (Next.js) │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ │ │Preview Canvas│ │Timeline & Store│ │ Tool Trace │ │ │ └──────┬───────┘ └───────┬────────┘ └─────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Reactive Project Store (Zustand) │ │ │ │ Committed Elements ↔ Staged Ghost Diffs │ │ │ └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ │Media Engine │ │ WebMCP Layer │ │ │ │(WebCodecs, │ │ (30 Tools, │ │ │ │ Canvas2D) │ │ Snapping) │ │ │ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ W3C document.modelContext / Web APIs │ │ │ │ VideoDecoder · VideoEncoder · OPFS · Mediabunny │ │ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 1. Camera Zoom Interpolation At any playback timestamp t , the camera transform state is represented by a 2D affine vector: T(t) = [ s(t), x_f(t), y_f(t) ]ᵀ where s(t) is the zoom scale factor and (x_f, y_f) ∈ [0, 1]² is the normalized focal target. For a zoom starting at t_k with duration Δt , the normalized transition progress parameter is: p(t) = clamp( (t - t_k) / Δt, 0, 1 ) Progress is mapped through a cubic easing curve E(p) : E(p) = 4p³ (for p < 0.5) E(p) = 1 - (-2p + 2)³ / 2 (for p ≥ 0.5) The camera blends smoothly from the current state to the target state: T(t) = (1 - E(p)) · T_start + E(p) · T_target To render this on a canvas of dimensions (W_canvas, H_canvas) letterboxing a source video (W_vid, H_vid) with base scale S_0 , the 2D transformation offsets applied to the context are: T_x(t) = (W_canvas / 2) - x_f(t) · W_vid · S_0 · s(t) T_y(t) = (H_canvas / 2) - y_f(t) · H_vid · S_0 · s(t) 2. Dual Time-Space Mapping The human editor and agent reason in timeline time ( t_timeline ), while underlying video chunks exist in immutable source time ( t_src ). Cuts and speed modifications cause these coordinate systems to diverge. For clip i with source interval [s_i, e_i] played at speed factor v_i , the timeline duration is: D_i = (e_i - s_i) / v_i The forward mapping function transforms source seconds into timeline seconds: t_timeline = ∑(D_j) + (t_src - s_k) / v_k When an agent proposes an edit, Panoptik immediately maps the timestamp back into source coordinates using the inverse mapping. Downstream timeline shifts caused by cutting dead air never invalidate or displace previously anchored keyframes. 3. Acoustic Word Boundary Snapping Rather than blindly executing raw timestamps emitted by an LLM, cut proposals are guarded against active vocal phonemes using an acoustic safety boundary: |t_cut - t_boundary(w)| ≥ 150 ms (for all spoken words w) If a proposed cut falls within 150 ms of a word boundary, the cut automatically snaps outward to the nearest preceding silence interval, preventing clipped syllables. 4. Token & Bandwidth Economics Comparing WebMCP structured tool calls against conventional multimodal vision scraping: WebMCP Payload: ~2.1 KB Screenshot + DOM Scraping: ~165 KB Efficiency Gain: 1 - (2.1 KB / 165 KB) ≈ 98.7% A complete multi-step edit session completes in ~6 lightweight JSON tool calls (~3 KB total context overhead), eliminating latency bottlenecks and model context exhaustion. Challenges we ran into Zero-WASM, Pure Browser Media Pipeline: Most web video editors rely on ffmpeg.wasm , which requires massive binary downloads (30 MB+), induces heavy CPU thermal throttling, and risks memory leaks. We built on native web standards: WebCodecs VideoDecoder / VideoEncoder , Canvas2D, and OPFS. Handling variable frame rate (VFR) screen recordings while maintaining microsecond audio synchronization required custom timestamp interpolation and frame-stepping logic. The "Dual Time-Space Paradox" in Agent Reasoning: LLMs reason sequentially based on current visuals: "cut dead air from 0:12 to 0:18, then zoom in at 0:25" . As soon as the first cut is staged, the visual timeline contracts by 6 seconds. If the subsequent zoom is evaluated against the old timeline, it lands on the wrong frame. We solved this by implementing an atomic batch execution pipeline ( propose_edits ) that evaluates all instructions against a single snapshot and performs dynamic cut-map rebasing. title: CommandCanvas
pitch: A shared spatial workspace where people and agents turn rough thinking into structured, attributable output on the same live canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared spatial workspace where people and agents turn rough thinking into structured, attributable output on the same live canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Meetings produce sketches, decisions, tasks, and commitments, but the useful deliverable is often reconstructed afterward in another application. CommandCanvas lets the meeting itself produce structured output. People, hands, collaborators, voice, and ChatGPT work against the same live spatial objects. Instead of sending an agent a stale transcript, CommandCanvas gives it bounded capabilities over the canvas everyone is using. What it does CommandCanvas is an infinite collaboration canvas built from semantic objects rather than untyped pixels. A participant can create notes, boards, schedules, sketches, diagrams, charts, tables, decisions, actions, and meeting packets; arrange them spatially; and see who changed what. The central workflow starts with rough human thinking. A participant draws a multi-stroke sketch while explaining it, then asks the agent to make it usable. CommandCanvas preserves the original, creates a separate structured result beside it, records provenance, and adds an immutable receipt. The result is not limited to architecture: the same system supports flowcharts, generic diagrams, bar, line, and pie charts, tables, boards, and written summaries. Every input follows one path: Hands / voice / pointer / collaborator / WebMCP ↓ validated capability ↓ canonical mutation ↓ revision + receipt + Supabase sync This lets a hand gesture, a remote collaborator, and ChatGPT change the same durable workspace without creating separate sources of truth. Mutations are visible and attributable. Destructive actions are recoverable. An agent may prepare a meeting packet and stage a send request, but the human host must approve the packet and authorize the external action. WebMCP Leverage WebMCP is the product boundary, not an integration badge. CommandCanvas registers a concise Site Tools catalog with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . A supported ChatGPT host can read the current canvas and selection, create or update semantic objects, organize work, use shared history, transform selected material, prepare a packet, and request a staged send. Each tool has a strict schema, read/write annotations, cancellation support, lifecycle cleanup, phase requirements, role checks, revision guards, and compact results. Registration can remain stable or change by phase behind one feature flag, while execute-time authorization stays identical in both modes. The agent never receives camera frames, database credentials, the user's ChatGPT credential, or authority to approve an email send. WebMCP makes CommandCanvas meaningfully better because selection, object identity, room revision, collaborator activity, packet approval, and receipts are live application context. ChatGPT acts against the same objects the participants can see and manipulate rather than a detached export. Execution CommandCanvas uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, and a custom DOM/SVG spatial canvas. Pointer, touch, stylus, voice, and hand input converge on one intent model. Stable object changes use expected revisions; high-frequency cursor and movement previews remain ephemeral. Supabase Postgres stores rooms, objects, receipts, packet snapshots, and send requests. Supabase Presence represents connected participants. Broadcast carries cursors, revision notices, and participant-bound small-room WebRTC signaling. The no-signup judge preview creates a bounded temporary authenticated identity only after entry; durable rooms use six-digit email OTP. Browser hand input uses local MediaPipe landmarks in a worker and keeps frames on the device. It implements index-finger drawing, pinch-to-grab, two-hand resize and canvas zoom, open-palm pan, minimize, recoverable side-edge trash, and visible interaction states. Pointer, touch, keyboard, typed command, and voice equivalents remain available. Optional in-page Live Voice uses gpt-realtime-2.1 through a user-owned API project key and a narrower capability catalog. The production release completed a real controlled provider chain from spoken transcription through a create_board function call, visible board creation, and a voice receipt. A separate production provider test rasterized a sketch to PNG, sent it to an image-capable OpenAI model, validated the structured result, and preserved the source beside the generated diagram. The current release also passed 1,723 automated tests across 164 files, responsive production acceptance at nine viewport sizes, two independent browser contexts sharing Supabase Presence, cursors, durable mutations, and receipts, controlled browser-to-browser WebRTC media, and native Chrome 153 WebMCP discovery, lifecycle, and cancellation. Potential Impact The gap between discussion and follow-through appears in planning, teaching, design review, research, technical interviews, and team decision-making. CommandCanvas turns live spatial work into reusable objects while the context and participants are still present. Rough notes can become decisions and actions. A sketch can become a chart or diagram. The room can become a reviewable packet. Because the system is domain-neutral, it can support a student drawing a study model, a team mapping a launch, or an analyst sketching a chart. Creativity & Ambition The memorable interaction is not gesture control or generation alone. It is a shared semantic world in which a person can draw with an index finger, explain the idea aloud, receive a structured result, physically reposition it, watch a collaborator modify nearby work, and let ChatGPT continue through explicit capabilities. Human, collaborator, voice, and WebMCP actions appear in one receipt stream. Preserving the rough source matters. It makes the transformation understandable, inspectable, and reversible instead of hiding the human contribution behind a generated replacement. Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was maintaining one trustworthy state model across fluid previews, durable collaboration, agent tools, undo, and consequential external actions. Spatial input became more reliable when gestures produced the same small intents as a pointer instead of owning separate business logic. Agent actions became safer when registration was treated as discoverability, while every execution still rechecked current room authority and state. We also learned to separate evidence boundaries. A green source test does not prove a physical hand, real email delivery, or a ChatGPT-hosted Site Tool call. Native Chrome 153 has verified the deployed registration and lifecycle behavior; the exact ChatGPT built-in-browser invocation and final named-device hand rehearsal remain required recording gates and will not be claimed from other evidence. Try it Open the temporary no-signup judge preview at https://commandcanvas.vercel.app/demo . It needs no signup, login form, password, third-party account, API key, or configuration for the core canvas path. The public preview intentionally reports packet delivery as preview-only rather than claiming an email was sent. title: LittleLibrary
pitch: LittleLibrary is an infinite wall for your files. Drop PDFs, notes, photos, and videos. A WebMCP agent files them into topic neighborhoods you can walk, drag, and inspect.
about_excerpt: LittleLibrary is an infinite wall for your files. Drop PDFs, notes, photos, and videos. A WebMCP agent files them into topic neighborhoods you can walk, drag, and inspect. Like 1 Comment Story Updates LittleLibrary Drop files onto an infinite plane. They file themselves by topic. What inspired me Most of the "AI organizes my files" demos I have seen end in a chat box. You dump a pile of stuff in, and it comes back as tags or a folder tree. You never actually watch a file land. You cannot walk the result. And if a second agent showed up, there would be nothing for it to share. It is not really collaboration. It is just a dump with extra steps. WebMCP felt like a different idea. The page itself can be the thing an agent acts in. Not a remote API with a chat UI glued on. A site that registers tools, and a person who is still sitting there looking at the same wall. I wanted that to feel obvious. Empty infinite plane, an intake pile, topic clusters you can pan around. You drop PDFs, notes, photos, videos, or try the samples that were given. An agent utilizing WebMCP reads the occupancy grid, picks a clip, and carries it to a cluster. That is the whole thing. LittleLibrary is just that wall. How I built it The whole app lives in the browser. Next.js 16 (static export) and React 19 Module stores for documents, camera, intake, and the agent. pdf.js for PDF text and first-page posters A Cloudflare Worker that serves the out/ folder There is no login, and no server that "is" the library. Nothing is kept or stored. On load, the page registers four site tools on document.modelContext : get_occupancy , place_tile , place_batch , and cluster_visible . The executes live in src/lib/tools.ts . Registration is in src/lib/webmcp.ts . The wall only reads state. The agent never imports the packer or the renderer. The agent speaks the page language: clip ids, occupancy slot ids ( "3,-1" ), and topic keys. Never pixel x,y . I tried that once. Had to quickly pivot. The built-in filing loop is: get_occupancy → pick a pending clipId → reach the intake pile → grab the card → carry it to the packed destination → place_tile → repeat until the pile is empty callTool uses the host when one is attached. If not, try the samples still runs the same executes. Occupancy slots are what the agent records. Humans act in the UI. Agents act with tools. Both land on the collaborative environment. What I learned Slots are a language. Pixels are a guess. place_tile({ clipId, slotId }) is something a model can actually use. (412, 880) is something it invents. Occupancy and drawing are different jobs. The agent needs a grid that does not stack. The wall needs organic sections. If I make the agent speak packed coordinates, it starts importing the renderer, and then I have two sources of truth. Tool success has to be visible. The hand shows WebMCP and the live tool name. You watch place_tile happen on a card, not in a log. If you cannot see it, it does not feel like the agent did anything. The human has to stay first-class. Pan, drag, marquee, inspect. If the next get_occupancy cannot see what you did, you are just taking turns. That is not a shared wall. WebMCP is the product surface here. If the host cannot see the tools, the agent cannot file. One write path for people, the built-in loop, and an attached model. One store emit used to re-render the whole wall. Pan has to write a transform, not React state. Visibility has to be a spatial query, not a list of every tile. Challenges I faced My first initial idea was to give the agent a planner that knew about sections, anchors, and links. It looked smart on paper. But ended up tearing it back to four tools and a loop the page already understands. Then the stage started lying. The hand would skip to the slot instead of carrying the card there. I had to ease the camera with the card, re-read the destination every frame, and let a user pan cancel the camera without dropping the card on the floor. On grab, the card in the hand was hidden behind the rest of the pile and the next cards slid up over it. The fix was a z-index, which is almost embarrassing, but the lesson stuck: pickup, carry, and drop are one action in three frames. If the layers disagree, the whole collaboration looks fake. The pile itself fought me. If the agent always took the front card, every drop stayed in one topic. I shuffle samples, promote a pending clip, and prefer a different topic than the last place, so the hand actually travels between sections. Performance showed up as soon as the wall had more than a handful of cards. A single snapshot subscription re-rendered every mounted tile on every agent phase. Camera motion went through React. Culling ignored the yaw, so we mounted five times what was on screen. I split the stores, pinned the world transform to a ref, and made visibility a grid query. Exporting for Cloudflare was the last constraint. The app is client-only, so output: "export" is honest. A leftover route handler and generated icons had to become static or the build refused to write out/ . The hard part was never "register a tool." It was making the tools a language good enough that a person and a model can occupy the same wall, at the same time, and both know where the chowder recipe actually landed. title: Fashion Learning Studio
pitch: A fashion eSchool where WebMCP agents guide the user's learning experience interactively using quizzes and essays.
about_excerpt: A fashion eSchool where WebMCP agents guide the user's learning experience interactively using quizzes and essays. Like Comment Story Updates Course page2 Course page Site open in Chatgpt Site home page Inspiration Fashion education is practical, visual, and highly dependent on guidance. A learner may watch a sewing demonstration and still need someone to identify the important control point, connect it to an exercise, review their understanding, and show them what to do next. Instructor-led delivery does not scale easily, especially for adult and working learners who cannot attend scheduled classes. Conventional online courses provide content, but learners must navigate long course structures and interpret practical activities largely on their own. Browser agents normally have to guess their way through changing page markup. I built Fashion Learning Studio to explore a more trustworthy collaboration: the school supplies the curriculum, demonstrations, assessments, and rules, while the learner's chosen browser agent supplies patient, contextual support. WebMCP lets the agent understand and interact with the same visible learning interface without replacing the learner or taking credit for the learner's work. What it does Fashion Learning Studio is a standalone WordPress learning experience for fashion design and sewing. It combines accessible course pages, practical video lessons, layered assessments, authentication, persistent learner progress, and five browser-native WebMCP tools. The demo includes three learning paths: Fashion Foundations : Fabric to Silhouette introduces fabric behaviour and an A-line skirt exercise. Fashion Design Studio : Concept to Collection has six ordered layers covering design signals, colour, silhouette, materials, mood-board editing, and a final rationale. Sewing Skills : Machine Control to Finishing provides 19 ordered video-led topics, practice reflections, and a final essay. The agent can inspect the signed-in learner's state, open the appropriate lesson, begin an available exercise, explain what to observe or practice, stage a proposed response in the visible form, and recommend the next step. Passed layers unlock the next task, and every learner has separate course progress. The agent cannot claim a video was watched, submit or grade an answer, or silently change progress. It stages assistance in the shared interface; the learner reviews, edits, and personally clicks Submit my answer. Without WebMCP, the school remains fully usable through its ordinary interface. What people and agents can do together A learner can ask, “What should I learn next?” Instead of guessing from the layout, the agent reads authoritative course state, opens the correct lesson, starts the available exercise, and helps stage a concise response in the visible form. The learner reviews or edits it and personally submits it. WebMCP gives the agent a reliable vocabulary for the course while preserving learner authorship and school authority. It turns static self-paced content into guided learning without requiring an instructor to repeat every basic explanation. How we built it We built the project as a lightweight WordPress plugin using PHP, the WordPress REST API, user metadata, semantic HTML, accessible CSS, and framework-free JavaScript. A companion WordPress block theme keeps the learning experience focused and responsive. After capability detection, the page registers five contextual tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(): The five WebMCP tools are: get_learning_state Reads the active course, progress, current assessment, choices, and available actions. open_next_lesson Opens the learner’s available lesson visibly. start_exercise Starts the assessment after the lesson prerequisite is satisfied. review_current_answer Reviews the learner-written answer, identifies weaknesses, and displays improvement advice without submitting or saving it. get_progress_and_next_step Reports the accurate completion percentage and recommends the next action. The tools use bounded JSON Schemas, enums, length limits, additionalProperties: false, structured errors, appropriate read-only annotations, same-origin exposure, and lifecycle cleanup with AbortController. Protected REST routes require an authenticated WordPress session and valid REST nonce. WordPress remains authoritative for state transitions, grading, and persistence. The design uses progressive enhancement: the human interface remains primary and WebMCP adds collaboration only when supported. Assessment and progress are deterministic. No external AI API or API key is required by the website; the learner's browser agent supplies the intelligence and invokes the site’s structured tools. Codex helped refine the product scope, translate the educational workflow into tool contracts, implement and review the plugin, improve the learner experience, define security and confirmation boundaries, create deterministic tests, and diagnose hosting and browser-support issues. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was understanding that WebMCP is not an embedded chatbot. It is a browser-native bridge through which an agent discovers capabilities supplied by the current page. That changed the design from “add an AI teacher” to “make the school understandable and operable by the learner's chosen agent.” The hardest product decision was where autonomy should stop. Automatically submitting an educational answer might look impressive, but it would undermine learner agency and academic integrity. We separated assistance from commitment: the agent explains and stages work, but only the learner can submit, grade, or save it. Browser support is still experimental, so we needed a complete standard interface and graceful fallback. We also had to create a public demonstration without exposing learner records, proprietary course data, or private video configuration. Hosting anti-bot protection challenged some automated requests. This revealed a broader deployment issue: agent-ready applications need authentication and hosting security that recognise legitimate, user-authorised agent activity without weakening protection. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built a coherent fashion-learning experience rather than a tool-registration proof of concept. Connected five task-specific WebMCP tools to authenticated learning state. Connected agent assistance to visible lessons, exercises, feedback, and progress. Preserved learner authorship through a clear human-confirmation boundary. Created three course structures, including layered design work and 19 video topics. Kept video configuration and learner information outside the public release. Built deterministic assessment without paid model calls from the website. Preserved full functionality when WebMCP is unavailable. Added structured evaluation journeys and deterministic client and server tests. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it communicates application intent and trust boundaries, not merely when it replaces clicks. Tool names, schemas, allowed actions, state responses, and visible effects must agree. We learned to distinguish between reading information, changing the visible interface, staging a proposed change, and performing a confirmed consequential action. In education, preserving a meaningful learner action can be more valuable than maximising automation. The website must remain authoritative for authentication, access, assessment, progress, and completion. The agent provides explanation and assistance but does not replace the school's rules or the learner's responsibility. Agent-ready education can reduce the instructor bottleneck. Educators encode the course sequence, demonstrations, rubrics, common mistakes, and escalation rules once, while agents help individual learners move through that trusted structure at their own pace. What's next for Fashion Learning Studio Next, we will integrate this interaction model into the full Unikon eSchool LMS, where it can work with real courses, sections, lessons, quizzes, projects, submissions, portfolios, progress records, and certificates. We plan to expose tools dynamically according to the learner's page and state, evaluate tool selection with more natural requests, add instructor-authored rubrics and feedback, and provide accessible transcripts and captions. We also plan to add personalised study timetables, evidence-based participation tracking, missed-session catch-up plans, and escalation to a human instructor. Future activities could accept photographs, pattern files, and CAD exercises so an agent guides the process while an instructor evaluates fit, construction quality, and final competence. Our long-term vision is an agent-guided, instructor-supervised mobile fashion school that serves learners continuously without requiring an instructor to repeat every basic lesson. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: Fantasy Draft Dash
pitch: Turn fantasy draft order into a live, verified football spectacle! Complete with chaotic runners, instant replays, announcer moments, a dramatic Toilet Bowl, and a provably random finish.
about_excerpt: Turn fantasy draft order into a live, verified football spectacle! Complete with chaotic runners, instant replays, announcer moments, a dramatic Toilet Bowl, and a provably random finish. Like Comment Story Updates Welcome to WebMCP Draft Day! Agents can enter your players, pick your colors and set your league name and channel Added in classic sounds, agents can Mute/Low/High music and FX A race to the bottom place in the toilet bowl your agent can't wait to watch! Watch the run with your agent (and players of course) Share in the drama with everyone Full screen for TV viewing, agents can set this to TV mode Instant reply chaos! Full draft order board your agent can use in other apps Verifiable results because every league has "that guy" Inspiration Every fantasy football league needs a draft order, but most leagues handle it by clicking a randomizer and reading a list, names in a hat, traditions that start the first argument of the season, etc. I wanted to turn that first moment into something people would actually gather around to watch and have fun with. Fantasy Draft Dash turns draft-order selection into a fake live football broadcast. League members become runners in a stadium race filled with penalties, bad decisions, phone distractions, questionable officiating, mascots, instant replays, and general fantasy-football nonsense. The goal was simple: Make a room full of adults scream at a television over a completely random draft order and solve the first major problem every draft day faces, free and easily. When someone complains you have a way to verify it was random. How it works The commissioner adds 4 to 16 players, picks a league name, chooses a fictional broadcast network, sets the race length, and decides how much chaos to unleash. Then you hit GO LIVE . The race plays out like a televised football event, complete with live standings, announcer updates, action replays, crowd energy, changing momentum, and a late-game Toilet Bowl for the final two runners. The important part is that the animation does not decide the draft order. Before the race starts, the app creates a cryptographically strong random seed and uses a deterministic Fisher-Yates shuffle to lock the official order. The race animation is generated separately from that locked result. It creates suspense, but it cannot secretly change who picks first. At the end, the app reveals the official draft board along with a verification seed so everyone can confirm the result. Fair randomness first. Completely unnecessary football drama second. How I built it I built Fantasy Draft Dash as a browser-based app using React, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Phaser 4, and OpenAI Sites. The app has one shared game controller that handles the league setup, roster, branding, race configuration, locked state, persistence, standings, results, audio, fullscreen mode, and reset flow. Phaser powers the animated race scene with runners, lanes, stadium visuals, weather effects, jumbotron moments, finish-line action, and the Toilet Bowl sequence. The rest of the interface handles setup, live standings, broadcast graphics, announcements, results, and verification. As part of this project I added WebMCP tools so an agent can safely configure the league, manage the roster, read the visible race state, validate the setup, and retrieve official results after the race is complete. The agent controls use the same guarded controller as the visible app, so tool access cannot bypass the locked-race rules. Challenges The biggest challenge was balancing fairness and drama. If the animation decided the winner, a visual bug could turn into a very real argument in the group chat. If the final order appeared immediately, the whole race would be pointless. Locking the result before kickoff solved both problems. The next challenge was designing for a television instead of a laptop. The app needs to work with anywhere from 4 to 16 players while keeping the field, names, standings, broadcast graphics, replay window, and controls readable from across a room. Timing was another big one. Early replay moments moved too quickly, so there was no time to react before the next thing happened. I slowed down the key action beats and gave tackles, phone distractions, sideline chaos, and other disasters more room to land. Audio also took some tuning. Music, crowd noise, whistles, impacts, cheers, and event sounds all sound great individually. Played at once, they sound like a soundboard falling down the stairs. Separating the layers and adding volume controls made the whole broadcast feel much more intentional. What I learned I learned that random results feel more trustworthy when people can understand how they were created. Showing the seed and explaining the locked shuffle makes the result easier to trust than simply saying, “Don’t worry, it was random.” I also learned that comedy is a systems problem. A funny event needs the right animation, camera framing, sound effect, announcement, text timing, and player name to arrive together. Treating race events as data-driven sequences made that much easier to tune. Most importantly, designing for a group changed the product. Bigger type, stronger contrast, persistent standings, longer replays, fullscreen support, and fewer competing messages mattered more than adding another setting. Put your league on the biggest screen you have, add everyone’s names, crank up the chaos, and let the draft order ruin somebody’s night. title: BenchPilot
pitch: Human evidence. Agent structure. Shared control for safer electronics troubleshooting.
about_excerpt: Human evidence. Agent structure. Shared control for safer electronics troubleshooting. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Hardware troubleshooting often becomes an unstructured stream of chat messages, photos, measurements, guesses, and repeated questions. The person can touch the physical system, but the agent can organize far more context than a person wants to track manually. BenchPilot gives both sides one inspectable workspace without letting the agent pretend it observed the hardware. What it does BenchPilot is a shared diagnostic canvas for safe low-voltage electronics. The human records symptoms and de-energized measurements. The app maps device topology, ranks evidence-linked hypotheses, maintains a safe test plan, preserves an append-only history, and produces a diagnostic report. In a WebMCP-capable browser, BenchPilot registers 12 typed tools over the same live case state. An agent can read the case and canvas, focus visible components, propose safe test steps, record only values explicitly supplied by the human, organize hypothesis updates, draft a cautious plan, and undo its own accepted changes. Every write is visible, attributed, reviewable, and reversible. Why WebMCP WebMCP is the product's collaboration layer, not a decorative integration. A troubleshooting agent needs structured topology, stable entity IDs, evidence provenance, unit and power-state validation, and a safe way to change the same workspace the person sees. Scraping page text cannot reliably provide those guarantees. BenchPilot's WebMCP tools use strict schemas and compact result envelopes. Human and agent actions share one command layer, so validation, revision checks, history, proposals, and undo behave identically from either interface. The site remains fully useful when WebMCP is unavailable. How we built it BenchPilot uses Vinext/Next.js App Router compatibility, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Zod, @xyflow/react, Drizzle migrations, and Cloudflare D1 on OpenAI Sites. A deterministic NEMA 17 seed and rule engine make the flagship journey repeatable without an external LLM or physical hardware. Safety is enforced at the domain boundary: allowlisted test templates, strict type/unit pairs, disconnected-power requirements for resistance, session/case isolation, optimistic revision checks, rate limits, proposal review, actor attribution, and targeted undo. The release gate includes unit tests, WebMCP contract tests, production builds, and desktop/mobile browser journeys. Challenges The hardest design problem was balancing useful agent autonomy with human ownership of physical truth. BenchPilot lets the agent organize and propose while preventing it from silently inventing measurements or replacing canonical wiring. We also kept tool results compact while still returning revision, changed IDs, and a visible verification target. Accomplishments that we're proud of Twelve discoverable WebMCP tools operating on live shared state. A production-verified read, focus, proposal, human accept, and targeted undo loop. Deterministic D1-backed guest sessions with no login or paid API dependency. Unsafe energized resistance writes rejected at the API/domain boundary. Responsive manual fallback, accessible canvas list, and shareable report. Public MIT-licensed source with automated release gates. What we learned The best human-agent interfaces make authority boundaries visible. Structured tools help, but collaboration becomes trustworthy only when users can see why the agent acted, review the exact change, and reverse it without damaging human evidence. WebMCP rewards strong internal state design: stable IDs, provenance, revisions, and narrow commands improve both the agent experience and the manual product. What's next for BenchPilot Next steps include team case sharing, richer but still allowlisted device templates, instrument imports that preserve provenance, image-assisted label capture, and organization-level diagnostic playbooks. The safety boundary will remain deliberately narrow until each new procedure has explicit validation and review behavior. title: Inference Chip Index
pitch: A source-linked MLPerf leaderboard that lets people and AI agents compare inference hardware safely in the same visible workspace.
about_excerpt: A source-linked MLPerf leaderboard that lets people and AI agents compare inference hardware safely in the same visible workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inference-hardware comparisons are easy to get wrong. A leaderboard can silently mix workloads, scenarios, accuracy targets, units, or system-level and per-accelerator numbers. Traditional browser automation makes that worse because an agent has to infer meaning from controls and tables. I wanted a safer collaboration model: the website should expose the exact research operations it supports, the agent should act on the same visible interface as the human, and every answer should remain traceable to immutable benchmark evidence. What it does Inference Chip Index turns official MLPerf Inference v6.0 results into workload-specific, source-linked comparisons. Its leaderboard now exposes four imperative WebMCP tools: list_inference_slices discovers valid exact comparison boundaries. configure_inference_leaderboard changes the filters visible to the human. compare_inference_accelerators compares 2–8 accelerator families inside one exact slice and renders the result on the page. clear_inference_comparison removes the shared comparison without resetting the leaderboard. The central safety rule is simple: a tool cannot claim that one chip is universally fastest. Every comparison is constrained to the same release, Closed division, workload, scenario, accuracy target, metric, and unit. Results include immutable GitHub source URLs and SHA-256 hashes. If evidence is missing, the tool returns an explicit missing-evidence reason instead of inventing a number. How I built it The application uses Next.js App Router, TypeScript, React, and Cloudflare Workers through OpenNext. The normalized data is generated deterministically from the pinned MLPerf Inference v6.0 commit 4d3916ac9cf474b679cdfcf492d43a0559418ad1 . During the WebMCP Challenge submission period I added the browser-native collaboration layer with the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Pure validation and comparison logic lives in src/webmcp/leaderboard-tools.ts ; registration and visible state updates live in the leaderboard React component. An AbortController unregisters the tools cleanly when the component unmounts. The WebMCP layer reuses the same checked-in dataset and exact-slice invariants as the site. It does not introduce a parallel ranking implementation, fetch untrusted runtime data, invoke paid endpoints, or expose secrets. Tool input schemas reject unknown fields and validate all slice IDs, vendors, submitters, grouping modes, metric views, and accelerator slugs. Challenge-period work The reproducible data index and Lucid API existed before the event. The WebMCP extension was built specifically during the challenge window. Public commits 7b89ee5 through fd9f65f add the imperative tools, shared-state UI, tests, documentation, security header, MIT license, and production URL documentation. The public deployment includes that extension. Challenges I ran into Converting a dense technical leaderboard into a small, predictable tool surface without duplicating ranking logic. Keeping agent actions visible to the human while preserving manual control of the same React state. Preventing incompatible benchmark dimensions from being compared even when an agent supplies plausible-looking inputs. Explaining absent results as evidence gaps rather than treating them as zero. Preserving immutable provenance in every structured response without overwhelming the visual interface. Accomplishments that I am proud of One agent call can build a three-vendor comparison that immediately appears in the human's browser. Every returned row stays inside an exact benchmark slice and links back to immutable source evidence. The tool surface is read-only with respect to servers and payments, while still making useful visible changes locally. The app contains 145 verified results, 50 submitted systems, 13 normalized accelerators, and 9 exact slices. The implementation passes type checking, 21 automated tests, and a production build. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes domain invariants, not when it merely turns every button into a tool. A good tool contract can make an unsafe action impossible, keep agent and human context synchronized, and communicate uncertainty as structured data. I also learned that browser-native tools can be a better accessibility and audit surface than invisible automation: the human sees the filters change, sees the comparison render, and can verify the same immutable sources the agent used. What's next Add WebMCP tools for methodology explanations and dataset-diff inspection. Let a human pin a baseline row and ask an agent for compatible deltas. Extend the importer to later MLPerf releases while preserving immutable snapshots and tombstones. Add signed dataset manifests so agents can verify provenance independently. Study how WebMCP tool descriptions affect agent selection and user trust in data-heavy workflows. Repeatable demo Open the live leaderboard in a WebMCP-capable browser. Ask: “List the available exact inference comparison slices.” Ask: “For the GPT-OSS 120B Offline slice, compare AMD MI355X, NVIDIA B200, and Intel Arc Pro B60 using official system results.” Observe the comparison appear in the shared page with values, source links, and missing-evidence handling. Ask the agent to clear the comparison or configure another visible slice. Verification npm ci npm run type-check npm test npm run build Verified locally: TypeScript passed, 21 tests passed, and the production build passed. The deployed leaderboard registered all four WebMCP tools, and a live three-vendor comparison returned exact-slice values with immutable sources.
