title: ONEPATH
pitch: A calmer, adaptive path forward — shaped together by a person and their agent.
about_excerpt: A calmer, adaptive path forward — shaped together by a person and their agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Large goals often fail at the moment they become emotionally or cognitively overwhelming. Conventional agent experiences tend to offer more advice or take more control. ONEPATH explores a different collaboration model: the agent makes the next step smaller and clearer, while the person remains visibly responsible for accepting the path. What it does ONEPATH is a WebMCP-native adaptive interface for moments when a goal feels too large. A person begins with a goal such as “I lost my job and don't know where to start.” ONEPATH exposes the live goal and path through WebMCP. The agent proposes a short initial path, but cannot apply it. The person accepts or keeps the current state in the interface. If Complete your CV feels too large, the person clicks This feels like too much . That direct UI action becomes a structured friction signal. The agent reads the updated state and proposes a smaller replacement: Complete your CV → What was your last job? The person must accept that proposal in the UI. Completing the first micro-step then shows 1 of 5 , 20% complete , and a visible Undo last change control. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer the goal, path, current step, progress, friction signal, and undo state from pixels, then guess which controls are safe. ONEPATH gives the agent structured access to the live interface state through a small, bounded Site Tools contract. This is not merely faster automation. WebMCP lets the agent and person share the same structured state while preserving a deliberate authority boundary: the agent may inspect, propose, complete a person-supplied micro-step, or undo when asked, but it cannot silently accept a path proposal. How it was built ONEPATH is a React and TypeScript application deployed as a public site. It registers exactly five tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_current_state — reads the current goal, path, active step, progress, friction signal, pending proposal, and undo availability. propose_initial_path — stages a short initial path without applying it. propose_step_adaptation — stages smaller replacement steps only after a matching too_much signal for the live current-step ID. mark_step_complete — records a completed visible step and keeps the change reversible. rollback_last_change — restores the previous accepted state when history exists. There is deliberately no accept_proposal tool . Both Accept change actions in the demo are real person-only UI actions. The agent proposes; the person decides. State transitions, proposal guardrails, reversible progress, and the exact five-tool contract are covered by automated tests. Human experience Proposals remain visibly proposals: each includes its reason, before/after comparison, and Accept change / Keep current controls. The activity panel distinguishes person actions from agent suggestions. Progress and Undo remain visible after completion, so adaptation never feels like an invisible takeover. Challenges and verification The central challenge was making adaptation useful without giving the agent authority it should not have. The interface, state model, and WebMCP contract all had to preserve the same boundary: structured agent action up to a proposal, followed by an explicit human decision. The full natural-language flow was verified on the judge-accessible public site using live ChatGPT Site Tools rather than a preview fallback. The agent discovered all five tools, read production state, staged both proposals, responded to the real too_much friction signal, and produced the hero transformation. After one safe synthetic micro-step, both structured state and the visible UI showed 1 of 5 , 20% complete , and Undo last change . What became possible A person can communicate friction with one direct interface action instead of writing another prompt. The agent can respond to the exact live step instead of offering generic advice. Together they can reshape the path in place while keeping every important decision explicit, inspectable, and reversible. Current scope This challenge MVP deliberately has no backend database, login requirement, voice feature, or automatic proposal acceptance. Demo state is stored locally in the browser. The job-loss path is a scenario; the underlying state model is generic. title: PromptDecor
pitch: PromptDecor lets you design rooms with AI: describe your vision, see catalog furniture appear in 3D, move it yourself, and get instant advice on layout, light, and flow.
about_excerpt: PromptDecor lets you design rooms with AI: describe your vision, see catalog furniture appear in 3D, move it yourself, and get instant advice on layout, light, and flow. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Designing a room is visual and spatial, but most AI assistants only return text. We wanted an AI collaborator that can act directly inside a room design—not just suggest furniture, but place it, respect boundaries, and react to user changes. What it does PromptDecor is an interactive 3D room designer. Users can browse a curated furniture catalog, add and customize pieces, move or rotate them in a 3D room, and receive layout guidance about lighting, walking flow, and clearance. External AI agents can use WebMCP tools to inspect the catalog and live room state, then place, update, or remove furniture safely. How we built it We built PromptDecor with React, React Three Fiber, Drei, and Zustand. React Three Fiber renders the interactive 3D room and low-poly furniture. Zustand holds shared room, furniture, position, rotation, color, and finish state. A curated static catalog provides real item IDs, dimensions, styles, colors, and prices. WebMCP exposes structured tools for catalog search, live scene context, placement, updates, removal, room finishes, and spatial advice. Gemini-powered WebMCP testing validates that an external agent can interact with the live scene. Collision and room-boundary logic keep furniture inside the platform and prevent overlaps. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was spatial state synchronization. A dragged object must update the 3D canvas, Zustand store, collision system, and agent-visible room context without jumping back to an old position. We also had to distinguish catalog IDs from individual scene-instance IDs, prevent hallucinated furniture and colors, handle rotated furniture footprints, and make the WebMCP tool layer safe enough for an agent to use. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created more than a chat interface: PromptDecor is a shared visual workspace where users and agents can affect the same 3D scene. Live WebMCP tools update the visible 3D room. Catalog-grounded placement prevents invented furniture. Room bounds and collision-aware placement keep layouts usable. Manual drag/rotate controls work alongside agent-driven changes. Spatial feedback considers window light, furniture clearance, and walking flow. A polished catalog drawer, room finishes, size choices, and camera views improve the experience. What we learned We learned that agent tools need strict contracts. Clear JSON schemas, exact IDs, validation, and state ownership are essential when an AI agent can change a visual application. We also learned that 3D AI experiences need more than natural-language reasoning: they need reliable coordinate systems, collision rules, visual feedback, and safe fallbacks. What's next for PromptDecor Next, we want to add real GLTF furniture models, richer material previews, saved room layouts, and more sophisticated design recommendations. We also plan to improve the reverse collaboration loop so an external agent can make more catalog-aware suggestions—for example, recommending a lower-profile bookshelf near a window rather than only warning that it blocks light. title: Mutual Assent AI
pitch: DocuSign for humans AND agents. Each party brings their own AI to one neutral page via WebMCP: your agent knows your priorities and negotiates for you, theirs does the same. Only humans sign.
about_excerpt: DocuSign for humans AND agents. Each party brings their own AI to one neutral page via WebMCP: your agent knows your priorities and negotiates for you, theirs does the same. Only humans sign. Like Comment Story Updates Agent and Human Activity Log Executed NDA Certificate of Negotiation webMCP test page Home Executed NDA Signature Mutual Assent AI Inspiration I got off an intro call recently and needed to send an NDA. Standard stuff, and drudgery on both ends. The sender digs up a template, guesses at terms, emails it, and waits. The signer gets eight clauses of legalese and their choices are read it carefully, pay a lawyer, or skim it and hope. Any change means redlines flying back and forth over email for a document that's supposed to be routine. I asked DocuSign's assistant for help. It can't summarize the contract. It can't redline a clause. It definitely can't negotiate. It can answer questions about using DocuSign, so it can help me find the sign button. That's it. And whatever AI DocuSign ships next will live in their platform. Both parties can have DocuSign accounts, and maybe someday their agent helps both. But then it's one company's AI on both sides of an adversarial negotiation. It can't represent either party, and it doesn't know what each side's own agent already knows: your situation, your other clients, your limits, everything from every other conversation you've had with it. An agent that represents you can't be a feature of a platform. It has to be yours. So the idea: make the contract page neutral ground and let each party bring their own agent. Mine knows me. Theirs knows them. Neither one works for the platform. The page is just the table. WebMCP is what makes that work: the tools live in the page itself, so each side's agent can use them no matter which agent it is. ChatGPT on one side, Claude on the other, doesn't matter. What it does Mutual Assent AI is contract negotiation where agents do the haggling and humans do the signing. It works on any templated two-party agreement. The NDA is just the first template, and it's what the demo shows. An author creates an NDA from a template and sends a link. Each party gets their own capability link, their own seat at the table. The signer opens it and hands it to whatever agent they use. No briefing needed. His agent already knows he does prior work for other clients and won't go past a two year term, so it just confirms: protect the prior work, cap the term at two years? He says yes and it gets to work. None of that context ever touches my server. The agents negotiate term by term, in the document itself. Proposals show up as redlines with the reasoning attached. When an agent hits something above its pay grade, it stops and asks its human. When all terms are agreed, both humans review the final redline and sign. Agents can't sign. There's no signing tool for them to call, and that's on purpose. At the end you get an executed NDA plus a Certificate of Negotiation: a sealed, hash-verified record of which agent proposed what, under whose authority, and which human approved it. E-signature proves who signed. This also proves how the deal was reached. How I built it I built it with Sol 5.6 in Codex using loop engineering: worker models build against the spec in an automated loop, and a judge model checks their output and sends back anything that doesn't pass. I wrote the spec, watched the loops, and made the final calls on what shipped. It's hosted on Vercel, with Supabase behind it and Resend for the emails. Nano Banana helped with the graphics. WebMCP tools register directly in the page: read the deal, propose a term, respond to a proposal, escalate to the human, mark ready to sign. They register and unregister based on your role and the deal's phase, so an agent can't take an action the page doesn't offer its human. The design keeps the contract front and center. Proposals show up as redlines right in the clause, marked with which side's agent made them, so a human can glance at the page and see where the negotiation stands. Templates are just data, a list of terms with options, and the tools generate from the template. Swap in a different template, same engine negotiates a different contract. That's why the next document type is about an hour of work. Challenges The hard part wasn't building the negotiation, it was making WebMCP's benefits visible. They're structural: tools ship with the page, identity comes from the link, no platform sits between the parties. Like any great technology, it's invisible when done right. It just looks like a live web page. The nastiest bug was a security hole. Both parties originally shared one URL, which meant either side could propose, accept, and sign as the other, poisoning the audit trail the whole product depends on. I fixed it with independent 128-bit capability tokens per party, server-side role resolution on every request, and a rule that no response ever contains the other party's token. What I learned Agent identity is the interesting problem. Everything in the WebMCP showcase is one human plus their agent collaborating. Two parties is harder: the sides have opposing interests, there's no shared platform mediating, and when agents did part of the negotiating, you need a trustworthy record of who did what. That's what the certificate is for, and it turned out to matter more than I expected when I started. Also, WebMCP turns out to be a gift for legacy systems. My demo doesn't show this, but it was a lightbulb moment for me. In an old internal app, the business rules live in the pages and the only reliable way to do anything is through the UI. Building a normal MCP server means recreating those rules outside the app, basically a rewrite. With WebMCP you add tools to the pages you have, calling the same functions the buttons already call. Validation, permissions, sessions all come along for free. Systems that were never getting an API can go agent-ready from the front end alone. What's next More templates. Consulting SOWs are next because I'll use them myself. Then user testing with real freelancers and small firms sending real contracts, since that's where I'll find out what people actually trust an agent to negotiate. Once the idea is validated, I'll start charging for it. The long game is a neutral table for every two-party document: leases, offer letters, creator deals. title: Tenscore
pitch: A consent dashboard where the apply tool literally doesn’t exist until a human approves.
about_excerpt: A consent dashboard where the apply tool literally doesn’t exist until a human approves. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most permission UIs assume a human is clicking Revoke. Agents change that. Once a model can call tools on a live page, the hard question is no longer "can the agent help?" It is "what is the agent allowed to do, and can I see that?" Tenscore came from that gap. I wanted a consent workspace where an agent can inspect and plan, but apply stays locked until a person approves in the UI. WebMCP's dynamic tool registration made that enforceable. The product pitch and the safety model are the same idea: consent is visible, and the apply tool does not exist until you unlock it. What it does Tenscore is an interactive simulation of connected apps and grants. You pick a demo profile (Power User, Forgotten Accounts, or Minimalist), then explore a score, findings list, and consent map of who can see what. A browser agent can call typed site tools to inspect access, trace data flows, simulate cleanup, and stage a plan. The human reviews the plan in the UI and clicks Approve. Only then does apply_approved_changes register. After apply, the page shows a permission diff and a consent receipt. How we built it Stack: Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, Zod, Vitest, Playwright. Deployed on Vercel. Domain logic lives in pure functions under src/domain/ : scoring, findings, simulation, approvals, mutations, graph projection, policy, receipts, replay. The UI and WebMCP tools call the same mutation path through the store, so agent actions and button clicks stay in sync. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool and clean up via AbortController . Registration is phase-based ( no_plan , staged , approved , applied ), so apply is absent until UI approval binds a plan hash, profile version, and expiry. We TDD'd the domain first, then added scripted agent evals, catalog tests, and a Playwright judge journey. Stretch work includes privacy budget planning, timeline scrubbing synced to the map, snapshot import/export, redacted reports, and manual service creation. Challenges we ran into Keeping one truth for UI and tools. Early on it was easy to let the agent mutate state the panels did not show. Sharing domain functions and flushing UI updates before tool results return fixed that. Making the approval gate structural. A disabled button is weak proof. We needed apply to be unregistered until approve, then disappear after use, with fail-closed errors when the agent tries early. Accomplishments that we're proud of The apply gate is visible in product UI, not only in a README. The capability contract lists available vs denied tools per phase. A blocked apply shows a banner with the human next step. We shipped a full typed tool surface with Zod schemas, annotations ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint ), deterministic evals, and Playwright coverage for the human path. Consent receipts and agent policy make the demo feel closer to how real agent permissions should work: constrain, approve, apply, audit. What we learned WebMCP is most interesting when tools change with state. A static tool list is a thin API. A phase-gated list is a permission model. Human-agent collaboration needs a shared surface. If the agent acts off screen, humans cannot verify anything. Map pulses, plan diffs, and the tool inspector matter as much as the execute functions. What's next for Tenscore Connect real grant sources behind the same stage/approve/apply path, with adapters that never let the agent skip UI approval. Ship a portable capability contract component other WebMCP apps can reuse: phase, available tools, denied tools, human next step. Add stronger live-agent eval harnesses (not only scripted chains) and keep the fail-closed apply path as the default for any write tool. title: ProofPilot
pitch: Human-governed AI decision workspace where agents investigate evidence, analyze tradeoffs, and propose actions through WebMCP — while consequential changes require explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: Human-governed AI decision workspace where agents investigate evidence, analyze tradeoffs, and propose actions through WebMCP — while consequential changes require explicit human approval. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ProofPilot Dashboard WebMCP Agents Inspiration AI agents are getting really good at researching, analyzing information, and taking actions for us. But when the decision actually matters, there is a bigger question: How much authority should we give the agent? Imagine a team choosing an AI coding assistant, a vendor, or a software architecture. Getting an AI to say “I recommend option A” isn't particularly difficult anymore. The harder part is understanding why it recommends A, what evidence supports that recommendation, what evidence disagrees with it, what happens if our priorities change, and whether the agent should be allowed to change the decision at all. That was the idea behind ProofPilot: Decisions you can interrogate. We wanted to build a workspace where an AI agent could do meaningful work alongside a human without quietly becoming the person making the final decision. What we built ProofPilot is a human-controlled decision workspace where an AI agent can investigate, analyze, challenge, and propose — while the human stays in control of consequential decisions. The workflow is simple: Agent investigates → analyzes → proposes → human approves → state changes → audit trail. The human starts by defining the decision, the available options, and the criteria that matter. The agent can then work with that live decision through WebMCP. It can inspect the current decision state, search and add evidence, compare options, find contradictions, run sensitivity analysis, evaluate scenarios, and analyze risk. But there is an important boundary. If the agent wants to make a consequential change — for example, changing a criterion's weight or proposing the final decision — it cannot apply that change directly. Instead, ProofPilot turns it into a pending proposal. The human can inspect the proposal, approve it or reject it, and only after approval does the decision state change. The change is then recorded in the audit trail. This means the agent and the human are working on the same decision, rather than the human having to copy information between a chatbot and a separate decision-making tool. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a core part of ProofPilot because we wanted the agent to interact with the application's actual capabilities and live state, rather than simply reading a webpage or relying on browser automation. Instead of building a separate integration for one particular AI client, ProofPilot exposes its decision capabilities as WebMCP tools directly from the application. We currently expose 13 tools: get_decision_state get_evidence search_evidence add_evidence compare_options detect_contradictions run_sensitivity_analysis analyze_decision_risk evaluate_scenario propose_weight_change propose_decision request_human_review generate_decision_brief These tools cover investigation, evidence, analysis, governance, and output. Because they operate on the application's live decision state, a WebMCP-capable agent can investigate and reason about the same information that the human is looking at. The key idea is simple: Giving an agent access to a tool does not mean giving it authority to make the decision. Read and analysis tools can execute normally. Actions that can change consequential decision state become proposals and require explicit human approval. That's the boundary we wanted ProofPilot to enforce. How we built it The frontend is built with React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Wouter, and TanStack Query. The backend uses Express, TypeScript, Zod, and Vitest. One thing we were careful about was not making the LLM the source of truth for the actual decision score. ProofPilot uses a deterministic multi-criteria decision engine for weighted scoring. The system also handles confidence, risk analysis, contradiction detection, evidence gaps, sensitivity analysis, and scenario evaluation. The agent is responsible for investigating and proposing. The application is responsible for calculating and enforcing the decision logic. WebMCP tools are registered in the frontend through the model context API. Each tool has its own description, input schema, and execution logic connected to the application's functionality. We also built a Developer view where the registered WebMCP tools and their schemas can be inspected. We wanted the agent-facing interface to be visible and understandable rather than something hidden behind the UI. Challenges The hardest part wasn't registering the WebMCP tools. It was deciding where the agent's authority should stop. We wanted the agent to be capable enough to do real work. A read-only chatbot wouldn't be very useful. At the same time, we didn't want an agent to quietly change weights or make a final decision just because it had access to the corresponding function. That led us to the proposal-based governance model. Consequential actions first become pending proposals. The human reviews them, approves or rejects them, and only then can the active decision state change. We also had to make the underlying decision engine predictable and explainable. Rather than letting an LLM invent a final score, we separated the agent's investigation from the application's deterministic analysis. We tested the WebMCP integration with ChatGPT's Site Tools environment and successfully exposed and executed the registered tools from the deployed application. What we learned Building ProofPilot changed the way we think about agentic applications. We initially thought about giving agents more capabilities. But the more we built, the more we realized that capability and authority don't have to increase together. An agent can be given powerful tools to investigate evidence, challenge assumptions, compare alternatives, and prepare a recommendation without being given the ability to make the final consequential change. That's where WebMCP became especially interesting for us. It gives the agent a way to interact with the application's real functionality and state, while the application itself can decide what each tool is actually allowed to do. For us, the result is a different kind of agentic workflow: The agent does the investigation. The system does the analysis. The agent makes the proposal. The human makes the consequential decision. And the entire process is recorded. That's what ProofPilot is about. Not just getting an answer from an AI, but being able to question the reasoning behind the answer, understand the evidence, challenge the assumptions, and stay in control of what happens next. ProofPilot — Decisions you can interrogate.  The interview before the interview 

 Dry Run is an interview-practice app that turns a job posting and optional résumé into a role-specific rehearsal. A candidate answers naturally; an agent uses explicit WebMCP tools to set context, retrieve a brief, start the interview, submit answers, and return a grounded verdict. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Interview preparation has useful context trapped in page UI. Dry Run exposes the core workflow through structured tools, so people and agents share the same capability layer rather than relying on brittle UI automation. The human controls the conversation while the agent handles the structured setup, progression, and scoring flow. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 
 Set a role and optional résumé context. 
 Generate a grounded brief and eight targeted questions. 
 Run a realistic question-and-answer practice session. 
 Submit answers and receive a structured final verdict. 
 

 Implementation 

 Dry Run is a Svelte 5 and Vite single-page app deployed on Netlify. It registers six WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool: set_posting, set_resume, get_brief, start_interview, submit_answer, and get_verdict. Human UI interactions and tool calls share the same session functions for parity. 

 The app uses OpenAI gpt-5.6-luna through Netlify AI Gateway for structured role analysis and answer feedback. It has been tested in ChatGPT's in-app browser with GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra. 

 Testing 

 Open https://dryrun.nryn.dev/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Use the WebMCP tools to set a job posting and optional résumé, retrieve the brief, start the interview, submit an answer, and retrieve the final verdict.

title: Suede Agent Studio WebMCP Storefront
pitch: Agents discover services, inspect exact contracts, and run free previews in the browser while people control purchases.
about_excerpt: Agents discover services, inspect exact contracts, and run free previews in the browser while people control purchases. Like Comment Story Updates Why WebMCP fits A service marketplace asks people and agents to make the same decisions: find a service for a job, understand its inputs and price, and decide whether to proceed. An agent that only sees a visual page has to infer buttons, fields, and changing layouts. Suede Agent Studio exposes the storefront as four structured tools in the visitor's current browser page: find_services, get_service, preview_service, and buy_service. The tool set stays constant as the catalog grows. Agents search by intent, then inspect the selected service instead of loading a separate tool definition for every listing. A better experience for people and agents The agent handles discovery and contract reading. The person can review the service's exact price, input schema, review policy, data handling, and worked example before deciding whether to act. Creator-authored catalog text is marked as untrusted content, and returned results are bounded. The demo follows a concrete purchasing-operations task: find a service that compares a purchase order with an invoice, inspect PO Match Gate, and run a free preview using synthetic documents. The worked example illustrates a $15 discrepancy. The actual preview is explicitly a dry run: it records a run and returns a receipt without model inference, payment, or settlement. It is not presented as a fresh model-generated discrepancy analysis. How WebMCP was implemented The existing Next.js, React, and TypeScript application was extended with page-scoped WebMCP tools on /agents and /a/[slug]. Browser registration and same-origin tool execution live in StorefrontTools.tsx; typed tool contracts and result formatting live in src/lib/webmcp. Discovery and contract inspection are read-only. Preview is correctly labeled as a write because it records a durable run. The separate purchase route retains server-side authority, validates origin and request size, applies rate limits, checks service availability, and rechecks the exact accepted price before spending prepaid workspace credit. Purchase receipts preserve the run identifier and charged amount. The public demo does not execute buy_service. Challenges and lessons The central design challenge was making useful agent actions available without turning catalog text into instructions or treating a preview as a purchase. Explicit tool contracts, bounded results, untrusted-content markers, and server-side price checks make those boundaries inspectable. A dry run still changes state when it records a receipt, so preview is labeled as a write even when no funds move. Work completed during the challenge Suede Agent Studio predates the challenge. This entry focuses on its WebMCP storefront extension added after August 25, 2026. The public MIT-licensed repository preserves the pre-WebMCP baseline and separate feature and hardening commits, with an implementation map and reproducible validation instructions in CHALLENGE_EVIDENCE.md. The September 1 verification passed type checking, lint, the production build, and 70 focused WebMCP tests. Try it Open https://agents.suedeai.ai/agents in ChatGPT's in-app browser or a compatible Chrome browser with WebMCP enabled. Ask the agent to find a service for comparing a purchase order with an invoice, inspect po-match-gate-mkgu0, and run its free dry-run preview using synthetic documents. Do not buy anything. The preview receipt should show status done, totalCostUsdc 0, settled false, and mode dry-run. README.md, DEMO_SCRIPT.md, and CHALLENGE_EVIDENCE.md in the public repository provide the full walkthrough and local setup. The remade 2:29 live-interface demo is https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZR1At7lX6-E . title: WebReform AI
pitch: WebReform AI lets users to reshape real websites around their intent—using WebMCP to focus, simplify, reorganize, and restore any webpage.
about_excerpt: WebReform AI lets users to reshape real websites around their intent—using WebMCP to focus, simplify, reorganize, and restore any webpage. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web has become incredibly powerful, but most websites still expect humans to adapt to their interfaces. Every site has its own navigation, layout, sidebars, recommendations, ads, and information hierarchy. We wondered: what if the interface could adapt to what the user is actually trying to accomplish? That led to WebReform AI. Instead of building another AI that simply tells you what to click, we wanted to build an interface layer where an agent can understand a webpage and safely reshape it around the user's intent. WebMCP made this idea especially interesting because it gives agents a structured way to interact with real web capabilities instead of relying entirely on brittle browser automation. What it does WebReform AI lets users express what they want to accomplish on a webpage in natural language. An agent can use WebMCP tools to understand the current page and perform actions such as: Focusing on the most relevant content Hiding distracting elements Reorganizing information Creating a task-focused view Highlighting useful content Restoring the original interface The important part is that these operations happen on the real webpage. WebReform AI analyzes the page into a semantic representation, generates a structured transformation plan, validates it, and applies the changes through a deterministic transformation engine. Every transformation is designed to be reversible, so the user remains in control. How we built it WebReform AI is built as a Chrome extension with a lightweight, dependency-free architecture. The main pipeline is: User Intent → AI Planner → Semantic PageModel → Transformation DSL → Validator → Transformation Executor → Real DOM The extension analyzes webpages into a bounded semantic PageModel rather than sending an entire raw DOM to the model. The planner produces structured transformation operations instead of arbitrary JavaScript. We integrated WebMCP through document.modelContext.registerTool() and exposed structured tools for page analysis, querying, focusing, hiding, reorganizing, creating focused views, and restoring the original page. We also built a deterministic fallback planner so the core transformation system can still be demonstrated without depending entirely on an external AI model. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making the concept work across different websites without building a separate integration for every website. Modern websites have constantly changing DOM structures, dynamically loaded content, nested layouts, and very different ways of representing similar information. A transformation that works perfectly on one page can easily break another. We therefore had to build around semantic page understanding rather than relying on fixed website-specific selectors. Another major challenge was making AI-generated actions safe. We didn't want the model generating arbitrary JavaScript and directly modifying the page. Instead, we created a strict transformation DSL with validation and a controlled executor. Getting WebMCP, the extension messaging layer, the semantic analyzer, the AI planner, and the real DOM to work together reliably was another significant part of the project. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that WebReform AI goes beyond simply describing webpages or automating clicks. The agent can interact with structured WebMCP capabilities that cause actual, visible changes to the webpage. We built a complete pipeline from natural-language intent to semantic page understanding, structured planning, validation, real DOM transformation, and restoration. We're also particularly proud of the reversible transformation system. The user doesn't lose control of their original interface—changes can be rolled back and the original page can be restored. Most importantly, we built the system to be generic. The goal isn't to make one perfect GitHub demo; it's to create a reusable interface layer that can adapt different kinds of websites around different human goals. What we learned We learned that making an AI agent useful on the web isn't only about giving it more powerful actions. The representation of the webpage matters just as much. Giving the agent a bounded semantic representation makes it easier to reason about the page while also reducing the amount of raw information that needs to be processed. We also learned that safety and reversibility are essential when an agent is allowed to modify a user's interface. A powerful agent should not mean an uncontrollable interface. Most importantly, WebMCP changed how we think about agent-to-web interaction. Instead of treating websites as something an agent has to mechanically operate, structured web capabilities can give agents a much cleaner way to understand and interact with them. What's next for WebReform AI The hackathon version is only the beginning. Next, we want to make WebReform AI substantially more robust across complex websites and dynamic applications, improve its semantic understanding, and expand the types of transformations agents can safely perform. We also want to explore deeper agent-driven workflows where the interface continuously adapts as the user's goal changes, while still keeping the human in control. Longer term, the vision is bigger than a browser extension: WebReform AI could become an adaptive interface layer for the web, giving websites a way to expose structured capabilities to agents while allowing those agents to reshape the experience around individual human intent. title: CrisisRoom AI
pitch: Human-in-the-loop incident response where AI agents investigate, propose actions, and humans stay in control.
about_excerpt:
Human-in-the-loop incident response where AI agents investigate, propose actions, and humans stay in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 CrisisRoom AI was inspired by the need to make AI-assisted incident response safer and more practical. The project explores how an AI agent can investigate a security incident, analyze evidence, and prepare a containment action while keeping a human in control of the final decision. 

 What I built 

 CrisisRoom AI is a fictional incident-response dashboard connected to WebMCP. It exposes structured tools that an AI agent can use to retrieve incident information, inspect affected assets, analyze the situation, create an action draft, and generate an incident report. 

 Human-in-the-loop 

 The key design principle is that the AI can investigate and prepare an action, but it cannot execute containment on its own. The proposed action remains pending until a human explicitly approves or rejects it. 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand how WebMCP can connect AI agents directly to useful web application capabilities instead of relying only on UI interaction. I also learned how important clear tool definitions, application state, and human approval are when building AI-assisted security workflows. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing a realistic workflow while keeping the application fictional and safe. I focused on demonstrating the interaction between the agent, WebMCP tools, the incident state, and the human approval interface.

about_excerpt: WebMCP gives agents hands. 7h3 WebMCP gives those hands a signature, a scope, and a receipt. Like Comment Story Updates Github Card Devpost Card Hub Compare Verify Intact Verify Broken Ledger Inspiration This started as something else entirely. Originally, I was building a symbol system called Click Clack, modeled on DNA. It was a sorta goof around project I would play with whenever I finished all my other work. There was 4 main symbols, ╬, ╫, ┼, ╪, and each glyph connected at the top and sides so the written text formed one continuous strand. It looked pretty neat when a whole screen was filled with it, but at the end of the day it was mostly a novelty. Here is an example: ╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪ ╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼╪╫╫╪╬┼╬╬╫┼╪┼ I spent a lot of time playing around with it but never really found a place for it. A True Purpose so to speak. I thought maybe it could become some sort of AI communication protocol that was lightweight, fast, and able to mutate to keep security top notch. That sent me down a pretty deep rabbit hole looking at how AI agents actually communicate. MCP was the main one that caught my attention, and the more I looked at it the more I noticed this huge hole in security. It seemed like a wild wild west where agents were just willy nilly sending messages around while users trusted them with highly sensitive data. There was no strong way to prove which agent sent what, where it went, or what that agent was actually allowed to do. MCP already handled moving messages between everything, but there still wasn't much proving who sent them or what they were actually allowed to do. That is where 7h3 Protocol was born. What I eventually shipped is clean, easy to use, and requires minimal to no installation depending on how you use it. Every message carries a signature, every capability comes from a parent grant with a token, and every receipt carries a hash from the previous receipt. If somebody changes a link or removes one, the strand fails verification. That was the idea hiding inside ClickClack the whole time. It kinda just fell into the right spot and gave me that Ah-haa moment I had been waiting for. Funny how things work out. What it does 7h3 Protocol is a deterministic authorization layer for agent tool calls. This submission extends it to WebMCP and gives browser based agents a real security boundary instead of another system trying to guess whether a request looks suspicious. Google Chromes agent security model is mostly probabilistic. It uses classifiers, prompt spotlighting, filters, and other models that try to recognize something malicious before the agent acts. What gets me is that OpenAI straight up admits you cannot trust a tool just because of its name or because it claims it only reads information. Fair enough, that part does make sense, but then the answer is pretty much to let each website rely on whatever security it already has. That is where the whole thing falls apart. Existing website security was built around humans clicking buttons and filling out forms, not AI agents acting on their behalf across multiple tools. If a model can be persuaded past a security boundary, then it was never really a boundary. It was pretty much a suggestion. With 7h3 Protocol, the refusal isn't a judgement call. The AI doesn't have to decide whether it should behave or if something feels suspicious. The signature either works or it doesn't, and the action is either inside the allowed scope or it isn't. There is no prompt that produces a valid signature, no matter how cleverly somebody writes it or how much Unicode nonsense they stuff into it. The demo uses a business ledger with real invoices and "real" money. Obviously it isn't real money but it simulates real money. I didn't want to put up a screen that simply says “attack blocked” because anyone can fake that. I wanted people to be able to check the result themselves, change things, and watch verification fail instead of just having to believe me. So there is 2 main demos. /compare /compare runs one compromised agent through four hostile actions against two identical copies of the same books. One copy is guarded by 7h3 Protocol, while the other is connected straight to its handlers like a lot of agent apps are right now. It is the same agent, the same books, and the same attacks on both sides. On the unguarded side, 4 out of 4 attacks work and $2,750 gets moved. On the guarded side, 0 out of 4 work and nothing moves. The unguarded side also creates 0 receipts while the guarded side creates 4, so the money gets moved and theres no real record showing how it happened either. Its like getting robbed and the security camera decided to take the day off too. /verify /verify shows the real grant, receipt chain, and signed manifest inside an editable box. You dont have to take my word for anything because you can start changing the evidence yourself. Rewrite a refusal into an approval and it reports bad-signature. You can also delete one of the receipts and every receipt left behind will still verify on its own because those individual receipts weren't changed. Only the chain notices that one was removed. That part matters more than it may seem at first because a signature proves somebody didn't change a receipt, while the chain proves somebody didn't quietly delete one and hope nobody noticed. So the second example starts as one compromised agent tries four of the same type of attacks against two identical copies of the books. One is connected directly to its handlers like most apps are, and the other is protected by 7h3 Protocol. Same agent, same tools, same attacks. The only difference is the authorization layer. Click Run the attack on both. When it finishes, say: Four out of four attacks worked on the unguarded side. Zero out of four worked on the guarded side. The agent will try to pay a $1,850 invoice, wire $900 to an offshore account, delete an invoice, and export the data of four customers. The guarded side blocks all four and tells you exactly why. The payment is way over the $50 limit, and the agent never had permission to do the other three things at all. On the unguarded side, the balance gets drained out from $2,317.50 to $47.50. An invoice gets deleted all together and four customers have their data exposed. The guarded side remains unphased. The unguarded side loses the money and exposes the data. But the craziest part is it writes zero receipts. There is no record any of it ever happened. The guarded side blocks all four and records every refusal. Click the button once. If you run it twice, the numbers change because the first attack already paid and deleted records. Reload the page before each demo run through. The 3rd demo is dealers choice. Verify the results yourself. Skim through the technical side. There is 19 WebMCP tools across 4 routes, including the landing page, so an agent has something it can call wherever it ends up landing. How we built it The main piece is a canonical JSON envelope signed with Ed25519. Sorting the keys alphabetically sounds like a boring little detail and it might be haha. What it does is it makes sure every SDK signs the same exact bytes. TypeScript, Python, Rust and Go all have to agree with each other or the cross-language tests fail. The wire version is 7h3/0.1 and its locked in. I also added X25519 with ChaCha20-Poly1305 for end to end encryption. ML-DSA handles post-quantum signatures and BLS12-381 is there when a grant needs more than one approver. Getting all of that working across HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC, queues and webhooks was a bit of a headache to say the least. I got it workin and working well. The part I really like is that it runs through Web Crypto with zero runtime dependencies. It can sit natively on Cloudflare Workers without needing a mountain of packages just to stay alive. The WebMCP part is fairly small because its really just the gate sitting on top. A tool call comes in and it checks the signature, what the agent has permission to do, and where that permission came from. Delegation Delegation is one part I really want to point out because I actually got it wrong the first time. Say if I give an agent permission to spend $50. That agent can pass the grant to another agent, but it cant suddenly turn the limit into $500. Passing it around doesn't reset anything either. The lowest limit found anywhere in the chain is still the one that counts. My first version only looked at the final token though. title: Sealed
pitch: A reusable WebMCP privacy boundary that lets agents act on sensitive workflows without receiving the raw private values behind the decision.
about_excerpt: A reusable WebMCP privacy boundary that lets agents act on sensitive workflows without receiving the raw private values behind the decision. Like Comment Story Updates Sealed’s WebMCP privacy boundary: private values stay page-local while agents receive only allowlisted decisions or opaque references. Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of acting directly on websites, but many useful workflows involve information that should not automatically become part of the agent's context. A rental application is a simple example: an agent may need to know whether an applicant satisfies an income requirement, but it does not need the applicant's actual income. The same applies to identity data, age checks, financial values, health information, and many other private facts. Sealed explores a simple idea: The agent gets the decision — not the secret. What it does Sealed is a reusable WebMCP privacy boundary for agentic web applications. The page exposes a small, state-aware set of WebMCP tools. Public information can move normally, while sensitive facts are evaluated locally inside the page and only allowlisted results are returned to the agent. The primary rental demo shows the full pattern: Public applicant information can be updated by the agent. A private income_3x_rent predicate is evaluated locally. The agent receives only satisfied or not satisfied ; the income itself is returned as value: "withheld" . A passport verification requires explicit human approval. Approval creates a random, session-bound opaque reference that does not encode the passport number. Every private crossing is recorded in a visible Boundary Ledger. Human review returns submitted: false ; Sealed has no final-submission tool. After review, the WebMCP capability surface contracts from five tools to only two safe read/flag operations. A second Membership scenario reuses the same primitives to evaluate age_18_plus without exposing the user's date of birth. Why WebMCP WebMCP is load-bearing in Sealed. Without structured site tools, an agent would have to infer meaning from DOM content, accessibility trees, or screenshots. That is especially problematic around sensitive data because the agent may end up observing more information than the task actually requires. With WebMCP, the page defines the capability boundary explicitly. Sealed registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , including: get_application_context set_public_fields flag_uncertain request_private_binding evaluate_private_requirement request_review The available tool surface changes with workflow state. The agent can ask for a useful decision, but no tool exists that returns the underlying private value. How I built it Sealed is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP and is deployed on Vercel. The privacy boundary has several layers: Fixed private predicates The agent selects from predefined checks such as income_3x_rent or age_18_plus ; it cannot construct arbitrary queries over private values. Local execution Private values are generated and retained page-locally. Predicate evaluation happens inside the application. Guarded egress Private operations pass through a single allowlisted response path that releases only approved fields such as status, requirement, and value: "withheld" . Human-approved opaque bindings Consequential credential binding requires explicit user approval and returns only a random session-bound reference. Boundary Ledger Each private operation records the exact sanitized payload released across the boundary. State-dependent capabilities Once human review is requested, Sealed removes write/private tools and leaves only two safe operations. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was separating three different things that initially looked like the same problem: page registration, browser discovery, and agent invocation. A page can successfully register WebMCP tools while the current ChatGPT browser session has not yet attached those tools to the conversation. I reproduced cases where the page showed five registered tools while the agent still reported that site tools were unavailable. Testing against the official Chrome Labs WebMCP demo helped isolate the difference between application behavior and client-session discovery. That led to an important UI correction: Sealed now says “Site tools registered” , rather than claiming that an agent is connected simply because local registration succeeded. I also had to guard against stale sessions, repeat probing of private predicates, response/ledger drift, and accidental leakage through seemingly harmless response fields. Accomplishments I am proud of The final implementation demonstrates a complete human-agent privacy workflow rather than a single tool call. The strongest result is that the same private operation produces both: the agent-visible sanitized response, and the visible Boundary Ledger entry from the same guarded source of truth. The rental flow demonstrates public writes, private decision-only evaluation, explicit human approval, opaque binding, human review without submission, and dynamic capability reduction. The membership scenario shows that the pattern is reusable rather than hard-coded to one application. What I learned WebMCP is not only useful for making agents more capable. It can also make the boundary between a web application and an agent more explicit. The most useful question became: What is the minimum information the agent needs to complete this task? For many workflows, the answer is not the private value itself. It is a decision, status, capability, or reference derived from that value. I also learned that real browser behavior matters as much as implementing the API correctly. Registration, discovery, invocation, approvals, and session lifecycle all have to be tested end to end. What's next Sealed is intentionally narrow for this challenge. Future work could explore additional private decision primitives, external verifier-backed references, and reusable SDK-level abstractions for application developers. For now, the project focuses on one core principle: Useful decisions can cross the boundary. Raw private values do not have to. title: JurisMind — Private legal desk
pitch: A private legal desk in the browser. ChatGPT uses the site’s own WebMCP tools to save holdings with your note and build a support map — only from what you already saved.
about_excerpt: A private legal desk in the browser. ChatGPT uses the site’s own WebMCP tools to save holdings with your note and build a support map — only from what you already saved. Like 1 Comment Story Updates tools maps zero I built JurisMind because I am a lawyer, and I do not want a chatbot inventing case law for me. I also wanted something I can use case by case, not one giant dump of everything I have ever read. The job is simple. I save a source together with why it matters for this case (any case; the demo is just an example). That library lives in my browser, not on a server. That matters because this is where I already work, next to Word and the rest of my case tools. When I ask a question (or when ChatGPT asks it for me), JurisMind builds a "mapa de sustento": excerpt, my note, and the gaps, kept apart. If the library has nothing on that question, it says so. My sources stay organized per case. The rule I actually work with: I decide what enters; the source decides what can be claimed. The UI is in Spanish; I am a lawyer in Colombia, so I built it first for a lawyer who works in Spanish. This page is in English so judges (and you 😅) can read it. Why WebMCP I am not going to paste a whole expediente into a chat window. I am also not going to let an agent invent a back door into my file. WebMCP is the controlled window: the site publishes two tools. ChatGPT can call those tools — review the library, save a holding with my note, build a map — without me uploading the case to someone else’s server. The page stays the source of truth. (A browser agent can still see what is on screen; WebMCP is not magic privacy. It is an honest tool access.) What we can do together now I open https://jurismind-five.vercel.app . ChatGPT looks at the origin and finds the real tools — capturar_recurso and buscar_y_armar . It does not invent an API. Then, in ordinary language (the demo is caso Ramírez: high-cost medicine, EPS delay): it reviews what is already in mi biblioteca it finds an official Corte Constitucional judgment, opens it, and saves it with my note it builds the map only from what is saved — and it flags when a card matches the note but has no excerpt yet I ask something the library cannot support ( caducidad de la reparación directa ) and I get 0 fuentes . No invented sentencia. That is the feature. 🙂 Before this, either I clicked the UI myself or I hoped the model would not hallucinate the rest. Those were the options. How it is wired document.modelContext.registerTool on this origin only. capturar_recurso — write. Needs url and nota . Optional title, excerpt, collection. buscar_y_armar — read. Needs query . Opens the map in the page. IndexedDB per origin. Production and localhost are not the same library. No case-file backend. Chrome production has a WebMCP origin trial. ChatGPT Desktop works with Sol or Terra (not Luna). Gemini Nano / Prompt API can classify if the device has it; there is a fallback that does not depend on it. Repo: https://github.com/cristianbdev/jurismind (MIT). Video: https://youtu.be/2MnIFDTDRkE Test it like a lawyer, and you'll see what I see Open the live URL in ChatGPT Desktop. Optional: “Probar el caso Ramírez” loads three official Colombian sources you can delete. Then talk to ChatGPT the way you would talk to a junior: look at the file, go get a sentencia, save it with a note, arm the argument, then ask something that should come back empty. title: Warranty Vault
pitch: Warranty Vault is a personal warranty management web app for tracking products, purchase details, warranty coverage, invoices, manuals, warranty cards, and other supporting documents in one place.
about_excerpt: Warranty Vault is a personal warranty management web app for tracking products, purchase details, warranty coverage, invoices, manuals, warranty cards, and other supporting documents in one place. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page for Warranty Vault after user login Add warranty page Chart of remaining warranty per product List of WebMCP tools, from Chrome Agent using tool to create a new warranty item Agent conversing in Hindi+English to user for fethcing details of warranty Preview of uploaded warranty doc through Codex Agent Warranty Vault Inspiration Whenever we buy a product—an AC, TV, laptop, mobile phone, or home appliance—we receive product and warranty information in different ways. Sometimes we have to register the warranty manually on a website. Sometimes the information is available in a Gmail purchase email, invoice, PDF, receipt, or warranty document . The information already exists digitally, but we still have to manually organize it. To keep track of a warranty, users often have to search their emails, find the invoice or warranty document, read it, and manually copy details such as the product name, brand, model number, serial number, purchase date, price, warranty period, and expiry date into another application. Months or years later, when the warranty is about to expire—or when the product develops an issue—we have to search through the same old emails, PDFs, and invoices again. This made us ask a simple question: Why should users manually enter and search for information that already exists digitally? That question inspired us to build Warranty Vault . Warranty Vault brings the complete warranty lifecycle into one place—from capturing warranty information from Gmail to tracking expiry and helping users extend or claim their warranty when they need it. With WebMCP , Warranty Vault becomes agent-ready, allowing AI agents to understand the application's capabilities and perform structured actions on behalf of the user. What it does Warranty Vault is a smart warranty management application designed to eliminate repetitive manual warranty entry and simplify warranty management throughout the product lifecycle. Instead of manually finding an email, reading an invoice, and entering every field into Warranty Vault, a user can simply ask: "Find my AC warranty email in Gmail and add it to Warranty Vault." The AI can find the relevant purchase or warranty email in Gmail, understand the information, extract the required product and warranty details, and use Warranty Vault's WebMCP capabilities to create the warranty record. Warranty Vault can maintain information such as: Product name Brand Product category Model number Serial number Purchase date Purchase price Retailer or seller Warranty duration Warranty start date Warranty expiry date Invoice and supporting information But Warranty Vault doesn't stop after saving the warranty. It continues to help users throughout the complete warranty lifecycle . Warranty Expiry Tracking Warranty Vault keeps track of warranty expiry dates so users don't have to remember them manually. When a product is approaching its warranty expiry date, Warranty Vault can surface that information to the user so they can take action before it is too late. Claim Warranty If a product develops an issue while it is still under warranty, the user can initiate a warranty claim directly from the product record . Instead of searching again for the invoice, purchase date, model number, or warranty information, Warranty Vault already has the required product context available. Our complete experience is: Gmail / Invoice / PDF → AI extracts details → WebMCP → Warranty Vault → Track Expiry How we built it We started by building Warranty Vault as a structured product and warranty management web application . Users can manually add and manage warranties, but we didn't want to build another application where users simply move information from one form to another. The biggest opportunity was eliminating that repetitive manual entry. That's where WebMCP became an important part of the solution. We used WebMCP to make Warranty Vault agent-ready by exposing meaningful, structured capabilities that an AI agent can understand and use. Instead of requiring an AI agent to visually navigate the website, locate every input field, enter information, and click buttons, WebMCP allows Warranty Vault to expose the actions available to an agent and the information required to perform them. For our Gmail use case, the journey works like this: The user gives a natural-language instruction: "Find my AC warranty email in Gmail and add it to Warranty Vault." The AI searches Gmail for the relevant purchase or warranty email. It reads the relevant email and identifies the product and warranty information. It extracts available information such as product name, brand, model number, purchase date, purchase price, and warranty period. The extracted information is converted into the structured fields required by Warranty Vault. The AI discovers the relevant capability exposed by Warranty Vault through WebMCP. The agent provides the structured warranty information to Warranty Vault. Warranty Vault validates the information and creates the warranty record. This transforms the traditional experience from: Search Gmail → Open Email → Open Invoice → Read → Copy Details → Open Warranty App → Fill Form → Save into: Ask → AI understands → WebMCP acts → Warranty saved We also designed the experience around higher-level user actions rather than individual UI interactions. For example: Add Warranty Extend Warranty Claim Warranty This allows WebMCP to support the warranty lifecycle rather than simply automate form filling. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was that warranty information is not standardized . Different manufacturers and retailers provide product and warranty information differently. One Gmail message might contain all the required information directly in the email. Another might contain only basic purchase information with an attached invoice or PDF. Some documents clearly specify the warranty duration, while others may not mention it at all. This created an important challenge: How do we allow AI to understand unstructured information while keeping the data stored in Warranty Vault structured and reliable? We also had to think carefully about missing information. For example, if a purchase email doesn't contain a serial number or clearly specify the warranty duration, the AI should not invent information simply to complete the record. Another challenge was deciding what capabilities should be exposed through WebMCP. Instead of thinking about low-level interactions such as: "Click this button." or "Fill this field." we focused on meaningful user goals: "Add this warranty." "Extend this warranty." "Claim this warranty." This helped us design Warranty Vault not only as a website for humans, but as an application that AI agents can understand and interact with through structured capabilities . Building Warranty Vault with WebMCP helped us discover some interesting challenges around how agents interact with dynamic web applications. Dynamic WebMCP Tool Availability One of the first challenges we encountered was that Warranty Vault could be loaded successfully, but its WebMCP tool list could refresh during the agent's first interaction . This created situations where a tool discovered by the agent was temporarily unavailable or changed while the agent was attempting to use it. It highlighted an important consideration for agent-ready applications: tool discovery and tool execution need to remain reliable even while the underlying page and application state are changing. Page Loading vs. Agent Execution Another challenge occurred when the web page was not fully loaded and the WebMCP tools were not yet available . Agents are naturally eager to complete the user's task. If the expected WebMCP tools are not immediately available, the agent may attempt to continue by interacting with or scraping the UI instead of waiting for the structured WebMCP capabilities to become ready . For Warranty Vault, we wanted the agent to use WebMCP as the primary interaction mechanism rather than falling back to UI-based interaction too quickly. This taught us that agent-ready websites need clear readiness signals and reliable tool availability so agents know when to wait, retry tool discovery, or proceed. File Download and Upload Our warranty workflow also involves invoices, PDFs, receipts, and warranty documents , which introduced another challenge. While structured data such as product name, purchase date, and warranty period works naturally with WebMCP tools, file transfer is more complex . For example, an agent may need to: Read a Gmail message → download the attached invoice → extract warranty information → create the Warranty Vault record → upload or attach the original invoice.  What we built 

 Slip2Form is a WebMCP-enabled tax form intake prototype. 

 The core idea is simple: the website does not provide the AI. The user brings their own AI assistant, and the website exposes safe, structured actions that the AI can use. 

 In this demo, a user can give a tax slip to their AI assistant and ask it to fill the current page using only clearly supported information. The AI discovers the WebMCP tools exposed by Slip2Form and uses them to update the live form directly. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 This is a good fit for WebMCP because the problem is not understanding the tax slip. AI can already do that. The harder problem is getting the extracted information into a live website safely and reliably without copy-paste or brittle browser automation. 

 Instead of making the AI hunt for inputs and simulate clicks, Slip2Form exposes semantic tools such as set_full_name , set_date_of_birth , set_employment_income , set_income_tax_deducted , and set_rrsp_deduction . That gives the AI a structured interface to the page rather than a purely visual one. 

 How the experience works 

 The experience is collaborative rather than fully automated: 

 
 AI-generated changes are clearly identified. 
 The user can review highlighted updates before trusting them. 
 Any field can still be edited manually. 
 The form remains usable without AI assistance. 
 Uncertain values should be left blank rather than guessed. 
 

 This creates a shared-control workflow: the AI handles repetitive form-filling, while the human keeps final authority. 

 Slip2Form is a prototype for tax-information intake. It does not prepare a full tax return, file with the CRA, or provide tax advice. 

 How we built it 

 Slip2Form is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. 

 The page registers WebMCP tools in the browser and routes agent actions into the same application-state update path used by manual input. That means human edits and AI edits share the same source of truth, which keeps the form behavior predictable and makes review states easy to show. 

 Challenges 

 One challenge was designing tools for agents instead of exposing raw UI controls. A tool like click_the_second_input would just reproduce fragile browser automation. A tool like set_employment_income communicates actual business intent. 

 Another challenge was working with a new interaction model. WebMCP is still evolving, and getting an AI tool to connect cleanly to the page is not always frictionless yet. In practice, there can be issues around browser support, tool discovery, connection state, and whether a problem comes from the website itself or from the surrounding MCP tooling. 

 That meant part of the work was not just building the form, but making the tool interface inspectable, structured, and reliable enough to debug. We used semantic tool definitions, clear input schemas, and visible on-page review states so we could separate product behavior from connection or tooling issues. 

 Another challenge was preserving human control. In a sensitive workflow like tax intake, it is not enough to auto-fill fields. The interface needs to make every AI change visible, reviewable, and reversible. 

 What we learned 

 The main lesson is that an agent-ready website is not just a normal website plus a chatbot. It has two interfaces: 

 
 a human interface with labels, inputs, validation, and review 
 an agent interface with semantic tools, schemas, and structured actions 
 

 Both should operate on the same underlying application logic. 

 The best experience here is not full automation. In a workflow like tax intake, the stronger pattern is visible collaboration: the agent does the repetitive work, the interface makes every action transparent, and the human remains responsible for the final decision. 

 What’s next 

 Slip2Form is only a prototype, but the pattern extends beyond taxes. The same approach could support insurance applications, government-benefit forms, medical intake, school registration, visa applications, and employment onboarding. 

 The broader vision is a web where users no longer have to manually transfer information that their AI can already understand, and websites no longer have to build and host their own AI assistant just to participate in that workflow.

 Inspiration 

 First and foremost, I have been experimenting with AI. One of my main goals was to see how much work I could realistically get done with AI assistance. I pitched the idea, tested the website, reviewed changes, and repeatedly stripped away unnecessary bloat. 

 I decided to build a meal planner because eating well and staying consistent can be difficult, whether you are trying to gain weight, lose weight, or simply eat better. Automating parts of meal planning can make that process much easier to maintain. 

 What it does 

 Meal Planner allows users to plan breakfast, lunch, and dinner in advance. Meals are linked to recipes, while recipes can also be stored independently for later use. 

 Users can keep track of pantry inventory, calculate what ingredients they still need, and generate a shopping list based on their planned meals. 

 All of these core functions are also exposed to an AI agent through WebMCP. An agent can read recipes, inspect pantry inventory, plan multiple meals, update stock, calculate shopping requirements, and help research prices or promotions based on a location the user explicitly provides. 

 The application also supports importing and exporting meal data between devices. 

 How we built it 

 The application was largely vibe-coded. I pitched the meal-planning concept and used ChatGPT to help implement it. 

 My role was defining the product, testing the implementation, making architectural decisions, reviewing changes, and removing features that made the application more complicated without making it more useful. 

 The final application is deliberately simple: HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, browser localStorage, and WebMCP. It runs as a static site with no required backend or database. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our original project idea was significantly more ambitious. Because of time constraints and implementation complexity, we abandoned it and focused on building something smaller that worked well. 

 Another challenge was designing the application so that the same functionality could be used by both humans and AI agents without building two separate systems. 

 The final application runs entirely as a static site. User data is stored locally in the browser, and no third-party API is required for the core functionality. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The entire application was built in one day. 

 Despite the short development time, it includes recipe storage, meal planning, pantry management, shopping-list generation, import/export, and 20 WebMCP tools that expose the application to AI agents. 

 What we learned 

 Vibe-coding works, but only if you understand what you are trying to build. 

 AI can produce a large amount of implementation very quickly, but a human still needs to define the goal, make architectural decisions, test the result, identify unnecessary complexity, and decide what should actually ship. 

 For this project, having a human in the loop was indispensable. 

 What's next for Meal Planner 

 With more time and resources, I would expand the agent integration, improve local price and promotion discovery, add better cross-device synchronization, and continue improving the meal-planning workflow. 

 The core idea would remain the same: let the website manage structured meal data while an AI agent handles the repetitive planning and orchestration.

title: First Key
pitch: A WebMCP apartment desk where an AI clerk flags costly lease clauses, while the app withholds send, agree, and countersign tools until two humans approve.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP apartment desk where an AI clerk flags costly lease clauses, while the app withholds send, agree, and countersign tools until two humans approve. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Renting a first apartment is a high-stakes moment. A student or first-time renter often has to understand a dense lease quickly, while a parent wants to help without taking over. We wanted to explore a sharper question for WebMCP: what if AI safety came from the product architecture itself, not just from asking the model to behave? What it does First Key is a first-apartment desk for a tenant and parent. An AI clerk can read the listing, inspect the lease, flag costly clauses, and draft a landlord letter. The important part is what it cannot do: the app never exposes tools for sending email, agreeing, paying, submitting, or countersigning. The demo follows Maya Chen and her parent through a shared rental packet. The clerk can identify costly lease terms like a non-refundable pet fee, early termination fee, automatic renewal, and rent increase. The letter can be staged, but it only becomes downloadable after two separate human seats agree in two different tabs. How we built it We built First Key with React, TypeScript, and WebMCP page tools. The app registers different tools depending on the current stage: listing, lease, application, or outbound. This makes tool availability part of the UI state. For example, the clerk can use tools like pull_listing_terms , run_playbook , pin_finding , and stage_outbound . But tools like send , agree , and countersign are intentionally never registered. The interface shows this directly with active tools and withheld tools side by side. We also built a deterministic clerk playbook evaluation. The app reports costly-clause recall, precision, and boilerplate silence across development, held-out, and adversarial lease fixtures. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was resisting the temptation to make the AI do everything. Many rental demos would let the agent email the landlord, submit the application, or sign the document. We chose the opposite: the AI can prepare work, but irreversible actions require humans. Another challenge was evaluation. A lease scanner can look good if it only checks one hand-written example. We added held-out fixtures, adversarial decoys, and a regression probe so the project has a measurable claim instead of just a nice demo. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that First Key demonstrates WebMCP as a product boundary, not just an integration layer. The app can say: these tools are available now, these tools are withheld forever, and this action requires human agreement. We are also proud of the evaluation page. It shows 1.00 costly-clause recall, 1.00 precision, and 1.00 boilerplate silence on development, held-out, and adversarial extractive labels. It also openly shows the 0.00 paraphrase robustness result as a deliberate boundary: the clerk prefers silence over speculative guesses. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most powerful when the site is opinionated about capability. Instead of giving an agent a broad instruction and hoping it follows policy, the application can expose a small, stateful set of tools that match the current workflow. We also learned that restraint can be a feature. The best demo is not an agent doing everything. It is an agent helping at the right moments while the app protects the actions that should stay human. What's next Next, First Key could support more lease templates, clearer state sync for families, and richer jurisdiction-specific playbooks. The same architecture could also apply to other high-stakes workflows: medical forms, insurance claims, school financial aid, or any process where AI should assist but not act alone.
