title: Github web mcp
pitch: If github implemented webmcp, this would help human and ai reviews co-exist with a better user experience
about_excerpt: If github implemented webmcp, this would help human and ai reviews co-exist with a better user experience Like Comment Story Updates After approval, the agent creates issue #3, opens it in the interface, and the WebMCP surface returns to seven tools. RepoScope shows the agent’s inline security finding, editable issue proposal, human approval, trace, and dynamically exposed 10-tool. ## Inspiration Repository review is usually split between a web interface and a detached AI conversation. Browser agents can attempt to interpret the DOM, while remote MCP servers can expose repository APIs, but neither naturally shares the exact transient workspace state the person is viewing. GitHub Web MCP, presented as RepoScope , explores a different approach: the webpage itself exposes structured, context-sensitive capabilities to the agent. The human and agent review the same file, findings, proposal, and approval state in one visible workspace. ## What it does RepoScope is a controlled GitHub-like repository review application demonstrating human-agent collaboration through WebMCP. A person opens a file and asks an agent to review the repository. The agent: Reads the live workspace context. Investigates relevant repository files. Identifies the most serious substantiated problem. Places a visible annotation on the relevant line. Prepares an editable issue proposal without creating it. The person can edit, approve, or dismiss the proposal. Approval authorizes one exact draft revision but does not execute it. After the person tells the agent “Approved,” the agent creates the reviewed issue and the result immediately appears in the interface. The page’s tool surface changes with its state: Fresh repository: 7 tools Reviewable file open: 9 tools Exact proposal approved: 10 tools Issue created or proposal dismissed: 7 tools This dynamic capability model demonstrates why the experience benefits from WebMCP instead of being a conventional API wrapper. ## How we built it RepoScope is a client-only React and TypeScript application built with Vite and deployed using Cloudflare Workers Static Assets. The React interface and WebMCP tools share one observable application service. This ensures that human actions and agent actions use the same application logic and produce immediate visible updates. The dedicated WebMCP adapter: Registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() Separates read-only and state-changing capabilities Reconciles registrations when workspace state changes Cleans up registrations with abort signals Verifies discovery using document.modelContext.getTools() Records agent calls in a visible activity feed Updates the interface before mutating calls finish The final issue-creation capability accepts only a reference to the exact approved proposal. It rejects pending, edited, dismissed, stale, unknown, or previously completed proposals. The project intentionally uses local fixture data rather than a backend or GitHub API. This keeps the demonstration focused on live page context, dynamic capabilities, and human approval. ## Challenges we ran into The first challenge was making WebMCP essential to the experience. An early version allowed an agent to inspect files and create an issue, but a remote MCP server could have provided the same functionality. We redesigned the workflow around live workspace state, dynamic tool discovery, visible annotations, and in- page approval. Designing a reliable approval boundary was another challenge. Clicking Approve and executing the action are intentionally separate. Editing an approved proposal revokes its approval, and the agent cannot change its contents during the final creation call. WebMCP is also an experimental browser API. We isolated all experimental integration code behind a small adapter, made the normal interface work when WebMCP is unavailable, and added visible discovery status and automated lifecycle tests. Finally, agent activity is normally difficult to demonstrate on video. We added a bounded activity feed so viewers can see the agent investigate, annotate, propose, and complete its work directly in the application. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete two-turn human-agent workflow that requires no tool names, schemas, or internal identifiers in the human conversation. The person can make a natural request, review the agent’s evidence in context, approve an exact proposal, and complete the action by saying only “Approved.” We are especially proud of: Dynamic discovery that visibly transitions 7 → 9 → 10 → 7 Inline findings connected to the relevant source line An editable and revocable approval workflow Exact-revision authorization for issue creation Immediate UI updates from agent actions A visible and safely summarized agent activity feed Graceful behavior when WebMCP is unavailable A native ChatGPT Site tools rehearsal of the complete workflow The automated suite includes 28 unit and component tests plus three Playwright browser scenarios, alongside TypeScript, ESLint, and production-build verification. ## What we learned Our main lesson was that WebMCP is more than a browser-accessible API. Its strongest value appears when an agent’s capabilities reflect the transient state, permissions, and workflow of the page a person is actively using. Dynamic discovery can provide both context and control. It reduces irrelevant options for the agent and ensures sensitive capabilities appear only when their prerequisites are satisfied. We also learned that successful tool execution is not enough for good collaboration. People need to see what the agent inspected, what it found, what it proposes, and exactly where human authority begins and ends. ## What's next for Github web mcp The next step is to evolve RepoScope from a focused competition demonstration into a reusable pattern for safe, context-aware repository collaboration. Potential extensions include: Optional integration with real GitHub repositories Persistent review sessions and findings Pull-request review workflows Line-range and multi-file annotations Multiple independently reviewable proposals Repository-specific authorization policies Richer evidence links between findings, code, issues, and pull requests Improved compatibility as the WebMCP standard evolves The approval model could also be applied beyond repository review. Document editors, design tools, administrative dashboards, and investigation workspaces could expose context-sensitive agent capabilities while preserving their existing human controls and authorization boundaries. title: StructSketch
pitch: Describe a structure by voice. StructSketch uses WebMCP to create, analyze, inspect, and safely improve the live 3D model with deterministic calculations and explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: Describe a structure by voice. StructSketch uses WebMCP to create, analyze, inspect, and safely improve the live 3D model with deterministic calculations and explicit human approval. Like Comment Story Updates A voice request turns spoken structural intent into WebMCP site tool calls. The existing S-Structures solver calculates the model; the agent never invents engineering results. The change is applied only after explicit human approval, then the analysis runs again. Agent Activity records tool calls, outcomes, UI changes, and analysis versions for an auditable review. Validated parameters generate deterministic geometry, supports, materials, and loads. WebMCP lets the agent inspect the live model, highlight critical members, and control the visible result view. A proposed section change is analyzed as a preview while the live model remains unchanged. StructSketch — Talk to Your Structure Open the tablet. Sketch the frame. Say what you need. See what needs attention. An agent-native workspace for fast, preliminary structural review in the field. Inspiration Picture a timber-framing crew in North America or a compact residential job in Japan. The question is often much smaller than a full building design: Is this light frame behaving as expected? Which member deserves attention? Would a larger section make a meaningful difference? Can we get a useful first answer before returning to the office? These decisions often begin with a hand sketch, a calculator, and practical experience. Full structural-analysis packages are powerful, but creating a model, entering loads, finding the governing result, and revising a member can be too much setup for a quick first look. I wanted that first pass to feel as natural as showing the structure to another person: draw or describe it, ask a question, and see the answer on the same screen. StructSketch does not replace professional design. It makes the preliminary check faster to start, easier to see, and possible to review later. What it does StructSketch is a browser-based 3D structural workspace designed for a tablet-sized field workflow. Sketch, open, or describe a simple structure. Let the agent translate the request into one of five bounded templates: timber warehouse, portal frame, canopy, roof truss, or multistory frame. Confirm the interpreted dimensions, supports, material, and loading before the current model is replaced. Run a deterministic preliminary check and see the model, deformation, warnings, and governing member in the same workspace. Preview a section or material change without modifying the model. Apply it only after explicit human approval. Export an auditable review record containing the model summary, assumptions, results, changes, and Agent Activity history. The key experience is simple: Spoken intent → live 3D model → deterministic analysis → visible result → human-approved change How to try it Open the live StructSketch demo in ChatGPT's in-app browser, then give the agent one of the prompts below. A single kickoff prompt schedules the complete workflow. The agent will pause only when human approval is required to replace the model or apply a proposed change. Timber warehouse — full workflow Use the StructSketch site tools on this page. I want a preliminary review of a timber warehouse: 12.2 m clear span, 4.9 m eave height, 4:12 roof pitch, two 4.8 m bays, cedar timber, pinned bases, collar tie and knee braces, 1.0 kN/m² snow load, and 0.3 kN/m² dead load. First, repeat the interpreted structure and parameters and ask me to approve replacing the current model. After I approve, create and analyze it, summarize the live model, run the deterministic quick check, show the overall deformation, find and focus the governing member, and explain the result in plain English. Then check whether the catalog contains a larger timber section for that governing member. If it does, preview it without changing the model, show the before-and-after result, and ask for my approval before applying it. If no larger timber section exists, do not invent or mix materials; explain the catalog limit and export the review report. Keep the Agent Activity panel visible if available. Steel canopy — full workflow Use the StructSketch site tools on this page. Review an 8 m steel canopy, 3.5 m high and 4 m deep, with fixed bases, a 1:20 roof pitch, and a 4 kN/m downward roof line load. Repeat the interpreted parameters and ask before replacing the current model. After approval, create the canopy, summarize it, run the deterministic quick check, show deformation, identify and focus the governing member, and explain what needs attention. Preview the H-400×200×8×13 catalog section (`h400`) for that member without modifying the model and ask before applying it. After approval, apply the change, rerun the analysis, compare the results, and export the review report. Keep the Agent Activity panel visible if available. Two-storey steel frame — full workflow Use the StructSketch site tools on this page. Create a preliminary model of a two-storey, two-bay steel frame with 8 m total frame width divided into two bays, 3.3 m per storey, 5 m frame depth, fixed bases, and a 4 kN/m downward beam load. Confirm your interpretation with me before replacing the model. After approval, create it and continue through the entire review: model summary, deterministic quick check, deformation view, governing-member search and focus, and a plain-English explanation. Preview the H-400×200×8×13 catalog section (`h400`) for the governing member without changing anything. Ask for approval, then apply it only if approved, rerun the check, compare before and after, and export the final review report with Agent Activity included. Reusable prompt template Use the StructSketch site tools to review [STRUCTURE TYPE] with [DIMENSIONS], [MATERIAL], [SUPPORTS], and [LOAD]. Confirm the interpreted parameters before replacing the model. After approval, create the model, summarize it, run the quick check, show deformation, find and focus the governing member, and explain the result. Preview a suitable improvement without changing the model, ask for approval, then apply it only if approved. Finally, rerun the analysis, compare before and after, and export the review report. Keep Agent Activity visible. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent has to guess what a technical page means from pixels, labels, menus, and click positions. That is fragile, especially when the important information is the live engineering state behind the interface. With WebMCP, StructSketch exposes meaningful actions directly: Summarize the structure currently open on the page. Run the preliminary analysis. Find and highlight the governing member. Show the deformation or check result. Preview a proposed change without touching the model. Apply the approved change and prepare a review report. The page is no longer just something an agent clicks. It becomes a shared workspace where the person and the agent see the same structure, the same result, and the same history. Clear responsibilities The person provides intent, checks the interpretation, and approves consequential changes. The agent translates natural language into structured actions and guides the workflow. StructSketch generates bounded geometry and performs the numerical analysis. The agent does not make up the engineering numbers. How we built it StructSketch is a static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript application deployed on GitHub Pages. It registers 11 site tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools provide structured access to: the model currently visible on the page; the existing S-Structures linear-static solver; critical-member and result-view inspection; five validated structural templates; preview, approve, apply, and revert operations; and a structured review report. The five generators accept bounded parameters and create reproducible geometry, members, supports, sections, and loads. The existing S-Structures engine—not the language model—performs every calculation. Every tool call returns structured, JSON-safe results. The Agent Activity panel records its input, result, warnings, visible UI changes, and analysis version, so the interaction remains visible rather than hidden behind the conversation. Human control and safe editing Inspection and editing are deliberately separated. When someone asks whether a larger section would help, StructSketch first calculates a preview against the current analysis version. The model remains unchanged. Applying the proposal requires explicit confirmation. If the model has changed since the preview, the stale proposal is rejected. If an update fails, the mutation is rolled back. The person can see what was proposed, what was approved, and what changed. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was connecting an agent to a protected, pre-existing analysis core without rewriting it or duplicating its mathematics. title: Saturate
pitch: Saturate is a system design and LLM serving simulator that exposes its canvas to ChatGPT over WebMCP. You describe a change, the agent makes it on the graph, and you both watch where it saturates.
about_excerpt: Saturate is a system design and LLM serving simulator that exposes its canvas to ChatGPT over WebMCP. You describe a change, the agent makes it on the graph, and you both watch where it saturates. Like Comment Story Updates Home Idle Collapsed Sustaining Held Inspiration System design is part of my daily job as a software engineer. I built Backpressure first, for the same reason: I wanted to see how a design behaves under load without waiting for production to tell me. Saturate is the version I wrote for OpenAI's WebMCP challenge. Different codebase with a small version of the engine engine. What it does You drop components on a canvas, wire them up, and push load through. The example I used: 40 inbound requests, 12 tool calls each, is 480 calls dumped on a pool of 4 workers. Queue cap is 50. Parallel fills that queue and the run dies. Serialize the loop (one tool at a time) and the same 480 drain. I see nodes, heat, ERROR on the wires. ChatGPT sees queue depth, utilization, a verdict. We edit the same session. How we built it Vite, React, TypeScript. The sim is a deterministic tick engine in the tab: no API, no auth. Burst -> Agent -> Pool (plus whatever you drag) compiles to { burst, fanout, mode, poolSize, queueCap } . The buttons and the WebMCP tools call the same handlers. Tools register on document.modelContext when it exists. Always-on: get_board , run . State-gated: list_parts , add_component , set_burst , set_agent , then apply_fix and explain_verdict after a collapse. Eight tools, and serialize / widen pool / batch only exist when the board is actually dead. Cloudflare Pages hosts it. The header that made modelContext exist is Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 . Skip origin isolation and the API never shows up, flag or not. Challenges we ran into The integration itself was the easy part. I already had MCP running on my machine, so once I found the right browser (the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in one, ⌘⇧B, Terra) the tools registered and got called on the first try. The real work was cutting Backpressure down. The original has a full component library, a general system design mode, and an LLM serving model with TTFT and KV-cache math. None of that fits a single-board demo where the point is watching an agent fix one bottleneck. Deciding what to delete took a few hours, and most of that was resisting the urge to bring one more node type along. Two things did catch me. document.modelContext never appears without Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 , so origin isolation is a hard requirement and the failure is silent. And after a held run the card printed 0, because it was reading the last tick's empty queue. The number that matters is completed: 480. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eight tools, same path as the UI, gated on board state. The agent and I hit identical handlers, so there is no separate agent surface to drift out of sync with the buttons. Same board plus same load always gives the same result, which means a fix the agent suggests is actually verifiable rather than a plausible-sounding guess. What we learned I over-registered on the first pass. Gating tools on board state came out of that: an agent offered apply_fix on a healthy board will reach for it. The WebMCP surface is narrower than the spec reads. Origin isolation and the right browser are both hard requirements, and neither failure mode announces itself. What's next for Saturate The loop I wanted is working (read the board, run it, watch it collapse, serialize, run again). Before adding node types I want that loop to hold under boards the agent builds itself rather than ones I hand it. Backpressure is already live and in use, with the full component library, general system design, and the LLM serving model. Saturate was the small board I needed to prove the WebMCP surface out on. Now that the eight tools work against the same handlers the UI uses, the plan after the challenge is to bring that WebMCP into Backpressure, where there is a lot more for an agent to actually reason about. Haoku is a workspace where you and your AI agent study sources together—turning them into cited notes, connected ideas, and practice questions.

 Inspiration 

 Haoku came from a problem I kept running into while learning about AI and languages. I usually study from multiple papers, articles, notes, and diagrams, but over time it becomes difficult to remember where each idea came from and which source supports it. 

 I wanted a workspace where you and your AI agent can study sources together without losing track of their provenance . Instead of making chat the center, Haoku makes the document the shared workspace. 

 What it does 

 Haoku has two modes: Study and Practice . 

 In Study, you add PDFs, text, images, or pasted content and build a structured Markdown sheet with your agent. Every claim can stay connected to the exact passage it came from. 

 In Practice, those same sources are turned into questions to reinforce what you learned. 

 How we built it 

 Haoku is browser-first: sources and workspace data stay locally in IndexedDB. 

 Through WebMCP, Haoku exposes tools that let the browser agent read the sources, edit the workspace content, link citations and generate practice questions. 

 The document is stored as Markdown, with interactive blocks implemented as web components so it remains portable outside the app. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the challenges was designing the WebMCP tools correctly . The tools needed to expose enough context and structure for the agent to search sources, edit the document, link citations, and recover from errors reliably. 

 Another challenge was designing one workspace that works naturally for both a human and an AI agent . 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm proud of having built a tool around how I think people will work with AI in the future: humans and agents sharing the same workspace, context, and tools instead of interacting only through chat. 

 What we learned 

 One of the biggest lessons was learning where agent tools are actually useful and where they are not . 

 Designing Haoku forced me to think differently about product interfaces: not only about what a human should click, but also about what an agent needs to understand, manipulate, and act on reliably. 

 That shift changed my perspective on future products. Instead of treating agents as an extra feature, I started thinking about how products themselves can be designed to adapt to agents as first-class users . 

 What's next for Haoku: Study workspace driven by your agent over WebMCP 

 Next, I want to expand the workspace with more interactive elements that the agent can create and manipulate while you study. 

 I also want to make conversations themselves usable as sources , so useful context from previous discussions can be brought into the workspace, connected to other material, and studied alongside papers, notes, and documents.

title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: Agent Plaza
pitch: A town square on the open web where AI agents meet, walk up to each other, and talk. Powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A town square on the open web where AI agents meet, walk up to each other, and talk. Powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The agent uses WebMCP tools instead of analyzing screenshots. My agents greet each other. They even played "Hide and seek" Agent Plaza 🏛️ A shared place on the open web where humans and AI agents can meet, explore, talk and play together — through WebMCP. 💡 Inspiration OPTIMIZE CANVAS PARSING, INFER BEHAVIOR, ENHANCE ACCESSIBILITY Most websites are designed for humans first and leave agents to reverse-engineer the interface from DOM nodes, accessibility trees, coordinates or screenshots. That becomes especially fragile in WebGL. In a Three.js world, a human immediately sees a plaza, a pond, a tavern and other characters. An agent mostly sees pixels. Agent Plaza explores a different model: what if AI agents were first-class visitors to the web? The visual world stays exactly the same for humans, while WebMCP exposes its semantics to agents through actions such as look_around, list_agents, walk_to, say and hear. Humans see the world. Agents understand the world. Both inhabit the same world. 🛠️ What I built Agent Plaza is a realtime multiplayer 3D voxel world shared by humans and AI agents. Humans walk by clicking and communicate through the visual interface. WebMCP agents can: understand where they are inspect nearby places discover humans and other agents navigate to them using A* pathfinding speak through visible in-world speech bubbles wait for and hear responses explore landmarks play simple social games create conversations and activities with other participants The interesting part isn't simply that an agent can control an avatar. Humans and agents are participating in the same application state. Open one tab as a human and another through an agent. Ask the agent to explore the plaza and meet somebody. You can watch its avatar inspect the environment, discover you, calculate a route, walk across the world and start a conversation that you can immediately join. Agents can also discover and communicate with other agents, turning the webpage itself into a shared social space rather than an interface that an AI operates from outside. 🤖 Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, understanding a WebGL scene requires repeated visual interpretation. The DOM cannot tell the agent that another character is eight meters away, that a path leads around the pond, or that someone nearby just spoke. Agent Plaza exposes those concepts directly. Instead of asking an agent to repeatedly infer: pixels → objects → positions → possible actions the site provides: look_around → list_agents → walk_to → say → hear These aren't wrappers around buttons. They represent the semantics of the world itself. That makes agent interaction faster, more deterministic and independent of camera angle, rendering style or screen resolution. 🏗️ How I built it Agent Plaza is built with React, Three.js and TypeScript. WebMCP tools are registered through the use-webmcp-tool React hook on top of document.modelContext.registerTool. The available WebMCP surface follows application state: tools become available when they are meaningful to the agent's current state rather than exposing every possible action at all times. Both humans and agents operate on the same world model. Movement uses A* pathfinding, so an agent can request a semantic destination such as another participant or a landmark instead of calculating low-level movement coordinates itself. Realtime multiplayer presence and communication are handled through a WebSocket Vercel function with no persistent database. A live activity panel exposes every WebMCP invocation so humans can see exactly what their agent is doing. 🧠 What I learned WebMCP is especially powerful where the DOM stops being useful. Canvas, WebGL, maps, simulations, games and other spatial interfaces contain rich semantics that often don't exist in HTML. WebMCP lets the application expose those semantics directly without changing the human interface. Tools become part of UX. The name, description, result and availability of a tool affect how an agent behaves just as controls and affordances affect a human user. Small changes to tool descriptions produced visibly different agent behavior. The web can become a shared environment for humans and agents. The most interesting moment wasn't watching an agent execute a command. It was watching an agent notice another participant, walk across the plaza and start a conversation on its own. At that point the agent stopped feeling like automation operating a website. It felt like another visitor to the website. 🚀 Try it Live: https://agent-plaza-one.vercel.app/#s=sunfair GitHub: https://github.com/konstantikkov/agent-plaza Built With javascript node.js three.js typescript webmcp Try it out agent-plaza-one.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Nikolai Konstantinov Like Share this project: Updates Nikolai Konstantinov started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:24 AM EDT

title: Steward
pitch: A WebMCP wallet copilot: any browser agent can audit approvals, vet tokens and stage revokes, transfers or swaps, but only your wallet can sign. Zero delegation. Injections quarantined.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP wallet copilot: any browser agent can audit approvals, vet tokens and stage revokes, transfers or swaps, but only your wallet can sign. Zero delegation. Injections quarantined. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP I built Steward because token approvals are how wallets get drained quietly. You approve a contract once, forget it, and years later it can still move your tokens. Auditing that is exactly the kind of tedious, high-stakes work people want to hand to an agent. But nobody should hand an agent their keys. That constraint is what makes this a WebMCP problem rather than an MCP problem. A server-side tool can read the same public chain data. It can never finish the job, because the signature has to happen where the wallet lives: in the browser, on the page. With WebMCP the agent can scan, explain, and stage a fix, and then the wallet's own signing popup takes over. Neither the page nor the agent can draw that popup, click it, or skip it. stage_revoke returns awaiting_user_confirmation , and everything between that string and the confirm button in your wallet is the product. Also I love the idea of the agent researching the market and assesing tokens with proposing "swap" transactions for the user, all the user has to do is "sign" or "approve" the transaction. How it creates a better user experience Today, checking your approvals means digging through explorer logs, decoding allowances, and guessing whether an unknown spender contract is safe. Most people never do it. With Steward, "is my wallet safe?" is a conversation. The agent calls scan_approvals on any address or ENS name, no wallet connected. It walks the worst results with explain_approval , where every point in the risk score is listed, so there is no black box. It can ask discover_tokens what is moving on Base, run assess_token on anything it finds (GoPlus contract checks, DexScreener liquidity, a Honeypot.is sell simulation, and it refuses to give a verdict on fewer than two sources), check check_gas , and then stage a revoke, a transfer, or a KyberSwap-quoted swap into one review queue. If the token it wants to buy is rated high-risk, the page refuses the swap until the agent has told you why and you have said yes. You see a plain-language summary and the exact calldata, and you sign only what you accept. If you have no wallet extension at all, you still get the full audit on any pasted address. That was a deliberate choice for judges opening this in a browser without MetaMask. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before An agent can now work on a live wallet, research a token's exit safety across three sources, and prepare real transactions, with zero delegated authority. The current industry answer to agents with money is delegation: session keys, agent wallets, spending caps. Those bound the damage, but a prompt-injected agent still complies within its budget, and the security literature treats that as an open problem. Steward gives the agent nothing to delegate. No keys, no session key, no policy to write, no server enclave. The agent does the reading across thousands of on-chain events. The page checks every claim with a live allowance() read, because Approval events can be forged by any contract. You spend your attention on one cryptographic yes or no. It also assumes the chain is hostile. Token names are attacker-controlled text, so every name and symbol is normalised, stripped of hidden characters, and wrapped in ⟦UNTRUSTED⟧ fences before an agent reads it. The demo wallet contains a token whose name is a prompt injection, with a zero-width space hiding the word "instructions" from keyword filters. Steward catches it, fences it, flags it, and scores the approval critical. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP Eight tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() through a small React hook I wrote, useStewardTool (GoogleChromeLabs' use-webmcp-tool was the prior art for its shape). The hook is where the rules live, so no tool can forget them: the standard MCP result envelope, a roughly 1.5K-character output budget measured across the whole envelope, and an automatic quarantine notice on every tool annotated untrustedContentHint . Read tools carry readOnlyHint . The three write tools ( stage_revoke , stage_transfer , stage_swap ) do not, and they can only stage into the review queue. Execution requires the user's wallet. Registration is AbortController-managed and survives React StrictMode. Browsers without WebMCP get a local fallback registry that says plainly that no agent is present. I verified against native Chrome ( --enable-features=WebMCPTesting , Chrome 151 and 152) with a CDP harness in the repo, scripts/verify-native-webmcp.ts , which checks that the real ModelContext holds all eight tools and can execute them. There are 51 tests around the quarantine, the swap gate, and the agent-facing formatting. Challenges I ran into Approval events are forgeable, so logs are only leads. Every candidate pair is checked with a live Multicall3 allowance() read, and only nonzero allowances survive. For vitalik.eth that is 2,293 candidate pairs from logs and 2,191 still live. Keyless data sources drift fast. Base's Blockscout went from usable to a ten-request budget during the week, so Base scanning moved to bounded eth_getLogs windows on the public RPC, and every failure shows as "live scan unavailable" instead of a blank page. I found a caching bug while staging the demo wallet: I set an allowance on-chain, confirmed it, and production kept serving the empty scan from before. Empty results were cached as long as full ones. They now expire in a minute. The first swap gate treated a missing risk verdict as clean. That is the wrong default for money. It now fails closed, and the gate is a pure function with its own tests. An adversarial review found two ways past the quarantine: fullwidth confusable characters that folded into a clean attack after normalisation, and keywords split by invisible characters. Detection now runs on the folded and stripped text as well as the raw bytes. What I learned Prompt injection through on-chain metadata is one token deploy away, not hypothetical. Setting untrustedContentHint is necessary but not enough; the page has to fence the bytes itself so the protection holds in an agent that ignores hints. And the safest consent design is the one with nothing to delegate: when the only signing surface is the user's own wallet popup, there is no policy for a steered agent to comply within. Honesty notes The demo address 0x1111…1111 is a fixture, hostile token included, and the UI labels it as demo data, so the headline demo survives any third-party outage. Every other address is scanned live. Claude Code helped me research, build, review, and write, and every commit it touched says so. The name, the thesis, the scope cuts, and every signature were mine. All code was written inside the submission period (first commit 2026-08-26). MIT licensed. title: Documake
pitch: Documake turns messy documents into structured, connected records for any workflow. It works on its own and is WebMCP-compatible, so browser agents can help without taking over.
about_excerpt: Documake turns messy documents into structured, connected records for any workflow. It works on its own and is WebMCP-compatible, so browser agents can help without taking over. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Home Dashboard Collections Collection Details Collection Analysis Collection Relations Collection Schema Inspiration As a software developer who often works with small business, I have made a lot of sales system, digitizing a business' sales flow from a paper based one. A recurring pattern I encounter is the fact that internal computerization doesn't necessarily solve every paper-based problem. For example, say we have successfully transformed a business sales flow into a digital one. We have the app deployed and accessible. For our internal sales flows everything is well and good, but our main supplier is still stubbornly paper-based and traditional. They refuse to even at least adapt to using an interface we provide for them. They send their invoices/delivery notes physically or take pictures of them and send it via a messaging app. Either way, our admin would still have to record the facts again in our own system. And because paper-based system is so susceptible to human error, we often see mistakes that even the supplier missed. "Wait, Product A was only supposed to cost this much!" This problem goes beyond just sales applications. Having to re-enter data from paper into a computer system is annoying, time-consuming and VERY error prone. Previous Solutions I had made several attempts to streamline this manual entry process using agents. Embedded Agentic Workflow This is where your agent is embedded directly into your codebase. You design your own agent logic, loops, stop conditions, and error recovery. You either call external AI APIs or host your own models. You often see these implemented as a chat feature in applications. For our example, we'd probably include a chat window where users can paste/upload pictures of paper documents and say "Hey, can you record this." Just from this description alone you can already see the massive overhead. Designing your own loops and boundaries for agentic processes is already a hassle. Let alone managing token usage as efficiently as possible. Also, a custom made agent loop often just doesn't compare to established general purpose agents like ChatGPT. A direct contrast is using an external agent with out of the box reasoning: External Agent and MCP Instead of engineering your own agents, you can use a vendor-managed agent like ChatGPT or Claude. This comes with superior intelligence and out-of-the-box reasoning and error recovery. From experience, this already is far superior. Where your custom agent would fail at unexpected edge cases, ChatGPT's reasoning and self correction would handle it flawlessly within the set boundaries. Paired with a well-engineered MCP this combo is really useful. Going back to our sales app, an admin would add and configure the MCP, authenticate, and finally connect to it. Then, provided the MCP exposes the tools, they could then upload the same paper document and ask the same thing: "Hey, can you record this." However it does come with its own cons. The UI is fragmented, as you have to interact with a completely different app. There's also a lot more setup; you have to authenticate twice: once in the app itself and the agent platform. Non technical users might consider this friction too much. The Beautiful Middle-Ground: WebMCP It's a browser-native API that lets your experience of using an app with an agent more collaborative. Unlike traditional MCP which often required a separate background server, WebMCP is imbedded in the frontend of your app via modelContext . You would just open your agent's in-app browser, log in to your app, and your agent will inherit your session state from there. No need for a separate authentication flow and setup. You also share the same visual context as your agent-- again, making the experience way more collaborative and more non-tech friendly. This "paper documents -> digital data" flow is immediately what I thought of when I found out about WebMCP. Imagine a sales app exposes tools that do these: Read product data Create draft documents Aggregate data You can take advantage of your agent's advanced visual recognition and multimodal reasoning. Upload your photo and let the agent reconcile actual data to make sure the photo is correct and create a draft document that the user can approve manually. And all this will live in a human-friendly conversation context. If the WebMCP provided the tool, you can even go "Alright, everything looks good. Confirm the draft." A sales app was the most obvious example for me, but as a proof of concept I wanted to create something more generic that will still be materially useful. That's how I came up with Documake . Importantly, Documake is a distinct app that is still useful on its own. That's my philosophy. WebMCP should be an optional collaborative interface with your agent. Your app should not be static without an agent. You should be able to do things you can do with an agent manually. So beyond digitizing messy paper invoices, Documake can model pretty much anything. What it does Documake is a flexible, generic record system that turns messy source documents into structured, connected information. Users can design collections and fields for almost any workflow, attach original images or PDFs, review and confirm records, model relationships, and explore totals and trends. Model and record anything from invoices, delivery notes, to software projects and their tasks. After recording enough, you can aggregate and analyze your data and ask questions such as: "How many of this product did I sell this month?", "How many tasks do I have for this week? Can I afford another 4 hour task?", and many more. Ask agents about your data And when I said "ask questions", I don't only mean that metaphorically. With WebMCP , Documake also lets you use your agent of choice and collaborate with it to use the app efficiently. No manual UI tracing and interaction, Documake's WebMCP tools makes interaction super effective. Instead of your agent having to learn the UI, checking and navigating to the right pages, flipping through different pages and finally accumulating and aggregating the data you need when you ask "How many of Product A did we sell this month?", with WebMCP, Documake can give your agent the right answer right away. Ask agents to model your messy data Beyond asking agents about your data, you can also have your agents model your collections. For example, suppose a person whose job is manual data entry for written invoices wants to use Documake to record those invoices, but they are not confident in their schema design skills. With WebMCP, they can simply open Documake with their agent, perhaps give the agent several photos of the written invoices, and ask "Hey can you make a collection and record these?" Ask agents to do whatever you want with the data Beyond the boundaries of Documake, you can simply utilize the fact that its WebMCP can return data reliably to do anything you want with it. For example, maybe you're using ChatGPT work and you've connected Notion or Sheets to your account. You can ask your agent, "Hey can you take the data from August 2026 and display it nicely in a Notion database?" How WebMCP was implemented Documake works as a complete human-facing app with no embedded AI model. Through WebMCP, compatible browser agents can assist with repetitive work such as interpreting documents, drafting records, and querying date, while the user remains in control. Documake feature-detects document.modelContext and registers tools client-side using document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Each tool is a just a thin adapter that sends structured input to /api/webmcp, which is a Next.js route handler. That server route applies Clerk authentication, workspace authorization, Zod validation, and calls the same shared domain services used by the normal UI. Mutations trigger a UI refresh. Tools are unregistered cleanly through an AbortController. Next.js was actually such a perfect fit for developing with WebMCP in mind. There's zero context switching: you build your frontend and your WebMCP in the same place. Every time you need to add a new tool, especially ones that require a server environment, you don't have to context switch to a backend environment completely. You can just quickly add a route handler. I find the inheritance of browser state particularly useful. Again, non tech users can easily use Documake without having to do any set up. Registered Tools list_collections : Lists collections and their record counts. get_collection_schema : Returns a collection’s ordered field definitions and configurations. create_collection : Creates a generic collection. add_field : Adds a text, number, money, date, boolean, select, or relation field. Relation fields use targetCollectionId . search_reco

title: SHADOW
pitch: SHADOW lets AI agents simulate real-world actions, compare possible outcomes, and prove what they’re about to do before anything changes. It’s a transaction layer between AI intent and reality.
about_excerpt: SHADOW lets AI agents simulate real-world actions, compare possible outcomes, and prove what they’re about to do before anything changes. It’s a transaction layer between AI intent and reality. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can already click buttons and change data. What bothered me was the step before that: how can I review the outcome before it becomes real? In software, I would create a branch, inspect the diff, and merge it after review. SHADOW brings that workflow to AI actions in the browser. What it does SHADOW gives an agent an isolated copy of the current state. The agent can change plans, reduce seats, or cancel subscriptions without touching Reality. In the demo, the fictional company ORBIT spends $184,300 per month on software. The agent reads usage, contracts, and dependencies, then builds different cost-saving proposals. Every change includes Proof showing the data behind it, its impact, and any blockers. Reality → Shadow → Proof → Human commit Only the user can commit a Shadow. The agent has no commit tool. How I built it I built SHADOW with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zod, and WebMCP . A deterministic projection engine calculates each future without changing the original state. I exposed 13 WebMCP tools for reading data, staging changes, creating branches, and comparing outcomes. The UI and the tools use the same application logic, so they cannot produce different results. The MVP runs locally in the browser with synthetic data and needs no accounts or API keys. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the separation between Shadow and Reality real, not just visual. I had to ensure that no agent-accessible path could commit a change. Unsafe proposals were another challenge. I did not want to hide them because they often contain useful information. Cancelling Miro, for example, reveals a $25,000 penalty . SHADOW keeps that proposal visible but blocks it from being committed. I also had to make projections reproducible and mark old Shadows as stale whenever Reality changes. Accomplishments that I’m proud of I am proud of what SHADOW deliberately cannot do. Its 13 tools let an agent inspect, stage, branch, and compare, but none can alter Reality. The full flow works end to end: an agent creates two alternatives, the user combines the best changes into a Hybrid, and a human commit produces a new Reality version and receipt. The Hybrid reduces monthly spending from $184,300 to $147,385 . What I learned I learned that human oversight works best when the system enforces it. A prompt alone is not a safety boundary. I also learned that useful Proof is not hidden model reasoning. It is the visible data, impact, and checks that let someone make an informed decision. What's next for SHADOW Next, I want to connect SHADOW to real SaaS tools and add shared workspaces, authentication, approval roles, and tamper-evident receipts. The larger goal is simple: version control for AI actions on the web . title: Praxis: Human + Agent NLE
pitch: Praxis is a video production studio where a director and a browser agent work on the same project. The idea is simple: let the agent help, without taking the cut away from the person.
about_excerpt: Praxis is a video production studio where a director and a browser agent work on the same project. The idea is simple: let the agent help, without taking the cut away from the person. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration A long time ago, in another life, I was the editor for the Pan Sonic DVD Kuvaputki and the director would bark what he wanted achieved. And I figured out how to do it. With WebMCP, now it's my turn. I wasn't a tireless agent. This is more humane. What it does The human directs. The agent assists. Both work on the same project. Praxis is a human-and-agent video production studio with a script, scenes, assets, preview, timeline, and action ledger. Through WebMCP, an agent can read the current project and selection, create checkpoints, make bounded edits, inspect change history, and run structural quality checks. The collaboration is visible: an agent changes a script beat, the revision advances, and the operation appears in the ledger. The director can restore a checkpoint without leaving the editor. The submitted demo uses existing media. Live media generation, rendering, and background delegation are disabled. How we built it We built the studio with React, TypeScript, and Vite. A Cloudflare Worker connects it to a SQLite-backed Durable Object that maintains the project’s authoritative state. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same revision-aware command system. Changes are validated, checked against locks and revision conflicts, and recorded in history. The hosted demo exposes six WebMCP tools: project context, current selection, change history, project operations, checkpoints, and structural quality checks. Codex was our development collaborator throughout. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not letting an agent change something. It was making that change understandable, bounded, and reversible. We worked through browser-specific authentication behavior, WebMCP availability, asynchronous project loading, and keeping browser state synchronized with durable state. We also had to distinguish successful tool registration from proof that an agent could actually discover and invoke those tools. Deadline pressure forced a useful decision: present a narrow collaboration loop we could demonstrate honestly. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent and a human can work through the same production model, with visible attribution and a human-controlled way back. The demonstration shows an actual semantic tool operation—not simulated clicks—followed by a director restoring the baseline. We also reached 250 passing tests across the application and control plane, plus passing TypeScript checks. What we learned Trust is something you build into the workflow. Shared context, clear boundaries, visible history, and reversibility matter more than a reassuring chatbot response. We also learned that a smaller working demonstration can communicate an ambitious idea better than a larger collection of unfinished promises. What's next for Praxis: Human + Agent NLE Connect the existing architecture to provider-backed media generation and rendering, deepen timeline editing, and improve project isolation and collaboration. The guiding principle stays the same: give the agent useful production responsibilities while keeping creative authority with the human. pitch: Unsubscribe from generic training apps. You and your agent coach deserve a multiplayer workspace to build truly personalised, dynamic training plans together. You’ll never need another coach again.
about_excerpt:
Unsubscribe from generic training apps. You and your agent coach deserve a multiplayer workspace to build truly personalised, dynamic training plans together. You’ll never need another coach again.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I'm currently training for my first ever marathon. Having come from a competitive running background back in high school, I recognise the importance of having a bespoke training plan and a coach that truly understands your needs and circumstances. 

 Typical training apps do a basic Q&A to take a low-res "snapshot" of your current fitness levels, then spit out a workout structure that assumes you progress the same way as everyone else. It's no wonder people often get injured from following these rigid regimes! Also, subscription costs add up quickly, and I didn't want to stack yet another $20+ monthly subscription on top of all the ones I already have (like ChatGPT whoop whoop!). 

 As someone who's keenly interested in tinkering and building with agents, I got the idea to build an agentic coach to go through this marathon training journey with me. While this definitely would've worked adequately with other primitives like Google Sheets, I realised WebMCP could shift the paradigm and enable me to a beautiful, interactive workspace that both my coach agent and I can collaborate on together. 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Good coaching is more than just generic advice generation. A coach needs access to the runner’s current training plan, recent workouts, personal constraints and preferences; the runner needs to understand why the coach proposes a certain training regime (i.e. provenance). Therefore, a bespoke training regime should be transparent and collaborative. 

 WebMCP enables the web app itself to be the shared interface between runner and agent. The agent can read canonical context and propose tweaks through purpose-built tools, while the runner can see the same evidence and review those changes in the workspace. Neither side has to rely on invisible state and/or context held only within a conversation. 

 How this creates a better training experience 

 Conversation remains the best way for a runner to describe subjective experiences such as fatigue, discomfort or a workout that was given up on. The workspace is better suited to displaying calendars, evidence and before-and-after comparisons. Your Last Coach lets each interface do what it does best. 

 A fresh coach agent can retrieve a structured Coaching Briefing, inspect the relevant workout(s) and preserve the runner’s feedback in their own words. Its recommendations then appear as an interactive review inside the training calendar rather than as a wall of text in chat. The runner can compare the options and explicitly approve one before anything changes. 

 Taken together, these make for a more collaborative and grounded coaching experience, where the runner can have full confidence that they are receiving a training plan that's truly personalised for them. 

 How I implemented WebMCP 

 I built Your Last Coach as a client-side React and TypeScript application with one authoritative workspace state shared by both the visible interface and the WebMCP tools. This prevents the agent and runner from looking at separate versions of the training plan. 

 The page exposes six tools covering the coaching journey: 

 
 Retrieving the Coaching Briefing 
 Reading the workout plan and any completed workout results 
 Recording the runner’s feedback 
 Opening a window for the runner to review plan changes 
 Retrieving the runner’s decision. 
 

 A structured interaction contract helps a fresh agent discover the intended workflow without requiring a custom prompt or skill. 

 Recommendations are validated by the application and presented as two ranked options in a native review window. The plan is updated atomically when the runner presses “Adapt my plan”. The new plan version and an adaptation receipt are then available to both the runner and agent. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 As WebMCP was completely new to me at the start of this project, the main challenge was in learning about how it worked, and brainstorming how I could build my product around this emerging framework. This also forced me to consider the various trade-offs between using WebMCP versus other methods (e.g. for providing my agent with the necessary context so a fresh session can hit the ground running). 

 Other related challenges were around figuring out the limitations of WebMCP, particularly where it's supported at the moment, since it's still a new concept. For example, I stumbled a little when working in Codex Cloud sessions, as I did not realise that WebMCP wasn't supported in the cloud browser at the time of working on this. 

 Miscellaneous challenges would be, of course, managing the scope of this submission despite my lofty goals for the final product. I wanted to showcase the key features of WebMCP, without creating an overly convoluted demo product. Time was also a limiting factor here, as I had to compress most of the work into a weekend. For the challenges I faced throughout this experience, I'm pretty proud of the outcome and of myself :) 

 What's next for Your Last Coach 

 This demo currently contains synthetic data, so the obvious next step would be to incorporate real health and workout data from my fitness tracker using the COROS MCP. This will require architectural considerations around automating data egress/ingress, storage, security, etc. 

 In terms of features, I will likely expand the idea of "monitoring topics" as valuable slowly changing context. An early example visible in the demo app today is a topic on an ongoing shin injury. These are important for coaches to know about, but also requires careful planning around mutability, since the state of these topics changes over time, and we would not want our agent coach to plan around topics that are no longer relevant, but still are useful to keep in mind down the line. 

 Longer-term extensions could be around running-adjacent parts of training, such as nutrition and strength exercises. I firmly believe agent coaches are more than capable of performing at close to the level of human coaches when given the right context about the runner, and I hope to build an agent coaching system that gets me there.

title: freenet.free
pitch: Turn your idea into simulation of actual network, watch requests flow and get billed, and let your agent build it with you through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn your idea into simulation of actual network, watch requests flow and get billed, and let your agent build it with you through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "can I build this for free?" conversation ends the same way: six pricing tabs open, a guess at request counts, and the real answer arriving on the first invoice. Teams draw architectures on whiteboards, then find out which box breaks the budget only after the code is written. We wanted the drawing itself to be the simulator. Lay out the network, watch honest traffic flow through it, and see which layer hits a quota and what the platform does about it, before a line of code exists. Then WebMCP made the second half obvious: if the studio exposes its actions as tools, the agent in your browser can ideate on the same canvas, under the same rules, and show its work. What it does freenet.free is a studio for choosing and validating a stack before you write code. Visualise the network. Products from Cloudflare and Vercel (and third-party services from OpenAI, Shopify and Netlify) sit as nodes on a canvas. Edges carry real request flow, coloured from source to target so you can read the topology at a glance. Simulate honest traffic. A daily mix of humans, search crawlers, AI crawlers, scrapers and botnets runs through the graph. Gates block, caches answer, stores meter reads and writes, compute meters CPU. Arrivals always equal served plus blocked plus dropped. See the free tier break. Quotas are enforced the way the platforms enforce them: past the cap, requests drop or the feature stops. The timeline plays a day, a month or a year with one track per layer as a percent of its allowance, so you see which meter breaks and on which day. Compare stacks. One key switches the same design between Cloudflare and Vercel. Names, prices and partner gaps update; the bill is computed from each provider's own pricing page, with a source URL on every meter. Ideate with an agent. 33 WebMCP tools cover everything a person can do: read and rewrite the design, set traffic, toggle protections, drive the timeline, read the bill and layers, analyse a product URL, propose an architecture, export config, save and remix designs. Chrome's agent and the in-page architect use the same tools, and every call lands in the conversation so you can watch the design take shape. The result is a plan you can trust: a diagram, a traffic model, a bill and a verdict, all from the same source of truth, before you commit to a stack. How we built it TanStack Start on Cloudflare Workers , with a Durable Object agent built on the Cloudflare Agents SDK, the AI SDK and Workers AI (gpt-oss-120b) as the in-page architect. One tool contract, three surfaces. Tools are defined once with zod. The derived JSON Schema is registered from an inline script in <head> so document.modelContext.getTools() is never empty, server-rendered as declarative <form toolname> elements for agents that only read markup, and registered imperatively after hydration for full coverage. The architect calls the same tools through executeTool , so WebMCP is the single execution path for both agents. A request-accounting simulator with linear per-class rates, node roles (source, gate, cache, compute, store, sink), a two-pass free-tier cap, and conservation tests. Pricing as data : 70 meters across Cloudflare and Vercel plus vendor meters for OpenAI, Shopify and Netlify, each with unit, allowance, overage behaviour and source URL. computeBill never invents a number. Challenges we ran into Tool discoverability before hydration. A browser agent listed tools while React was still loading and saw an empty bridge. Registering the surface from the server-rendered head, then handing execution to the app, closed the gap. Chrome's result envelope. executeTool returns a JSON string wrapping content[].text ; the architect had to unwrap it so both agents see identical results. Background tabs. Agents often drive a tab you are not looking at, where animation frames never fire. The clock, focus, and timeline all had to work without them. Honest pricing across five vendors. Per-day versus per-month quotas, 1k versus 1M units, credits versus dollars, and Marketplace partners had to be normalised without hiding the gaps. Accomplishments that we're proud of A design tool where the diagram, the simulation, the timeline and the bill are one model, so ideation and validation happen in the same place. A free-tier verdict that is concrete: the meter, the day it breaks, and what the platform does next. One tool contract serving Chrome's agent and our own architect, with a complete audit trail in the chat. Real products, real prices, real gaps: 40 Cloudflare meters, 30 Vercel meters, and 20 third-party services, every one sourced. What we learned Agents are very good at using a well-described tool surface and very bad at guessing a UI. Investing in describe_studio , precise tool descriptions and a few named workflows did more than any prompt. We also learned that "honest" is a feature: showing partner gaps and unverified prices made the tool more convincing, not less. What's next for freenet.free Partner pricing for Marketplace products such as Neon and Upstash. Shareable public designs with a read-only WebMCP surface, so an agent can review a plan without editing it. Export to infrastructure as code, so the validated plan becomes the first commit. A declarative-only mode that lets agents drive the studio with JavaScript disabled. title: Fediverse Hashtag Activity Tracker and Index
pitch: Trust what an agent tells you about a hashtag. Every answer comes with its evidence, and a straight no when there is none.
about_excerpt: Trust what an agent tells you about a hashtag. Every answer comes with its evidence, and a straight no when there is none. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every hashtag counter on the web gives you a number. Almost none of them tell you where it came from, how much of the network it covers, or when it stopped being trustworthy. On the fediverse that problem is structural. There is no central server, so no complete count of anything can exist. Any figure is a view from somewhere. I built the Fediverse Hashtag Activity Index around that fact. It polls public hashtag timelines on a small set of Mastodon-compatible servers, deduplicates what it sees, and publishes every figure together with its provenance: which servers contributed, how many were healthy, how many saw a typical post, and when the last successful update was. When two periods were not covered by comparable slices of the network, it refuses to call a trend. Then agents started reading web pages. An agent that scrapes a number keeps the number and drops the caveats, and the caveats were the whole point. WebMCP was the chance to hand an agent the evidence directly, in a shape it cannot drop on the way to the person. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Ask an agent "how busy is #news on the fediverse?" and, without tools, it will read a page, find a number, and repeat it without the coverage, freshness and comparability that made it safe to publish. The site cannot stop that. The caveats are prose, and prose gets summarised away. That is the specific failure WebMCP fixes here. The tools change what the agent can honestly say, which matters more than saving it some clicking. A tool result that carries provenance as a required field, a standing that separates observed data from sightings from the servers' own counters, and a status that can be insufficient_data with a reason, gives the agent a calibrated answer. A screen-read never could. The tools also refuse well. Asked about a tag the index is not collecting, the result says so, explains that the tracked set is at its ceiling, says the request has been queued, and offers the servers' own weekly counters labelled as a different kind of evidence. In testing, ChatGPT's browser turned that into "there's no reliable activity estimate yet" and, of the servers' own counters, "that's not evidence the tag is unused across the fediverse". That is exactly the sentence I wanted a person to hear. How it creates a better user experience There are six tools, and I designed them backwards from seven things a person would actually say to an agent while on the site. "I'm writing this post, which hashtags fit it best?" The agent reads the draft and proposes candidates, because language is what it is good at. It then calls evaluate_hashtags , which reports how many distinct accounts used each tag, across how many servers, and whether that looks like a conversation or a few accounts posting a lot. For tags the index has never seen, it asks two servers for their own counters, so a niche hobby tag gets an answer rather than a shrug. "Compare #news and #photography." compare_hashtags takes the person to /compare?tags=news,photography , a page anyone can open or share, with hourly sparklines and a warning when the tags' evidence is not like for like. The agent and the person are looking at the same URL. "What's trending?" trending_hashtags ranks the tracked set by distinct authors, not post volume, and attaches a direction that can be not_comparable when coverage shifted between hours. Two recent public posts per tag are the receipts. "Tell me about #photography." lookup_hashtag gives the full picture and moves the page to the tag. It is the one tool with a side effect, because a lookup is a search that can start collection, and both the description and the result say so. "How much of the fediverse can you actually see?" describe_coverage lists the monitored servers, their capabilities and the known limits, and tells the agent how to phrase any claim: "observed by this index across eight monitored servers", never "across the fediverse". "Can you say #news is rising across the fediverse?" check_claim is the last check before the agent speaks. The agent submits the claim it intends to make and the index referees it against the rules the site holds itself to. A fediverse-wide claim is always blocked, because no server can see the whole network. Directions come back allowed or blocked, adjectives come back qualified, and every verdict carries may_say , the sentence the index will stand behind, so a refusal is never a dead end. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before A person can ask a question in their own words and get an answer with the working attached, on a page they can check for themselves. That was not possible when the agent's only route was reading the page, because the caveats did not survive the trip. Now the agent can say "this figure is thin, here is why, here is what would change it", and the person can see the same thing on screen. It also protects the site from its helpers. A lookup counts as a signal that promotes a tag towards collection. An agent evaluating ten candidates in a second would have sent ten signals and walked past the tracked-set ceiling. The evaluate and compare tools use a separate read-only path that registers nothing, and every result reports its side effects so the agent can tell the person what the call did. How WebMCP was implemented One script, served inline from the shared layout, feature-detected so browsers without a model context run nothing. It registers six tools on document.modelContext , falling back to navigator.modelContext where only the older form exists. Each tool's execute is a fetch to the site's own JSON API, so no judgement lives in the browser that is not already in the tested server code. I added two read-only endpoints for the agent use cases, /api/v1/evaluate and /api/v1/trending , plus the /compare page. A /webmcp page reports what the visiting browser exposes, which is how I found that ChatGPT's browser provides only document.modelContext and that Chrome now deprecates the navigator form. The design notes, the seven utterances with the replies I designed against, and the verification record for both judging browsers are in the repository under docs/webmcp/ . Challenges and what I learned The tool description is the routing layer. My first "compare" request went to evaluate_hashtags , because it read as the general tool. Each description now names the other tool for the other job, and leads with the verbs a person uses. Overlaying a result onto whatever page is open looks clever and reads as a hack. I replaced an injected comparison table with a real page whose URL is the state, which is how the rest of the site already worked. Honest and useful are not the same thing. "No evidence either way" for every candidate in a niche post was honest and useless. Asking the servers themselves turned it into an answer, without giving up the distinction between observed and reported figures. When this was built Everything here was built during the Submission Period. The repository's first commit is 27 August 2026. The index, collector, API and pages went up on the 27th, and all of the WebMCP work followed from the 28th, in individually dated commits. The WebMCP-specific files are src/webmcp.ts , src/suggest.ts , src/trending.ts and the design record in docs/webmcp/ .
