title: Haggle
pitch: Your agent haggles with the seller's agent so you don't have to Price, pickup and terms get negotiated agent to agent, the site enforces the limits you set and nothing closes until both people say yes
about_excerpt: Your agent haggles with the seller's agent so you don't have to Price, pickup and terms get negotiated agent to agent, the site enforces the limits you set and nothing closes until both people say yes Like Comment Story Updates Main Web MCP Tools Inspiration Every time I try to buy or sell something on a marketplace it's the same thing. I message, they answer three hours later, I'm at work, they're at dinner, someone forgets, and a $150 bike takes a week of messages and then nothing happens. The negotiation is not the hard part. The hard part is that two busy people have to be online at the same time to close something simple. So I wanted to try this: you bring your own agent, it talks to the seller's agent, and you get out of the loop. You come back only to say yes or no. And then the obvious problem. If my agent is negotiating for me, how do I make sure I don't end up buying something it picked because "it fit"? That's why the mandate and the double approval exist. They're not extras, they're what makes the first part safe. What it does Haggle is a bike marketplace where the agents do the back-and-forth and you only show up to decide. You bring whatever agent you use (I tested with the ChatGPT desktop browser). The page gives it WebMCP tools to search listings, set your limits, make and counter offers, wait for the seller to answer, and check where things are. It doesn't click around or scrape anything. On the other side, the seller sets up an agent in Seller Studio: how it negotiates, a floor price, some rules. Your agent can't read any of that. They negotiate everything, not just the price. When to meet, where (public place), and what's included, like a lock. Before you send your agent, you give it a mandate: max price, when you're free, public pickup only, what has to come with the bike. That's saved on the server and enforced there. If your agent tries to accept $195 and your max is $180, the site says no, and you see it in the timeline as "Blocked by your mandate, not by your agent." When they reach something, you see each term next to what you asked for. You approve, or you decline and leave a note for your agent, and it keeps going. The seller sees the same screen against their own limits, and those numbers never leave the server. Nothing closes until both people approve. How I built it Next.js and TypeScript on Vercel, Postgres with Drizzle. Tools are registered with document.modelContext, with a fallback to navigator.modelContext. The tools change depending on where the negotiation is: read-only ones are always there, the action ones only appear when that action actually makes sense. The seller's agent runs in the background, so I added a read-only wait_for_seller_response tool. Otherwise the agent had to guess when to check again, and it usually didn't. Tools have readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint. All the checks (budget, mandate, seller limits, valid pickup options) run on the server. Whatever the seller's agent writes comes back marked as untrusted. There's a panel called Agent Lens that shows you what tools your agent can see on each screen. If your browser doesn't support WebMCP yet, it still shows you the list. Challenges I ran into The main one was giving the agent room to negotiate without losing control of it. I tried doing it with prompts first. It didn't work. Moving the limits into the site fixed it. Then keeping everything consistent with the seller running in the background, tools appearing and disappearing, and private info on both sides. It's easy to end up in a state where nobody knows whose turn it is. And the small one that turned out to matter: at first, declining ended the negotiation. Now declining is a message to your agent. Accomplishments I'm proud of Two agents with opposite interests, private information on both sides, limits the site enforces, and two separate human approvals. All of it through tools the page exposes. I'm mostly happy with how the site ended up being the referee, not just a place where agents click things. What I learned Exposing tools is the easy part. The real decision is what the agent must never be able to do. Once that lived on the server I could stop babysitting the prompt. Also, "no" has to be information for the agent, not a stop button. And the state of the deal should decide what tools exist, not the prompt. What's next for Haggle Sellers bringing their own agent, with Haggle staying in the middle as the referee. Delegation levels, from "ask me everything" to "close it if it fits." And going past bikes to anything two people sell to each other. Bikes today. Any local deal tomorrow. Note for judges Seller Studio is a labeled persona simulator so you can play both sides in one session. It's not authentication. title: Circuit Sim
pitch: One circuit, two native interfaces: people edit visually while agents inspect, author, highlight, and simulate the exact same design through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: One circuit, two native interfaces: people edit visually while agents inspect, author, highlight, and simulate the exact same design through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Electronic design is naturally visual, but agents are usually forced to guess their way through pixels or work in a separate text-only model. That creates two competing versions of the circuit. Circuit Sim explores a better model: one authoritative circuit that a person can see and edit while an agent can inspect, change, simulate, and explain through structured browser-native tools. What it does Circuit Sim is a collaborative schematic workbench for people and agents. A user works in the visual editor while an agent uses four WebMCP tools exposed directly by the live page: inspect_circuit discovers instructions, the component catalog, exact terminal keys, project state, ERC findings, and simulation freshness. author_circuit applies a validated complete circuit graph using an optimistic project hash. highlight_components focuses the same objects in the human-visible schematic for explanation and review. simulate_circuit runs the selected SPICE engine and returns measurements tied to the exact circuit snapshot. The demo shows Codex designing a beta-100 NPN bias stage from a natural-language target, creating the complete connected schematic, highlighting the bias network, running ngspice, and reporting node voltages and branch currents. It then changes the emitter resistor from 1 kΩ to 2 kΩ and simulates again to explain the stability-versus-headroom tradeoff using measured evidence. Why WebMCP is the right fit Without WebMCP, an agent would have to click through a dense CAD interface, infer component geometry, and scrape results from pixels. With WebMCP, the page advertises its capabilities and schemas directly. The agent can make precise, validated edits while every result remains visible to the user in the same workbench. This creates a workflow that was previously difficult: a person can describe design intent, watch an agent turn it into a real schematic, inspect exactly what changed, and challenge the design with another simulation—all without copying netlists between tools or maintaining a hidden agent-only circuit. How we built it The browser editor is React and TypeScript. Effect Schema defines and validates the canonical CircuitProject , edit operations, WebMCP inputs, and simulation responses. The page registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Agent edits cross the same domain validation used by the human interface. Connectivity and the SPICE netlist are derived from the saved project; the server runs ngspice in an isolated process and returns a validated simulation run associated with the project snapshot hash. IndexedDB persists validated projects and runs. The app is containerized and deployed on Render. The project is intentionally human-in-the-loop: hashes prevent stale agent writes, ERC findings stay visible, simulation evidence is inspectable, and component highlighting connects the agent’s explanation to the schematic. Challenges and learning The hardest part was keeping a visual editor, structured agent tools, connectivity extraction, and SPICE results consistent without creating a second source of truth. We learned that WebMCP is most valuable when tools expose domain operations and evidence—not a thin wrapper around UI clicks. Accomplishments Circuit Sim delivers a working deployed product rather than a mockup: four live WebMCP tools, validated authoring, shared human/agent state, ERC feedback, ngspice simulation, snapshot identity, undo/redo, persistence, and an end-to-end demonstration inside the Codex in-app browser. title: Arcana Table: RPG with an AI DM: Do push-ups for natural 20s
pitch: Everyone wants to play tabletop RPGs (50 million people) but nobody wants to run them, and everyone wants to exercise but the couch is winning. Arcana Table brings the dungeon; you bring the muscle.
about_excerpt: Everyone wants to play tabletop RPGs (50 million people) but nobody wants to run them, and everyone wants to exercise but the couch is winning. Arcana Table brings the dungeon; you bring the muscle. Like Comment Story Updates Instructions Explore the Area - Encounter Monsters Real World Exercise to Get bonus points on the roll. Timed Goals for Extra Bonus Points on rolls Use real world activities as micro goals to get done. Break cleaning a room into 5 minute or ten minute bursts. Fight Monsters Leveling Up - Micro Reward in Game - Hit those Endorphins Diagram Inspiration Literally, there are multiple influencers with millions of followers who act as DM while their clients lose weight and get in shape. ie link The first version of this was just a board that exposed some WebMCP tools and waited for you to bring your own agent. It was dead on arrival. You opened it and clicked buttons at yourself. What made it a game was putting an actual Dungeon Master in the seat, but making it go through the exact same tools an outside agent would have to use. Now when I say the tool surface is real, the DM playing the game is the evidence. What it does You open the URL and you're playing. The DM (GPT with function calling, talking through OpenAI TTS) sets the scene. You type or say what you do. It answers on a cartoon battle map: narrates, moves the tokens, lifts the fog, drops monsters in, runs initiative, rolls dice where you can see them. Click the map and your party walks there. There's a five-beat quest called The Ember Crown so a session has an ending. Each beat you clear levels the party up, hands out loot, and heals everyone. The last one is a boss called the Cinder Wight. The thing I actually care about is Heroic Effort. When a roll matters, the DM offers you a deal. Ten push-ups gets you +5 on the roll. Twenty-five gets you a natural 20. You count them on a big tap ring, or out loud if you're in hands-free mode because your hands are on the floor. There are timed holds too (a 30-second plank counts itself down), and a task list where it puts up three small things at once and you tick off whichever ones you did. Two out of three still pays. And there's the Oath. If you can't exercise, or just don't want to today, you can pay with something real that the page can't see. Clear the sink. Twenty minutes of studying. The email you've been avoiding. The whole table locks for however many minutes you agreed to, and when you come back you click "I kept it" on your honour. It pays the same as push-ups. You can also set the table to "Oaths only" in the party panel and it will never ask you for anything physical, so the game works for people who can't do any of this. If a hero drops to 0 HP, time stops. The board freezes and almost none of the tools work, including for the DM. You get out with a death save on a d20, or by doing a Heroic Effort, which always works. I like that effort is the guaranteed way out of dying. That's kind of the point of the whole thing. How we built it It's plain JavaScript with no build step. Canvas for the board, localStorage for state. There's one Cloudflare Worker, about 200 lines, that holds the OpenAI key so it never ends up in a browser. It's locked to the site's origin and rate-limited per IP. The page ships the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill (MIT) so document.modelContext exists in any browser without a flag. If the browser has WebMCP natively, that takes over and the badge in the header says so. There are 25 tools on document.modelContext. 21 are always there. Three more (advance_turn, update_hp, apply_condition) get registered when combat starts and unregistered when it ends. death_save only exists while somebody is bleeding out. Every tool is registered with an AbortController and removed with abort(), which fires toolchange the way the spec says. Read tools have readOnlyHint. The destructive ones, like deleting a token or damaging a player character, pause inside execute() until the player clicks approve. There's a 45-second timeout on that so a judge who walks away doesn't leave the DM hung forever. The DM loop is about 180 lines. It calls getTools(), turns the result into OpenAI function specs, sends the conversation to the Worker, runs whatever tool calls come back through executeTool(), feeds the results back in, and repeats up to seven times before it has to say something. There's no other path for it to change the game. The DM Panel tab in the app shows you the same registry live, every tool with a form built from its JSON schema, and running one goes through the same executeTool() and shows up in the same log. There's a Playwright test suite, 435 assertions in eleven files, that drives everything through the real document.modelContext in headless Chromium. It checks the registry growing and shrinking with combat, both approval paths, all the effort modes, a full five-beat run, and it samples pixels off the canvas. That last part exists because I once shipped a scope bug that made every monster disappear from the board and all 196 tests at the time still passed. I used Claude (in Cowork) as a pair programmer for most of the build. A lot of the test suite and the refactoring described below came out of that. Challenges we ran into Wiring up tools was the easy part. The hard part was that the model is a great storyteller and a bad referee. I'd put a rule in the system prompt, it would follow it for a few turns, and then it would drift. I told it to offer push-ups often. It didn't. I told it to move the tokens when the party moved. It described the walk and left everyone standing there. I told it not to change maps with set_scene. It walked the party into the forest that way, never called advance_quest, and the beat never paid out. Every one of those got fixed the same way, and it turned into the rule for the whole project: if it matters, the tool enforces it. The attack tool checks reach, so if you swing from across the room it refuses and tells you which square to move to. The dice enforce pacing now. Two rolls without anything staked and roll_dice refuses once and tells the DM to make an offer first. The map only changes through advance_quest. Monsters take their own turn when initiative gets to them instead of waiting to be asked. The player's effort preference gates the effort tools directly, and there is on purpose no tool to change it, because an agent that can decide what it's allowed to ask of your body isn't respecting a preference. The other big one was hands-free mode hearing itself. The DM would talk, the mic would pick it up, and it would come back as the player's turn. That took three separate layers of echo suppression and a test that fakes the SpeechRecognition API to replay the exact failure, since headless Chrome has no microphone. Accomplishments that we're proud of Someone who has never seen this can open the link and play a real ten-minute dungeon with zero explanation. And when the DM offers push-ups for a natural 20, people stand up. Everyone I've tested it on has stood up. The DM has no special access. It finds its tools with getTools() and uses them with executeTool() exactly like a ChatGPT or Claude agent would from outside. You can watch every single call in the log while you play. I'm also glad I didn't fake verification on the Oath. The card literally says "Nothing here can check, which is rather the point." I could have added a webcam check. It would have limited the whole mechanic to things a camera can see, and the things people most need a push on (reading, practicing, that email) aren't those. What we learned Rules belong in the tools, not the prompt. Every time I tried to fix behaviour with better wording it worked for a while. Every time I turned it into a counter or a refusal it stayed fixed. A good refusal that says what went wrong and what to call instead does more than a paragraph of instructions. Passing tests don't mean the game works. I had 196 green assertions and no monsters on the screen. Now the suite looks at pixels, and I don't trust anything I haven't watched. And accessibility turned out not to be a separate feature. Once the Oath paid the same as push-ups, "I can't exercise" stopped being a reason you couldn't play. It's a setting now. What's next for Arcana Table Webcam rep counting with MediaPipe Pose, running in the browser, so push-ups count themselves. The Oath stays unverified on purpose. Multiplayer, with a few people sharing one DM. Campaign art generated per run from my ComfyUI setup. And I want to record a Claude or ChatGPT browser agent running the same dungeon through the same 25 tools, next to the built-in DM, because that comparison is the thing WebMCP makes possible and I haven't shown it yet. title: Cadence
pitch: An issue tracker where your agent is a real teammate: it triages, dedupes, and reprioritizes with tools that change live as you select issues, not a fixed list.
about_excerpt: An issue tracker where your agent is a real teammate: it triages, dedupes, and reprioritizes with tools that change live as you select issues, not a fixed list. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every judge on this panel works at a company that lives in an issue tracker. "Triage my backlog, dedupe these, split this ticket, reprioritize the sprint" is a request any engineer has typed into Slack at 5pm on a Friday. It's also genuinely tedious for a person and genuinely tractable for an agent, but only if the agent can act with real authority inside the tool instead of clicking through a UI it's guessing at from a screenshot. We also noticed a gap. The official showcase and the community demo list are full of storefronts, flight bookers, and games. Nothing engineering-tool shaped. Nothing where the agent has to hold a real permission boundary, share an undo stack with a human, or watch its own available capabilities change as the page changes under it. That felt like the actual hard part of WebMCP, the underexplored part, so we built toward it instead of around it. What it does Cadence is an issue tracker where an agent is a real teammate on the board, not a chatbot bolted onto the side of one. Ask it to triage an untriaged backlog, find and merge duplicate bug reports, split an oversized epic into sub-issues, or reprioritize a sprint, and it does real analysis against real board state through the same functions the UI itself calls. Here's the part that's actually WebMCP-specific, not just "an app with an AI feature": the registered tool set changes live with what's on screen. Select an issue and add_comment , split_issue , and link_issues register. Apply a filter or multi-select and bulk_update shows up. Switch to cycle view and summarize_cycle appears. None of that is expressible as a static, pre-declared tool list, because a server-side MCP server has no idea what a human currently has selected in their browser. It can't. Agents also carry real identity and real permission scoping. A workspace owner grants each agent a scope, read, triage, write, or full, and that grant filters which tools registerTool even offers before the agent ever sees them, live. Every agent edit lands on the same undo stack the human uses too. Cmd+Z undoes an agent's change exactly like it was your own, because both write through one shared reduce() function against one shared state. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite on the client. Cloudflare Workers plus a Durable Object (SQLite-backed, free-tier eligible) as the authoritative backend, syncing over the WebSocket Hibernation API so multiple humans and agents can work the same board live. webmcp-kit , a small library we published alongside this entry: defineTool / registerTools with full JSON-Schema-to-TS inference, and useScopedTools , a React hook that registers a tool set while a condition holds and cleanly unregisters when it stops. That hook is what makes Cadence's dynamic tool surface a one-liner instead of a pile of manual AbortController bookkeeping. Every mutation is a pure (state, actor, action) → state function in one reducer, shared by the client store, the Durable Object, and every WebMCP tool handler. There's exactly one place a board mutation is defined, which is also what makes the shared human/agent undo stack possible. Only one code path to undo. Seed data is deliberately messy on purpose: real duplicate bug reports worded three different ways, vague untriaged titles, missing estimates, so the higher-order tools have genuine work to do instead of a tidy board with nothing left to fix. A hash-chained audit log on the Durable Object records every mutation with actor attribution, queryable via get_activity . Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's in-app browser only supports a subset of the spec: imperative registration only, no declarative HTML tool attributes, and no cross-frame tool discovery even for same-origin iframes. We designed single-origin from day one because of this, and honestly it shaped the whole architecture more than anything else did. Then there was the embarrassing one. Our seed data computed Date.now() at Cloudflare Workers module scope instead of inside a request handler. Turns out Workers doesn't guarantee wall-clock time outside a request's I/O context, so every "recent" issue and cycle date came out silently wrong, offsets from epoch, not from actual "now". We only caught it by inspecting live state over a raw WebSocket and noticing the numbers just didn't add up. find_duplicates had a similar quiet failure. It used Jaccard similarity on tokenized title and body text with a default threshold that, on inspection, was too strict to ever catch our own deliberately seeded duplicate cluster. Real paraphrased duplicates scored around 0.23 to 0.28 against a 0.4 cutoff. Tuned it down and documented why right in the tool description, since it's a real limitation an agent calling the tool should actually know about. And demo-state entropy: a Durable Object's seed loads exactly once, ever, so every round of testing permanently mutated the same live board. Later testers kept hitting an already-triaged, already-deduped board with nothing left to demonstrate. Fixed it by giving every visitor their own isolated board, auto-fresh on first visit, plus a visible in-app reset button, instead of trying to guess when it's "safe" to reset something shared. Accomplishments we're proud of A genuinely dynamic tool surface, verifiable live in Chrome's Model Context Tool Inspector: select an issue and watch the registered tool count change in real time, no faith required. Per-agent permission scoping that changes what tools even exist for an agent, not just what it's allowed to call, enforced before registration ever happens. A free, LLM-free benchmark comparing tool calls against real Playwright-driven DOM interaction on the live app. Single actions cost about the same either way, but a 7-item bulk task runs roughly 3x faster over tool calls, because the DOM path re-pays a fixed per-item navigation cost that a tool call just doesn't. Real accessibility work, not just a claim. Full keyboard operability, and a code-level WCAG audit that actually found and fixed two real bugs, custom buttons not activating on Space, confirmation dialogs with no Escape-to-dismiss, instead of asserting AA compliance from a README and hoping nobody checks. What we learned The most interesting property of WebMCP isn't that it lets an agent call functions instead of scraping a page. It's that tool registration lives in the same runtime as the UI state, so the tool surface can be a live function of what's actually on screen, and permission boundaries can be enforced at the moment of registration rather than only at call time. Neither of those is something a server-side MCP server wrapping a REST API can do, no matter how well-designed that API is. What's next Publishing webmcp-kit to npm proper (it's a GitHub dependency right now), a full screen-reader session to go with the code-level accessibility audit, and pushing the duplicate-detection scoring past bag-of-words Jaccard now that we know exactly where its ceiling is. title: FitzYo
pitch: FitzYo - Deeply personalized shopping. Zero-knowledge retail Fully Automated shopping experience through the power of WebMCP, personalized with zero data stored.
about_excerpt: FitzYo - Deeply personalized shopping. Zero-knowledge retail Fully Automated shopping experience through the power of WebMCP, personalized with zero data stored. Like Comment Story Updates Look Book created by Agent Inspiration I hate shopping online as it is today. Every e-commerce site assumes the retailer has to know the customer. Sizes, preferences, family members: either you re-enter them on every site, or you hand them over to be stored forever. Meanwhile, "AI shopping" mostly means a bot that clicks through the same UI a human would. Adding a brain and tools to an ordinary website through WebMCP is revolutionary. The moment I came across WebMCP, I realized this is the future. I wanted to build a showcase application that shows how retailers can serve shoppers like me, who hate manual shopping, using WebMCP. The user's AI agent already knows the user. The retailer already knows its products. WebMCP is the missing interface between them. So the guiding line for FitzYo became: your agent knows what fits you. The web doesn't have to. The scenario that drove every decision was one sentence: "We're going to Hawaii for seven days in September. Plan what everyone should wear and find what we're missing." What it does FitzYo is an ordinary-looking apparel store with one difference: every commerce operation is also exposed to an AI agent through WebMCP, and the human and the agent share the same live page. Shop for your whole family without registering family members or storing measurements in the retailer's application. The store has no intelligence of its own. An external WebMCP-capable agent attaches to the page, discovers the tools, and shops using private context that lives only on the user's side. Tools are semantic, not DOM-based. search_products, filter_products, find_matching_variants, compare_products, get_size_guide, add_to_cart, propose_cart, and so on. Nothing clicks a button. The agent sends constraints, never the profile. The store learns "size XL, blue or black, not red, relaxed fit, under $80, label: Dad". It never learns Dad's chest measurement, and it rejects any payload that tries to include one. "Fits Dad ✓" badges appear on product cards. The agent registers each family member as derived constraints once, and the store badges every product that fits each person. The store never knows who Dad is. The human sees everything the agent does. Filters the agent set show as chips marked "✦ agent", with a count of how many products each one hides. An activity feed narrates every tool call. A plan panel and a day-by-day lookbook show the trip taking shape. The agent has to earn the cart. Cart tools are locked until the shopper grants the capability with a spend ceiling and an expiry, and the ceiling is enforced on every write. The shopper can revoke any tier at any time. Decisions come back to the human. ask_human pauses the agent with a question. propose_cart presents one priced, grouped basket that the shopper edits and accepts in a single action. There is no checkout tool. Ordering is a press-and-hold gesture the page only accepts from trusted input with a single-use nonce. Every line in the order records whether a human, an agent, or an accepted proposal put it there. How we built it Elixir, Phoenix LiveView, and Ash Framework, deployed on Fly.io. One LiveView process owns the shared human/agent state: filters in the URL, results, selected product and variant, party members, capability grants, and the cart. Ash domains for the catalog (categories, products, variants, and structured size guides with per-size chest, waist, hip, and inseam ranges) and commerce (session carts and a human-only checkout). The seeded catalog has 56 products and 754 variants across Columbia, Patagonia, Nike, Levi's, Teva, and others. WebMCP registration in a LiveView hook. The page registers its tools on document.modelContext (and navigator.modelContext for the older spec) the moment a WebMCP surface appears, and also exposes a same-origin postMessage bridge for embedding shells. Every tool call round-trips over the LiveView socket and runs in the same process that renders the human's page, so the UI updates in the same frame as the reply. Any WebMCP agent can drive the store using the registered tools. Challenges we ran into Agent state and user state. I wanted the site to work for user interaction and agent interaction at the same time. Making the agent's filters, badges, and recommendations first-class citizens of the same LiveView state, with clear provenance on every chip and cart line, took most of the design effort. The user can always tell which products the agent selected and which they selected themselves. Privacy that is enforced, not promised. Sending "size XL" instead of "chest 45 inches" sounds simple until the agent needs a size it doesn't have. The answer was to serve size-guide ranges from the store and have the agent match locally, then have the store actively reject measurement fields. Blocking tools inside a request/response protocol. ask_human, propose_cart, and request_capability need to wait minutes for a person. We had to make these calls suspend cleanly, allow one pending decision at a time, handle supersede and timeout as normal outcomes, and let the shopper keep using the store meanwhile. Human override that the agent respects. When the shopper removes a chip the agent set, the agent must not re-impose it. We surface removed_by_human in store state and flag re-imposition in the activity feed as a warning. State survival across remounts. Party members, grants, plan, and lookbook lived only in the LiveView process. A reload, a dropped socket, or clicking the logo silently dropped all of it while the cart carried on. Late in the build we moved agent session state into a session store and switched navigation to patches. Making checkout unreachable to agents without making it hostile. A press-and-hold gesture gated on trusted input and a nonce keeps a scripted click inert, while still feeling like a normal confirm to a person. Accomplishments that we're proud of A store that looks and works like a normal retailer, where every commerce concept is also a structured, validated WebMCP capability. The "Fits Dad ✓" experience works end to end, and the retailer genuinely never receives who Dad is or what his measurements are. A capability model for agents: read and suggest on connect, cart by explicit grant with a spend ceiling, checkout never. The ceiling is enforced on every write, including accepted proposals. propose_cart: one priced basket with alternatives, optional lines, and per-person budgets, live budget math as the shopper edits, and a result the agent has to read rather than assume. Full provenance. Every filter chip, badge, and cart line knows whether a human, an agent, or an accepted proposal created it, and the order confirmation says so. A rehearsal script that runs the whole demo against a real browser with no LLM in the loop, which doubles as an executable specification of the tool surface. What we learned Tool design is product design. The moment we named a tool after a UI element, the agent got worse. Naming tools after what the shopper wants (find_matching_variants, not click_size_dropdown) made both the agent and the human experience better. Agents need to see what humans see. get_store_state returning the human's overrides turned out to matter more than any search tool. Without it, an agent argues with the person. The retailer should serve data for reasoning, not do the reasoning. Structured size guides let the agent stay private and the store stay simple. Trust has to be granular and visible. A blanket "let the agent shop" is scary. "Let it fill a cart up to $500 for the next 30 minutes" is something people will accept. LiveView is a very good fit for WebMCP. Running tool calls in the same process that renders the page eliminated an entire class of sync bugs. What's next for FitzYo Run the demo with real WebMCP agents as browser support lands, and publish the playbook as a reference for other retailers. Multi-retailer shopping. The same private context and the same agent, driving several stores' tool surfaces in one trip plan. Wardrobe feedback loop. Accepted orders flow back into the user's local wardrobe file, so the next trip starts from what they now own. Broader domains. Shoes, outdoor gear, travel, gifts: the architecture is not apparel-specific. Richer fit. Stretch, cut, length, and past-purchase fit feedback, so "Likely fits Dad" can become a confidence the agent explains. A portable private-context format, so a user's family, wardrobe, and preferences work with any agent, not just ours. Beyond apparel. The same approach works for flight booking or picking parts in a big-box hardware store. title: Handoff
pitch: Handoff is where AI agents inspect projects, propose plans, and make approved changes while humans stay in control. Every decision and action is tracked in one shared workspace.
about_excerpt: Handoff is where AI agents inspect projects, propose plans, and make approved changes while humans stay in control. Every decision and action is tracked in one shared workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Workflow Thumbnail Live Board Why we built Handoff AI agents are getting good at taking actions, but there is a simple problem: who decides what the agent is actually allowed to do? We built Handoff to explore a different interaction model. Instead of telling an agent exactly what buttons to click, a person gives Handoff a goal and constraints. The agent can then inspect the real project, gather evidence, identify problems, and propose different ways to solve them. The person reviews the options and approves what should happen. For example, in our demo, Handoff connects to a real GitHub repository. The agent inspects the codebase, issues, pull requests, commits, and CI status, then identifies problems with the application's content-management flow. Rather than immediately changing anything, it turns its findings into an implementation plan with cost, risk, tradeoffs, and proposed actions. The plan appears in Handoff's Decision Room . The human can approve, reject, or change the constraints before anything consequential happens. Once approved, the authorized actions execute. External GitHub actions are treated as a separate boundary: the agent can propose creating an issue, branch, or pull request, but it cannot authorize those actions itself. Every step is recorded in the Shift Ledger , including what the agent investigated, what it proposed, what the human approved, and what was executed. The entire collaboration can then be replayed. What we learned The biggest lesson was that human-in-the-loop interaction works better when the human is involved at the decision point , rather than being asked to supervise every individual agent action. We also learned that WebMCP is most interesting when the tools expose meaningful application capabilities rather than simply reproducing buttons as agent commands. Handoff uses the same underlying application state for both the human interface and the agent tools, so an agent is working with the actual project state. How we built it Handoff started as a small HTML, CSS, and JavaScript task board. We deliberately kept the implementation lightweight so the WebMCP integration was easy to understand and inspect. We then built the collaboration layer around it: missions, task state, agent activity, proposals, approvals, permissions, and replay. The project was extended with a backend for GitHub OAuth and repository access, allowing agents to inspect real repositories through WebMCP. The current implementation exposes 19 WebMCP tools. Read operations such as repository inspection, issues, pull requests, commits, CI status, and blocker detection can be performed autonomously. Consequential GitHub operations are represented as proposed changes and only execute after a human approval. Challenges The hardest part was making the approval boundary real rather than cosmetic. We wanted an agent to be able to reason about an action without being able to silently perform it. We therefore put the permission checks in the application logic itself. An agent can propose a change, but execution of an external action is only reachable through an approved decision. We also had to handle the practical parts of building a real WebMCP application: keeping the agent and human UI synchronized, recording every state transition, handling GitHub authentication securely, and making the system work with the live state of an external repository. Handoff is our exploration of a simple question: What if an AI agent could do the work, but the human could always see what it wants to do before it crosses an important boundary? title: AgentOps
pitch: AgentOps gives AI agents real WebMCP tools to act on the web and a Sentinel security layer that keeps you in control of every risky move.
about_excerpt:
AgentOps gives AI agents real WebMCP tools to act on the web and a Sentinel security layer that keeps you in control of every risky move.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give AI the web and keep yourself in control 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give AI the web and keep yourself in control 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give AI the web and keep yourself in control 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every "AI agent that browses the web for you" demo I'd seen was binary, either the AI does everything unsupervised unsettling the moment money or personal data is involved or the user has to approve every single click, which defeats the point of delegating anything. I wanted to build the middle ground: Which is an agent that acts freely on low-risk actions, but hits a real, structural trust boundary the moment something consequential is at stake. WebMCP made that possible in a way ad-hoc browser automation never could because a registered tool is structured data , a security layer can actually reason about what a call means before it runs, not just watch pixels get clicked. 

 What it does 

 AgentOps takes a plain-language goal "book me a flight to Venice under $600," "order pizza for a get-together" and turns it into a mission: a sequence of real WebMCP tool calls. Every one of those calls passes through Sentinel , our trust/policy layer, before it executes: 

 
 Low-risk actions (search, compare, read) run automatically. 
 Consequential ones (bookings, purchases above a user-set threshold, sending messages) pause and ask for a one-click approval, with a plain-English reason and a risk score. 
 A fixed set of categories (credentials, password changes, financial transfers) are never auto-approved, full stop. 
 Anything a tool returns is treated as untrusted content if it contains an embedded instruction trying to override the agent (a prompt injection), Sentinel blocks it outright. Not a setting. A boundary. 
 

 The user sets their own risk tolerance once in a Trust Policy screen; every mission afterward respects it without further supervision. Missions pause and resume in place no restarting and every decision is logged. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is a Vite/React app with a Three.js "Agent Core" that visually reflects the agent's state (idle, thinking, executing, awaiting approval, blocked). Every mission step is registered as a real tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() / navigator.modelContext native on Chrome behind the WebMCP flag, or through the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill package everywhere else, so the same code path works across environments. Before executing anything, the mission engine calls getTools() a genuine discovery step, not a hardcoded list. 

 Sentinel's gate lives inside each tool's execute() , so the enforcement isn't UI-only it applies no matter who calls the tool, our own runner or, in principle, an external agent. Mission plans are generated at runtime by an LLM (via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint) rather than picked from a fixed script, and one mission's flight-search step calls a real (sandboxed) flight-search API through a small serverless proxy the only place any secret key lives, since real commerce/travel APIs explicitly block direct browser calls. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 A few things broke in ways that shaped the final architecture: 

 
 My first pick for real flight data, Amadeus's free self-service tier, was decommissioned mid-build . We moved to Duffel's test-mode API instead. 
 Duffel (like most real commercial APIs) explicitly blocks direct browser calls you cannot safely hold a real secret key client-side. That's what pushed me to add a minimal Vercel serverless function as a proxy: the smallest amount of backend that makes a genuinely real API call possible without leaking credentials. 
 The LLM provider deprecated the model I was building with mid-hackathon, silently breaking AI planning until I caught it and swapped to their current recommended model. 
 The most important bug we found: Sentinel's purchase-risk check used (amount || 0) > threshold , so a step with no amount attached like an AI-planned "order pizza" step that omitted a price silently defaulted to "safe" and auto-approved. I fixed this as defense-in-depth: a missing amount now escalates to "ask" rather than being treated as zero risk, and a second, independent check flags any step whose own description implies a real commitment (ordering, paying, booking, canceling) even if the planner mis-categorized it. Sentinel's judgment isn't purely downstream of a label the LLM chose. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 Getting Sentinel to feel like a real trust boundary rather than a UI decoration the prompt-injection detection in particular, where content a tool returns is scanned as untrusted data before the agent can act on it, not just the request being sent. And getting at least one mission wired to genuinely real external data (not just simulated), despite hitting a dead API provider and browser CORS restrictions along the way, without ever compromising a secret key. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP's ecosystem is still very early almost no production site implements it yet, which shaped an honest choice to have AgentOps register its own actions as tools rather than pretend arbitrary sites already support this. I also learned, the hard way, that any security layer built on top of an LLM's own categorization needs a second, independent check trusting a model to always self-report risk correctly is exactly the kind of single point of failure a "trust boundary" is supposed to prevent. 

 What's next for AgentOps 

 Wiring real external data into the Shopping and Finance missions the same way I did for Travel; giving AgentOps a second, fully independent WebMCP surface (a separate site registering its own tools) so the External Agent → Sentinel → WebMCP Tool → Website story is completely literal instead of self-hosted; and letting a real external agent not just our own UI discover and drive AgentOps' tools directly.

title: ACKB Handshake
pitch: Design together. Approve with proof
about_excerpt: Design together. Approve with proof Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of suggesting and executing changes, but consequential design decisions still need clear human control. In kitchen and bath planning, even a seemingly simple suggestion—moving a fixture, changing an appliance, or adjusting a room layout—can affect cost, accessibility, clearances, utilities, and usability. We built Handshake to explore a better collaboration model: an AI agent can inspect a shared design, search for products, evaluate constraints, and propose improvements, but it cannot silently change the approved plan. Our guiding principle became our tagline: Design together. Approve with proof. What it does Handshake is a WebMCP-enabled kitchen and bath co-design workspace where a person and an in-browser AI agent collaborate on the same room plan. The agent can: Read the current room and design state Search a synthetic kitchen and bath product catalog Evaluate budget, geometry, clearances, openings, and planning guidelines Propose placing, moving, swapping, or removing products Propose changes to room dimensions and openings Explain warnings before a decision is made Generate a bill of materials from the approved design Retrieve evidence receipts for protected actions The agent cannot approve its own proposal or bypass the page’s consent controls. Every proposed change is versioned and shown to the person for review. Approval is bound to the exact proposal contents using a canonical hash, so an approved proposal cannot be silently replaced with something different. Consequential actions pass through an additional human-only confirmation step. Successful actions produce evidence receipts that record what was approved, which checks were shown, and what happened. How we built it Handshake is a TypeScript monorepo built with pnpm and deployed around a Cloudflare architecture. A Cloudflare Worker serves the application and API. Each synthetic design session is owned by a Durable Object, which maintains the authoritative room state, proposal versions, idempotency records, confirmations, and audit events. The browser exposes a governed WebMCP tool surface. Tools can read state, search the catalog, create proposals, apply an already-approved proposal, request protected actions, and retrieve receipts. Human approval and confirmation endpoints are deliberately excluded from the agent-callable tool surface. The policy layer is deterministic and side-effect free. It handles: Canonical proposal hashing Proposal expiry and state transitions Expected-version checks Idempotency and replay prevention Actor and authorization boundaries Budget and room-boundary evaluation Fixture overlap and approach clearance Door and appliance-opening conflicts Kitchen work-triangle guidance Work aisles, walkways, and landing areas Service-location warnings Accessibility-oriented turning-space checks Bill-of-materials calculation Rule thresholds are represented as named, reviewable constants with source information rather than unexplained numbers embedded in the implementation. The current project uses synthetic data and presents its checks as planning guidance—not as building-code certification. We use Vitest for unit and policy testing, Playwright for browser verification, GitHub Actions for continuous integration, and Wrangler for Cloudflare development and deployment workflows. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was preserving meaningful human control without making the agent collaboration feel artificial. It was not enough to place an “Approve” button beside an unrestricted mutation endpoint. We needed to prove that: The person reviewed the exact proposal that would be applied. The proposal was still valid for the current room version. The agent could not approve or confirm its own work. Replayed requests could not apply the same change twice. A protected action could not proceed without fresh, explicit confirmation. The resulting receipt accurately described the approved action. Another challenge was keeping the product claim aligned with the implementation. Handshake was described as a kitchen and bath workspace, but the earliest catalog and rules were primarily bathroom-oriented. Rather than hide that gap, we documented it and expanded the domain model to include kitchens, doors, windows, service anchors, appliance interactions, work-triangle evaluation, landing areas, and a bill of materials. We also had to distinguish authorization from design guidance. Authorization rules fail closed, but planning warnings should remain reviewable. A person may knowingly approve a design that carries a recommendation-level warning; Handshake’s job is to ensure that the warning was visible and recorded, not to pretend the agent owns the final decision. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Handshake treats consent as part of the architecture rather than a decorative UI step. The project now includes: A versioned proposal state machine Canonical hashes that bind approval to exact proposal contents Human-only approval and confirmation endpoints Replay-resistant and idempotent state transitions A shared, server-authoritative design session A governed WebMCP tool surface Protected-action evidence receipts Deterministic budget and geometry checks Kitchen and bathroom planning-rule support A derived bill of materials Negative-path tests for replay, self-approval, stale versions, expired consent, and altered proposals Continuous-integration validation for formatting, types, and tests We are especially proud that the system is explicit about its limits. It uses synthetic project data, does not claim code-compliance certification, and does not treat a green automated check as proof that deployment or final submission is complete. What we learned We learned that trustworthy agent experiences require more than permission prompts. The approval must be attached to the exact state transition, and the system must preserve enough evidence to explain the decision afterward. We also learned that deterministic policy code and generative agent behavior work best when they have separate responsibilities. The agent can help interpret goals and propose creative changes. The policy engine owns authorization, consistency, geometry, and repeatable checks. A third lesson was that missing information should not be invented. If a room has no modelled door, Handshake does not fabricate one and claim to have checked its swing. Evidence is only useful when it clearly distinguishes what was evaluated from what remains unknown. Finally, we learned that human control does not have to eliminate useful automation. The agent can still inspect, search, calculate, and prepare a complete proposal. The boundary is simple: the agent proposes; the person decides; the system records the proof. title: ClaimGate
pitch: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions.
about_excerpt: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP exposes privacy-safe candidate matching while private proof stays manual. Staff reviews aggregate eligibility and a redacted timeline, never evidence values. Atomic handoff completes the claim, returns the item, and resolves the report. ClaimGate — privacy-first lost-property claims with human release decisions. Problem Lost-property desks need enough public detail to find a likely item without publishing the details that prove ownership. Giving every field to an Agent would turn private proof into searchable material. ClaimGate separates public matching from private proof. The Agent handles structured preparation and safe reads. People publish, submit evidence, decide the claim, issue the pickup credential, and complete the release. Why WebMCP This workflow changes as the claim moves from draft to match, review, pickup, and collection. WebMCP lets the page expose the few actions that are valid now, with typed inputs and bounded results. The Agent does not have to infer controls from page layout, and sensitive actions can stay absent from the tool set. Better experience A Claimant can describe a loss once, let the Agent structure the public fields, and receive explainable candidates without copying data between screens. Staff gets a short queue and a redacted summary. Each person sees the next action in the same claim instead of reconstructing context after every role change. Before and after Before ClaimGate, the demo journey is a sequence of manual forms and page searches, with a risk of mixing public clues and ownership proof. With ClaimGate, the Agent prepares, searches, and summarizes through explicit tools while the UI reserves publication, proof, judgment, credential transfer, and handoff for visible human controls. What it does A Claimant starts a fresh two-hour instance with fictional Northbridge Campus inventory. The Agent can create or update a lost-report draft, list reports, find up to three candidates, and stage one candidate. Results contain broad fields, confidence bands, and public reasons, not internal inventory IDs. The Claimant publishes and submits masked evidence manually. Two correct slots are sufficient even if a third submitted slot is wrong. The browser receives only aggregate eligibility, insufficiency, or the third-attempt LOCKED state. Staff reads a bounded queue and redacted review summary, then decides manually. After approval, the Agent can read pickup instructions. The Claimant manually generates and copies a ten-minute, one-time credential, then Staff pastes it into the handoff form. One transaction marks the claim collected, item returned, and report resolved. The normal web flow also works without WebMCP. How implemented ClaimGate is one Next.js 16 application with separate report, matching, evidence, claim, authorization, audit, and WebMCP modules. SQLite scopes every record to a demo instance. Signed HttpOnly sessions and server routes enforce role, ownership, state, version, CSRF, origin, idempotency, and rate limits. The browser uses native document.modelContext.registerTool() . A page and state registry selects nine tools, and an AbortController removes the previous generation on navigation or state change. Tool visibility assists selection; the server remains authoritative. The tools are create_lost_report_draft , update_lost_report_draft , list_my_reports , find_candidate_matches , stage_claim_candidate , get_claim_status , get_pickup_instructions , list_pending_claims , and get_claim_review_summary . Publishing, evidence, decisions, pass issue or reissue, role switching, and handoff have no WebMCP tool. Matching uses fixed category, time, area, color, and tag rules. Runtime evidence comparison uses salted HMAC digests and a fixed three-slot shape. The public repository contains the readable fictional seed answers so judges can run the demo; the privacy boundary covers runtime clients, pages, APIs, WebMCP, logs, and stored raw evidence, not repository readers. Only a successful issue or reissue response returns the full pickup credential. The current Claimant page keeps it in memory and can reveal, mask, or copy it. Navigation or refresh clears it and cannot recover it. The server stores only a digest, and reissue invalidates the previous generation. Challenges we ran into State-aware tool lifecycle: Chrome 151 can briefly change membership while registrations are replaced. A serialized generation manager and server state checks make stale calls fail safely. Runtime privacy evidence: We separated public DTOs from private transports, signed opaque candidate handles, bounded outputs, and scanned tool results, HTML, logs, storage, history, and public build assets. Visible cross-role continuity: Claimant and Staff must resume the same authorized claim without hidden navigation. Contextual role switching and a 14-scenario visible Playwright suite cover that path. Accomplishments that we're proud of The complete report, match, proof, review, pickup, and handoff flow works in the normal UI and the WebMCP-assisted path. Nine tools appear only in valid page and state scopes; human-only actions stay absent. A clean production build completed three independent native Chrome 151 runs. Each used fresh SQLite state, exercised all nine tools, completed the manual transitions, and ended with Home tools [] . All 14 visible Playwright E2E scenarios passed after commit 04c618d added contextual cross-role claim navigation. The release path isolates its runtime, data, processes, ingress, and Nginx resources from unrelated services. These are implementation and test results, not claims of awards, adoption, users, or judging outcome. What we learned Tool discovery improves planning but is not authorization. Runtime privacy needs separate data paths, not hidden UI fields. Human control is clearest when a sensitive transition has no tool at all. Stateful WebMCP also needs navigation, stale-version, delayed-completion, and teardown tests, not only a happy path. What's next A production pilot would need institutional identity, enrolled Staff, accessibility and abuse review, retention policy, backup and recovery, and a database architecture for multiple application instances. Configurable matching and evidence policies should preserve the same public-match, private-proof, and human-release boundaries. title: Chip
pitch: Talk directly to your hardware. Chip links AI models straight to physical microcontrollers through browser-based Web Serial APIs for instant flashing.
about_excerpt: Talk directly to your hardware. Chip links AI models straight to physical microcontrollers through browser-based Web Serial APIs for instant flashing. Like 5 Comment Story Updates 1 Dashboard page: Connect microcontroller, view live firmware flashing Setting: See all available Webmcp tools and also copy Setup: Copy agent prompt / Live url or Setup Standard MPC Inspiration Building hardware with AI still has a missing link. An agent can write firmware, explain wiring, and debug errors, but the real ESP32 is sitting on the user’s desk, connected by USB to an IDE. Chip was inspired by that gap: how do we let an AI assistant move beyond “here is some code” and actually help with the real compile, flash, and debug loop? ESP32 development is powerful, but the beginner experience is long and requires process. Users often need an IDE, board drivers, local toolchains, flashing commands, serial monitors, and a lot of context just to blink an LED. Chip asks a simpler question: what if the user could plug in a board, open a dashboard, and let an AI agent guide the rest? What it does Chip connects AI agents directly to live ESP32 hardware through a browser dashboard. The user plugs in an ESP32, grants browser USB access through Web Serial, and Chip becomes the bridge between the agent and the physical board. Chip uses two kinds of MCP-style integration: Standard MCP connects the AI agent to the cloud/backend side of the system. Through the standard MCP server, the agent can work with higher-level project tasks like compiling firmware, starting flash jobs, checking job status, and coordinating the build pipeline. WebMCP connects the AI agent to the live browser session. This is the unique part: the browser actually has access to the USB-connected ESP32. Chip exposes browser-side WebMCP tools such as list_devices , get_board_status , read_serial_logs , read_job_status , read_dashboard_state , post_agent_message , set_agent_note , request_user_action , and erase_board . Beyond firmware, Chip includes Circuit Studio, allowing the AI agent to visually design, inspect, and modify hardware circuits directly on an interactive canvas. Through WebMCP and backend SKiDL integration, the agent searches real KiCad symbols on demand, inspects pinouts, places components like microcontrollers, passives, and sensors, wires nets, and runs Electrical Rules Checking to keep the schematic valid across versions. Together, Standard MCP handles cloud-side intelligence and workflow, while WebMCP gives the agent eyes and hands inside the browser session that is physically connected to the board. How we built it Chip is built as a three-part system: a React/Vite client dashboard, a backend service for compile, relay, and circuit synthesis workflows, and a standard MCP server for AI tool access. The client dashboard uses Web Serial and esptool-js to communicate with the ESP32 over USB. This is important because cloud servers cannot access a USB cable plugged into the user’s laptop. The browser owns the physical connection, so the browser performs board operations like flashing and erasing. On top of that, the client registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . These tools expose live browser state to the agent: connected devices, board status, serial logs, dashboard state, active jobs, and user-visible messages. The agent can also post notes into the dashboard and request physical actions from the user, like connecting the board or pressing reset. The result is a loop where the AI agent can reason, the backend can build, and the browser can safely touch the real hardware. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was the physical boundary between cloud AI and local hardware. An AI agent running in the cloud cannot directly access an ESP32 plugged into a user’s computer. Browser security also correctly prevents silent USB access, so the user must grant Web Serial permission. AI cannot directly generate a binary file accessible by Microcontrollers. That forced a better architecture: the backend should not pretend to flash the board. Instead, Chip makes the browser the active hardware bridge. The cloud compiles and coordinates, but the browser performs the physical write. Another challenge was separating Standard MCP and WebMCP cleanly. Standard MCP is useful for cloud/backend tools, while WebMCP is useful for live browser state and hardware access. Chip uses both instead of forcing one protocol to do everything. Handling schematic generation also required solving symbol storage constraints. Bundling full KiCad symbol libraries into production containers is heavy, so we built an on demand symbol loader using Cloudflare R2 to stream lightweight part definitions during synthesis without bloating backend storage. We also had to think carefully about destructive actions. Erasing a board is powerful, so the WebMCP erase_board tool checks for a connected board and is described as something that should only happen after the user clearly asks for it. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Chip is not just an AI code-generation demo. It creates a real bridge between an AI agent, a browser, and physical microcontroller hardware. The WebMCP implementation is especially important. The client exposes browser-side tools that let an agent inspect live board state, read serial logs, understand job progress, post messages into the UI, save guidance notes, request user actions, and erase the connected ESP32 when appropriate. We are also proud of the architecture split. Standard MCP handles the cloud workflow. WebMCP handles live browser interaction. Web Serial handles the actual USB connection. Each part does what it is naturally good at. The result is a more believable path toward AI-assisted hardware development: not just “copy this code into Arduino IDE,” but “connect your board and let the agent help you iterate.” What we learned We learned that connecting AI to hardware is less about making the model powerful and more about designing the right bridge between digital reasoning and physical constraints. The key insight was that the browser is not just a frontend. In Chip, the browser is the hardware runtime. It holds the USB permission, talks to the board, streams logs, flashes binaries, and exposes that live state back to the agent through WebMCP. We also learned that Standard MCP and WebMCP solve different problems. Standard MCP is great for remote services, build systems, and backend workflows. WebMCP is powerful when the agent needs to interact with the user’s live browser context, especially when that browser has access to local capabilities the cloud does not. What's next for Chip Next, we want to make the full agent-to-hardware loop smoother: ask for a firmware change, compile it, flash it, read the serial output, and let the agent debug the result automatically. We want to link Circuit Studio schematics directly to code generation, automatically assigning firmware pin definitions based on the visual wiring. We also want to improve safety and trust around hardware actions, especially destructive actions like erasing flash. Clear user confirmation, better action history, and stronger board/session pairing will make the system safer. Future work includes richer serial-log analysis, support for more boards, PCB layout export, saved project history, and a cleaner demo path for WebMCP-capable browsers. Long term, Chip could become a general bridge between AI agents and physical computing: a way for students, makers, and hardware teams to build with real devices using natural language, while still respecting the security boundaries of the browser and the real world. title: Overturn
pitch: Analyze, recommend, and convert any website to WebMCP—in one shot.
about_excerpt: Analyze, recommend, and convert any website to WebMCP—in one shot. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web was built for people clicking. Some sites later gained APIs; many accumulated PDFs, hidden rules, multi-page forms, phone-only support, and offline handoffs. Browser agents can read those pages, but they still have to guess at the interface and often stall at the one consequential step that matters. WebMCP changes that by letting a website expose an explicit, typed contract for agents. The remaining adoption problem is substantial: a site owner still has to inspect an existing workflow, decide what should be a read, what should become an editable proposal, and what must wait for a human, then implement and verify the resulting tools. We built Overturn to make that retrofit process a product. For the end-to-end proof, we chose one of the hardest common workflows: appealing a health-plan prior-authorization denial. In Medicare Advantage in 2024, plans processed nearly 53 million prior-authorization requests. Only 11.5% of denied requests were appealed, even though 80.7% of appeals were partially or fully overturned ( KFF ). The fictional Larkspur Health Plan portal in our demo starts where many real workflows still start: a PDF letter, a six-page form, rules that are referenced but not exposed, and a fax or mailing address. What it does Overturn Retrofit takes a public URL and: Scans up to eight same-origin pages for forms, tables, detail pages, documents, offline submission instructions, cited policies, phone-only support, iframes, sign-in requirements, and WebMCP headers. Produces a 0–100 agent-readiness score and evidence-backed findings grouped as blockers, gaps, and notes. Recommends a typed WebMCP tool inventory. Reads are marked read-only, writes become on-page proposals, and consequential actions are explicitly human-gated. Generates a starter document.modelContext.registerTool() module and a Markdown implementation report. Exposes its own WebMCP meta-tools— analyze_site , get_readiness_report , list_recommended_tools , and get_generated_code —so a developer’s agent can drive the retrofit itself. The analyzer does not pretend it can infer and safely wire every site’s private business logic. It generates the tool layer and concrete fixes; a developer or coding agent connects app-specific handlers. To prove that the plan is actionable, we ran Retrofit against the fictional legacy portal, implemented its recommendations, and shipped the complete before-and-after experience on the same live site. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This project depends on WebMCP rather than merely adding it as a feature. On the Retrofit page, an agent can run the audit, inspect the findings, list the proposed tools, and retrieve the generated code through four page-native tools. On the rebuilt appeals portal, 14 tools expose the actual workflow: member context, denials, deadlines, policy criteria, drafting, evidence completeness, review type, submission, status, and external review. The tool surface is state-scoped. Drafting tools appear only in the appeal workspace; after filing, they disappear and status tools take their place. Every agent call is visible in the Activity panel, and every proposed write is rendered on the page for the person to inspect or edit. Without WebMCP, an automation agent must inspect the DOM, open PDFs, infer what fields mean, and eventually stops at the fax instruction. With WebMCP, the site itself tells the agent what it may read, what it may propose, and where the person must take over. How it creates a better user experience For a site owner, Overturn replaces a blank page with an actionable plan: what blocks agents today, which tools to expose, how to describe and scope them, which actions need confirmation, and the code to start from. For a person using the retrofitted site, the agent handles the repetitive work—reading the denial, matching records to five policy criteria, drafting one evidence-backed argument per criterion, checking completeness, and calculating deadlines. The person keeps the decisions that are actually theirs: choose records, edit the language, select standard or expedited review, and sign. The work never disappears into a chat window. Drafts are on the page, labelled and editable. Tool calls are logged. The person sees exactly what changed and remains in control. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Before: an agent can read a denial letter and locate the appeal form, but the workflow is unstructured and ends at a fax or mailing address. It cannot reliably know the plan’s five criteria, prove that the evidence is complete, or safely file the appeal. After: in one sitting and on one shared page, the agent reads the structured denial and criteria, opens the appeal, drafts five arguments tied to named records, and re-checks completeness as the member attaches evidence and edits the draft. The agent can request submission, but it cannot file. It returns pending_confirmation , the site renders a Sign & submit card, and only the member’s click creates a case number and starts the decision clock. That read → proposal → human commit pattern can extend beyond appeals to any claim-shaped dispute or regulated legacy workflow. How we built it Application: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, and Vercel. Analyzer: deterministic server-side heuristics using Cheerio. Crawling is SSRF-guarded: HTTP(S) only, private network ranges refused, and redirects, response size, page count, and time are capped. WebMCP layer: document.modelContext.registerTool() with a legacy navigator.modelContext fallback, one AbortController per tool, duplicate-safe registration, readOnlyHint annotations, concise descriptions, and bounded outputs. Safety: reads are free; writes render as proposals; submit_appeal and request_external_review return pending_confirmation . The server rejects submission without the human-click marker using 403 human_confirmation_required . State and judge access: each visitor receives an isolated localStorage sandbox. There is no login or database. A replay demonstrates the same flow for browsers without site-tools access. Verification: a comprehensive Puppeteer smoke suite exercises route scoping, the full appeal flow, generated code, analyzer guards, human-gated submission, and the post-filing tool transition. We also tested the deployed tools in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and WebMCP-enabled Chrome. Build workflow: we used Claude Code on an NVIDIA DGX Spark for research, implementation, debugging, testing, deployment, and the reproducible FFmpeg/edge-tts video pipeline. The submitted application does not depend on an LLM at runtime. Challenges we ran into Designing real human confirmation. WebMCP does not currently provide a tool-level confirmation primitive. We created an application protocol instead: an agent can propose a consequential action, the page renders a confirmation card, and a server-side gate accepts only the person’s click. Keeping tools synchronized with application state. The useful tool set changes as the member moves from denial to draft to filed case. We built one registry that derives tools from both the route and appeal status, unregisters stale tools, and remains stable under React Strict Mode and hot reloads. Analyzing arbitrary URLs safely. A URL analyzer can easily become an SSRF proxy or an unbounded crawler. We had to reject private addresses and tightly cap redirects, bytes, pages, and request time while still returning a useful partial report when some pages fail. Drawing an honest conversion boundary. Static HTML can reveal affordances, but it cannot reveal every private API or JavaScript-only state transition. Generated handlers therefore make app-specific wiring explicit instead of hiding it behind a false “one-click” claim. Accomplishments we are proud of Shipped the analyzer, legacy portal, agent-native portal, and readiness record as one coherent live product. Turned the legacy portal’s 40/100 audit—two blockers, two gaps, and nine recommended tools—into a working portal with 14 domain tools plus four Retrofit meta-tools. Made the agent’s work visible and editable while enforcing consequential consent on the server, not in a prompt. Built a complete, reproducible before-and-after demo and an automated verification suite during the hackathon window. What we learned Structured reads alone do not complete workflows. Agents also need typed proposals, deterministic validation, explicit commit paths, and post-action status. Human control works best as product architecture, not as a prompt instruction. Tool names, descriptions, scope, and lifecycle are part of the user experience. A generated scaffold is valuable only when it clearly shows what has been inferred and what a developer still needs to connect. WebMCP tooling for FullCalendar React applications without replacing the UI or the backend.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story

 Inspiration 

 I mainly got inspired because two of the projects I developed for a couple of small businesses use FullCalendar (React), so I was hoping to add agent functionality for scheduling. This was the perfect opportunity and the perfect tool. 

 What it does 

 Exposes six tools for reading calendar context, finding events, and reading individual events, and interact with them to create, update, and delete. 

 How we built it 

 I used AI agents like Codex and Cursor. I did have experience with the FullCalendar implementation, what I did not have experience with was Chrome-specific or Chromium-specific developer tooling. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest challenge was to contain the boundary between the adapter and the host application because it could really easily outgrow and become opinionated about the implementation, which is contradictory to the ergonomics I'm looking for. 

 Coding agents have this tendency that makes us overbuild, so I actually created three implementations before actually trimming about 60% of features I'd say, before freezing. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I think is easy to understand, and it can be very developer-agent-friendly. 

 What we learned 

 I learned that less is more and clarity is the best way to communicate a tool description for agents. I mean, AI has come so far that it can pretty much understand intent even if you mess up your prompts. 

 What's next for FullCalendar WebMCP 

 I think this implementation can grow as an open-source project, especially since FullCalendar is used in production by many devs (9M+ monthly npm downloads). And not only FullCalendar, I actually bought a domain called protocoltooling.com that I probably would like to convert to a webmcp-focused tool creation organization for widely-used web-integrations like FC.
