title: innpilot hotel pms
pitch: Hotel PMS with WebMCP tools for AI agents
about_excerpt: Hotel PMS with WebMCP tools for AI agents Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 innpilot landing page dashboard Inspiration Hotel management involves constant operational work: checking room availability, making reservations, updating room status, checking guests in and out, and monitoring occupancy and revenue. We built InnPilot because we wanted to explore a different question: what if a hotel management system was designed to be used by both people and AI agents? Instead of adding an AI chatbot that only answers questions, we wanted the agent to interact with the actual hotel system through structured capabilities. WebMCP gave us the opportunity to make InnPilot's hotel operations directly discoverable and usable by agents while keeping the application responsible for enforcing its business rules. Our goal was simple: make hotel software something an agent can actually operate, not just talk about. What it does InnPilot is a multi-tenant hotel management platform for hotel owners, managers, and staff. Through WebMCP, InnPilot exposes real hotel operations as structured tools that agents can use directly. An agent can: View hotel rooms and their current housekeeping status Check room availability for specific dates Filter availability by room type Create reservations List and filter reservations Check guests in and out Cancel reservations or mark no-shows Update room status, including Cleaning, Maintenance, and Out of Service Retrieve occupancy information Retrieve revenue and financial performance The tools are designed around hotel-domain actions rather than generic database operations. For example, an agent doesn't get a generic "write reservation" function. It gets a purpose-built innpilot_create_reservation tool with a defined schema and hotel-specific validation. This also means the agent cannot simply bypass InnPilot's rules. Overlapping reservations are rejected, and rooms under maintenance or out of service cannot be booked. The result is a collaboration model where: Human intent → AI agent → WebMCP tool → InnPilot business logic → Result How we built it InnPilot is a web-based multi-tenant hotel management application. We integrated WebMCP by registering structured tools that expose important hotel capabilities to agents. Each tool provides: A unique tool name A clear description explaining when it should be used A structured input schema An execution handler connected to InnPilot's existing application logic We deliberately exposed domain-level operations such as innpilot_check_room_availability, innpilot_create_reservation, innpilot_set_room_status, innpilot_get_occupancy, and innpilot_get_revenue. This allows the agent to interact with InnPilot through well-defined capabilities instead of trying to navigate buttons, forms, or pages. The underlying application continues to perform validation and enforce hotel rules, so WebMCP becomes a reliable agent interface to the existing product rather than a separate parallel system. Challenges we ran into: The biggest challenge was making agent interaction reliable enough for real hotel operations. Reservations aren't just simple database writes. Availability depends on dates, existing reservations, room status, and operational constraints. We had to make sure that: Availability reflects the requested stay rather than only the room's current status Existing and legacy bookings are considered Maintenance and out-of-service rooms cannot be sold Reservation creation rejects conflicting bookings Reservation status transitions are handled correctly Tool inputs are strictly validated Agents receive useful results after each operation Another challenge was deciding what should become a tool. We learned that exposing too much low-level functionality can make an agent interface harder to use. We focused instead on meaningful hotel actions that map directly to tasks a manager or staff member would actually perform. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that InnPilot is more than a WebMCP proof of concept. We connected WebMCP to an actual hotel management workflow with real operational state and business rules. An agent can go from: Finding an available room → creating a reservation → managing the reservation lifecycle → updating housekeeping → checking occupancy → analyzing revenue. We're particularly proud of the validation layer. If an agent tries to book an occupied room or create an overlapping reservation, InnPilot doesn't blindly execute the request. The application rejects the operation according to its hotel rules. That demonstrates what we believe agent-native applications should look like: agents get powerful capabilities, but the application remains responsible for correctness. What we learned WebMCP changed the way we think about web applications. We learned that a website can be designed not only as a visual interface for humans, but also as a structured capability layer for agents. The most useful agent tools are not necessarily complex. A small collection of well-designed, domain-specific tools can allow an agent to accomplish an entire workflow when those tools compose naturally. We also learned that agent-native design requires more than exposing functions. Tool descriptions, schemas, validation, error handling, and business rules all become part of the experience. Most importantly, we learned that human + agent collaboration can be a product feature in itself. What's next for InnPilot We're continuing to develop InnPilot as an agent-native hotel PMS. Next, we want to expand the range of workflows that hotel staff can delegate to agents while keeping humans in control of important decisions. We see opportunities for agents to coordinate more complex workflows across reservations, housekeeping, restaurant operations, conferences, payments, reporting, and hotel administration. Our bigger vision goes beyond InnPilot. Today, most websites are built primarily for humans to navigate. We believe the next generation of the web can expose structured capabilities that agents can discover and operate safely. InnPilot is our exploration of what happens when a real-world business application is built for both humans and agents from the start. title: Investigation Canvas
pitch: Investigation Canvas turns messy data into a shared, visual investigation where humans spot what matters and AI agents test it with auditable WebMCP tools
about_excerpt: Investigation Canvas turns messy data into a shared, visual investigation where humans spot what matters and AI agents test it with auditable WebMCP tools Like Comment Story Updates About the project Inspiration Most AI data tools force people into one of two interfaces: a chat window that hides the underlying evidence, or a dashboard that an agent can only understand by scraping text, pixels, and DOM elements. Real investigations work differently. A human notices an unusual cluster, questions an assumption, or recognizes missing context. An agent can search hundreds of records, compare cohorts, inspect documents, and track several explanations simultaneously. We built Investigation Canvas around one idea: the human and the agent should work on the same visible investigation—not exchange disconnected summaries. What it does Investigation Canvas is a visual reasoning workspace for exploring datasets, evidence, relationships, hypotheses, findings, and possible causes. Humans can: Filter, search, and visually select records Explore linked scatter plots, timelines, tables, and relationship graphs Inspect evidence and its trust level Challenge the agent with contradictory examples Arrange findings and evidence on a spatial canvas Review every action through an auditable provenance trail Through WebMCP, an external agent receives 48 structured tools operating on the same workspace. It can query records, compare cohorts, rank distinguishing features, find correlations and outliers, inspect evidence, navigate relationships, create competing hypotheses, search for counterevidence, record findings, build causal links, save views, and branch an investigation. Every agent action changes the visible workspace. The human can inspect, rearrange, question, or reject the result. The project includes three complete example investigations: A checkout conversion regression with two independent causes An ML model-quality regression involving preprocessing and optimizer behavior A suspicious transaction network with explicit evidence-trust boundaries Why WebMCP A scatter plot may be immediately meaningful to a person but opaque to an agent. Investigation Canvas already knows which records each point represents, which cohort is selected, how evidence relates to a hypothesis, and which actions changed the investigation. WebMCP exposes those semantics directly instead of making the agent reverse-engineer the rendered interface. This creates shared attention . A human can select an unexpected group of records and ask the agent to investigate exactly that selection. The agent can focus a source, create a hypothesis, or place a finding on the canvas, and the human immediately sees the result. WebMCP turns agent reasoning into inspectable product actions. How we built it Investigation Canvas is a dependency-light static web application built with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. A deterministic state store drives both the visual interface and the WebMCP tool implementations. Human interactions and agent actions therefore operate on the same investigation state rather than separate copies. The page registers its tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Read-only tools are marked accordingly, while tools returning third-party evidence identify that output as untrusted. Mutating tools use the same state operations as the visible interface, making their effects observable across selections, filters, evidence, hypotheses, findings, canvas artifacts, branches, and provenance. We also implemented: CSV, JSON, JSONL, and NDJSON imports Public JSON API snapshots Schema inference Investigation export and restoration Browser-local persistence Undo and redo Saved analysis views Restorable investigation branches Web-worker processing for larger local datasets Three deterministic example datasets The Do example experience lets a judge choose an investigation, understand its mission, load an isolated workspace, and copy a prompt for an external WebMCP agent. It never fakes an agent conversation or silently runs a scripted simulation. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was making agent activity understandable. Our early demo concepts moved too quickly, displayed too much information, and blurred the distinction between a real external agent and a scripted presentation. We replaced that approach with a clear handoff: choose a dataset, understand the mission, copy a prompt, connect through WebMCP, and watch durable actions appear in the shared workspace. We also had to preserve spatial context. Selecting a record or focusing evidence should not unexpectedly reset the canvas or camera. Data-state changes and view-state changes were separated so human exploration remains stable while the agent works. Finally, evidence is not automatically truth. The suspicious-transaction scenario contains both verified internal material and untrusted external claims. Investigation Canvas makes this distinction explicit instead of allowing an agent to treat every document as authoritative. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most powerful when a website already possesses rich domain semantics. Structured tools make agents more reliable, but the larger benefit is collaboration: agent actions become visible and reviewable instead of disappearing inside a chat response. We also learned that a serious investigation tool must make disagreement easy. Competing hypotheses, contradictory evidence, falsification questions, human-selected counterexamples, and provenance are not optional additions. They are what keep fast agent analysis accountable. What’s next Next, we would add authenticated streaming data connectors, server-side processing for very large datasets, real-time multi-user investigations, and exportable investigation reports. The central interaction would remain unchanged: humans direct attention and exercise judgment, while agents perform structured analysis through visible, auditable tools. The saved version is also available in SUBMISSION.md . title: Versailles — The Thread of Time
pitch: Explore Versailles across five eras. The player reasons; a WebMCP agent reads real game state and offers bounded help, without taking over.
about_excerpt: Explore Versailles across five eras. The player reasons; a WebMCP agent reads real game state and offers bounded help, without taking over. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Versailles is not just a monument. It is a place shaped by power, ambition, art, diplomacy and history. We wanted players to work out where and when they had arrived through observation and action, rather than turning pages or receiving answers from an AI. Our principle is simple: the player reasons; the agent supports, without taking over. What it does The Hall of Mirrors becomes an interface to time. The player restores five fragments: WITHDRAWAL → POWER → RUPTURE → MEMORY → INFLUENCE . Across 1623, 1682, 1789, 1837–1919 and 2026, the mechanics change with the historical role of Versailles: examine a map, letter and seal; match six royal orders to their recipients; find a concealed passage by observing the woodwork; arrange discovered objects into sequences; and connect evidence about the palace's changing function. The final mirror returns to the present. Versailles is no longer the seat of royal power, but its history gives diplomatic encounters symbolic weight. This is historical interpretation, not political endorsement. Why WebMCP matters WebMCP gives an external agent a bounded, structured view of actual game state. It does not have to guess progress from pixels or inspect unrestricted internal data. The game reports the current phase, discovered evidence, relevant errors and permitted assistance. Zero relevant errors means SILENT and refusal of a hint request. One permits NUDGE ; two or more permit GUIDE . Hints are selected by deterministic game rules, not freely generated by a language model. In the 1682 demonstration, an order goes to the wrong recipient. A real request_hint call returns a reading strategy, not the recipient's name. A later sequence error in 1919 produces a different method hint. The player makes the next choice. How we built it Native HTML, CSS and JavaScript ES modules support a pure state reducer and filtered public projection. The static game needs no account, backend, database or API key. Five tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(): get_mission_state reads filtered state and assistance policy. inspect_evidence examines one to six discovered observations. request_hint requests policy-bounded help. compare_evidence compares two or three discovered observations. submit_hypothesis submits an available hypothesis to normal domain validation. JSON Schema describes inputs; runtime validation and abort signals enforce boundaries. Read tools do not change progress. A valid hypothesis may advance through the normal reducer, but cannot force success, bypass prerequisites or ask for hidden solutions. Challenges and what we learned The main challenge was making assistance useful without replacing historical reasoning. Each era needs a different puzzle, while the agent needs one coherent contract. Filtering discovered evidence, enforcing error thresholds and validating every action matter more than offering unrestricted context. We also kept filming evidence honest: cards labelled RECORDED TOOL RESPONSE are editorial layouts of actual recorded responses, not invented game UI or a simulated autonomous conversation. Filming begins at chapter checkpoints; the video is not an uninterrupted public playthrough. Validation and limitations The reviewed local candidate passed 97 automated tests . Eight boundary tests cover repeated errors, hidden evidence, prerequisites, cancellation, restart and final-fragment idempotence. After the contemporary visual replacement, 17 affected tests passed , and the arrival/welcome interactions were checked in Edge. There is no persistent save : reloading starts a clean game. Tool filtering is not source-code secrecy; the JavaScript remains inspectable. We do not claim measured learning outcomes or universal browser compatibility. Media and provenance The 2:40 jury film uses the author's approved English transcript, narrated by Charles through ElevenLabs . Historical illustrations are AI-assisted reconstructions, not archival photographs. Contemporary 2026 visuals in the prepared release use credited Official White House Photos by Daniel Torok , taken at Versailles on June 17, 2026. No endorsement is implied. Detailed credits and historical sources are included in the repository. Open source The project is released under the MIT License . The complete source code, assets, automated test suite and reproducible setup instructions are available in the linked public GitHub repository. What's next Broader player testing and accessibility refinement, while preserving the central boundary: assistance should help the player reason, not remove the reason to play. title: TaskBridge
pitch: Your AI-powered bridge to better job opportunities.
about_excerpt: Your AI-powered bridge to better job opportunities. Like 2 Comment Story Updates TaskBridge — A job workspace designed for humans and their AI agents Inspiration Job hunting is full of repetitive, low-judgment work: searching through dozens of listings, reading requirements, comparing them against your skills, and tracking interesting opportunities. As someone who has personally experienced this process, I started thinking about where AI agents could genuinely help. Agents are well suited to discovery, filtering, and repetitive tasks, yet most websites still force them to interact like humans, clicking through interfaces that were never designed for them. When I discovered the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore the opposite approach: what if an application treated the AI agent as a first-class user? That idea became TaskBridge. TaskBridge is a job workspace where humans and AI agents collaborate. The agent discovers opportunities, compares them against a candidate's profile, and shortlists relevant jobs. The human remains responsible for judgment and final decisions. Saving a job can be automated. Applying for one is always the human's call. What it does TaskBridge allows users to browse and manage job opportunities through a familiar web interface while exposing structured capabilities to AI agents through WebMCP. The agent can: Search for job opportunities. Retrieve detailed job information. Access the candidate's profile. Save relevant opportunities. Retrieve saved jobs. Draft a tailored application. For example, a user can ask an agent to find remote jobs matching their experience. The agent retrieves their profile, searches available opportunities, compares requirements, and saves the strongest matches for the user to review. TaskBridge also supports live remote job listings and allows users to maintain an editable candidate profile. Users can upload a CV, which can be parsed to help populate their profile. The goal is not to replace the job seeker, but to reduce the repetitive work surrounding job discovery and applications. How we built it TaskBridge is built with Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The application registers six tools using the browser-native WebMCP API ( document.modelContext.registerTool ): search_jobs get_job_details get_candidate_profile save_job get_saved_jobs apply_job One of the key architectural decisions was making the human interface and AI agent tools share the same underlying logic layer. The dashboard and the agent therefore use the same search, ranking, and application-generation logic rather than maintaining separate implementations. Job matching uses a simple and explainable overlap score between a job's tags and the candidate's skills and interests: $$ \mathrm{match}(j) = \mathrm{round}\left( 100 \cdot \frac{|T_j \cap (S \cup I)|}{|T_j|} \right) $$ where Tj represents a job's tags, while S and I represent the candidate's skills and interests. Live remote jobs are fetched from the Remotive feed through a route handler, with bundled sample data acting as an automatic fallback so the application remains functional even if the external feed fails. Users can edit their candidate profile and upload a CV. PDF and DOCX files are parsed locally, with optional AI-assisted parsing available through the user's own OpenRouter API key. The apply_job tool can generate a tailored cover letter, but deliberately never submits an application. The user reviews the draft and decides whether to apply through the original job posting. The project itself was also built through human and AI collaboration. I directed the product and technical decisions while using an AI coding agent to help scaffold, refactor, and verify parts of the application. Challenges we ran into Working with an emerging browser API WebMCP is still an emerging standard, which meant dealing with browser implementation quirks during development and testing. Chrome's testing environment can return inputSchema as a JSON string and reject certain tool execution paths. I handled this by normalizing schemas and ensuring the same underlying handlers could execute consistently. React StrictMode also introduced double-mount behaviour that could interrupt tool registration. This required careful lifecycle handling using AbortController . Hydration-safe persistence Saved jobs, applications, and candidate profiles are stored using localStorage , but the application also needs to render correctly on the server. I used useSyncExternalStore with server snapshots to manage client-side persistence without introducing hydration issues. Unstructured job data Live job descriptions often arrive as messy HTML. Instead of injecting raw HTML into the application, I built a small parser that converts headings, paragraphs, and lists into structured content for safer rendering. Demo reliability A live external API can fail at exactly the wrong moment, especially when a demo is involved. Because computers apparently sense deadlines. To avoid this, every data layer gracefully falls back to bundled sample data. I also built a development-only agent demo using an OpenRouter tool-calling loop and a smoke script to verify all six tools end-to-end without requiring a WebMCP-capable browser. Accomplishments that we're proud of Building a complete human-and-agent collaboration workflow in less than a day. Successfully exposing six structured capabilities through the browser-native WebMCP API. Designing the agent with clear trust boundaries, allowing it to assist with discovery and drafting without autonomously submitting job applications. Creating a shared logic layer so the human UI and AI tools always operate on the same underlying functionality. Supporting both live job data and reliable fallback data for a resilient demo experience. Building an accessible interface with visible focus states, reduced-motion support, a skip link, and an aria-live agent transcript. Demonstrating that WebMCP can enable a more intentional relationship between web applications and AI agents. What we learned WebMCP changes the integration model There is no traditional integration layer to build between an application and an agent. The page declares its capabilities, and compatible agents can discover and use those tools directly. The application's responsibility is to expose clear, reliable, and honest capabilities. Tool descriptions are part of the user experience Agents don't navigate an application by looking at buttons. They rely on tool descriptions and JSON schemas to understand what they can do. Writing clear tool definitions turned out to be just as important as designing the human interface. Trust boundaries improve agent experiences Giving the agent the ability to search, compare, save opportunities, and draft applications while keeping final submission in human hands made the collaboration model clearer. Trust boundaries are not necessarily limitations. They can be product features. Designing for agents improves applications for humans too Thinking in terms of structured data, explicit actions, and predictable states resulted in a cleaner application architecture and a simpler interface for human users. What's next for TaskBridge TaskBridge is currently a proof of concept exploring how job platforms can be designed for both humans and AI agents. Future improvements could include: Integration with more job sources. Improved candidate-job matching. Application tracking. Interview and follow-up management. TaskBridge started with a simple question: what happens when we stop forcing AI agents to navigate websites designed exclusively for humans? The answer I wanted to explore is simple: the future of the web may not be agents becoming better at pretending to be human users. It may be applications becoming better at working with both humans and their agents. So I had a different idea: instead of learning how to operate a complex 3D tool myself, I wanted to describe the video I imagined to an AI and let the AI operate the tool for me. It can load Gaussian Splatting assets, create camera paths, add visual effects, build a timeline, render videos, and export them directly from the browser. The most important feature is AI control. I can describe the camera movement or effect I want in natural language, and the AI operates the virtual camera, adds effects, and builds the timeline for me. I’m an engineer, not a professional video editor, but Splat Studio lets me create videos that feel far beyond my editing skills. How we built it I chose Spark 2.0 because it already had the visual effects I wanted and could use WebGPU for fast rendering directly in the browser. The first version was a local tool built only for myself. It used a local API, so although it worked for creating my own videos, it was difficult to share with friends. Later, I integrated WebMCP, which made it much easier to turn Splat Studio into an AI-native web tool that other people could use. For the implementation, I worked with Codex, which handled essentially all of the coding and the WebMCP integration while I focused on the product idea, workflow, and creative direction. Creative intent is often vague, so translating instructions like “make the camera orbit around the subject and slowly pull back” into predictable editor actions was an important part of the project. Codex allowed me to focus much more on what the tool should do rather than spending all of my time implementing every part manually. What’s next for Splat Studio Next, I want to make Splat Studio easier for anyone to use, not just for my own projects. I want to improve AI camera direction, add more effects, make timeline editing more flexible, and make it easier to create polished videos from Gaussian Splatting scenes with only natural-language instructions. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Orqenta
pitch: Orqenta is a human–agent collaboration layer that makes the open web agent-ready, enabling AI to discover tools, perform tasks, and collaborate with people—securely and under human control.\n
about_excerpt:
Orqenta is a human–agent collaboration layer that makes the open web agent-ready, enabling AI to discover tools, perform tasks, and collaborate with people—securely and under human control.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 a detailed media overview 
 
 1 2 



 
 About Orqenta 

 We built "Orqenta" around a simple question: "What if the web was designed for both humans and AI agents from the start?" 

 Today, AI agents are increasingly good at understanding intent, but interacting with real websites can still be fragile. An agent may know 'what' a user wants but struggle with buttons, forms, page structure, and application-specific workflows. We were inspired by the idea behind "WebMCP": instead of forcing agents to interpret every interface visually, websites can expose their capabilities as structured tools that agents can understand and use. 

 That became the foundation of "Orqenta", a human–agent collaboration layer for the open web. Our goal was to explore a future where "websites expose capabilities, agents execute them, and humans remain in control". 

 What We Built 

 Orqenta connects human intent with agent-accessible web capabilities through WebMCP. A user can describe what they want to accomplish, while an AI agent can discover available tools, understand their schemas, perform structured actions, and return meaningful results. 

 Rather than treating an AI agent as an external chatbot, Orqenta treats it as a "participant in the web experience". 

 The core interaction looks like: 

 "Human intent → Agent discovers tools → Agent performs structured actions → Human reviews the result" 

 This creates a more reliable interaction model than asking an agent to independently guess how a webpage works. 

 How We Built It 

 We designed Orqenta around a modular web architecture so that the product remains useful even when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 At the application layer, we expose clearly defined capabilities through WebMCP tools using structured names, descriptions, input schemas, and executable functions. The frontend provides the human-facing interface, while the tool layer acts as the bridge between agent reasoning and application actions. 

 We focused heavily on making every tool: 

 
 "Discoverable" — agents can understand what the tool does. 
 "Structured" — inputs and outputs follow predictable schemas. 
 "Controllable" — humans can remain involved in consequential actions. 
 "Composable" — multiple tools can be combined into larger workflows. 
 "Progressively enhanced" — the application still works as a normal web application without WebMCP support. 
 

 What We Learned 

 The biggest lesson was that "agent-native web design is different from traditional UI design". 

 A traditional interface is primarily designed for a human to visually interpret. An agent-facing interface needs something else: explicit capabilities, predictable inputs, clear outputs, validation, and well-defined boundaries. 

 We learned to think about application features not only as UI components, but also as "machine-actionable capabilities". 

 For example, instead of only building a "Search" interface, we ask: 

 
 What exactly should an agent be able to do with search? 
 

 That shift led us to define tools around intent and actions rather than around individual UI elements. 

 We also learned that human oversight remains critical. Giving agents more capability does not mean removing people from the workflow. In many cases, the better experience is agent-assisted execution with human control at the right moments . 

 Challenges We Faced 

 One of our biggest challenges was working with an emerging technology and designing around capabilities that are still evolving. 

 We had to make architectural decisions that would support WebMCP without making the entire application dependent on it. This led us to separate the core application logic from the agent interaction layer. 

 Another challenge was determining the right level of tool abstraction. Exposing every UI interaction as a tool creates noise and makes agents harder to use. Exposing too few tools makes useful workflows impossible. We therefore focused on high-value, task-oriented capabilities instead of exposing raw interface actions. 

 We also had to think carefully about security. An agent capable of taking actions on behalf of a user introduces questions around authorization, validation, sensitive operations, and human confirmation. We designed Orqenta so that agent capability does not automatically mean unrestricted authority. 

 Why Orqenta Matters 

 We believe the next evolution of the web will not be purely human-facing or purely agent-facing. 

 It will be "collaborative". 

 Humans bring goals, context, judgment, and creativity. Agents bring speed, automation, reasoning, and the ability to execute structured workflows. 

 "Orqenta explores what happens when the web becomes a shared environment for both." 

 Instead of AI merely reading the web, "Orqenta explores a web where agents can actually work with it—while people stay in control."

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Mission Control is a shared operations surface for teams and their AI agents. The challenge was to make agent access useful without turning a real operations system into an open door. 

 What we built 

 Mission Control: Shield Wall is a public-safe, fictional dashboard where a person and WebMCP agents can observe a synthetic fleet, create an ephemeral task, run six local security checks, preview a simulated scheduled report, prove tool behavior with a five-scenario harness, and walk through a reversible incident drill. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 A person can see the same state an agent is using, while the agent receives explicit schemas instead of guessing through buttons. The tools are bounded to fictional memory: one read, one validated task write, one local scan, and one reversible incident action. Invalid inputs and external-workflow attempts are rejected by the evaluation harness. 

 Privacy and implementation 

 The demo has no backend, database, analytics, credentials, cookies, external calls, or production integrations. It uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zod, and the experimental document.modelContext.registerTool pattern. Every visible organization, operator, task, check, and incident is fictional. 

 What we learned 

 Designing the human and agent surfaces together made least privilege visible as a product feature. Shield Wall and the repeatable harness turn safety claims into something a judge can inspect and run.

title: Team Rocket Command Center
pitch: 6 agent drivable builds, one Team Rocket.
about_excerpt: 6 agent drivable builds, one Team Rocket. Like Comment Story Updates 6 agent drivable builds within one command center Inspiration Team Rocket started as six small AI builds for the DC DevFest 2026 Buildathon, where we took third place. When we heard about the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge we could not help ourselves. Every one of those builds already had a human interface worth using, and WebMCP asked a question we wanted to answer: what does it take to hand that same interface to an agent without taking it away from the person? The answer we wanted was not a separate API. It was the same screen, driven from either side. What it does Team Rocket Command Center is six AI apps behind one Next.js site: a kanban board whose cards are segments of one effort-weighted progress bar, a group restaurant picker decided by counting swipes, a policy diff that ranks changes by who they land on, a resume-to-posting gap finder with a two-week plan, an ambient note taker that files what you say, and a reader that illustrates a chapter scene by scene. Each runs on the visitor's own Gemini key. Every build is drivable by an AI agent through WebMCP. Each page registers its actions as tools on document.modelContext , 44 in all, and every tool calls the same function the button calls, so a person and an agent are always looking at the same page. An "Agent is driving" pill in the header names the running tool. A WebMCP button lists what an agent could do on the current page before one arrives. The full surface, with schemas, lives at teamrocket.website/webmcp and is rendered from the same definitions the pages register. Anything destructive stops at an in-page confirm bar and waits for a human. No tool can read, accept or set an API key. How we built it A single client hook, useWebMCPTools , registers a page's tools while it is mounted and unregisters them through the registration's AbortSignal on unmount. It reads document.modelContext , the current spec and Chrome 153+, falls back to navigator.modelContext for Chrome 149 to 152, and degrades to a console.debug where neither exists so the site works in every browser. Each build keeps a static tools.js with names, descriptions and JSON Schemas, and wires handlers in its component next to the state they touch. Handlers read live state through a ref, so a tool always sees the current board, deck or workspace without re-registering on every render. ok() and fail() build the result shape; failures always carry a next-step hint and nothing ever throws. Four site-wide tools live in the shell: list the builds, open one, check which keys are set as booleans, and open the key panel for the human to type into. One tool is declarative: the name form in This or That carries toolname , tooldescription , toolautosubmit and a toolparamdescription , and answers agent-invoked submits with respondWith() . Destructive tools call gate() , which blocks on a confirm bar in the shell and resolves when the human presses Confirm or Cancel, the agent aborts, or a minute passes. The toolactivated and toolcancel events drive the header pill. Everything is committed in small steps in the open, MIT licensed. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. Articles still said navigator.modelContext and unregisterTool ; the current draft says document.modelContext with an AbortSignal, and Chrome 149 and Chrome 153 disagree. We read the Chromium IDL rather than the blog posts and support both. Agents arrive through different doors. The Codex Chrome extension drives the DOM and never saw our tools, while Codex's in-app browser called them directly. The first agent to reach the site used the buttons, which is exactly why the human UI had to keep working. That agent also found a real bug. Giving plan() parameters for the tool meant React handed it the click event when a person pressed the button, and the event's DOM node broke JSON serialisation. One-line fix, and a good reminder that adding an agent path can break the human one. Smaller ones: React's compiler lint rejects setting state in effects, so adopting saved state after hydration needed a useSyncExternalStore pattern instead; and transcribing a three-minute demo in one pass drifted ten seconds by the end, so captions are now generated in silence-aligned chunks. Accomplishments that we're proud of 44 tools across six real multi-stage pipelines, not a to-do list, each with the screen as the record of what the agent did. A safety model you can see: the pill, the confirm bar, and zero ways for a tool to touch a key. A tool catalog generated from the same code that registers the tools, so the documentation cannot drift from what is live. A pattern small enough to copy: one hook, one tools file per page, handlers beside their state. A clean lint run, a compile-checked build, and a commit history that shows the work as it happened. What we learned WebMCP is at its best when it is a second door into an existing room rather than a new building. Because our tools call the button functions, every agent action is visible, undoable where the UI allows it, and testable by clicking. The places where we were tempted to add tool-only shortcuts were the places bugs appeared. Descriptions are the interface. An agent decides what to call from the description alone, so "when to use this" matters more than "what this does", and every error message is a chance to steer the next call. And the confirm bar earned its place. Watching an agent stop and wait for a person on camera made the case for human-in-the-loop better than any paragraph could. What's next for Team Rocket Command Center Re-record the six walkthroughs against the current builds, and add an agent-driven clip for each the way Taskboard has now. Give the site's own player a proper caption track. Add outputSchema to the tools once the spec lands it, and revisit readOnlyHint and consequentialHint as agents start honouring them. Then keep using the site as what it has become: a worked example anyone can fork to wire their own app the same way. about_excerpt: VIA keyboard configurator with WebMCP Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I got a new mechanical keyboard a few months back and was configuring it through the via configurator (usevia.app). I found it difficult to search up key codes and configuration syntax but when I heard about WebMCP, it seemed like the right tool to help. I used Redux (the app's existing state system) to store the agent's activity log and pending proposals, right next to the app's normal state. Some tools only exist temporarily. For example, "write this proposal" only appears as an available tool once a human has actually approved it, and disappears again afterward. Challenges I ran into I ran into a case that looked like a bug but wasn't: a keyboard that was visible to the browser but wasn't actually running keyboard firmware that supports VIA at all. That took real time to track down before I confirmed it was a hardware/firmware issue, not something wrong with my code :P Accomplishments that I'm proud of An actual working setup that lets your agent talk with the hardware! What I learned That WebMCP helps both human and agent to collaborate without needing any additional setup. What's next for remap Support for more QMK features (like tap dance and key combos), and a history view so a human can look back and see everything an agent has proposed and why, not just what's happening right now. title: WORLDLINE
pitch: WORLDLINE is a WebMCP science lesson where you and a browser agent test possible futures for a probe near a black hole, learn from the evidence,and decide what to save.
about_excerpt: WORLDLINE is a WebMCP science lesson where you and a browser agent test possible futures for a probe near a black hole, learn from the evidence,and decide what to save. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Space science is full of ideas that are fascinating but difficult to experience. A light-year is an enormous distance. A signal can travel at the speed of light and still take 23 years to arrive. A spacecraft may have enough fuel to escape or enough time to transmit its discoveries, but not both. A video popped up on my Youtube feed while I was on a walk and gave me the inspiration for the base idea. I wanted to make them something a person could investigate with an AI agent. WORLDLINE began with a simple question: What if WebMCP could turn a webpage into a shared science lesson, where the agent investigates the evidence, the learner contributes their own thinking and the final decision remains human? What WORLDLINE does A probe near a black hole has recorded measurements showing how gravity bends space and changes light. Its computer has processed those measurements into two files. The probe is 23 light-years away and has only 71 seconds of radio contact remaining. An early, powerful burn can help it escape, but turns its antenna away from Earth. A later, gentler burn can keep the antenna connected long enough to send both files, but cannot save the probe. The browser agent receives the mission objective through WebMCP. It reads separate information about the files, radio connection, engine and maneuver limits. It forms hypotheses, predicts what each burn will do and uses a limited simulator to test possible worldlines. A worldline is the path something takes through space and time. Each tested maneuver creates a different possible future. The experience unfolds through three exchanges: The agent investigates the two clearest possibilities: saving the probe and sending the files. The learner calculates the transmission time and predicts why one burn may not achieve both goals. The agent reads that answer, tests a compromise and a counterexample, then explains what the evidence shows. The learner decides what to save. That decision creates one exact, temporary WebMCP action that the agent can execute once. The central calculation is intentionally approachable: $$ 18\text{ MB} + 12\text{ MB} = 30\text{ MB} $$ $$ 30\text{ MB} \div 1.2\text{ MB/s} = 25\text{ seconds} $$ The lesson then connects that calculation to the probe's remaining communication window, antenna alignment and escape requirements. Why WebMCP matters WebMCP is not an extra control attached to a fixed animation. It is the mechanism that makes the lesson responsive. The page initially registers six tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These expose separate mission facts, scientific files, maneuver constraints, a bounded simulator and presentation checkpoints. The agent must decide: Which evidence it needs Which possible burns are worth testing What each test is expected to prove Whether the learner's prediction matches the evidence Which outcome it recommends and why The learner's calculation and prediction become part of the shared page state. The agent reads that work and chooses tests that examine it. The resulting explanation develops from the evidence and the learner's participation rather than following a prerecorded sequence. When the learner makes the final choice, the page registers a seventh tool. This tool takes no arguments and is locked to the exact tested maneuver the learner selected. It can run only once. After execution, all planning and action tools disappear, leaving two read-only tools that verify the final state and transmission receipt. The visible lifecycle is: $$ 6 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow 2\text{ tools} $$ The agent investigates. The learner decides. The page controls the resulting action. How we built it WORLDLINE is built with WebMCP, TypeScript, React and Vite, and is deployed on Vercel. It was coded using Codex. A revisioned TypeScript state machine is shared by the visible experience and the WebMCP tools. It records the mission evidence, simulation budget, tested worldlines, learner calculation, learner prediction, recommendation, human choice and final receipt. Tool schemas are closed and reject unexpected properties. Revision checks prevent stale operations. The simulator permits no more than five tests. The final execution tool closes over the selected maneuver, so the agent cannot change its timing, speed or payload after approval. Every visible path, result, calculation, animation and final receipt is derived from this shared state. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was making the agent's intelligence visible. Agents can call several tools quickly, but a learner needs time to understand why each test matters. We redesigned the experience so results remain on screen until the learner chooses to continue. We also had to make the difference between agent mode and ordinary page interaction unmistakable. WORLDLINE does not secretly replace a missing agent with a scripted imitation. If WebMCP is unavailable, the page clearly explains what is required. Another challenge was keeping the science understandable without pretending this is a precision spacecraft simulator. The mission is fictional, but its lesson uses clear relationships between file size, transmission speed, communication time, burn timing and speed change. Finally, we needed to preserve human authority without reducing the learner to an approval button. The learner performs the calculation, proposes an explanation and makes the value decision that physics cannot answer. What we learned We learned that WebMCP can support more than task automation. It can give an AI agent access to the structure of an educational experience while allowing the webpage to remain the shared visual workspace. We also learned that a useful educational agent should not simply reveal an answer. It should test competing possibilities, respond to the learner's thinking, explain why an idea succeeds or fails and stop when the remaining question is a human judgment. WORLDLINE is an interactive science lesson about black holes, light-years, spacecraft communication and possible futures. It lets people investigate those ideas with an AI agent instead of merely watching them. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: AffiliateTresur
pitch: AffiliateTresur reimagines e-commerce affiliate platforms by exposing its product catalog, filtering system, and discount engine directly to browser-based AI agents.\n

AffiliateTresur reimagines e-commerce affiliate platforms by exposing its product catalog, filtering system, and discount engine directly to browser-based AI agents.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Conventional affiliate discovery platforms are designed exclusively for human navigation through ad banners, cluttered lists, and search bars. However, as local client assistants and autonomous AI agents evolve into the primary portal for research and shopping, web content must become programmatically actionable for machines as well as visually readable for humans. Driven by this shift, we set out to create an agent-native affiliate marketplace. Our goal was to enable seamless visual browsing for users while empowering local AI agents to query structured product catalogs, discover tools, and deliver verified deals using modern browser standards. 

 
 What it does AffiliateTresur. 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Frontend: Built with vanilla HTML5, modern CSS, and JavaScript to keep asset delivery lightweight and responsive. 
 Agent Interface: Implemented declarative WebMCP tool handlers that bind directly to DOM forms and programmatic schemas, responding with structured JSON when invoked by browser-level AI agents. 
 Edge Hosting & Delivery: Configured for edge deployment via Cloudflare using Wrangler, delivering static assets globally with instant edge caching. 
 Version Control & CI/CD: Maintained via GitHub with automated Cloudflare Worker build triggers and custom domain routing on affiliatetresur.com . 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Edge Environment vs. Browser Code: Reconciling Cloudflare Worker deployment pipelines with a purely client-side static application required fine-tuning wrangler.jsonc asset routing rather than compiling edge server handlers. 
 Build Configuration Hurdles: Diagnosing configuration file syntax issues—such as multi-root JSON parsing bugs in package.json —and configuring compatibility dates under automated Wrangler pipelines. 
 Standardizing Agent Discovery: Aligning custom mock product query filters (spanning hardware, mobile tech, and automotive accessories) with strict WebMCP schema definitions so simulated agents could query data cleanly without format errors. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Seamless Tool Discovery: Successfully implemented in-browser agent discovery, enabling Chrome DevTools agent simulators to detect and execute catalog queries instantly. 
 Zero-Bloat Architecture: Delivered a full-featured, functional prototype without heavy framework overhead, ensuring sub-second load times and zero unnecessary dependencies. 
 Live Domain Deployment: Successfully deployed and routed the platform to the live production custom domain affiliatetresur.com . 
 

 What we learned 

 
 Agent-First Web Design: Structuring data and forms for both browser DOM events and agent-invoked events requires thinking about web applications as APIs and visual dashboards simultaneously. 
 Declarative Browser Standards: Practical hands-on experience navigating emerging browser AI APIs and testing agent interaction pipelines locally and in staging environments. 
 Cloudflare Static Assets on Workers: Mastering modern Wrangler asset-binding patterns to serve high-performance client code reliably at the edge. 
 

 What's next for AffiliateTresur 

 
 Live Affiliate API Feeds: Connect the platform beyond mock datasets to real-time affiliate network APIs (e.g., Amazon Associates, CJ, ShareASale) with dynamic pricing updates. 
 Autonomous Agent Price Tracking: Enable background agent monitoring where users can instruct their local assistant to alert them when a specific product drops below a target price threshold. 
 Decentralized Attribution: Explore cryptographic verification and transparent commission tracking for agent-referred conversions.

title: GovBridge AT
pitch: Don't replace legacy e-government. Upgrade it. GovBridge AT: a browser extension adding WebMCP tools to track public insurance payouts. Local, privacy-scoped, and the government app stays unchanged.
about_excerpt: Don't replace legacy e-government. Upgrade it. GovBridge AT: a browser extension adding WebMCP tools to track public insurance payouts. Local, privacy-scoped, and the government app stays unchanged. Like Comment Story Updates About GovBridge AT Inspiration Dealing with government services should not mean deciphering confusing forms, switching between portals, and maintaining your own spreadsheet just to know where things stand. Yet that is often the experience with legacy e-government systems. We wanted to explore whether WebMCP could make these services easier to use without waiting for institutions to rebuild them. As a first example we tested the reimbursement process of the Austrian public health insurance (OEGK), which is the first step before chasing the remaining amount through your private insurer. The individual systems work. The workflow between can be improved. Keeping track of "Which invoices have I submitted? Which claims are still being processed? How much was reimbursed? What can go to private insurance next?" is manual spreadsheet work across multiple portals. At the same time, AI agents are getting genuinely useful at everyday tasks. But the services that create the most administrative burden are legacy applications, and no government can rewrite them overnight. WebMCP offered a third path: add the agent layer from the user's browser instead of waiting for the institution. And it forced a second question we cared about: how can an agent help without getting a screenshot of your entire health insurance account? That privacy boundary became the core of the design. What it does GovBridge AT is an open source Chrome extension that adds a WebMCP layer to the existing Meine SV (OEGK) claims pages. The site itself does not change. On supported pages the extension registers: three read-only query tools: list_claims , get_open_claims , and get_claim , which return normalized claims rendered on the current page one bounded action for convenience: search_claims , which fills and submits the page’s own date-range form (never a claim application) So an agent can answer "Which of my claims are still open?" or "How much was reimbursed this year?" through structured tool calls. No screenshots, no unrestricted page access. Only allowlisted claim fields cross the boundary. Person, social security number, bank account, and claim reference fields are never exposed, even when visible on the page. The extension’s claim processing runs locally in the browser, with no claim-processing backend, telemetry, or claim persistence. The demo has its own server, and normalized tool results are returned to the connected agent. Reads are strictly current-page and results carry explicit environment provenance. For the hackathon we run the demo against a hosted synthetic replica of the Meine SV claims area (20 fictional claims, public demo login, English/German). Not everybody has an account for the Austrian public insurance site or speaks German, so the demo is fully self-contained. How we built it Spec-driven development with automated regression coverage. We built the whole project with Codex (SOL, Luna), using the Codex Google Chrome extension for browser control. A Manifest V3 Chrome extension in TypeScript, built with esbuild, with no additional extension API permissions, explicitly scoped page access, and no service worker. A MAIN-world content script registers tools via the experimental document.modelContext API, with a pinned, locally bundled polyfill as fallback A separate demo server, built with OpenAI Sites, replicates the site's routes, forms, and landmarks with fictional data, served bilingually A reusable agent skill handles the workflow: external Chrome, user-operated ID Austria login, and WebMCP-only reads and summaries within the user’s requested scope. Challenges we ran into The Codex in-app browser does not support extensions, and we found no good way to inject our own code. So we used the early WebMCP support in current Chrome instead. The ChatGPT app's Chrome extension does not yet expose WebMCP tools directly, so our integration currently requires CDP to discover and call them. This dependency is outside our control. We expect direct WebMCP access to become available in the future, which would remove the need for CDP in this workflow. The selected e-government service requires a 2FA account from an Austrian citizen and supports only German. For the hackathon judging process and for faster development, we built a synthetic replica of the site. Accomplishments that we're proud of An end-to-end WebMCP story: extension, hosted bilingual demo, and a reusable agent skill A better privacy story than browser-use or computer-use approaches, and more efficient as well What we learned WebMCP is still fresh and experimental Spec-driven development with automated regression coverage kept the codebase verifiable even while the architecture pivoted mid-project. What's next for GovBridge AT More adapters on the same bridge and privacy model: private health insurers, the tax office, and other Austrian services The private-insurance half of the workflow: comparing remaining costs against private coverage is on the roadmap, explicitly not implemented Local PDF response parsing, behind the already-specified parser boundary: responses are commonly attached as print-ready PDFs The adoption path: show institutions real evidence of which WebMCP capabilities citizens use, so they can implement them natively Success means the extension gets smaller: when an institution ships native WebMCP tools, its adapter retires Built With chrome codex sites webmcp Try it out govbridge-at-demo.manuel857067.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Manuel Zach Like Share this project: Updates Manuel Zach started this project — Sep 03, 2026 04:47 AM EDT
